#6417. Comets probably didn’t deliver life’s building blocks to Earth

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The speed and angle of impact would have destroyed most organic compounds from comets

Comet McNaught shines over Australia a safe distance from Earth in this photo taken in 2007. Most comets that collided with the early Earth would have been moving too fast and at too steep an angle for prebiotic molecules to survive the collision and kick off chemical processes that gave rise to life, a new study suggests.

The chemical building blocks that gave rise to life on Earth probably didn’t come from comets.

Most comets would have been traveling too fast and at too steep an angle to Earth for prebiotic compounds to survive impact with the planet, researchers contend October 28 in Scientific Reports. While the study doesn’t completely rule out the possibility that comets brought these molecules to Earth, it contradicts the long-standing idea that comets seeded Earth with the chemicals necessary for life to arise.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“Even though we see that comets contain all of these molecules in really high concentrations, it’s not straightforward to go from there to saying we’re going to have all of these available for prebiotic chemistry on the surface of the Earth,” says Richard Anslow, a planetary scientist at the Met Office, the national meteorological service for the United Kingdom in Exeter.

Comets carry carbon- and nitrogen-containing molecules left over from early in the solar system’s formation. These molecules can react to form biologically important compounds like sugars and DNA. Scientists have long thought that comets could have delivered these building blocks to Earth when they collided with the planet during its first billion years.

But it’s important to revisit these ideas as our understanding of both comets and the early solar system improves, says Nicolle Zellner, a physicist at Albion College in Michigan who was not involved in the study.

In the new work, Anslow and colleagues used computer simulations to predict the likelihood that a chemical called hydrogen cyanide would survive a comet’s journey through Earth’s present atmosphere and its impact with the planet’s surface. The early Earth’s atmosphere was probably much denser, so would have been even more destructive.

The strong chemical bond between the carbon and nitrogen atoms in hydrogen cyanide can release energy that drives later chemical reactions necessary for life. It also makes the molecule particularly stable compared to other carbon-based chemicals.

“It’s probably one of the more robust molecules to surviving impacts,” Anslow says. “So if things look bad for hydrogen cyanide, then we think it’s going to be much harder for other, more complicated molecules that are more likely to be broken down during these impacts.”

Based on the simulations, a comet impact that kept hydrogen cyanide intact would be extremely unlikely, the team found. On average, the simulations suggest that only one impact would have been able to deliver a meaningful amount of hydrogen cyanide to the planet’s surface over more than a billion years. For hydrogen cyanide to survive the crash, the comet would have to be larger than 100 meters across, slow moving and traveling at an oblique angle to Earth.

A comet that met those narrow criteria would also have had to crash into land, rather than an ocean, to kick off any biologically useful chemistry. If the comet landed in the ocean, any hydrogen cyanide that survived would be diluted too quickly to trigger those reactions.

While still improbable, comets may have been more likely to deliver carbon-based molecules to Mars than to Earth, the simulations showed. Mars’ thinner atmosphere and smaller size meant that comets would impact at lower speeds. That could mean that more compounds could survive the collision.

If Earth’s carbon-based chemicals didn’t come from comets, they may have come from carbon-rich asteroids called carbonaceous chondrites, says Gordon Osinski, a planetary geologist at Western University in London, Canada, who was not involved in the study. Other sources might have included volcanoes and hydrothermal vents.

The study “definitely will make people think twice about comets being the originator for the delivery of organics,” Osinski says. “I hope other people will try to reproduce these results [and] then potentially try something similar with carbonaceous chondrites as well.”

#6416. Your clothes could soon work like a smartphone touchscreen

Scientists have developed the world's first wearable fabric touchscreen, creating washable clothing that displays images, plays videos, and responds to touch.

Phone and laptop screens are built on flat, stiff panels. Clothing is made of soft threads. Until now, those threads couldn’t form a full-color screen that responds to touch.

In Singapore, engineers have built that kind of screen into the forearm of a sleeve, and it kept working after 50 trips through a washing machine.

There’s no rigid screen anywhere in the sleeve.

Tural Khudiyev, an assistant professor in the Department of Materials Science and Engineering at the National University of Singapore (NUS), led the work. His team at the university’s College of Design and Engineering published it on October 21, 2026.

The menus and buttons people tap on a phone make up what engineers call a graphical user interface, or GUI.

Khudiyev’s team built one from electronic fibers, creating a working touchscreen on the forearm of a sleeve.

“What made this possible was our ability to construct the GUI system from electronic building blocks in fiber form – similar to traditional yarn, but with the sophisticated electronic functionality built directly into the fibers,” Khudiyev said.

Fabric that lights up isn’t new. A 2021 paper in the journal Nature described large display textiles, while another study in 2025 described a single-fiber computer.

Khudiyev’s team cites both. Earlier approaches, the researchers wrote, don’t readily give each pixel its own digital address or move information fast enough for touchscreen menus.

One obstacle was a fiber’s round, thin shape.

“A fiber has a one-dimensional, axially symmetric geometry, which makes it difficult to build complex circuitry using approaches developed for conventional two-dimensional electronics,” Khudiyev added.

“We overcame this limitation through a new interconnection architecture, which enables thousands of microelectronic devices to be integrated and interconnected along a fiber.”

The team started with tiny wires wrapped in insulation. A laser exposed the metal only at the spots where each microchip needed a connection.

The engineers controlled where molten solder, a metal alloy used to join electronic parts, could spread, allowing it to bond only at the exposed spots.

With that method, the team joined more than 5,000 chips through over 20,000 electrical connections. Next, the engineers built the strip of LEDs into a layered fiber.

They used thermal drawing, in which heated material is pulled into a long, thin strand. The finished thread is about 0.04 inch (1 millimeter) thick and about 33 feet (10 meters) long.

For the prototype, the team threaded 54 of these fibers into the forearm of a sleeve. Each fiber carries 96 LEDs, so the screen is 96 pixels wide and 54 pixels tall.

Underneath the LEDs, a separate layer senses touch. Pressing the fiber completes a circuit, and the signal shows where the finger landed, so the nearest pixel lights up.

The whole screen measures about 6.6 by 4.1 inches (168 by 105 millimeters), a little larger than a postcard. It refreshes 30 times a second and supports 8-bit color.

A full-HD TV picture has 400 times as many pixels, so the sleeve shows far less detail.

Each fiber has its own control channel. If one line fails, the fibers next to it keep working normally, and the screen can register several touches at once.

Other fibers, built the same way, carry a microphone, a speaker and sensors that track movement, find magnetic north, measure temperature and gauge how bright the surroundings are.

Together, the fibers handle jobs that early smartphones could do.

The sleeve runs a calculator and a photo gallery, and it plays video at 30 frames per second, or 25 when the sound is synced. It works as a compass, responds to voice commands and receives images over Bluetooth.

The sleeve can rotate the screen on its own. It adjusts its brightness, too.

When the temperature fiber is placed under the arm, the sleeve reads the wearer’s body temperature and shows it on the display.

The team ran the sleeve through 50 detergent washes in a typical washing machine. They also bent it 1,000 times around a curve just 0.2 inch (5 millimeters) in radius.

After both tests, the light it gave off and its response to touch were nearly unchanged.

The display lets air through about as well as cotton, polyester and denim do. It also stays within established safety limits for contact with skin.

Smaller chips and thinner fibers also fit the team’s method, and they could lead to sharper, larger screens. Thinner fibers could be knitted, woven and embroidered on the standard machines factories already use.

Smartwatches and other wearable technology already track some body signals from the wrist.

“Healthcare is one particularly promising application,” Khudiyev said.

“A garment could continuously collect physiological information through fiber-based sensors and allow the wearer to access and interact with that information directly through their clothing.”

“Combined with artificial intelligence (AI), this could enable personalized health monitoring, feedback and assistance,” Khudiyev added.

“Just as smartphones enabled applications that were difficult to imagine when they first appeared, garment GUIs could ultimately enable entirely new applications that do not yet exist.”

Tracking more health signs and giving touch-based feedback are uses the team describes for the future, not results from the prototype.

Future versions could offer sharper displays, more built-in sensors and AI-powered features that expand what clothing can do.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6415. Four Decades Ago, Scientists Dropped Gophers Onto a Volcano. They Might Try It Again.

Scientists’ experiment on Mount St. Helens suggests rodents can deliver fungi that plants need, but the repair crew has an appetite.

In 1982, scientists brought a pocket gopher to Washington’s Mount St. Helens and put it inside a small enclosure around a plant growing on the Pumice Plain. Two years after the volcano’s infamous eruption, the plant had taken root among volcanic deposits. The gopher stayed for 24 hours before the researchers returned it home.

Michael Allen and his colleagues were testing whether gophers could carry fungi themselves, rather than simply uncovering fungi in buried soil. Allen describes experiments around two plants in different volcanic deposits. When the researchers returned the following year, both plants had mycorrhizal fungi, while nearby plants outside the enclosures showed no traces of them.

“We concluded that the gophers themselves transported these critical fungi, likely in their feces as they are known to feed on these fungi in their meadows,” he tells Popular Mechanics.

The experiment went viral after a 2024 paper in Frontiers in Microbiomes reported microbial differences associated with the old gopher enclosures. That paper dates the Pumice Plain experiment to 1982, rather than the 1983 date repeated in some coverage. The researchers sampled the soil in 2014, when the gopher had been gone for about 32 years.

Allen, a soil ecologist and distinguished professor emeritus at the University of California, Riverside, thinks the gophers give us something else to consider. When we plant a damaged landscape, how do the microbes those plants need get there? Could gophers do the job? If so, people planting a former mining or industrial site would have a reason to let gophers stay, even when they eat some of the seedlings.

Some native gophers survived the May 18, 1980, eruption by hiding underground, beneath the snow cover. Allen says the snow and soil protected them in patches of meadow and land that had been logged. Where the ash wasn’t too deep, the gophers dug their way out, bringing the old soil up with them. They also brought microbes with them, including mycorrhizal fungi, which help plant roots obtain nutrients and water in exchange for carbon.

But the Pumice Plain was buried under more than 20 meters of sterile volcanic ash and debris, far beyond any gopher’s reach. Allen wanted to know whether a gopher could carry fungi onto ground like that from somewhere else. That’s why his research team took a gopher from a nearby clearcut and put it in the enclosure on the Pumice Plain. The results of the experiment were clear. The plants inside the enclosures had mycorrhizal fungi, but nearby plants outside did not. Allen suspects the fungi arrived in the gopher's droppings, although the experiment didn’t show how.

Decades later, the landscape around the experimental site had changed considerably. Allen says plants, gophers, and fungi have spread across the Pumice Plain, beyond the original plot. The later study, led by mycologist Mia Maltz, found differences in the microbial communities associated with historic gopher enclosures and comparison plots. It also examined the lasting influence of forest conditions before the eruption.

That finding leaves plenty to investigate. A different assortment of microbes doesn’t automatically mean healthier soil or faster recovery. Allen says that analysis of the communities is continuing. He wants to know whether gophers could bring those helpful microbes to other places where people are trying to get plants growing again.

When the nearest healthy soil is too far away

Allen thinks the question could matter most where damaged ground lies far from surviving vegetation. If healthy soil and vegetation are close by, he told Pop Mech, microbes may find their way back on their own. But microbes struggle to return to places like industrial sites, where healthy soil is scarce, and Allen thinks those sites could be worth testing to see whether gophers can help.

Allen’s work extends beyond volcanoes: at a Wyoming strip mine, his team moved gophers and soil from a healthy ecosystem onto disturbed ground. He suspects gophers deliver a broader mix of microbes than commercial treatments do, though he calls that a question for further research. Success would depend on conditions, though. As David Lindenmayer, a conservation biologist at the Australian National University, notes, an introduced animal first needs a habitat, and Allen adds that gophers need enough food to get started. Timing matters too, because the soil microbes that survived the eruption, which Lindenmayer calls “biological legacies,” die off without host plants, so the longer a site waits, the fewer remain to help new roots take hold.

That requirement brings an awkward complication. A gopher could make a meal of the seedlings it was brought in to help. The animals “could well destroy the restoration effort if they ate the plants desired for restoration and did not eat undesirable plants,” Allen says.

Lindenmayer also cautions that returning an animal to a changed landscape can produce surprises, because it’s hard to know how a gopher will affect the plants and animals that have moved in since it disappeared. Researchers would need to track whether gophers deliver useful microbes, whether those benefits outweigh the damage the animals do, and how the approach compares with other ways of helping a site recover. Allen’s experiment gives them a place to start: in a single day on volcanic ground, a gopher carried fungi to plants. The question now is whether more plants would survive with a hungry gopher around than without one.

#6414. Exercise is good for your brain, but too much may alter its chemistry

Excessive exercise may alter brain chemistry, raising dopamine levels during rest and offering clues to the sleep problems linked to overtraining.

Skipping a rest day might seem like a good way to get more out of a workout. But pushing the body too hard may also change what happens in the brain.

Mice that completed eight weeks of increasingly demanding treadmill running had higher dopamine levels in a brain region involved in memory and mood than untrained mice.

The difference appeared during their usual rest period, when this chemical, which helps regulate alertness and motivation, might affect their ability to settle down.

Serotonin, another brain chemical associated with exercise fatigue, showed no significant difference between the groups.

The finding offers a possible clue to why some overtrained athletes report poor sleep and anxiety, although the researchers measured neither.

Alisson Luiz da Rocha carried out the experiments as a doctoral student at the University of São Paulo‘s School of Physical Education and Sport of Ribeirão Preto.

“Our findings show that excessive physical exercise affects not only skeletal muscle but also has a pronounced impact on the brain,” said da Rocha.

The mice first spent five days getting used to a treadmill. They ran for 10 minutes a day at about 20 feet per minute (six meters per minute).

In the first week, they ran for 15 minutes at 60% of their top speed. By week five, the treadmill sloped 14% downhill, which puts more strain on muscles than running on level ground.

The sessions grew longer, and recovery time shrank. By week eight, the mice ran twice daily for 75 minutes each time, with only four hours between sessions.

Running tests at the start, at four weeks and at the end showed what this schedule did to their fitness. The mice improved halfway through the program, then lost those gains by the end.

Two days after the final running test, the researchers collected a brain region called the hippocampus. It helps with memory and mood and responds to exercise, including by growing new cells.

They collected samples at 6 p.m., midnight, 6 a.m. and noon, using four mice from each group at each time.

The lab lights stayed on from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., covering the daytime hours when these nocturnal animals normally rest.

At noon, the overtrained mice had more dopamine in the hippocampus than the untrained mice. They also had more tyrosine hydroxylase, an enzyme that helps make dopamine.

Serotonin remained similar between the groups, so the balance between the two chemicals shifted toward dopamine.

That noon measurement showed a difference 48 hours after the final test, but it didn’t show that dopamine stayed high throughout those two days.

A separate group of 20 mice completed just one run in the early evening. They ran at 60% of their top speed until they could no longer keep up with the treadmill.

Their dopamine levels were also higher immediately afterward.

However, levels of the enzyme that helps produce dopamine fell, along with activity in the gene responsible for making it.

The researchers think this combination might reflect fatigue, with demand for dopamine getting ahead of the machinery that makes it.

They couldn’t confirm that explanation because they measured the amount in brain tissue, not how quickly the brain produced it.

After eight weeks of overload, both dopamine and the enzyme were higher two days after testing. The authors see this as a possible sign of a longer-lasting change, beyond the immediate effects of one demanding run.

The idea that serotonin drives exercise fatigue dates to 1987. A British biochemist proposed that rising serotonin during long exercise makes the effort feel harder and encourages an athlete to stop.

The team expected serotonin to rise, or at least increase relative to dopamine. Neither happened in the single-run experiment or the eight-week program.

To reduce the chance that the chemical broke down during handling, the researchers froze each hippocampus within five minutes. A 1989 rat study using a similar method also found no change in serotonin.

Research in people has raised questions, too. When Finnish researchers scanned severely overtrained athletes a year apart, they found similar patterns in how their brains handled serotonin.

The team also examined public genetic data from 71 strains of laboratory mice. They looked for patterns linked to the gene that helps produce the dopamine-making enzyme.

Strains with more activity in that gene also showed more activity in genes involved in inflammation.

Mice from those strains froze longer during a fear test and spent less time in exposed parts of a maze, behaviors researchers associate with anxiety.

These mice also performed worse on a rotating rod used to test balance. That result can point to poorer coordination.

But these data came from other mice at rest. The team did not measure inflammation or behavior in its trained mice, so this analysis cannot show that overtraining caused those problems.

The researchers did not measure sleep, anxiety or alertness in the overtrained mice.

Higher dopamine during their usual rest period may offer a clue to athletes’ symptoms, but that link still needs testing.

The groups were small, with four to five animals at each sampling time. All were male, and sex can affect both dopamine regulation and the body clock.

The chemical tests also had limits. They measured dopamine in tissue, without showing how much passed between brain cells or how quickly the brain broke it down.

Overtraining syndrome is a condition diagnosed in people. The mouse running program models some aspects of it, but it cannot fully reproduce the condition.

Serotonin has many jobs in the brain, including helping regulate sleep. This study suggests researchers should also examine its balance with dopamine when looking at the effects of excessive training.

Other research has linked brain signals to how long people can keep exercising, often over minutes. This work raises a different question: what happens to brain chemistry after weeks of training without enough recovery?

Study coordinator Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva said similar changes in humans could help explain links between excessive training, brain regulation and sleep problems.

His group is now working on an international project to identify which biological systems first shift away from exercise’s usual benefits.

The study is published in the journal Neuroscience.

It seems like a simple question, but it needs serious taxonomic sleuthing. Are sharks or trees the oldest?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You may have heard that sharks are older than trees. And yes, sharks are truly ancient, with an evolutionary lineage dating back hundreds of millions of years.

But are they really older than trees? Experts told Live Science that the answer depends on what we classify as a shark.

"It's all in the fine print," John Maisey, the curator-in-charge emeritus of fossil fish at the American Museum of Natural History in New York, told Live Science. "The takeaway is that the shark lineage within the fishes generally does go back further than trees. But it really depends on how you define what we mean by shark."

The modern sharks we see today first emerged around 195 million years ago, during the Jurassic period. Fossils of ancient sharks from this time can be traced to living lineages, namely Hexanchiformes, an order of sharks identified by their six or seven gills and single dorsal fin.

This means that modern sharks, at least, are not older than trees. Experts generally agree that trees first evolved in the Middle Devonian epoch, around 380 million to 390 million years ago. "I think it's not very controversial, when we had the first trees," Cindy Looy, a paleobotanist at the University of California, Berkeley, told Live Science.

For instance, the first true tree in the evolutionary record is considered to be Archaeopteris, an extinct genus discovered in a 385 million-year-old fossil forest near Cairo, New York. Looking at these fossils, Archaeopteris has many characteristics of trees we have today, including a tall, woody trunk; leaves; and a deep root system. Other early trees ‪—‬ such as Eospermatopteris found in ancient forests near Gilboa, New York, and Calamophyton in southwest England ‪—‬ also appeared in the fossil record 390 million and 393 million years ago, respectively.

But when we look at the extinct relatives of modern sharks, "that's where it gets a bit wobbly," Maisey said. There are fossils from the sister groups of modern sharks that can be traced back through the Permian period and into the Devonian period (around 359 million to 420 million years ago). The most abundant group are hybodonts, an extinct group of spiny fish that have a unique calcification pattern in their cartilage that is similar to that of modern sharks.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

A microscopic image of skin cells from the dogfish shark.

"It’s called tessellated calcified cartilage, and that's a very important hallmark of most of the shark-like fishes and their ancestors," said Maisey, who has studied a spiny fish fossil called Doliodus problematicus from the early Devonian. If this definition is used, these sharks first appeared around 400 million years ago, before trees emerged.

Sharks' rough skin can be traced even further back, with the dermal denticles — the tooth-like scales that roughen a shark's skin — first appearing in the fossil record around 450 million years ago.

These transition fossils, where fish were evolving into sharks and gaining shark-like traits, introduce a gray area in the definition of sharks. "When you get back into the ancient past, when you're not dealing with things that we have living examples to compare with anymore, then it becomes a bit more tricky [to figure out what they are]," Maisey said.

Fossils also present a very limited picture. Many contain only fragments of an animal, like a fallen tooth, so scientists are still piecing together the clues of exactly how and when sharks arose. That means every fish fossil discovery often leads to more questions about what other transition fossils could be out there, Maisey said.

There is also much to be discovered about trees, Looy added. Terrestrial fossils, especially ones that clearly show parts of a tree, are quite rare. Finding a fossil forest requires a lot of luck, she said, although there is little indication that trees were present before the Middle Devonian.

"That's why I think the fossil record is so intriguing," Maisey said. "Because it may not give us all the answers, but it certainly raises questions."

#6412. Why do flamingos dance while they eat? This scientist found out

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Erin Garcia de Jesús, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

On a family trip to Atlanta, Víctor Ortega Jiménez spent time taking pictures and videos of flamingos as they fed in their pond. It wasn’t to admire their long legs or flamboyant pink color. Instead, he noticed the “beautiful” ripples spreading across the water as the birds ate under the surface. But he didn’t know why the waves were happening.

It took “more than four years to answer that question,” says Ortega Jiménez, of the University of California, Berkeley. “But I think the answer was fascinating.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Ortega Jiménez’s focus is biomechanics, or the study of how mechanics applies to animal movement and structure. His goal is to understand how animal behaviors might lead to human-made engineering feats.

He discovered that, by retracting their heads, flamingos produce vortexlike traps with water to scoop up algae. They stomp around — or dance, if you will — amplifying the vortex. The series of motions brings the food to their crooked beaks. The beaks then filter in food, releasing silt and mud.

The impressive process can weed out particles the size of a single cell. This kind of self-cleaning filter for extremely small particles can be applied to remove microplastics and so-called forever chemicals called PFAS from water, Ortega Jiménez says.

“Nature is always full of secrets,” he says. “And I think that’s the riddle that keeps me going, trying to understand nature. That’s my way to see science: by observation and trying to be inspired and trying to solve a problem.”

#6410. Webb traces a mysterious cosmic signal to a tiny ancient galaxy

NASA's James Webb Space Telescope traced the most distant fast radio burst ever detected to a tiny, star-forming galaxy in the early universe.

Today’s Image of the Day from the James Webb Space Telescope reveals a tiny galaxy with an extraordinary story to tell.

Hidden among countless distant galaxies, this faint patch of light is the source of one of the most mysterious signals in the universe.

The signal, known as a fast radio burst, traveled across billions of years of cosmic history before reaching Earth.

It lasted only a fraction of a second, yet it carried clues about the galaxy where it began.

Astronomers have now traced the burst to a surprisingly small galaxy that existed when the universe was just three billion years old.

The discovery could help scientists understand what produces these powerful cosmic flashes.

Fast radio bursts, or FRBs, are incredibly brief explosions of radio waves that arrive from distant regions of space.

Although they typically last only milliseconds, they can release enormous amounts of energy in that short time.

Scientists first discovered these signals in 2007, but their origins remain uncertain.

Some bursts repeat, while others appear only once. Their unpredictable behavior makes them particularly difficult to investigate.

One of the biggest challenges is identifying the galaxy where a burst originated.

Without that information, astronomers cannot easily determine what kind of environment produced it.

The signal featured in Webb’s latest discovery, called FRB 20240304B, was detected on March 4, 2024, by the MeerTRAP team using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa.

Initial observations suggested that the burst came from an exceptionally distant location.

However, even the largest ground-based optical telescopes could not detect a galaxy at its position.

Astronomers needed a more powerful instrument to uncover its source.

NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope provided the missing piece of the puzzle.

Using its Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam), Webb detected a faint galaxy precisely where the radio burst had originated.

The accompanying image shows a field filled with distant galaxies.

A white box highlights the region containing the burst’s host galaxy, while an enlarged view reveals its faint blue glow.

A white cross marks the location of the radio signal.

Webb’s Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec) then measured the galaxy’s redshift, which describes how much its light has stretched as the universe expanded.

The measurement, 2.148, confirmed that the burst originated when the universe was only about three billion years old.

That makes FRB 20240304B the most distant fast radio burst identified to date.

The galaxy itself turned out to be just as remarkable as the signal.

Astronomers had expected to find a large, well-developed galaxy containing an enormous population of stars.

Instead, Webb revealed a dwarf galaxy roughly 1,000 times less massive than anticipated.

Despite its small size, the galaxy was actively producing new stars.

It existed during a period known as “cosmic noon,” when star formation across the universe reached its peak.

The researchers estimated that most of the galaxy’s stars may have formed within just 30 million years.

This youthful environment offers an important clue about what might have generated the mysterious burst.

“We thought it would be a big, nicely formed galaxy with lots of stars, and instead it was a little dwarf galaxy, although it was actively forming stars,” said Manisha Caleb of the University of Sydney, who led the study.

Astronomers have proposed several explanations for fast radio bursts, but two possibilities are particularly relevant to this discovery.

One involves the collision of two neutron stars, the extremely dense remnants left behind when massive stars die.

Such mergers can take billions of years to occur, making them more likely in older stellar populations.

Another explanation involves magnetars, neutron stars with extraordinarily powerful magnetic fields.

A magnetar can form after a massive star explodes as a supernova. Under certain conditions, activity within or around the magnetar could generate an intense burst of radio waves.

Unlike a neutron star merger, this process could happen relatively soon after the original star’s death.

The newly discovered galaxy’s youthful population makes the magnetar explanation especially compelling.

“Our work suggests that it’s very unlikely that this FRB was produced by a merger,” Caleb said.

Although the finding does not establish exactly what produced the burst, it strengthens the case for young magnetars as possible sources of these mysterious signals.

The burst also provided astronomers with information about the vast stretches of space between its host galaxy and Earth.

As radio waves travel through the universe, they interact with matter along their path.

Those interactions leave subtle signatures that scientists can study to investigate otherwise difficult-to-detect cosmic structures.

The researchers identified evidence of two such structures in the burst’s signal.

One was a previously unknown galaxy cluster approximately 3.5 billion light-years away. The other was the much closer Virgo Cluster, located around 54 million light-years from Earth.

These findings demonstrate how fast radio bursts can serve as probes of the cosmic web, the enormous network of galaxies, gas, and dark matter that stretches across the universe.

“A fast radio burst is almost like a cosmic flashlight. It lights up everything along the path,” said study co-author J. Xavier Prochaska of the University of California, Santa Cruz.

Astronomers expect future radio telescopes to identify many more distant fast radio bursts.

As those discoveries accumulate, Webb will help researchers examine the galaxies that produced them, revealing how their environments and stellar populations differ.

Each new detection could bring scientists closer to understanding the physical processes responsible for these extraordinary flashes.

For now, this image captures a remarkable achievement: a tiny, faint galaxy that remained invisible to powerful ground-based telescopes has finally come into view.

And within that distant galaxy lies a clue to an explosive event that occurred billions of years before our solar system formed.

The study was published in the journal Science.

Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Themiya Nanayakkara (USYD); Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI)

#6409. The Missing Engine Behind Quantum Computing Is Literally All Around Us

Scientists say they can corral up to 40 quantum-ready photons from everyday light, even at room temperature.

The answer to one of the biggest questions in quantum computing might have been all around us this whole time: light. In newly published research, a team of scientists from Louisiana and Mexico say they’ve found a way to corral up to 40 viable photons of light “at room temperature under high levels of noise and decoherence,” for use in quantum information crunching. If this finding is validated by further research and implementation, it could help move quantum computing closer to real life.

The paper was recently published in the peer-reviewed journal Advanced Science. The research starts from an understanding that quantum computing, or quantum information processing, is something fundamentally different from the paradigms we have today. The team explains in the paper how their field, reservoir computing, differs from the von Neumann setup that the vast majority of computers have now. Instead, it’s closer to a neural network, with “highly-interconnected quantum networks as reservoirs.”

In a von Neumann system, information marches through a central processing unit (CPU) almost on a ticker tape. One minuscule math problem at a time is crunched onto that ticker tape, then returned to its host area of the computer—like memory, hard drive, software, or your mouse—to be applied. Everything the computer does gets crunched, one math operation at a time, through the CPU. In a neural net, including a reservoir computer, multiple things can happen at the same time. The computing style is nonlinear, involving clouds of quantum particles.

If that setup sounds thrilling, you’ve now joined a large group of people who feel excited about it, even if they aren’t sure yet how it can be implemented. The industry is bottlenecked by logistics. There’s no general purpose quantum computer. “Scalability and fragility have long represented two major challenges to the practical realization of quantum technologies,” the team writes. But in their simulation, the scientists were able to extract little quantum pockets from everyday “classical” light sources, corralling reservoirs that they say show a marked improvement over classical computing.

“We demonstrate the potential of our platform to perform complex tasks by using random multiphoton reservoirs to map input signals into higher-dimensional spaces, which are then optimized by low-level neural networks,” the team writes. In other words, the simulation shows that the reservoir system can set up and explore functions, taking an input and turning out the function performed on that input, like an algebraic expression and then the integral of that expression.

The secret in this experimental setup is the Fock space, which lets scientists gather particles under one umbrella in order to study how they behave, mathematically. Once a number of particles within the classical light source are corralled in a special circuit, they can be used to do quantum computing, despite their “losses and noise.” Light is bent and manipulated at “room temperature,” which in quantum mechanics means above freezing.

This work is the next step down a path that has, so far, worked only in much smaller setups. “While these effects have been explored in the context of nanophotonic systems and quantum sensors, their implications for multiphoton quantum information processing have yet to be investigated,” the team explains. “These results highlight the robustness and scalability of hybrid quantum technologies against decoherence.”

Caroline Delbert is a writer, avid reader, and contributing editor at Pop Mech. She's also an enthusiast of just about everything. Her favorite topics include nuclear energy, cosmology, math of everyday things, and the philosophy of it all.

#6408. Mountains are eroding fastest where you least expect it

Scientists have discovered why some gentle mountain landscapes erode faster than steep rocky slopes, revealing hidden effects on Earth's carbon cycle.

Every mountain range is, in geological terms, falling apart. Rivers cut downward, slopes shed material, rock weathers into soil and sediment and eventually finds its way to the sea.

Geologists have been measuring this process – denudation – for decades, using a clever trick involving cosmic rays.

When high-energy particles from exploded stars hit quartz grains at the surface, they create a rare isotope, beryllium-10, at a known rate.

The longer a grain sits exposed, the more ¹⁰Be it accumulates. Measure it, and you get an erosion rate.

The problem is that this has always worked better on some rocks than others. In granite, sandstone, and other coarse-grained rocks, quartz grains are large and easy to isolate.

In shale – one of the most common sedimentary rocks on earth, soft, fine-grained, and widespread across mountain landscapes – the quartz is too small and dispersed to extract cleanly using standard techniques.

As a result, shale has often been left out of erosion measurements, creating a significant gap in our understanding of how mountain landscapes change.

A team led by Eyal Marder at the University of Massachusetts Amherst has now fixed that. Their study describes a new method for extracting ¹⁰Be from fine-grained sedimentary rocks.

The researchers applied this method to the East River watershed in the Elk and West Elk mountains of Colorado.

This is a 465-square-kilometer catchment where resistant igneous rock and Cretaceous Mancos Shale sit side by side, subject to the same climate and the same tectonic forces.

“Shale’s erodibility is three times that of the harder rocks in the East River Watershed,” Marder said.

The shale catchments in the study erode at rates ranging from 0.05 to 0.38 mm per year, with a median of 0.11 mm per year. The intrusive igneous catchments erode at 0.03 to 0.07 mm per year.

That gap, on its own, is not surprising: geologists have long assumed weaker rock erodes faster. What the measurements reveal is the consequence of that contrast playing out over millions of years.

When weak and strong rocks sit next to each other in a landscape, they don’t erode in sync. The shale comes down faster while maintaining comparatively gentle, subdued topography.

The harder rock develops steeper slopes and higher relief as it adjusts more slowly. The result is that the fastest erosion in a mountain range is happening in the rounded, lower-relief shale terrain.

“When we look at landscapes, we are only seeing a snapshot in time,” Marder said. And that snapshot is misleading.

A steep cliff face of hard granite looks like where the action is. The quiet shale valley is where the ground is actually disappearing.

Shale and igneous rock don’t just erode at different rates. They also have opposite effects on atmospheric CO2.

Intrusive rocks like granite and monzonite undergo silicate weathering, a process that draws CO2 out of the atmosphere and locks it into dissolved carbonate.

Shale, by contrast, can contain pyrite and organic carbon, whose weathering can contribute to CO2 release.

In the East River watershed, chemical weathering accounts for roughly 10 to 70 percent of the total denudation rate.

Because the shale is eroding three times faster than the igneous rock, it is contributing disproportionately to CO2 release.

The landscape evolution modelling in the study suggests this imbalance persists for millions of years.

The models suggest that shale continues to erode faster than harder rock over extended periods, sustaining the difference in their contributions to the carbon cycle.

The cumulative CO2 implications are large.

“Scale our work up from the Elk and West Elk mountains to all the mountainous regions of the world, and getting erosion rates and their equivalent impact on CO2 release right has a marked impact on what we know about biogeochemical global cycles and climate change,” Marder explained.

Model simulations predict that the watershed could release approximately 85 teragrams of CO2 over 2.6 million years of continuous landscape adjustment.

That could potentially rise to 135 Tg if repeated glacial topographic resetting drives repeated transience cycles.

These are first-order estimates, and they exclude CO2 from oxidative weathering of fossil organic carbon in shale, which would push the numbers higher still.

The deeper lesson of the study is about what topography alone cannot tell you. Slope, relief, and channel steepness are the standard proxies geologists use to assess erosion rates and landscape equilibrium.

The steeper the terrain, the assumption goes, the faster it’s eroding. That assumption holds when the rock type is uniform.

Where it isn’t, the fastest erosion is hidden in the gentlest terrain. Models that ignore lithological contrasts will systematically misread both the erosion and the carbon flux.

The new ¹⁰Be technique for fine-grained sediments should allow researchers to fill in those gaps across other mixed-lithology mountain belts – the Appalachians, the Alps, the Himalayas.

There, shale and weak sedimentary sequences are common and their contribution to erosion and chemical weathering has been poorly constrained.

Getting that accounting right matters for anyone trying to understand how mountains regulate Earth’s carbon cycle over geological time.

The study is published in the journal Science Advances.

Writer Olivia Maule spoke with biologist James O'Hanlon about his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats." In it, he explores deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it amounts to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most deception in nature happens without much awareness from the creature involved. From a moth that has evolved to look like a hornet to orchid mantises that mimic flowers to lure in pollinators, deception is part of these animals' nature. But in his book "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), biologist James O'Hanlon turns to tactical deception aimed at manipulating what another animal believes — and whether we can consider this as lying.

Live Science spoke with O'Hanlon about his book, and why so many scientists are reluctant to say "yes, animals can lie."

Read an excerpt: Can animals lie? This sneaky bird might be proof.

James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. He is the author of "Eight-Legged Wonders: The Surprising Lives of Spiders" (2024).

Olivia Maule: The chapter opens with a moment from a talk you gave, where a woman at a senior citizens' club asked you a question about orchid mantises that left you stumped: "How does the mantis know to look like a flower?" Why did that moment stick with you enough to open the chapter with it?

James O'Hanlon: Because it was such a simple, straightforward question that I couldn't give a simple, straightforward answer to. At the time, I was thinking about what's going on in the brains of the animals I was looking at — does a camouflaged animal actually know it's camouflaged? Does an insect that looks like a leaf know what a leaf even is?

And it got me thinking: they don't need to. This stuff just sort of works because it works. That's a completely different type of deception to the other things dealt with in this chapter, which is: Do animals actually know that they can lie? Can they intentionally deceive, like we can?

OM: So would you say you have an answer to that question now? And if so, what would it be?

JO: If I had to answer, it would be yes. It looks like it. But scientists are paid to be pedantic, so it's always going to be a "yes, but" or a "possibly." There's a ton of behaviors that look like animals can lie, and they're really good at it, but with any type of science, we're never going to know for certain what's going on in their brains. It's a best-guess situation.

The Pink Orchid Mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) is an insect that uses camouflage as a form of protection in the wild.

OM: How would you help readers hold those two ideas at once — that this is genuine deception in an evolutionary sense, but not necessarily lying in the way we mean it as humans?

JO: When we talk about lying in humans, there's a value judgment attached. We're judging each other on whether we're good or bad people, doing right or wrong things. We kind of have to relax that judgment a bit when we're talking about other animals.

I guess it becomes an ethical question — we look at deception as being right or wrong, morally good or bad, and that's a very human-centric way of thinking. Ethics and morals are things we've developed to help us get along in our own societies. Who knows what's going on in animal societies?

There's an example in the book of golden snub-nosed monkeys that use deceptive alarm calls to scare off other members of their group and steal their food. After a while, those monkeys start to get ignored, and the group stops responding to their calls. So maybe there is some sort of animal-society rules and regulations keeping lying in check. Maybe. We'll see.

OM: I do want to ask about the chimpanzee study, in which chimpanzees intentionally misled competitive handlers to boxes without food, and compare it to the 2017 dog study, where dogs learned to mislead handlers much faster than the chimps did. What did that result do to the assumption that big brains equal better lying?

JO: There's always been this idea that lying is a really cognitively complex task — you need the brains not just to realize what's going on in the real world but to imagine a false possibility, and then to describe that false possibility as if it were real. We talked that up as something you need big brains to do, and there was also a bit of patting ourselves on the back for being such smart animals — maybe we lie a lot because we're such smart animals. But the more we learn about animals and what they're capable of, the more we realize they can do so much more than we thought was possible with the brains they've got.

OM: Does that suggest lying is less about raw intelligence and more a byproduct of needing to survive in a group?

JO: As far as all the examples of tactical deception in the book that look like they're intentional, they all, or mostly all, come from social animals. We don't seem to see it in solitary animals. That's a big sign that maybe it's something that's evolved because individuals can exploit it in a social setting. But it's still such early days, so it's hard to say for definite how different levels of sociality, and how bonded individuals are within groups, correlate with more deception.

OM: Could you elaborate on the distinction between deception and something like the camouflage you introduce in the book with the tiger's stripes?

JO: Compared to the intentional deception we've been talking about, things like camouflage still work regardless of whether the animal doing it is aware of it or not. The idea behind lying and tactical deception is that it only works because it's intentional — there's some sort of choice to do it.

Whether the animals are aware of that choice is another question. Think about the way we do it as humans — are we always aware of it? Whenever your friend asks whether you like their new haircut and you just go, "Yeah, it's great," you don't really think about the fact that you're probably lying. It's just part of our social norms. So it becomes a very blurry gray area very quickly.

OM: It sort of boils down to the choice of it all — whether they can choose to do it or not, which raises the question of whether it's conscious or unconscious.

JO: It's tricky, because as soon as you start talking about it being a conscious decision these animals make, you start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches, giggling at how evil they are for pretending to hide nuts. And you start to think, maybe this isn't the right exact way to think about lying and deception.

OM: The drongo — a bird renowned for its ability to deceive meerkats — doesn't just have one trick, it cycles through different alarm calls and borrows calls from other bird species. Does that put it in a different category of liar than squirrels or monkeys, or is it the same trick with a different toolbox?

JO: It could just be the same trick with a different toolbox. It's essentially doing the same thing as the golden snub-nosed monkeys we were talking about before. But birds are incredible singers and have very flexible call structures, and there are tons of birds that can mimic other birds. Maybe you just pair that ability with this deception adaptation, and it looks a bit different, but it's the same kind of trick.

OM: Do you think these behaviors are inherited, or just innate characteristics of the drongos themselves?

JO: I don't know — I'd be interested to find out. The evolutionary aspect would be that the ones who can do it get more food and are better able to survive and reproduce. Whether they learn it from their parents, it's entirely possible. We know from birds in general that they learn calls from their parents and their social groups, and there are even studies showing birds will start learning calls while they're still in the egg, listening to their parents' calls. So it's entirely possible they learn this trick socially, as far as I know.

Male cuttlefish can change their body pattern to trick competing suitors.

OM: In writing this book, what did you find is the best way to approach understanding animal behavior as it relates to human traits like lying or deception?

JO: I think there's still a little bit of baggage from old-school thinking, that you need bigger brains to be deceptive and tricky in this way, and there are still people who think it must be things like the higher apes and great apes that are capable of this stuff.

As soon as you start studying that in something like an invertebrate, it's really hard to get the idea out there — other scientists will come back and say, "No, that couldn't be possible, this must be some other type of behavior, or it just looks like tactical deception, but it's not." This happened with the researchers who did the work on cuttlefish that change one side of their body to look like a male and the other to look like a female — there was a lot of resistance to that idea, seemingly just because it was a cuttlefish, this little invertebrate, so it couldn't possibly be capable of such cleverness. But as far as the actual evidence goes, and what we can see, it's really no different from what we see in these big-brained mammals, so why not assume the same thing is going on?

A lot of it comes down to the culture and practice of science, and the people doing the science. We're supposed to be as objective as possible, but we're still humans, we're still animals. It takes a while for ideas to change.

OM: Is there a risk that this caution has become its own kind of bias, where we assume human specialness by default until proven otherwise?

JO: Yeah, definitely. It's important, as part of scientific practice, to be as objective as possible, and as a general rule, to not anthropomorphize. But at the same time, we're just animals too — we're just another one of the great apes. We share characteristics with lots of different animals, so it's not a huge stretch to think that what's going on in our brains is also going to be similar to what's going on in other animal brains.

It's just a question of when we apply that kind of thinking, and when it's useful or not. Something similar happened in the field of understanding pain in animals — scientists studying this were always trying not to anthropomorphize, not to assume animals experienced pain the way we did. Then, the more we understood it, it became quite clear that they probably did, and it almost became an ethical question to stop with the anti-anthropomorphizing and instead go, no, we know what pain feels like, we can say that.

We're never going to be able to see what's going on in their brains, but that doesn't excuse us from recognizing what's going on. So I think it became okay not to anthropomorphize but to recognize the similarities between humans and other animals, as opposed to always hinging on the differences between us.

OM: At the end of the chapter, you say that if you buy a scientist a few drinks, they'll eventually admit that animals can lie. I obviously can't buy you a drink over email, so I'll just ask you directly — do you think animals can lie?

JO: Yeah. I'll give a straightforward yes, because I can.

You need to get scientists out of their professional mindset, where they're trained to give the most correct answer that they can. And yes is a bit of a broad-stroke answer for a scientist when they're in professional mode, which is why you need to get them out of the lab and out to a bar or a cafe, and get them talking in human terms again.

OM: What would you say is your favorite example in the book — what are you most excited for readers to walk away with?

JO: I'll go with the cuttlefish example — the one where a male cuttlefish will put male color patterns on one side of its body and female patterns on the other, to trick other male cuttlefish. It might be my favorite because, as a young student, I worked on this particular species of cuttlefish. We were studying them, watching all of their crazy color-changing abilities, and just wondering what on earth they must be talking about, what was going on there. Then, years later, seeing the aforementioned research come out was this sort of lightbulb moment — that's what I was watching them do all along. I think that has a personal connection for me. I spent so much time looking at these creatures, being mesmerized by what they were doing, with no idea what was going on. So it was great to see scientists come in and figure it out, and answer those questions.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

To understand how these creatures swindle their way to survival, Liars, Cheats, and Copycats reveals the science behind camouflage, mimicry, and masquerade. Taking readers on a journey from tropical rainforests to the darkness of deep ocean trenches, James O’Hanlon explores how animals and plants use deception to avoid predators, lure in prey, and even reproduce.

Olivia Maule is a former Live Science intern and science journalist whose beats include space, biotechnology and the environment. She holds a B.A. in biology and a B.S. in anthropology from the University of Florida and completed a master's degree in science communication at U.C. Santa Cruz. A 2025 AAAS Mass Media Fellow, she wrote stories and produced videos during a summer at El Nuevo Día, Puerto Rico's largest newspaper, and has written for Eos, Mongabay, Science magazine and Stanford Report. #6406. Foraging for Purple Sea Urchins Along California's Sonoma Coast

This article is part of a series of stories about hunting, fishing, and foraging experiences across North America. Joseph Ogilvy is the author of Tin Can Coast, published in July 2026.

It’s low tide, not long after dawn, and we’re about to disturb the tide pools of a small Sonoma cove in a hunt for sea urchin. Our group of would-be foragers are in Sea Ranch, a couple hours north of San Francisco, on the tough end of the California coast, where fog-pressed hills tumble into the Pacific. The tide pools of Pebble Beach are covered in shaggy mats and bundles of kelp, and the spots that aren’t blanketed in seaweed are a carnival of alien creatures: sea stars, anemones, crabs, abalone, a muddled parade of luminous colors and implausible body shapes.

Nathan Maxwell Cann, a foraging guide with Flora & Fungi Adventures

Nathan Maxwell Cann, our guide, spectacled, moustachioed, and clad in a well-worn chore jacket and waterproof boots, talks the group through the principles and practice of sea urchin gathering. He tosses out the explanation of what we’re looking for with the easy, self-deprecating banter of a former bartender. For a long time he worked in restaurants in North California, but a few years ago he caught the tidal foraging bug and became a self-professed ‘kelp guy’ with a sideline in urchins.

He shows us our prey. Out of the water, urchins look like curled-up hedgehogs, which is the root of their name in Spanish, Italian, and even English (many years ago our word urchin was used for the hedgehog). Their purple spikes project outward from a roughly hemispherical shell, known as a test. Most are somewhere between the size of a golf ball and a fist, and their only real feature is a malevolent-looking mouth armed with five overlapping teeth for grinding and shearing kelp.

The purple sea urchins devastating California's kelp forests is one of the few seafoods that exist in abundance—or rather, overabundance.

In the water, their flare of spines look like dark starbursts against the rock. At first you only see the big ones, but the longer you stare into the pools, the more urchins you will make out; what seemed shadows resolve themselves into potential pickings, far more than could possibly be taken by hand.

There are huge number of purple sea urchins in this cove, and there are even larger numbers of purple sea urchins throughout California’s coast. Whole swathes of seafloor where kelp forests used to stand are now home to nothing but thousands of the prickly echinoderms, so-called urchin barrens. Similar barrens can be found in Alaska, Tasmania, New Zealand, South Africa, and beyond. Sea urchins have become one of the few seafoods that exist in abundance—or rather, overabundance.

The idea of urchins as a pest wasn’t intuitive for me. When I first encountered them, they were luxuries, delicacies for the gourmand who'd graduated beyond oysters, requiring a great deal of time and discomfort, most of it mine: I was a commis chef in a London restaurant, and one of my duties was cleaning urchins. The restaurant served the roe raw in the shell or tossed with spaghettini; I was busy pulling shards of their spines out from underneath my fingernails.

With California's sea otters hunted to the brink of extinction and sea stars struck down by an uncontrollable plague worsened by the state’s warming waters, the sea urchins have few natural predators left.

In the restaurant business, at least, urchins were still precious things. Only a few years later did I see the other side of their nature. After various twists and turns I found myself writing a book about the history of California and its ocean. The story followed the back-and-forth of human and marine life; how fishing and the sea shaped the state and how the state’s history shaped them in return. For most of the story, the urchin was a minor character compared to sea otters or sardines. In recent years, however, the unsuspecting urchin has moved to center stage: It’s not really coherent to call a brainless shellfish a villain, but within the drama of the intertidal zone, it’s not totally incorrect either.

To put it bluntly, the urchins are out of control. They’re blindly mowing down kelp forests, leaving barrens in their place. And those kelp forests are—or were—marvels of diversity, providing a shelter for a wild array of ocean creatures from jeweled top sea snails to barrel-bodied harbor seals. The problem is the urchins' insatiable appetite for seaweed; unchecked, they will graze through the kelp stipes, dooming them to float away into the deep ocean.

For most of California’s history, predators have kept urchin numbers down, but there aren’t many predators that can get past the wall of spikes and shell. The ones that really make a difference are sea stars and sea otters: Sea stars spew out their stomachs and envelop the urchins, dissolving the edible parts in their digestive juices then ejecting the empty shells. Otters just bash and bite their way through.

The problem in Sonoma and the shore north of it, is that it’s been 150 years or more since a wild otter smashed open an urchin. In the early 19th century, California’s sea otters were hunted to the brink of extinction, the unparalleled softness and value of their fur drawing fur trappers all the way from Russia into California. Two centuries after the hunt, the sea otters’ range is still restricted to a couple hundred miles of the Central California coast.

For a time the sea stars did double duty controlling the urchins, but in recent years they have been struck down by an uncontrollable plague, worsened by the state’s warming waters, called, quite literally, sea star wasting disease. The stars have grown lethargic and limp, with lesions spread across their bodies, their arms falling off or disintegrating. Their population has collapsed, allowing the urchins to chew kelp and multiply at their leisure.

The real skill in urchin foraging lies in not falling over—the kelp-slicked rocks are slippery under the feet, and the ocean pulls at our ankles.

So, ecologically speaking, the job of our small group of foragers is to be the otters. The principles of urchin harvesting internalized, we ditch our shoes and move on to the practice, clambering around the rocky intertidal zone. Our little group is still shaking off our early morning bleariness while scattering over the rocks, bending over to peer closely into the tide pools. Gathering urchins has much the same feeling as mushroom picking or birdwatching (or indeed easter egg hunting). You quickly enter into a kind of focused flow state, punctuated by little jolts of childish joy as you spot what you're looking for. But compared to other forms of foraging, urchin gathering is easy as pie. None of my companions, mostly ocean-curious thirty-something Californians from the Bay and beyond, have been urchin foraging before, but their coolers and bags are soon brimming. The primary motivation of my fellow foragers is split: half are most excited by the prospect of eating our catch, the other half by the experience of going out and catching it.

Once your eye settles on the color and shape of them, they’re everywhere. Picking the urchins up from their niches just takes a little clasp and a wiggle with a pair of tongs. The real skill in urchin foraging lies in not falling over—the kelp-slicked rocks are slippery under the feet, and the ocean pulls at our ankles, while the busy strangeness of the tide pool creatures makes it easy to get distracted.

As Cann puts it, urchin gathering is really just “a reason for being out in the tide pools.”

As my net bag begins bulging with spines, I find myself more and more absorbed with what John Steinbeck called the ‘hurrying, fighting, feeding, breeding animals of the tide pools’; the scuttling of a hermit crab fleeing from my shadow, the respiration holes of an algae-camouflaged abalone peeking from a crevice, the waft and flicker of an anemone’s tentacles. The coos and camera clicks of my fellow foragers suggest they are just as absorbed. Which is kind of the point. As Cann puts it, the urchin gathering is really just “a reason for being out in the tide pools.” The constraint of the task encourages a deeper looking, and gives us, part of a society suspicious of aimless activity, an excuse to mess around and explore a strange world.

And besides, they taste good. Back on dry ground, we each grab a stout pair of kitchen shears and crunch a rough circle out the top of an urchin, scooping and tossing its muddy, briny viscera, rinsing the creature in a bucket of seawater and using a mussel shell to spoon out the five golden tongues of roe, arranged in a star shape. The roe is rich and buttery, starting off savory and briny, then mellowing into a higher note of sweetness. It’s bracing stuff, especially at 8:15 in the morning. It tastes powerfully of place. Cann explains that the umami savor comes directly from the kelp it feeds on. No wonder that, at the Sea Ranch Lodge just down the coast from our expedition, the head chef Ryan Seal makes a sea urchin zabaglione as the base for a carbonara, introducing urchin-hesitant guests to the delicacy while showcasing an intrinsically Sonoman flavor.

Sea Ranch Lodge chef Ryan Seal uses the local sea urchins to make an “uni carbonara” with squid ink chimaera pasta, pancetta, and furikake.

Still on the shore, we stand around in a group chatting while we open more urchins and swallow the meat inside. Even with the appeals and distractions of the intertidal world and a few early morning tongues of uni, our bags are still overflowing. But our gathering has barely made a dent in the cove’s urchin numbers. As substitute otters we have come up short; the real thing can eat dozens of urchins in a day.

And still, uni foraging workshops are increasingly common all over Northern California, adding to the many beachcombers who pick urchin on their own. The urchins are still dominating the coast though. From an ecosystem perspective, our efforts are little more than “a drop in the bucket”, as Cann acknowledges. Restoring the kelp forests will require a more forceful campaign. The Giant Giant Kelp Restoration Project in Monterey has an enormous submarine vacuum to suck urchins from the barrens. In Northern California, scuba divers just crush them with hammers. Entrepreneurs all over California and the West Coast have begun ranching operations, gathering the often underweight urchins from the barrens and fattening them up on sustainably harvested kelp before selling them to restaurants. Another company in Mendocino, Marblis, is compacting the shells into what they call urchinite, pitched as a substitute for marble countertops.

Our morning workshop of tongs and kitchen shears, by contrast, is a symbolic gesture. By mid-morning, my fellow foragers and I will be heading back home with fond memories and a few meals worth of seafood delicacies. The urchins will continue to chomp their way through the kelp forests of Sea Ranch.

Kelp forests—which simultaneously serve as a carbon sink, wildlife habitat, and protection against erosion—are vital to Sonoma's coastal ecosystem.

Before we split to find the coffee we both need, Cann and I stand in the parking lot and talk through what the urchin gathering is really about, given that we’re not singlehandedly saving the kelp. It’s a form of education or consciousness-raising for sure. There’s nothing like feeling the kelp between your toes or swallowing urchin roe just minutes after it has left the water to make the stakes of ocean conservation feel close to home. You can make the case that activities like this develop virtues of generosity and curiosity in ourselves; my fellow foragers filter out of the car park smiling and carrying dripping containers; they tell Cann what they’ll do with their haul, who they’ll invite for dinner or share their newfound knowledge with.

Steinbeck advised his readers to look “from the tide pool to the stars and back to the tide pool again.” Maybe that’s what the foraging is really about. The focus on one small creature opens you up to its myriad connections to everything else. At the same time, it puts you in that web, gives you a visceral way to feel the relationship between yourself, the urchin, and the rest of the tide pool world; you can quite literally taste the kelp forest in the uni. I’ve seen the sea urchin as a pest and a delicacy, an ecosystem villain and a precious treat worth getting splinters for. But it was only when I planted my feet in its rock pool home and plucked one from the water and threw back its roe that I really saw it in its place.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6405. A diving pioneer found a Roman wreck off Portofino in 1959, then it vanished until police divers found it again 66 years later

Carabinieri divers training off Punta Chiappa, Italy, found 9 Roman wine amphorae at a Roman wreck first reported in 1959 and lost since 1960.

On November 7, 1959, the Italian diving pioneer Duilio Marcante went down off Punta Chiappa, near Camogli in northwest Italy. At about 150 feet (45 meters) he found Roman amphorae jammed between the rocks, the first sign of a Roman wreck.

Six months later the pile he had described was gone. Nobody found the site again for 66 years.

During a recent training dive, Carabinieri divers came across an intact amphora at the spot. Italian heritage officials said on October 22, 2026, that it is Marcante’s lost wreck. The announcement mentions no remains of the hull.

The divers belong to the Nucleo Carabinieri Subacquei of Genoa, the diving unit of Italy’s military police. During the exercise they spotted a complete Dressel 1 amphora, a standard Roman wine-jar type, at more than 130 feet (40 meters).

The spot lies inside the Portofino Marine Protected Area, a very busy diving area. The divers reported it at once to the regional heritage office, the Soprintendenza for Liguria.

Follow-up dives were run with the office’s own diving unit, the Servizio Tecnico di Archeologia Subacquea (S.T.A.S.). The first map counted nine amphorae in a small area along cracks in the cliff.

The jars are hard to spot because they are fused to the rock under a thick coralligenous crust, a hard pink layer built mainly by calcareous algae.

According to the official press release, the team lifted the two most exposed jars of the nine, because large numbers of divers pass over the area.

Marcante (1914-1985) ran the Centro Subacqueo Mediterraneo and a spearfishing school in Genoa. In 1958 he had joined the first campaign on the Roman ship of Spargi, in Sardinia.

On his 1959 dive he saw two amphorae stuck to the rocks by stony coral and calcareous algae. He swam around the area and saw more jars nearby. At the foot of the cliff there seemed to be a mound, covered by muddy sediment.

On Monday, November 9, the team dove again and brought up two intact jars. They feared looters would take them. The next day Marcante reported the site to the heritage office and to the underwater archaeology center in Albenga.

The difficulties of the season prevented an immediate follow-up. Nino Lamboglia, who directed the Albenga center, later wrote that the depth and steep seabed also argued against sending the ship Daino, then in its first year of work.

On May 8 and 9, 1960, Gianni Roghi went back with Marcante and the Carabinieri. Roghi worked for the Albenga center, run by Lamboglia (1912-1977), a founder of Italian underwater archaeology.

The mound in the mud was gone. They found one amphora tied with a thin line, ready to be carried off by looters. Three broken jars were still locked in the crust.

Lamboglia described the case at an underwater archaeology congress in Barcelona in September 1961. He wrote that the site had probably not stayed “immune from clandestine hoarders.” After that, nobody found it.

Simon Luca Trigona, who heads S.T.A.S. Liguria, said the survey and a first look at the jars confirm that this is Marcante’s site.

The amphorae form a uniform cargo of Dressel 1A wine jars from the Tyrrhenian side of Italy. The type dates them to between the late second century BCE and the first decade of the first century BCE.

Trigona tied the cargo to the years just after Rome conquered southern Gaul. Genoa and the other Ligurian ports were then important for Roman trade.

A second wreck from the same period was found off Pegli, on the western side of Genoa, in the early 1950s. It has not been located since either.

Other cargoes from the Roman era have survived in very different places, from a ship off Adrasan in Turkey with its plates still stacked to intact goods in Lake Neuchâtel.

The heritage office says the site now needs regular checks and rules for divers. Colonel Samuele Sighinolfi, who commands the Carabinieri naval and diving group, said it is under constant surveillance.

Major Alessandro Caprio leads the Genoa unit of the Carabinieri heritage command. He said his officers watch auctions, websites and illegal markets for the work of “tombaroli del mare,” or sea tomb robbers.

Tips from divers have mattered elsewhere in Italy, as when off Sardinia a diver alerted authorities to a hoard of about 50,000 Roman coins. Busy dive sites carry risks too, and a study that tracked more than 700 divers found that most reef damage is accidental.

Superintendent Vincenzo Tiné said the find shows how much work remains, “even in areas that we consider well studied.” He noted that thousands of divers visit them every year.

Giovanni Anelli, the mayor of Camogli, hopes the jars can one day go on display. Guglielmo Caversazio, president of the marine protected area, offered to help protect the site.

So far the divers have recorded only jars. No timber from the ship has been reported. The release does not say how many amphorae the vessel carried.

“Difficult to imagine the size of the vessel,” Trigona said. Only the more detailed surveys planned for the near future can confirm other remains, he added.

The release also does not say where the two jars raised in 1959 are today. Nor does it explain what became of the mound at the base of the cliff.

Alessandra Cabella, an art historian on the S.T.A.S. Liguria diving team, put the story in three words. “Discovered, lost, rediscovered,” she said. Carabinieri divers were there in 1959, and again for the rediscovery.

The information was obtained from the Soprintendenza Archeologia, Belle Arti e Paesaggio per la Liguria.
