#6404. Three-quarters of NFL football players may end up with CTE

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

It’s the first population-level estimate for the neurogenerative disease among NFL players

The neurodegenerative disease CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy. The condition has been identified most frequently among American football players.

An estimated three-quarters of NFL players who died in a 16-year period had the devastating neurogenerative disease called CTE.

Back in 2017, researchers reported that an estimated 99 percent of former NFL players developed CTE, or chronic traumatic encephalopathy, from an analysis of donated brains. But the families who provided the donations may have done so because their football-playing relatives had symptoms related to CTE, which could skew the results. A new study, which accounts for this potential bias, estimates that nearly 75 percent of former NFL players have CTE at death. It’s the first population-level estimate for NFL players, researchers report October 28 in JAMA Network Open.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The development of CTE is linked to repeated blows to the head over time. The disease can occur in people who play contact sports, experience intimate partner violence or engage in military combat. A study of American football players suggests that the longer the duration of repeated head trauma, the higher the risk of CTE and the more severe the condition. During life, people who are later diagnosed with CTE can experience symptoms including memory issues, difficulty concentrating, depression and poor impulse control.

A brain protein called tau, which usually helps nerve cells communicate and performs other jobs, goes awry in CTE. Brains with the disease are snarled with irregular, damaging clumps of the protein. The condition is diagnosed after death, during an autopsy, and has been identified most frequently among American football players.

The new study, by a Boston University research team, included all previous NFL players who passed away from January 2008 through December 2023. The more than 2,300 players included almost 400 with samples in the university’s UNITE Brain Bank, with the remainder identified from records in the U.S. National Death Index. The research team determined that families of NFL players who had CTE-related symptoms in life were five times more likely to donate their relative’s brain than families whose relative did not experience symptoms. Taking that into consideration, the team landed on a population-level CTE estimate for NFL players of 74.5 percent.

The research team notes that determining the true prevalence of CTE is important to understanding the public health impact of the disease.

#6403. Archeologists Found a 1,000-Year-Old Viking Treasure That May Have Touched a Saint’s Hand

It was first sorted with English pennies, until its inscription revealed it had a run-in with Norway’s future saint.

Experts cataloguing the largest Viking Age coin hoard ever discovered in Norway were stunned when one 1,000-year-old coin stood out from the more than 5,000 in the find. As archaeologist Anne Skogsfjord sorted and catalogued the coins, she found herself face-to-face with King Olaf Haraldsson, known as Saint Olaf. The coin’s inscription confirmed it: ONLAF R+ NORMANORV, which translates to “Olaf, King of the Norwegians.”

“Could this really be a coin of Olaf Haraldsson that I was holding? And it was,” Skogsfjord said in a statement from the University of Oslo’s Museum of Cultural History. “It was a very special moment. I realized that we had found a national treasure.”

The discovery came from what is already a remarkable find. Since its discovery in April 2026, the Mørstad Hoard has grown to about 5,500 coins, so cataloguing it is no simple task. Skogsfjord came across the Olaf coin while working through a group of Anglo-Saxon coins issued by Æthelred II, where it had first been sorted. However, its inscription soon revealed who had really issued it.

The find is extraordinarily rare. Fewer than 20 of Saint Olaf’s coins survive today, and most have turned up outside Norway. Only four examples of the type found in the Mørstad Hoard were previously known, and just one of those was found in Norway, in a hoard uncovered during the restoration of the church ruins at Stein in 1924.

“For those of us interested in Norway’s earliest monetary history, it hardly gets any better than this,” said Svein H. Gullbekk, professor of numismatics at the University of Oslo. “Here we have a coin bearing the king’s portrait and a cross, with another cross on the reverse. It is a Christianization coin on a grand scale. We can see how King Olaf used coinage to legitimize the new faith and to establish himself as a Christian king of European standing.”

The coin was struck around 1024–1028, near the end of the Viking Age, and minting it was itself a political act. “This is branding,” Gullbekk said. Olaf himself appears on the coin, facing left and wearing a conical battle helmet, which gave this coin type the nickname “Pointed Helmet.”

“Olaf Haraldsson himself decided what these coins should look like, and perhaps he was present when they were struck,” Gullbekk said. “It is entirely possible that this very coin from Mørstad was once held in the king’s own hand.”

Yet the coin was more than a political statement, as it was, unsurprisingly, used as money. Both sides bear numerous small knife cuts, likely made to test the silver content during transactions. “On that basis, we may assume that the coin changed hands several times during the approximately 20 to 25 years between its production and its deposition in the Mørstad Hoard,” said Associate Professor Florent Audy, who leads the museum’s cataloguing of the hoard. “That is yet another fascinating chapter in the coin’s history.”

The hoard itself was first found on April 10, 2026, by metal detectorists Rune Sætre and Vegard Sørlie in Rena, in eastern Norway’s Innlandet County. This autumn, the two detectorists searched the field again and, with landowner Ole Erik Hørstad, unearthed coin number 5,000. County archaeologists also carried out a follow-up investigation of the site in late September. And the count may keep climbing. “I am beginning to think that the hoard may soon exceed 6,000 coins,” Audy said.

In the meantime, the public will get its first look at the find. The Olaf coin will be shown when an exhibition on the Mørstad Hoard opens at the Historical Museum in Oslo on November 20, while cataloguing continues behind the scenes.

“When you think this Viking treasure cannot become any more exciting, new surprises emerge,” said Hanna Geiran, Norway’s director general of cultural heritage. “This St. Olaf coin is yet another reminder of how extraordinary this find is. The coin is not only a rare object, but also tangible testimony from a time when the foundations of the Norwegian kingdom and the Christianization of the country were laid.”

Tim Newcomb is a journalist based in the Pacific Northwest. He covers stadiums, sneakers, gear, infrastructure, and more for a variety of publications, including Popular Mechanics. #6402. The Key to Stress-Free Travel Is the Right Gear—These Travel Accessories Pull Their Weight

The secret to a seamless travel journey is having the right travel accessories at your side. Whether you're boarding an early flight, hopping on a cruise ship, or catching a cross-country train, it pays to be prepared with smart gadgets and gear that make all the difference. From the packing cubes and laundry bags that help me fit the excessive amount of clothes I insist on bringing to the eye mask and neck pillow that make getting sleep at 30,000 feet possible, the best travel accessories pull their weight every time. After more than six years as a travel editor, I've figured out which essentials are worth bringing along. My lineup of foolproof travel accessories keeps me comfortable on long-haul flights, protects my suitcase from getting lost in transit, and ensures all my things are exactly where they should be.

To help every trip you take be a smoother one, I've put together a list of the very best travel accessories to pack on your next vacation. From in-flight necessities and organization hacks to tracking devices that deliver even the most anxious travelers peace of mind, these are the essentials I recommend most.

A tote bag is the ideal personal item—it's roomy enough to store all of your in-flight essentials and is usually pretty pliable, meaning you can squeeze it under the seat without taking up all of your foot room. Look for one with comfortable shoulder straps, a zipper or magnetic snap closure, and a few interior pockets to store your phone and passport. A trolley sleeve is a nice feature, too, so you can slide it over your suitcase while cruising through the airport. My personal favorite is MZ Wallace's Metro Tote—it's got more pockets than I know what to do with, and its super-soft straps never dig in to my shoulders. Cuyana's sleek System tote, L.L.Bean's iconic Boat and Tote, and Calpak's expandable Luka tote all come highly recommended by my fellow editors too.

A good toiletry bag keeps your products organized and your suitcase spill-free. These smaller options from Dagne Dover and Away offer enough space for your skincare essentials without taking up a ton of space in your suitcase. If you're going on a longer vacation or want to keep all of your products in one place (skincare, makeup, shower essentials, etc.), you might want to opt for Bagsmart's hanging toiletry bag that can be hooked onto the back of the bathroom door at the hotel. It keeps the counter clutter-free, and makes finding exactly what you need a breeze. Peak Design's best-selling wash pouch is another smart pick for longer journeys—commerce director Madison Flager has used hers for over five years and it's still in good shape.

Browse more toiletry bag recommendations.

A rule to live by: Never check your valuables, especially jewelry. Keep necklaces, earrings, bracelets, and rings safe and neatly organized inside a jewelry case that gets stowed in your carry-on luggage or personal item. These durable, compact cases have enough room to store a few different jewelry options. Mark and Graham's case is on the larger side, making it ideal for destination weddings, special events, or longer vacations.

Browse more jewelry case recommendations.

Rather than buy plastic minis every time you travel, get yourself a set of leakproof travel bottles to hold your at-home favorites on the go. My holy grail product, the Cadence capsules, are great for storing toiletries and beauty products, as well as small loose items like vitamins and bobby pins. I also regularly travel with a few of these silicone bottles from Amazon to hold shampoo, conditioner, and body wash. They're leakproof, easy to refill, and aren't super bulky in my toiletry bag.

Browse more toiletry bottle recommendations.

Instead of bringing entire bottles of medication or vitamins, pack a compact pill case that holds only as much as you'll need for the length of your trip. No matter where I'm headed, I always pack the Holii pill organizer—it's small enough to fit in my Dopp kit and has enough compartments to separate what I'll need for each day. Dosey's seven-day pill case is a nice pick for weeklong trips—and it looks so cute on any hotel bathroom counter.

I've recommended Afform's makeup bag to my mom, my sisters, my friends, and even strangers in the airport bathroom. It really is that good! The standout feature is its foldable shape: After you unzip the bag, each side can be pulled down to lie flat, allowing you to see all of your products at once. It's designed to keep each product secured in an upright position, reducing the risk of any spills. The bag's structured silhouette and flat base offer the stability and durability I want all of my breakable—and pricey—beauty products to have while in transit. For something less expensive, Eachy's best-selling makeup bag has a lot to offer—with plenty of room for full-size blushes and bronzers, as well separate compartments and multiple pockets to hold smaller products.

For years, I tossed my makeup brushes in a cosmetic pouch when I traveled—and I suffered the consequences. Not only did it make finding the right brush I need difficult, it also meant the rest of my makeup products ended up covered in leftover powder, blush, and bronzer. This all changed when I finally caved and tried out a dedicated brush holder a few years ago. With this $15 Amazon find, all of my makeup brushes stay in one place and can lay flat in the same direction, keeping them organized and away from other products. It’s large enough to hold several long, thin eyeshadow brushes and thick, dense foundation brushes (and a Beauty Blender too). The case's magnetic flap keeps my brushes secure and the soft silicone material means I can wash it off with ease.

All of those tech items you're bringing along mean you're going to have plenty of charging cubes and cables to keep track of. Save space in your backpack by keeping everything wrapped up in a travel organizer designed specifically for your electronic accessories, like the ones below from Peak Design and Bellroy. These are especially great for long flights where you're more likely to switch between devices.

Browse more travel tech organizer recommendations.

There's no sense in bringing your full-size day-to-day wallet on vacation—chances are, you only need a few cards and some cash. A slim travel wallet allows you to carry just those essentials, and makes it less of headache if it gets lost or stolen. Bellroy's RFID-blocking wallet is a smart choice for travelers, while Coach's sleek leather card holder fits in even your tiniest purses.

Browse more travel wallet recommendations.

A crossbody bag makes the most sense for travel—whether you're sightseeing around London or exploring the Disney parks, you want something to keep you hands-free and ready to go no matter what's on the agenda. These lightweight bags take up little suitcase space and have enough room for your daily essentials: wallet, keys, sunnies, lip balm, and hand sanitizer. Senior features editor Megan Spurrell swears by Baggu's nylon Crescent bag for its versatility and roominess, while commerce director Madison Flager's go-to crossbody is this sleek convertible style from Lo & Sons (you can remove the long strap and re-clip the sides to make it a shoulder bag whenever you need!).

Some instances call for a slim bag that holds your phone and little else. Whether you're headed to dinner on a cruise ship, down to the hotel pool, or to an outdoor concert, these tiny bags will keep your phone and a few cards secure, without the extra bulk that comes with carrying around a larger purse or tote. Senior commerce editor Hannah Chubb is a big fan of the Hailey crossbody phone case from Bandolier—she's had it for over four years and it's still going strong.

Also handy: a high-quality passport case (bonus points if it has space to hold your credit cards) to keep your most important document protected. Made of genuine Italian leather, Mark & Graham's sleek passport case is a thoughtful gift for any traveler in your life (especially since it can be monogrammed).

Is there anything more humbling that trying to fit a floppy sunhat into your suitcase? It takes up so much space and often leaves your favorite hat completely squished. Last summer, Chubb shared her top tip on how to pack the bulkiest thing in your vacation wardrobe: Use a hat clip. With one, your hat can hang securely from your personal item or suitcase without any fuss. Chubb's favorite one, the Toptote, fits in the palm of your hand. Its design is simple: Stick the brim of your hat between the two magnets, and it gets locked in place, letting your bag do all the heavy lifting.

For a comfortable journey at 30,000 feet—especially long trips where you’re hoping to get some shut-eye—an eye mask is crucial. The 100% silk option from Zimasilk and the soft, sculpted eye mask from MZoo are two highly rated Amazon finds. Both mold to fit to your face, provide total darkness, and stay in place.

Another comfort essential: a travel pillow. It can take some time to find the style you like best, and your pick might vary depending on whether you're in-flight or in a car or on a train. Cabeau's Evolution S3 and Ostrichpillow's Go memory foam pillow are among our editors' go-to's. They offer great head and neck support and are soft on the skin.

Alright, alright, a pair of foldable slippers isn't exactly a necessity for travel, but it is a simple in-flight luxury that makes your time in the clouds a little bit cozier. This one is for the travelers out there who insist on taking off their shoes on the plane (leave your socks on, please!), but still want to be kind to their neighbors. As you prepare for takeoff, slide on a pair of these lightweight slippers. They're not too structured, meaning you can fold them back up and tuck them into a small compartment of your personal item.

Frequent fliers who run cold would be wise to invest in a travel blanket—it'll keep you warm, and if you're on a red-eye, may help you actually get some sleep. Go for something lightweight that can be packed into a small pouch when you're not using it.

We love a good pair of compression socks to fight that pins-and-needles feeling that comes from sitting still for too long, be it on a long-haul flight or a road trip. Our editors swear by socks from Bombas and Comrad—they're comfortable, stay in place, and help reduce swelling.

#6401. Your brain follows bad advice even when you know better

A new study reveals why people continue to follow unreliable information even when they know it could be misleading.

Knowing that information is unreliable doesn’t necessarily stop us from believing it.

A new study found that even when people were warned that certain clues were no more accurate than a coin toss, they still allowed those clues to influence their decisions.

Even more surprisingly, participants recognized that the unreliable clues were influencing their decisions.

It shows that simply being aware of a bias doesn’t always stop it from affecting our choices.

Keiji Ota, an assistant professor at the University of Tsukuba in Japan, carried out the research with Lucie Charles of Queen Mary University of London. Both also work with the UCL Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience in London.

The pair tested people’s choices in a simple color-guessing game. It wasn’t a test of real news, but the findings raise questions about how much a warning label alone can do.

The study involved 140 adults in the United Kingdom, who played one of five versions of an online game.

In each round, a computer chose red or blue as the correct answer, and players scrolled at their own pace through six colored squares that predicted it.

A percentage above each square showed its chance of being right, so a 65% square gave the right answer about two-thirds of the time.

The instructions described a 50% square as “as reliable as if the square’s color had been determined by flipping a coin” and told players to ignore it.

Some clues were wrong more often than right. A 35% square could still help, but players needed to reverse its answer, much as they might do with advice from someone who usually lies.

After seeing all six clues, players chose a color and immediately learned whether they were right.

Each person played close to 300 rounds, without a time limit, while the five versions used different mixes of clues.

Players did fairly well overall, choosing the right color in 58% to 64% of rounds, depending on the version. Guessing alone would give an average of 50%.

A player who used the percentages perfectly would ignore every 50% square. Yet in all five versions, people chose blue more often when more of those random squares showed blue.

The researchers built a computer model of each person’s choices to measure the effect.

The model estimated that players treated these squares as though they were right about 54% to 62% of the time.

That was more trust than the clues deserved, but it rarely made much difference to scores. In only one version did people who relied more on the random clues perform noticeably worse.

A clue that’s wrong 65% of the time can tell you just as much as one that’s right 65% of the time. You just have to use the opposite answer, and players found that harder.

In the version with only reversed and random clues, volunteers got 58.2% of answers right. In a matching version with trustworthy clues, they reached 64.4%.

Players also gave the last clue more weight than the first, especially when most clues needed reversing.

The researchers suggest that earlier clues may have faded from memory as new ones appeared.

Mentally flipping each answer could add to that strain. The extra effort might leave people with less ability to remember the clues they had already seen.

In two versions, players answered a question after each choice about one randomly selected kind of clue. They moved a slider to show whether they had followed its color, ignored it, or chosen the opposite.

Their ratings matched patterns in their choices: when more squares of a given kind agreed with their final answer, they reported more influence from that kind.

The most informative clues drew the strongest ratings, whether players needed to follow or reverse them.

The random clues showed the same pattern, suggesting that participants could recognize how unreliable information affected their choices.

People who relied most on a kind of clue also generally felt most influenced by it, although this did not hold for every kind in both versions.

A second model compared how likely a player was to choose an answer with and without a clue.

The difference matched people’s ratings and was closely tied to confidence, according to the authors.

The researchers offer several possible explanations for the bias. Seeing the same color repeatedly may make it feel like the right answer, an idea psychologists call the mere exposure effect.

People may also expect whoever provides information to be trying to help. That expectation could make it difficult to accept that a clue contains nothing useful.

Or players may have turned to random clues when the useful ones left them almost evenly split between red and blue. In that case, a useless clue could serve as a tiebreaker.

Ignoring those clues might also take more work than it was worth. Since the bias barely hurt scores, the authors suggest that players had little to gain by resisting it.

Reliability labels already appear alongside social media posts, product reviews, and health advice. Research on whether they reduce misinformation has produced mixed results.

Some studies found that star ratings for news sources reduced people’s willingness to believe and share false stories.

A 2022 study, however, found little average improvement in the quality of news people read and no reduction in mistaken beliefs.

The volunteers’ awareness also differs from earlier research in which people often missed influences on their choices, including the order of search results.

Those studies used cues that weren’t spelled out, while this game clearly stated how reliable each clue was.

Colored squares are much simpler than real headlines, and each version of the game used only three reliability levels.

The slider used to measure people’s awareness is also new and needs testing with other wording, labels, and instructions.

The questions asked about kinds of clues rather than their place in the sequence. That means the study couldn’t show whether players noticed how much more they relied on the last clue.

Fact-checking labels aim to limit the influence of false information, but this experiment cannot tell us exactly how people respond to them online.

Still, the findings reveal something important about human decision-making: Knowing that information is unreliable doesn’t necessarily stop us from using it. Recognizing a bias and overcoming it may be two very different things.

The study is published in the journal PLOS Computational Biology.

#6400. Einstein had a packed schedule in Pittsburgh in 1934, but he made time for a group of amateur astronomers

In 1934, Albert Einstein visited a Pittsburgh astronomy exhibit organized by a plumber, highlighting his respect for amateur scientists and their work.

In December 1934, Albert Einstein came to Pittsburgh with a tight schedule. One stop he made a point of keeping was an exhibition by the city’s amateur astronomers.

The group’s co-founder, Leo J. Scanlon, was a plumber. Four years earlier, he had built a backyard observatory topped with a homemade aluminum dome for about $428.

Einstein was in town to give a lecture. The amateurs had invited him to see their display at the Mellon Institute, in Pittsburgh’s Oakland neighborhood.

In June 1929, Scanlon, who lived from 1903 to 1999, and Chester B. Roe founded the Amateur Astronomers Association of Pittsburgh.

In 1930, Scanlon and a group of friends traveled to the Stellafane convention of amateur telescope makers, which drew just under 100 registered guests. He kept a 41-page journal of the trip.

Back home, Scanlon built the Valley View Observatory beside his house on Van Buren Street. He ordered about 415 square feet (38.6 square meters) of sheet aluminum for the dome.

Its curved panels, called gores, were joined with an external double-turned seam. On November 15, 1930, with finishing touches still to come, the dome was lifted into place.

A dedication followed on November 23. The observatory without its dome cost $250, and the dome itself cost $178, according to Scanlon’s journal entries shared by the Springfield Telescope Makers.

A plaque near the site calls Valley View the first known astronomical observatory with an aluminum dome. Its shiny metal dome became a model for later observatories worldwide, the plaque adds.

In 1934, a national science convention met in Pittsburgh, with exhibits in the unfinished Mellon Institute building. Scanlon collected telescope-making materials from amateurs around the country for a free booth there.

He also wrote to Einstein, saying that a visit would encourage amateurs. Einstein answered that he would come if his schedule allowed.

“It would be my pleasure to examine the exhibit of the Amateur Astronomers,” Einstein wrote.

On December 28, 1934, Einstein, author of the general theory of relativity, lectured at the Carnegie Institute of Technology, now Carnegie Mellon University. His topic was mass-energy equivalence, the idea summed up as E = mc².

“People clambered to see Einstein’s lecture because he was one of the world’s first rock-stars,” said Gregg Franklin, a physics professor at the university.

A foggy photo taken from a balcony of the Little Theater is the only known picture of Einstein with a variant of that equation.

After his lecture in a nearby hall, Einstein asked the audience where the astronomers were, according to the club’s account. A professional astronomer in the room stood up.

“No, no,” Einstein replied. “I want to meet with the amateur astronomers.”

He reached the booth with a group of 40 or 50 people and stayed about 20 minutes. The display held equipment, material samples and photographs from telescope builders in eight states.

Scanlon’s brother Frank was working at a noisy grinding table. Scanlon showed Einstein the Foucault knife-edge test, which reveals tiny bumps and hollows on a telescope mirror.

On a 6-inch (15-centimeter) mirror, Scanlon pressed five fingertips to the glass. The test then showed five “hills” about one wavelength of light high, raised by the heat of his hand.

“I’m a plumber,” Scanlon replied when Einstein asked about his profession near the end of the visit. “Good,” Einstein answered, before asking him where the bathroom was.

David Topper, a Pittsburgh native, is a historian of science at the University of Winnipeg and the author of several books about Einstein.

“He had a thing about amateurs, whom he respected as much as professionals,” Topper said.

Another club member photographed Scanlon thanking Einstein at the booth. Scanlon kept Einstein’s written reply to his invitation.

“It is a letter that I still treasure,” Scanlon recalled many years later.

Steve Hill, a citizen scientist, showed that he could map Jupiter’s atmosphere with special color filters and a backyard telescope.

He then joined Patrick Irwin at Oxford University, whose team had studied Jupiter’s clouds with the MUSE instrument on the Very Large Telescope.

Their combined study concluded that the upper clouds are most likely ammonium hydrosulfide mixed with smog, not frozen ammonia, the European Southern Observatory reported in January 2025.

Clouds of ammonia ice may form only occasionally, when strong vertical convection carries ammonia to the top of the atmosphere.

Dan Caselden, a volunteer with the Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 citizen science project, co-discovered the cold brown dwarf W1935, the American Museum of Natural History announced in April 2024.

The James Webb Space Telescope later detected methane emission from W1935, a possible sign of aurorae.

The information was obtained from the Amateur Astronomers Association of Pittsburgh

#6399. The 6 Best Cell Phone Boosters to Supercharge Your Signal

Improve your phone's reliability both at home and the next time you're off the grid.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

We’ve all lost cell service at home at the worst time. Maybe a call to the insurance company drops when you walk into the kitchen, or a meeting with your boss starts cutting in and out until you step onto your front porch. Usually there’s some signal outside your house. It just gets too weak to reach your phone while you’re inside your home.

A cell phone signal booster can fix dropped calls and slow data when your signal is weak and unreliable. An antenna on your roof or an outside wall picks up whatever signal reaches your house, an amplifier boosts it, and an indoor antenna rebroadcasts it so your phone can hold a steady connection from room to room. Boosters help most in houses far from the nearest tower, like in rural areas where towers are spread miles apart. If your home Wi-Fi is strong, turning on Wi-Fi calling in your phone’s settings routes calls over your internet connection, and a mesh Wi-Fi system can carry that connection to the rooms your router doesn’t reach.

Before you buy one, though, check how much your booster amplifies signal, how many square feet it covers, and which carriers it works with, since those specs decide whether it will actually help where you live. Below, we break down each spec, then list our picks for the best signal boosters for home use.

To find the top-performing cell phone signal boosters, we researched cell signal booster brands across the market, focusing on top consumer brands including HiBoost, weBoost, SureCall, and Winegard. We narrowed our selections by considering customer insights and feedback, price point, product descriptions, and overall user satisfaction before selecting the top product in each category.

Say goodbye to tangled wires and unsightly equipment with the SureCall Flare 3.0, a sleek signal booster that delivers professional-grade cellular enhancement in your home or office.

This powerful booster amplifies weak cellular signals across two to four rooms, making it ideal for medium- and small-sized spaces where reliable connectivity is essential but, for whatever reason, absent.

The intelligent dual-antenna system combines a directional outdoor antenna with an omnidirectional indoor antenna, creating stronger signal amplification that translates to faster data speeds, improved network capacity, and significantly fewer dropped calls.

Installation of the SureCall Flare 3.0 is refreshingly straightforward. This unit requires minimal technical expertise to get up and running. Plus, its competitive pricing is a deal compared to similar-class competitors with lower dB gain ratings, without sacrificing performance. However, it only supports Verizon, AT&T, Sprint, and T-Mobile, so if your phone uses a different carrier, you'll want to look elsewhere.

This affordable but mighty booster punches above its weight class at under $300. The HiBoost for Home Cell Phone Signal Booster boasts an impressive 62 dB gain and comprehensive coverage up to 2,000 square feet, which isn't the most you'll find, but more than satisfactory for single or multiple rooms in average-sized homes, as well as small office spaces.

The intuitive, bright LCD screen provides real-time monitoring of cell connection strength, making it easy to track signal improvements and optimize performance without guesswork. Installation is straightforward and user-friendly, requiring no technical expertise to get the results you want.

This booster is relatively affordable compared to similar options, and HiBoost backs its product with a money-back guarantee and an extensive three-year warranty.

Off-grid with no service? No problem. Built for backcountry exploration, the weBoost Drive Reach is a rugged, durable, reliable cell signal booster for outdoor enthusiasts who refuse to sacrifice connectivity when venturing into remote wilderness areas where traditional cell towers can't reach.

The Drive Reach includes a mount bracket that securely attaches to the roof rack of your car, truck, RV, or off-road vehicle, ensuring stable performance even on the roughest terrain. The adjustable outside antenna easily folds down if your garage has a low ceiling or you’re passing under a low tree canopy. And its all-weather omnidirectional antenna is built to withstand harsh backcountry conditions, including rain, snow, dust, and extreme temperatures.

In most cases, users can expect an additional two bars of boost wherever they explore, turning dead zones into areas with reliable communication for emergency calls, GPS navigation, and staying connected with basecamp or family back home.

Trust us: This isn't just another signal booster—it's your lifeline to the outside world when you're miles from civilization, whether you're camping in deep mountain valleys, traversing desert landscapes, or exploring dense forest trails where cellular signals struggle to reach.

The weBoost Home Complete covers up to 7,500 square feet, more than double our top pick from SureCall, and enough for a two-story house with a basement. A directional antenna on your roof or an outside wall picks up signal from the nearest tower and sends it by cable to an indoor amplifier. The amplifier boosts it by up to 72 decibels, and a panel antenna rebroadcasts it to your phones.

WeBoost’s free app shows your signal strength while you aim the outdoor antenna. The 7,500-square-foot figure assumes a strong signal outside. WeBoost says that with a moderate outside signal, coverage drops to multiple rooms rather than the whole house, so test where the antenna will go before you buy.

The Cel-Fi GO C41 amplifies signal by up to 100 decibels because it boosts only one carrier. The FCC allows single-carrier boosters more gain than universal ones like our SureCall and weBoost picks, which top out at 72 decibels. That extra 28 decibels is roughly 600 times more amplification, enough to make a usable signal out of one weak bar at a rural house.

You choose Verizon, AT&T, or T-Mobile in the Cel-Fi WAVE app, and you can switch carriers there later. If people in your house use different carriers, the phones on the other networks won’t get any boost. Cel-Fi rates the kit for up to 15,000 square feet, but that number assumes open floor space. Interior walls block some of the rebroadcast signal, so expect less in a house with lots of smaller rooms, especially with only one indoor antenna.

The WeBoost Home Studio puts the amplifier and the indoor antenna in a single unit about the size of a paperback, so there’s no separate panel to mount on a wall and only one cable to run from the outdoor antenna to the box. By setting it in the room where your calls drop, it boosts AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon at the same time, so you and your roommates can have different carriers.

WeBoost only rates the Home Studio for one room, so it fits a studio apartment or home office. Its 60 decibels of gain is lower than the SureCall’s 72 decibels, so it works best when you have at least a bar or two outside.

Cell phone signal boosters use “gain” to describe how much a signal is amplified. Gain is measured in decibels (dB), and most cell phone signal boosters range from 50 dB to 100 dB. The larger the gain value, the greater the amplification, or strength, of the signal. You can use a tool like the weBoost app to test your phone's signal strength. An ideal signal strength for a cell phone falls between -50 and -67 decibel-milliwatts (dBm) or lower. If your signal reads between -100 and -109 dBm, it’s poor. Anything beyond -120 dBm is very poor.

Most wireless providers require you to register a signal booster with them before you use it. (This lets the provider identify a specific booster if it causes interference for users in the area.) Also note FCC regulations on how much consumer signal boosters can amplify a given signal, typically restricting gain between 64 dB and 72 dB. That said, most single-carrier boosters, which amplify only one network, can go up to 100 dB.

Is your new signal booster for your home? Is it for a single room or for your entire house? Do you want to take your cell signal booster with you? Ask these questions before purchasing a device.

In your home, you’ll want a model that provides service based on total coverage area in square feet. If you'll use it more for driving in your car or RV, or while camping or in a rural area, consider a compact model you can use while stationary or on the go.

Omnidirectional antennas pick up signals 360 degrees around, whereas directional antennas must be pointed directly toward a cell phone tower to pick up signals. Omnidirectional antennas can serve multiple providers from all directions. Directional antennas generally provide greater gain from a single provider but must be fine-tuned directionally for the best possible signal connection.

Most home and office cell signal boosters include both an outdoor antenna to capture exterior signals and an indoor antenna to broadcast the amplified signal from room to room. Offices with users of several cell phone carriers should invest in an omnidirectional booster that picks up signals from multiple carrier towers. If you use one carrier and need a big boost, a directional antenna is the way to go.

For most users, the best signal boosters work with all cell phone carriers. Put another way, universal boosters are carrier-agnostic and support all carriers—AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon, U.S. Cellular, Sprint, and more—not just one. You can also check which frequency bands (e.g., 700 MHz, 850 MHz, 1900 MHz, etc.) your booster supports, since different carriers operate on different bands.

As mentioned, the FCC regulates how much any consumer signal booster can amplify a signal: 64 dB and 72 dB for most boosters. That said, “single carrier" boosters that amplify a signal for one network can go up to 100 dB—best for cell phones that need a big boost on a single network.

A cell phone booster signal works like a megaphone for your cellular connection—it captures the weak signal from nearby cell towers using an outside antenna, amplifies it electronically to make it stronger, then broadcasts the boosted signal through an inside antenna so your phone can connect more reliably.

Think of it like having a friend with really good hearing who listens to a distant conversation and repeats it back to you louder and clearer. The booster doesn't create a new signal from nothing; it takes whatever weak signal exists and gives it the power boost it needs to reach your device consistently.

Installing a signal booster is easier than you might think. Whether you're boosting signals at home, the office, or on the road, the key is finding a device that boosts your signal efficiently and reliably wherever you need to connect.

For exterior home and office installations, mount your outdoor antenna on the roof or highest exterior wall, facing your nearest cell tower.

For boosters with an indoor antenna, keep it properly separated from its outdoor counterpart to prevent signal feedback that could shut down your system faster than you can say “Can you hear me now?” Some home setups require running coaxial cable through walls or attics (if one doesn't already exist), so basic DIY skills help, but if you're in doubt, hire a professional to install it.

Vehicle installations are usually even more straightforward. External antennas mount magnetically to your roof or via brackets, while internal antennas sit on dashboards or clip to sun visors. Vehicle systems draw power from your 12V outlet, so consider battery capacity before you buy if you plan to use a booster during repeated, extended off-grid adventures.

Remember, signal boosters amplify existing signals rather than create them from thin air, so check carrier coverage maps and ensure frequency compatibility with your provider. Finally, register your booster with your carrier as required by FCC regulations—it's the law.

#6398. Microplastics can make toxic metals less dangerous, study finds

Scientists discover that sunlight-aged microplastics can transform toxic heavy metals into less harmful forms, revealing surprising new chemistry.

A recent study has found that, under the right conditions, microplastics can detoxify heavy metals.

The research was led by scientists at the Northeast Normal University. They found that polystyrene microplastics, after sitting in sunlight long enough, become chemically active in a specific and surprising way.

The particles start converting hexavalent chromium, a toxic industrial pollutant, into a far less dangerous form.

The researchers emphasize that this discovery does not make plastic pollution beneficial. Instead, it reveals an unexpected way that plastic can influence water chemistry.

It ultimately suggests that the standard picture of microplastics as passive, chemically inert contaminants is incomplete.

Chromium-6 can enter waterways through waste from metal finishing plants.

It dissolves readily in water, travels easily, and is toxic enough to be classified as a hazardous substance in China’s pollutant lists. It was also the contaminant at the center of the Erin Brockovich case in the United States.

In the environment, it exists alongside a much less dangerous cousin, chromium-3. This form tends to bind with other substances and become less mobile in water.

Getting from Cr(VI) to Cr(III) is a detoxification reaction, and natural organic matter in sunlit water already drives it to some degree.

The question is whether microplastics, which are accumulating in aquatic environments faster than anyone is cleaning them up, participate in that chemistry too.

The experiments showed that they can, particularly after prolonged exposure to ultraviolet light.

A fresh polystyrene microplastic is smooth, spherical, and unreactive. Leave it under UV light and the story changes.

The benzene rings that give polystyrene its structure absorb radiation and start breaking down.

Chemical bonds break, creating reactive molecules called free radicals, while oxygen-containing groups accumulate on the surface.

What builds up are environmentally persistent free radicals. These are reactive chemical species that, unusually, don’t vanish in milliseconds the way most radicals do.

They stay stable on the particle surface and remain available for electron transfer reactions.

The team aged polystyrene particles under UV light for 0, 6, 12, 24, 48 and 96 hours, then put them in chromium solutions.

Fresh particles reduced 38 percent of the Cr(VI) under UV irradiation. Ninety-six-hour-aged particles reduced nearly 90 percent.

Without UV light, the reaction barely happened at all.

To understand how the reaction works, the researchers ran parallel experiments under normal air and pure nitrogen.

The nitrogen blocked one of the two pathways, allowing the researchers to examine their contributions separately.

The direct route is the aged particle surface itself. Persistent free radicals transfer electrons straight to Cr(VI) molecules, reducing them on contact.

A chemical analysis confirmed that after the reaction, over 90 percent of the chromium on the particle surface had converted to Cr(III).

Removing oxygen reduced the reaction’s overall efficiency by about 20 percent, suggesting that direct electron transfer from the aged plastic surface plays an important role.

The second pathway involves chemicals released as the plastic breaks down.

Aging microplastics continuously shed dissolved organic matter into the surrounding water – fragments, additives, small aromatic breakdown products.

Under UV irradiation, this microplastic-derived dissolved organic matter generates superoxide radicals, which reduce Cr(VI) through a separate chemical chain.

That indirect pathway accounts for about 78 percent of what the dissolved fraction contributes on its own.

“Our findings suggest that microplastics are not simply passive carriers of pollutants. As they age under light exposure, they can become chemically active participants in environmental processes,” said senior author Jiunian Guan from the Northeast Normal University.

“Understanding these reactions is important for evaluating how plastic pollution may alter the behavior of heavy metals in aquatic ecosystems.”

Because the experiments took place under controlled laboratory conditions, researchers still need to determine whether similar reactions occur in natural waterways.

What happens at the pH, ionic strength and organic matter concentrations found in actual rivers is unknown.

Polystyrene’s aromatic structure makes it unusually susceptible to radical formation. Polyethylene and polypropylene, which are far more abundant in the real world, may behave differently.

Microplastics are already known to carry pollutants, break into even smaller particles, and provide surfaces where microorganisms can grow.

Now, researchers have shown that sunlight can also turn certain microplastics into active participants in chemical reactions that influence the behavior of toxic metals.

Whether these reactions make contaminated waterways safer or introduce additional environmental risks remains uncertain.

For now, the discovery offers another reminder that plastic pollution doesn’t simply sit in the environment.

It continues to change, interact with surrounding chemicals, and influence ecosystems in ways scientists are only beginning to understand.

The study is published in the journal Environmental and Biochemical Processes.

#6396. Birds that are supposed to be completely safe from extinction are actually losing their genetic diversity very quickly

Sixty-two common songbirds lost nearly half their genetic diversity in 50 years, and the most abundant species lost the most.

A songbird you can find on almost any hillside seems like it would be part of an abundant bird species with nothing to worry about in terms of population decline. In the Gaoligong Mountains of southwestern China, the bigger a songbird’s population, the faster it has been losing genetic diversity.

Across all 62 species the researchers compared, genetic diversity fell by an average of 43% to 49% in about 50 years. Every one of those species is listed as Least Concern, the lowest level of extinction risk.

Ri Liu, Feng Dong and their colleagues at the Kunming Institute of Zoology, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, sequenced DNA from birds collected in the 1960s and 1970s. Then they compared it with DNA from birds sampled in the same mountains since 2000.

Only songbirds were sampled, and only in this one range. Birds have lost more genetic diversity than any other major animal group worldwide, so the team expects other animals here to be losing some too.

Genetic diversity is the sum of the small differences in DNA across a population. A species with a lot of it has more ways to adapt when conditions change.

The team measured that diversity two ways. Across a whole population, variation fell by an average of 48.8%, with species ranging from 18.1% to 77.2%.

Within a single bird, variation between the two copies of its genome fell by 42.9%, ranging from 21.8% to 80%. Not one of the 62 species held steady.

By either measure, that’s a far steeper fall than earlier work had suggested. A 2019 analysis of 91 species, which used short repeating stretches of DNA rather than whole genomes, estimated a loss of about 6% over roughly a century. The Gaoligong birds lost more than that every decade.

The losses do match the steepest theoretical forecast. A 2021 projection, built on the 73% drop in monitored vertebrate populations since 1970, predicted that genetic diversity could fall by more than half in 50 years.

The team then asked which traits went with the biggest losses. Several did. The unexpected one was the size of a species’ population worldwide.

In an interview with Earth.com, Dong said the direction of that result surprised the team. “We expected large populations to buffer against genetic erosion,” he said.

“Instead, we found the opposite: the more abundant a species was, the more genetic diversity it lost over the past five decades.”

The reason, in Dong’s account, is that a large population only stays genetically rich because birds keep moving and breeding across one continuous stretch of habitat.

Cut that habitat into pieces and a big population becomes many small, isolated ones, each losing variation on its own. “So the very species we assumed were safest turn out to be experiencing the heaviest genetic erosion,” Dong said.

Population size was a minor factor, though. It accounted for less than a tenth of the variation between species in how much they lost. And the population figures are global estimates, which may not match how many of each bird actually live in these mountains.

When people clear a forest, two things happen to the birds. Some habitat disappears outright, so fewer birds fit in what’s left, and what remains breaks into patches, so birds in one patch stop meeting birds in the next.

If the problem were outright loss, species that produce few young should suffer most. If it were isolation, strong fliers should suffer least, because they can still cross the gaps.

Strong fliers lost the least. The team scored each species’ ability to travel from its wing shape, and the better travelers lost less diversity per generation.

Clutch size, adult survival, and breeding elevation made no measurable difference. The only stronger predictor was the size of a species’ recent population decline.

Forest patches across the Gaoligong range have multiplied more than tenfold in recent decades, and the average patch is now under a tenth of its old size.

The worst breakup is at low to middle elevations, and that matters because rivers and steep terrain already isolate the range. The lowlands are the routes birds use to move between neighboring mountains.

Conservation planning “should treat connectivity – not just population size or protected area coverage – as a core conservation target,” Dong told Earth.com. In practice, he said, that means keeping and rebuilding low-elevation corridors between otherwise isolated populations.

The old birds came from a museum. The Kunming Natural History Museum of Zoology holds specimens collected across the Gaoligong Mountains in the 1960s and 1970s, and the team extracted DNA from them.

The modern DNA came from tissue samples taken between the 2000s and 2020s and stored in a tissue bank for wild species in Kunming.

Each species was represented by four or five birds per era. That’s a small number, and the team cites earlier work showing it is enough to capture how much variation a population holds.

The median collection year was 1973 for the old birds and 2022 for the new ones. For these small birds, 49 years is about 20 generations.

And those museum specimens were collected before forest fragmentation here intensified, so they show what the birds’ genomes looked like beforehand.

On the IUCN Red List, all 62 species are in the lowest-risk category, Least Concern, and Yunnan province’s own red list rates them about the same. The range itself already has formal protection.

The Gaoligong Mountains lie where the eastern Himalayas meet the mountains of Indo-Burma and southwest China, and they are part of a World Heritage site. They hold nearly a tenth of the world’s songbird species on about 0.02% of Earth’s land.

The losses are also larger than the world’s biodiversity agreement treats as tolerable. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in 2022, set a 10% loss of genetic diversity as the limit for a species to keep its ability to evolve. The Gaoligong songbirds are already well past it.

Dong said conservation groups should stop treating “Least Concern” as a synonym for “genetically safe,” and that genetic monitoring should extend to common species rather than stopping at the rare ones.

The study ruled out mutation rate and elevation as explanations for the losses. It can’t say whether past hunting, climate change, or invasive species added to the damage alongside fragmentation.

The oldest birds in the comparison date from the 1960s, and the authors wrote that their figures may still understate the true historical loss.

The bigger open question is whether other animals and plants in the same mountains are losing diversity the way these songbirds are. The team expects they are, to a lesser degree, and hasn’t measured it.

Dong said genomic monitoring should start where the gap between a species’ official status and its actual genetic health is likely to be widest.

That means biodiversity hotspots with rapid recent fragmentation, and common, widespread species that go unmonitored because they aren’t listed as threatened. Low-elevation corridors in mountain hotspots, where connectivity loss is most severe, would be among the priority regions, he said.

Genetic indicators have been proposed for the global biodiversity framework, but they aren’t yet part of routine monitoring. The baseline for that monitoring, Dong said, already exists in museum collections like the one in Kunming.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6394. Scientists discover hidden genetic clues that may help explain autism

Scientists have discovered overlooked DNA sequences that may help explain autism, revealing genetic changes missed by conventional testing.

Scientists have linked hundreds of genetic changes to autism, yet genetic testing can identify a cause in only about 15 percent of cases.

A new study suggests that some of the missing answers may be hiding in overlooked stretches of DNA.

Benjamin Blencowe of the University of Toronto‘s Donnelly Centre co-led the work with Quaid Morris of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. Blencowe also works at King’s College London and the Francis Crick Institute.

The results are computer predictions checked against thousands of family genomes, and there’s no clinical test yet.

A gene isn’t read straight through. Cells copy it into a working message, then cut out some pieces and keep others, so one gene can make slightly different proteins in different tissues.

Some of these retained pieces, called microexons, are only three to 27 DNA letters long. Despite their tiny size, they can influence how proteins function in the brain.

Neurons use microexons much more than other cells do, and the same ones show up across vertebrates. Blencowe’s lab had already found that the brains of autistic people often use them incorrectly.

Mice with only one working copy of the main switch for them show autism-like behavior.

What nobody had was a full list. Most earlier searches used whole brain tissue, which can miss a fragment that only certain kinds of neurons use.

Guillermo Parada, a postdoctoral fellow in Blencowe’s London group and co-lead author, built a tool that scans RNA data, the working copies of genes, for microexon-shaped pieces.

He ran it over more than 100 terabytes of public data. He also included data from single cell nuclei, so a piece that only one kind of neuron uses could still show up.

The scan covered 4,790 human tissue samples and 47,380 single nuclei from the cortex.

It turned up 1,514 human microexons that no catalog had listed, and 292 of them are used differently in nerve cells than elsewhere. A matching search in mice found another 1,115.

Many of the new pieces, more often than known ones, insert a stop signal that makes the cell destroy the message instead of altering a protein. That gives neurons a way to turn a gene down.

The next question was what tells a neuron to keep a microexon included when editing the message for making a protein.

Parada and co-lead author Hannes Bretschneider worked with Morris to train a machine learning model on about 1,800 known neuronal microexons and 91,920 look-alike stretches that cells don’t use.

It reads 300 letters on each side of a fragment and scores how likely a neuron is to use it.

The team then changed every letter in those windows on the computer and recorded how the score changed.

The positions that mattered most matched the DNA that evolution has kept the same across vertebrates.

“What surprised me was that the sequences the model identified as important closely matched those conserved throughout vertebrate evolution,” Parada said.

The model also flagged a short pattern just upstream of some fragments as a signal to leave the piece out. In mouse cells, lowering the protein that binds there, QKI, made those microexons show up more often.

With their model in place, the researchers could investigate how genetic changes found in autistic people might disrupt the way neurons use microexons.

Working with Stephen Scherer and Brett Trost of The Hospital for Sick Children, they applied it to whole genomes from three large collections.

Two of them together held 2,666 pairs of siblings in which one is autistic and the other isn’t.

Rare changes, those seen in under 1 percent of reference genomes, had larger predicted effects than common ones. The same subset of microexons turned up as affected in all three collections.

“Using our model, we were able to show that rare genetic variants generally have the largest predicted effects on the splicing of neuronal microexons,” Blencowe said.

The results showed that autistic siblings carried more predicted genetic disruptions than their non-autistic siblings.

The three collections together held 25,132 people from 7,391 families, and in that group 72 of the genetic variants were tied to an autism diagnosis.

They turned up in 2.5 percent of the autistic participants and in none of their unaffected siblings.

Although these variants appeared in only a small percentage of autistic participants, they offered potential explanations for cases in which previous genetic testing had found no cause.

Of the people carrying those variants, 82 percent had no previously identified genetic cause.

The affected genes cluster at synapses, the junctions where neurons pass signals, and several were already on autism gene lists.

Nearly all of this is prediction. The team tested a few of the flagged variants in lab-grown human neurons, and those did change how the microexon was used.

A flagged variant isn’t a diagnosis, either. More than a third of everyone in the study, autistic or not, carries at least one change predicted to affect a microexon. The ones tied to autism were the rare few with large predicted effects.

The model learned its rules from known microexons, and only 59 of the new human pieces followed them, so others may obey a code it doesn’t yet have.

And only 12 percent of the new brain-specific human pieces have a clear match in mice, which limits what mouse experiments can check.

How a disrupted microexon changes the proteins a neuron builds is the open question.

“In terms of future work, it will be important to understand how disrupted microexons affect interactions between proteins that are important for nervous system development and function,” Blencowe said.

The team has published its prediction for every variant it scored, so other groups can run new genomes against it.

That includes genomes from people with schizophrenia or epilepsy, where microexons may also be disrupted.

The findings suggest that some of autism’s missing genetic explanations may lie not within genes themselves, but in overlooked DNA sequences that help determine how those genes are used.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6393. Why people with ADHD struggle to stop watching short videos

In a survey of 302 adults, people with ADHD more often lost track of time while using short-video apps, and felt regret and guilt afterward.

A short-video feed never ends. Swipe past one clip on TikTok, Instagram Reels or YouTube Shorts and the next one is already playing, chosen to match what you’ve watched before.

In a survey of 302 adults, people with ADHD said those picks matched what they’d opened the app for just as well as they did for people without ADHD.

What set them apart was everything else: more trouble stopping, more lost time, and more regret once the app was closed.

The problem, the researchers wrote, isn’t bad recommendations. It’s a feed with no built-in place to stop.

The work comes from Elisabeth Lex and colleagues at Graz University of Technology (TU Graz) in Austria.

The research was released as a preprint ahead of ASSETS 2026, a computing accessibility conference held in Portugal in late October.

Earlier studies have tied heavy social media use and short-video habits to attention problems, but few have put numbers on how these feeds affect people who have ADHD.

The team recruited 302 adults through Prolific, a website that pays people to take part in research.

Of those 150 participants, 65 reported a formal ADHD diagnosis, while 85 identified themselves as having ADHD. This allowed the researchers to compare responses between the two groups

Splitting the ADHD group this way let the team check whether a formal diagnosis changed the answers. Participants ranged from young adults to people in their 70s.

YouTube Shorts was the most popular app, ahead of Instagram Reels and TikTok.

Each person rated 15 statements about their own viewing on a scale of 1 to 7, such as “Once I start watching short-content videos, I find it difficult to stop.”

The whole questionnaire took a typical participant under five minutes.

Participants with ADHD agreed more strongly that they often watched longer than they meant to and found it hard to stop once they’d started.

Asked how hard it was to pull away from the feed, the typical person with ADHD answered 5 on the 7-point scale. The typical person without it answered 3.

People with ADHD were also more likely to say they lost track of time while watching. Researchers call that time blindness – losing the sense of how many minutes have gone by.

Lex’s team named the pattern the engagement trap.

“By the ‘engagement trap,’ we mean a situation in which (video) recommendations are, on the one hand, perceived as highly relevant, but, on the other hand, people find it very difficult to tear themselves away from the screen and consciously control their own behavior,” Lex said.

The differences continued after people closed the app. Participants with ADHD more often said they regretted the time they’d spent, felt it hadn’t been valuable, and had put off things they meant to do.

They also reported lower mood after a long session than before it, and more guilt.

The biggest gap of all was frustration with their own difficulty disengaging. Even so, the differences were modest – small to medium by standard statistical yardsticks.

The team found no statistically reliable difference between people whose ADHD had been diagnosed by a doctor and people who identified it themselves.

“Our findings show that recommender systems optimized for engagement place a disproportionate emotional and behavioral burden on people with ADHD,” Lex explained.

Earlier research from a team led by Thomas Mildner found that people with ADHD were better than others at spotting manipulative design on social media.

Lex’s team wrote that a short-video feed works differently. There’s no deceptive visual element to spot, only a stream with no end.

With nothing to tell a viewer when to quit, stopping depends on self-control and a sense of how much time has passed. Those are the same abilities ADHD tends to strain, the authors wrote.

This may contribute to hyperfocus, a state of intense concentration that can make it difficult to disengage without an outside cue.

The survey also described seven possible app features, none of them built yet. They ranged from a gentle usage reminder to a mode that turns off the feed entirely.

None of them would require people to step away from the apps altogether.

People in every group liked the ideas, giving a typical rating of 5 on the 7-point scale. A fixed number of videos per session and an enforced break after a set time scored highest.

“To redress this imbalance, we must move away from optimization focused purely on engagement towards human-centered design practices that explicitly support users’ sense of time and their intentional control,” Lex said.

Everyone reported on their own habits from memory, and no one’s screen time was measured.

People with ADHD may also experience more guilt about scrolling, potentially influencing how negatively they describe their viewing habits.

The researchers did not independently verify ADHD diagnoses or ask about medication use, which may have influenced participants’ ability to stop watching.

The authors want future studies to compare how long people think they watched with how long they really did, using recorded watch time.

Whether a fixed video limit or a forced break actually cuts viewing time will take working versions of those features to find out.

The full study has not been published in a journal yet and is available as a preprint on arXiv.

In his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats," biologist James O'Hanlon surveys deception across the animal kingdom and asks whether any of it adds up to lying.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most trickery in nature happens without a shred of awareness behind it. An orchid mantis (Hymenopus coronatus) doesn't know it looks like a flower, and a moth with eyespots on its wings has no concept of the predator it's startling. These are adaptations shaped by natural selection over countless generations, not conscious choices. But a smaller set of animal behaviors look like something else entirely — deliberate tactical, and aimed at manipulating another individual's beliefs, the same way human lies do.

Figuring out which is which turns out to be one of the trickiest questions in animal behavior research, James O'Hanlon, zoologist and science communicator, told Live Science.

In this excerpt from his new book, "Liars, Cheats and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature" (Columbia University Press, 2026), O'Hanlon explores camouflage, mimicry and misdirection throughout the natural world, building toward the book's central question: Can animals tell lies?

In it, O'Hanlon examines one of the strongest candidates for an animal that deliberately lies: the fork-tailed drongo (Dicrurus adsimilis), a small African bird whose ever-changing repertoire of false alarm calls has made it a favorite subject for scientists studying tactical deception.

James O'Hanlon interview: 'You start painting pictures of squirrels twirling their mustaches': A biologist on whether animals can lie

This is a Live Science Pro article that we're publishing for free to all our readers. If you'd like more exclusive book excerpts, as well as news analysis, scientist interviews and in-depth features, please consider subscribing.

Fork-tailed drongos are remarkable vocal mimics and can do an uncanny impression of a meerkat alarm call. The meerkats respond to it just as they would one of their own and scamper to safety. Meanwhile the drongo flies in once more to steal the meerkats' abandoned food.

They don't stop there; drongos mimic a whole range of other animals' signals, mimicking various avian neighbors like the caped glossy starling or the pied babbler. Those ever-watchful meerkats fall for the ruse once more, leaving their meals behind. Researchers have identified over fifty unique deceptive vocalizations in the drongo's arsenal.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

By constantly rotating their "cry-wolf" tactics, these birds ensure their victims don't grow wise to the deception, allowing the theft to continue unabated. Yet, their cleverness isn't reserved solely for exploited meerkats.

This remarkable talent for mimicry extends to other creatures as well. Pied babblers and sociable weavers, who both forage in groups upon the earth, frequently find themselves bamboozled into fleeing their food by these false warnings. Had the legendary boy who cried wolf possessed such adaptive ingenuity, he might have successfully maintained his trickery.

It would, however, have resulted in a peculiar fable with an entirely different, perhaps darker, moral lesson.

It's early days in our understanding of whether animals can tell lies. Social group-living animals are likely candidates for finding animal tricksters in the wild, and we have only scratched the surface of what kinds of trickery goes on in these societies. Time will tell whether similar forms of deception are happening in the subsonic songs of whales and dolphins, the chemical mists of ants and termites, or the barks and howls of wild dogs.

Meerkats are tricked by fork-tailed drongos mimicking the alarm calls, so the birds can swoop in and steal their food.

Despite the growing list of evidence, scientists are still hesitant to conclude definitively that animals can intentionally deceive another, in a similar way to humans. This might have more to do with the professional conduct of scientists than it has to do with the reality of what goes on in animal societies.

Firstly, one of the most important rules in studying animal behaviour is to not anthropomorphise animals. In other words, don't project human-like qualities or emotions onto other species. Scientists must be completely objective and not assume that other animals think, behave or make decisions for the same reasons we do.

Since lying has always been perceived as a human behaviour, scientists are incredibly hesitant to conclude that it could be happening in other animals.

The second reason is that scientists are trained to never definitively conclude anything. There is an idea in science that you can disprove things, but never really prove things. This is why you will find scientific writing littered with phrases like "the evidence suggests," "it's probable that," or — my personal favourite — "the most parsimonious explanation is," and so on and so forth.

A professional scientist will often give a direct "No" answer but rarely a direct "Yes." It's like squeezing blood from a stone. But this is a good thing. What often sounds like indecisiveness or a lack of certainty is actually just good professional practice. It's part of a scientist's job description — to consider all possible explanations for the observations they have made and examine every possibility on its own merits.

Then the conclusions that are drawn come down to which of these possibilities is most likely. In a universe of infinite possibilities and scales of enquiry, it would take an impossible amount of overwhelming data for scientists to exclude all possibilities but one.

To understand how these creatures swindle their way to survival, Liars, Cheats, and Copycats reveals the science behind camouflage, mimicry, and masquerade. Taking readers on a journey from tropical rainforests to the darkness of deep ocean trenches, James O’Hanlon explores how animals and plants use deception to avoid predators, lure in prey, and even reproduce.

James O’Hanlon is the author of "Liars, Cheats, and Copycats: Trickery and Deception in Nature." He is an award-winning science communicator. He has published more than thirty academic papers, and his popular science writing has appeared in ABC News (Australia), Australian Geographic, The Conversation, and Biosphere Magazine. He is the author of "Eight-Legged Wonders: The Surprising Lives of Spiders" (2024).

#6391. 8 Theories About What Actually Happened to Amelia Earhart, Ranked From Most to Least Plausible

Was she eaten by crabs? Abducted by aliens? Here’s how the claims all stack up.

The story is famous, but the details are worth retelling. On July 2, 1937, Amelia Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan departed Lae, New Guinea, bound for Howland Island, where the Coast Guard cutter Itasca was waiting. Her final confirmed radio transmission at 8:43 a.m. local time said: “We are on the line 157 337... We are running on line north and south.”

Then she vanished. The U.S. launched the largest air-sea search in history to that point—two weeks covering an area roughly the size of Texas—and found absolutely nothing. Ever since, theories about what really happened to Earhart and Noonan have abounded. Here are the leading ones, ranked from the most plausible to the most outlandish.

⚬ What the theory is: Unable to locate Howland Island, Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan ran out of fuel and ditched in the Pacific Ocean, where the aircraft sank in waters up to 18,000 feet deep.

⚬ Where it originated: This was the U.S. Navy’s official conclusion in 1937 and remains the U.S. government’s documented stance.

⚬ How likely it is to be true: Highly likely. This is the consensus view of most aviation historians, as it requires no extraordinary assumptions and directly aligns with Earhart's final radio transmissions reporting she was “running low” on fuel. But frankly it’s a bit depressing, so let’s consider some alternatives!

⚬ What the theory is: Earhart missed Howland and landed on the reef of Gardner Island (now Nikumaroro), surviving briefly as a castaway. A grisly sub-theory suggests giant coconut crabs scavenged her remains, explaining why only 13 bones were found in 1940.

⚬ Where it originated: Developed since the late 1980s by The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery (TIGHAR).

⚬ How likely it is to be true: The most plausible alternative to an ocean crash. Despite dozens of post-loss radio signals, recovered 1930s artifacts, and multi-decade scientific investigations, no definitive evidence has successfully linked Earhart to the island. That includes a recent trip to Nikumaroro by Purdue University researchers, which came up empty-handed. But the whole eaten-by-crabs thing remains a tantalizing, if not entirely appetizing, possibility.

⚬ What the theory is: Realizing she had insufficient fuel for the journey, Earhart reversed course toward New Britain or New Guinea and ultimately crashed near Buka Island.

⚬ Where it originated: Advanced by researcher William Snavely, who spent 13 years investigating a coral-encrusted aircraft wreck reported by local divers in the area.

⚬ How likely it is to be true: Unlikely. This theory directly conflicts with the U.S. Coast Guard cutter Itasca’s radio logs, which showed Earhart's signals growing stronger as she approached Howland, proving she was not flying away from it.

⚬ What the theory is: Earhart landed or crashed in the Japanese-controlled Marshall Islands, was taken into custody, and transported to Saipan where she died in prison or was executed as a spy.

⚬ Where it originated: Popularized by Fred Goerner’s 1966 bestseller The Search for Amelia Earhart, relying on eyewitness testimony from island residents who recalled an American female pilot.

⚬ How likely it is to be true: Highly improbable. Despite strong popular belief and sheer volume of islander testimony, there is zero physical evidence, key photographs have been thoroughly debunked, and the islands sit roughly 800 miles off course. But it makes for great reading!

⚬ What the theory is: President Franklin D. Roosevelt secretly tasked Earhart with overflying Japanese-held islands to photograph military installations, resulting in her being shot down or forced to land.

⚬ Where it originated: The theory stems largely from the 1943 Hollywood film Flight for Freedom, featuring a thinly veiled Earhart character who deliberately disappears to allow a Navy search.

⚬ How likely it is to be true: Extremely unlikely. Historians have found no reliable documentary evidence for such a mission, her plane lacked camera equipment, and the route makes no sense for reconnaissance. But it makes for an exciting movie script!

⚬ What the theory is: Following her capture by Japanese forces, Earhart was forced to broadcast wartime propaganda over the radio as one of the infamous “Tokyo Rose” voices during World War II.

⚬ Where it originated: This rumor circulated widely among the American public during the war.

⚬ How likely it is to be true: False. Earhart’s husband, George Putnam, listened to the broadcasts at the Army’s request in 1944 and unequivocally stated none of the voices belonged to his wife. The “Tokyo Rose” persona was later shown to be multiple women.

⚬ What the theory is: Earhart survived Japanese captivity, was secretly returned to the U.S. after the war, and lived out her life under the assumed identity of New Jersey resident Irene Craigmile Bolam.

⚬ Where it originated: Proposed by Joseph Gervais and published in Joe Klaas’s 1970 book Amelia Earhart Lives.

⚬ How likely it is to be true: Thoroughly debunked. The real Irene Bolam called the claim a “poorly documented hoax” and sued the publisher. Forensic comparisons and verified documentation proved Bolam had a life history that predated 1937. So if you thought you’d never have to fight claims that you’re really a vanished celebrity living incognito, think again!

⚬ What the theory is: Extraterrestrials intervened during the flight over the Pacific Ocean, abducting Earhart, Noonan, or their Lockheed Electra aircraft and taking them off-world.

⚬ Where it originated: A fringe claim that emerged within popular culture as a sci-fi explanation for the total and sudden disappearance of the aircraft.

⚬ How likely it is to be true: Zero probability. This is a purely speculative fringe explanation lacking any credible evidence, serving only as a testament to the enduring public fascination with her vanishing. That is, unless there really is something out there.
