#6357. What is the physical size of a 1-billion-solar-mass black hole compared to the Sun?

When a supermassive black hole is measured as 1 billion solar masses, what would be its actual physical size relative to the size of our Sun?

The size of a black hole is generally taken to be the size of its event horizon. The event horizon is a mathematical boundary around the black hole that marks the “point of no return” — anything that crosses this boundary is trapped inside and becomes part of the black hole forever.

The size of the event horizon can be calculated from Einstein’s field equations, and it depends on (1) the mass of the black hole, and (2) how fast the black hole is spinning. For a nonspinning black hole that has the same mass as our Sun, the radius of the event horizon (also called the Schwarzschild radius) would be about 1.8 miles (3 kilometers). A nonspinning supermassive black hole that is a billion times more massive than our Sun would have an event horizon radius that is a billion times larger, or 1.8 billion miles (3 billion km). This is 4,300 times larger than the radius of the Sun, or about the typical distance between the Sun and Uranus. However, if a billion-solar-mass black hole is spinning very rapidly, then the radius of the event horizon would shrink by about 30% (to around 1.3 billion miles or 2 billion km) because of the way the black hole distorts and drags space around it.

It is important to note, however, that while the event horizon is considered the outer boundary of the black hole, the mass inside the black hole has likely collapsed into a much smaller size under its own self-gravity, often referred to as a singularity. But we don’t actually know if the mass has collapsed into an infinitely small point in space, and, unfortunately, we can’t really say more than that because our understanding of physics breaks down under the extreme conditions that are present inside a black hole. So we use the event horizon as a convenient reference for the black hole’s size, because everything inside the event horizon is part of the black hole.

Misty BentzProfessor of Physics and Astronomy, Georgia State University, Atlanta

#6356. The 7 Best Car Battery Chargers for Roadside Emergencies

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Maintain your car battery—or bring a dead one back to life.

The 12-volt battery is one of the least complex components in modern vehicles but one of the most crucial. If it’s not in good condition, the engine won’t start, and none of the vehicle’s fancy systems will work. Car batteries have a limited lifecycle and deteriorate with time. This can happen for many reasons, including extended inactivity, extreme temperatures, or even something as simple as accidentally leaving the lights on after you turn off the engine.

That’s why it’s handy to have an external car battery charger so your engine is ready to go when you need it. A charger can also help extend your battery's life, for instance, in a vehicle you don't drive often—a weekend getaway camper or an old classic cruiser. Some chargers also have a jumpstart feature, eliminating the need for jumper cables (and the inconvenience of a required second vehicle).

You might be surprised to hear that electric vehicles use the same 12-volt car batteries as their internal combustion counterparts. Regardless, modern vehicles rely on this ancillary battery to power lights and onboard electronics when the ignition is off. Here, we’ve compiled the best chargers for cars and motorcycles, including everything from a solar-powered charger to a model that can revive several vehicles at once.

Noco’s Genius 10, the brand’s flagship single-vehicle charger, offers many cool features, including the ability to “force charge” a battery so dead it won't generate any voltage when you hook it up. (Most modern chargers won’t do this.) Maintenance and “desulfation” modes extend your battery's useful life while keeping it ready to go.

Unlike smaller, less ambitious chargers, the Genius 10 charges a vehicle battery to full power in the shortest safe time. It can even charge the new generation of lithium-ion car batteries, like the complex, expensive units fitted to many newer BMWs.

All the basic features are here at a very low price, including protection from reverse clamping and a “float mode” for fully charged batteries.

The included set of bolt-on leads lets you quickly connect and disconnect the charger. Operation couldn’t be simpler: a green light shows the Motopower is on, and a red light indicates charging status. With 1.5 amps of power, it charges slightly faster than most competitors in the low-price bracket.

Think of this 15-amp charger as a miniature version of the shop-grade Schumacher. It’s also the form and function that will be most familiar to older or experienced users. The included clamps are high-quality and should fit most cars. Just clamp on, plug in, and select one of three modes.

The 15-amp rapid charge is slightly more than the competition can manage, and a carrying handle makes it easy to place where you want it.

This charger is compact, light, easy to operate, and almost bombproof. It delivers a 3-amp charge, then automatically switches to float mode to maintain proper voltage and prevent overcharging.

A two-color LED indicates charging status, and if the battery voltage drops below a certain level, it resumes full charging output in adaptive mode. It’s compatible with most automotive batteries and can switch between 6- and 12-volt batteries with the push of a button. Its battery clamps are spark-proof, and the Battery Tender 3-Amp will automatically detect reverse polarity. It comes with a 5-year warranty and lifetime customer service.

Dealerships and race shops that used to scatter CTEK individual chargers throughout the building are now switching to the multi-vehicle Noco 2x4 model. It weighs just under 8 pounds, mounts to a wall, and can handle four vehicles at the same time, each in a different mode.

Want to float charge one car, recondition another, and bring two other dead batteries back to life in force-charge mode? Not a problem.

If you own a vehicle you only drive occasionally, an under-the-hood charger saves the hassle of disconnecting it from the battery and storing it each time you want to go for a cruise.

The compact Schumacher SC1300 mounts under the hood to supply up to 1.5 amps, while a built-in microprocessor automatically adjusts the charging rate to maintain an ideal charge state. Float mode delivers a small current when needed.

Reverse hook-up protection prevents the charger from working if the battery clamps are installed in reverse polarity, and the Schumacher automatically detects 6-volt or 12-volt batteries.

If an electrical outlet isn’t available or if you just want to use the sun to keep your battery topped off, the Sun Energize solar-powered charger is a reliable option. It trickle-charges a variety of automotive batteries, as well as some lithium batteries.

A built-in charge controller prevents overcharging; charging stops when a battery is topped off and automatically resumes when it drains.

An LED indicator shows charge and battery conditions. The 20.1 x 13.8 x 0.7-inch solar panel is larger than the other chargers here, but it’s built to handle high winds and heavy loads and is IP65 waterproof.

We tested some external battery chargers under varying weather conditions, while others were chosen based on feedback from car enthusiast friends. The selections represent a wide variety of chargers with different capabilities to match a broad range of use cases. We have years of experience traveling the country with these chargers and know their performance very well.

If you store a vehicle for long periods, you’ll want a charger to keep the battery from fully dying and turning into a paperweight. (It’s also nice to know it will start without jumper cables.) But a battery charger can make a difference in plenty of other situations.

If you regularly experience below-freezing temperatures at night, a charger with a maintenance function can significantly extend your battery's life. If you rarely drive more than a few miles at a time, a charger can prevent your battery from discharging too far—leaving you with a no-start condition. Last but not least, older vehicles often struggle to recharge slightly depleted batteries on the move, so starting the day with a fully charged battery can also extend the life of your alternator and charging system.

Charging power is traditionally measured in amps. Think of amps as the amount of juice that can be put back into the battery at any given time; for example, a 10-amp charger puts twice as much charge into the battery as a 5-amp one. A quick stroll through a listing of battery chargers can be confounding, though. Some have 40 amps, and some have 0.75 amps, and yet they do the same thing. In reality, the difference is easy to understand. The more power a charger has, the more quickly it can bring a dead battery back to life. The tradeoff is cost, size, and weight.

If you’re charging a small motorcycle battery or maintaining a good-condition battery in a cherished collector car, then a 0.75-amp charger will do just fine. If you’re worried that your pickup won’t start in the winter, 2 to 10 amps is a better bet. Any capability above that is mostly for mechanics who need to quickly charge or recondition batteries in the shop.

Every charger here can “maintain” a charged battery, keeping it from slowly discharging between uses. Most chargers can also bring a depleted battery back up to full power. A few chargers offer specialized modes like “desulfation,” which helps a battery regain its chemical balance through carefully timed charge-and-discharge cycles. A “quick charge” can very rapidly (but safely) prepare a battery for use. A few battery chargers also offer a “jump start mode” that can start a car or motorcycle with a dead battery, but this is rare, and most of the time you’ll need a separate jump starter for that task.

Most chargers in this roundup are designed for conventional lead-acid (flooded cell) or Absorbent Glass Mat (AGM) batteries, which you’ll find in newer vehicles. If you have a vehicle with a lithium-ion battery, like some new BMWs, or a customized car with ultra-compact batteries from manufacturers like Braille, you’ll need a charger with that capability—different battery chemistries require specific charging protocols.

If you are dealing with a cramped garage, or travel between storage spaces throughout the seasons, consider a “wall wart” or direct-mount charger. The former keeps all the charging mechanisms in a large plug that some people might compare to model-train transformer plugs. The latter bolts into your car and plugs directly into the wall.

Not anymore. Today's smart chargers, like the ones in our article, won't overcharge a battery or give it more than it can handle. And choosing a more powerful charger won't shorten your battery's lifespan; quite the opposite, in fact!

It's usually as simple as removing the bolt from both battery clamps, slipping the thin copper loops between the bolt and washer, and reinstalling. Then you can coil the quick-disconnect cord in a convenient place, like inside a motorcycle fairing or under a car hood. The cables can melt when exposed to serious heat, so don't let them touch an exhaust pipe.

Yes, if the batteries are in reasonably decent condition. Any charger rated at 2 Amps or more should be able to rotate between multiple vehicles. If you have more than three or four, consider buying multiple chargers.

Live Science spoke with psychiatrist Anand Kumar about the next edition of the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual Of Mental Disorders", which will include biological factors like genetics in studying and diagnosing psychiatric conditions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For decades, psychiatrists and other mental health professionals have used the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders," or DSM, to diagnose patients with conditions such as major depression, anorexia and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). To reach diagnoses, mental health practitioners identify symptoms via interview, case history, questionnaire, or observation to paint a clinical picture.

But for the next version of this "psychiatry bible", the DSM-6, scientists are planning to add other factors into the diagnostic criteria.

Dr. Anand Kumar, a psychiatrist who served for two years on the DSM Strategy Committee, says one of the most important potential changes is the introduction of biological factors into the diagnostic framework. While Kumar, the head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois Chicago, no longer serves on the committee, he was influential in discussions about how biology could be incorporated into the DSM-6. Some of these biological factors include data from genome-wide association studies of hundreds or thousands of genes that each increase the risk of a mental disorder by a tiny amount. Other biological factors include signs of inflammation or immune-system dysfunction that may show up in blood tests or brain scans.

Live Science spoke to Kumar about how this update to the DSM could change the way mental disorders are understood and potentially help improve treatment.

Dr. Kumar is the Lizzie Gilman Professor and Head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois at Chicago. Dr. Kumar's research focuses on late-life depression and mental disorders of the elderly, including Alzheimer's disease. He has served as Treasurer, Program Committee Chair, and President of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry (2004-2005). Dr. Kumar is Associate Editor of the American Journal for Geriatric Psychiatry and has served as reviewer for numerous NIH review committees.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: How is the DSM-6 going to be different from the DSM-5?

Anand Kumar: Up to this point, the distinctions between the different major groups — who has clinical depression, or what we call major depression; who has an eating disorder; who has PTSD, etc. — have been based exclusively on clinical grounds: You meet certain criteria, and you fall into this category. If you meet some other criteria, you fall into another category.

An attempt that's being made now, one of the major attempts for the next DSM, is to introduce biological factors into the manual.

The idea is not new. It's been discussed in the past, but it was difficult to get a consensus on what goes in and what should not go in. That's still going to be tricky, but at least there's a broad acknowledgement that the time is ready to start introducing biology into the DSM.

It's very likely that, at the end of it, there will be meaningful changes in a positive kind of way. It's not going to make everyone happy. There are going to be gaps, but the idea is to incrementally improve this and make it more modern as we go along.

KHC: What sort of biological markers have you seen that we can actually correlate with these disorders?

AK: What the committee is doing is taking a more nuanced approach. Outside the realm of Alzheimer's disease, which I'll get into in a minute, there are no clear-cut diagnostic biomarkers — meaning no blood tests or brain scans that you can look at and say, "This person has a diagnosis of depression," or "This person has PTSD," or "This person has schizophrenia."

The committee talked about how, in addition to biological biomarkers, there's a concept of biological factors. What I mean by that is biological pathways and mechanisms that have a role in the development of a particular disorder, but the findings have not crystallized into a laboratory test.

For example, immunology — the study of the body's response to a variety of stresses, including infections and others — has been shown to be impactful in about 30% of cases of major depression. Yet there is no single biological laboratory test that is currently available that can be used [to diagnose immune-mediated depression] in clinical practice. So these come under the category of what we call biological factors.

In the Alzheimer's disease field there are clear-cut biomarkers. There are now blood tests for proteins called tau and amyloid that have been approved by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] as biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease. Meaning, if you have a clinical picture and a mental-status exam consistent with intellectual decline, you must have a positive biomarker test to be categorized as having definitive Alzheimer's disease.

And that's new. Ten or 15 years back, there were brain scans, and if you did a lumbar puncture, you could find these proteins in the spinal fluid. But those are invasive. Now you actually have a blood test.

A neuron, in blue, is surrounded by a plaque of amyloid-beta protein, in yellow, which causes the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease. Tests can be used to detect biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease.

But that degree of precision, for lack of a better term, is not available in the other branches of psychiatry. Nonetheless, there are clues that other pathways and mechanisms are involved.

I mentioned immunology as one. Another big elephant in the room is genetics.

Most people think of genetics as an abnormal gene or a mutation — meaning a gene switches or changes and confers increased risk — as one mutation causing one disease. That's how most people in the general public think about mutations: They cause disease.

But when you get into complex diseases like heart disease and diabetes, there are multiple genes involved. And diseases may or may not be caused by a gene. Abnormal genes may or may not cause the disease, but they increase risk.

With mental disorders, the situation becomes immensely more complicated. It's not just a few genes here and there. There are hundreds of genes, each increasing the risk for depression, schizophrenia and anxiety disorders by a small amount.

So while there is no single genetic test that can now be used, large numbers of genes have consistently been shown — and many of the recent studies are strong — to be associated with certain disorders. But because there's no single gene or small group of genes, we cannot walk away from the science. Complexity doesn't mean we throw our hands up and say, "Well, it's all too much."

It may seem overwhelming, but genetic profiles are better understood today than they were 20 years ago. So that's something else this committee is thinking about and I think should take into account going forward: to somehow incorporate that into the diagnostic categories.

KHC: Do you think there's any sort of risk with adding those biological factors into the DSM?

AK: I don't think so, because if you think about genetics, it's not going to be introduced as a biological test.

Most folks know that mental disorders, like other medical disorders, run in families. And genetics is the most plausible explanation for that. What this does, I hope, is introduce a degree of more comprehensive description of these disorders. So when a busy clinician looks at it, it confirms what they already suspected: There's a family history here, and family history means genetics.

It's complex, many genes are involved, and it produces a better characterization of this. The diagnosis is still going to remain clinical, but this provides a biological context, very much like, say, diabetes or heart disease.

Genes and environment cause a variety of medical disorders. With heart disease, there's no one gene. When cardiologists develop a risk profile for heart disease, it includes genes, other physiological factors such as BMI, which is the weight-height ratio, diet and a variety of environmental factors.

That degree of classification is missing today in mental health and psychiatry. We hope this is a first step in correcting, if you will, those conceptions about what causes these disorders.

KHC: How would you end up using this in a psychiatrist's office to guide treatment?

AK: I can give you one possible example. I'm reaching a bit.

There's a term commonly used in clinical psychiatry and psychology called comorbidity. What it means is that people who are diagnosed with depression also have anxiety, or people who are diagnosed with an anxiety disorder also have substance abuse or alcoholism in general.

That is not coincidental. It's not something that we just somehow find. A lot of these disorders share genes.

For example, about 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with a major mood disorder also have an anxiety disorder. And you flip that around: About 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with an anxiety disorder — it could be generalized anxiety disorder, what we call PTSD, or a phobia — also have a mood disorder.

Patients with anxiety may also be diagnosed with a mood disorder.

I think when clinicians classify them together, not as the same disorder but as sharing a lot of psychological as well as genetic risk, clinicians should be on the lookout for both. A patient with a mood disorder, for example, could either now or at some later point develop an anxiety disorder. Or someone with an anxiety disorder is at risk for substance abuse.

So treatments need to be tailored a little more broadly. I'm hoping that'll be something clinicians think about when they talk to patients and their families.

KHC: What do you think is the most unique aspect, from your perspective, of this upcoming DSM-6?

AK: My bias is the biology. I say this because a lot of the other things, the cultural factors, etc., are largely appreciated, and they'll be better characterized. Some things like cognitive changes, such as working memory and attention [tests], are not unique to any given disorder.

Biology will be qualitatively new when introduced into the DSM, and I hope it's done well. I hope that they do it appropriately, and I think they will [do it] correctly.

It's not going to be perfect, but it's going to be a first step. I think introducing the idea that genetics, immunology and other factors are very important in the causation of mental disorders, and explain some of the phenomena that we previously could not find an explanation for, is — I hate to use the word "leapfrog" — but that's kind of what it is.

It moves the field conceptually forward, and not as a slow, steady, gradual increase. For the DSM, it would be an important step forward.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

#6354. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column.

Monday, November 2The Moon slides 1.1° south of Mars at 9 A.M. EST, then passes 0.5° south of Jupiter at 6 P.M. EST. Some parts of the world will see these planets disappear behind the Moon, although this is not visible from North America. Instead, we’ll focus on the trio’s appearance before this in the early-morning sky, where they dominate in the hours before sunrise.

By 5 A.M. local time, western Leo is more than 50° high in the southeast. The Moon lies just to Mars’ upper right, roughly 1.5° southwest of the Red Planet’s position and 6.3° west-northwest of Jupiter.

This view offers a great opportunity to see just how far the Moon travels through our sky in a day. By tomorrow morning at the same time, Luna will have moved some 14° to the east, passing close to Regulus and standing southeast of the star in the early-morning sky at the same time.

Sunrise: 6:30 A.M.Sunset: 4:56 P.M.Moonrise: —Moonset: 1:41 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (36%)

Tuesday, November 3The Moon now passes 0.8° south of the bright star Regulus in Leo at 4 A.M. EST. Some regions of the world will see our satellite pass in front of Regulus in an occultation, but again, the event is not visible from North America.

The pair rises together shortly after midnight on the 2nd. By 5 A.M. local time on the 3rd, the Moon-star pair is nearly 50° high in the southeast. The waning Moon has shrunk from roughly 43% lit yesterday morning to 33% lit today. It is just under a week from New phase, which occurs on the 9th.

Sunrise: 6:31 A.M.Sunset: 4:55 P.M.Moonrise: 12:34 A.M.Moonset: 2:07 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (26%)

Wednesday, November 4Venus sits 2° south of Virgo’s brightest star, Spica, in the early-morning sky. The pair is joined by a lovely crescent Moon just over 20% lit, high above them in Leo.

Sunrise: 6:32 A.M.Sunset: 4:54 P.M.Moonrise: 1:44 A.M.Moonset: 2:30 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (17%)

Sunrise: 6:34 A.M.Sunset: 4:53 P.M.Moonrise: 2:50 A.M.Moonset: 2:53 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (10%)

Sunrise: 6:35 A.M.Sunset: 4:52 P.M.Moonrise: 3:56 A.M.Moonset: 3:16 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (5%)

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

#6353. Newborn survival improves when families receive financial support

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Rx Kids, a cash transfer program, boosted infants’ health in Flint, Michigan

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield announces Rx Kids' Detroit debut in 2025. The program began in Flint, Mich., in 2024. “We know how to deliver this support efficiently and with dignity," pediatrician and Rx Kids director Mona Hanna told Science News.

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.

“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.

Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

#6351. South Korea eyes rocket debut and China lines up four launches

On Monday, Nov. 2, Rocket Lab launched The Sea God Surveys on an Electron rocket from its Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula at 11:41 a.m. EST. Aboard was a QPS-SAR satellite for private Japanese company iQPS It marked Electron’s 10th flight for iQPS. The company is building out a fleet of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites with the goal of handing customers worldwide radar views in close to real time.

On Monday, Nov. 2, CAS Space — the commercial launch company founded by the Chinese Academy of Sciences — is targeting 7:10 p.m. EST for a Kinetica 2 launch from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been disclosed, but the only prior Kinetica 2 launch carried a batch of SpaceSail satellites. SpaceSail, also known as Qianfan or “Thousand Sails,” is a Chinese broadband megaconstellation designed to beam internet service from low Earth orbit (LEO).

On Wednesday, Nov. 4, SpaceX will launch the classified USSF-432 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California at 8:28 p.m. EST. After stage separation, the Falcon 9 first stage will aim for a landing on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You, stationed in the Pacific Ocean.

On Wednesday, Nov. 4, South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development (ADD) may attempt a demonstration flight of its Mir rocket from Jeju Island, off the country’s southern coast. That date comes from Next Spaceflight’s tracking; South Korean officials have said only that the launch will happen before the end of the year. ADD, the military research arm of South Korea’s defense ministry, has been developing the solid-fueled rocket since 2021. The military plans to use it to launch small military reconnaissance satellites into orbit. The demo was originally set for June 30 but slipped over safety concerns.

On Thursday, Nov. 5, China’s state-owned launch provider, the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), has two launches scheduled, according to Next Spaceflight. First, a Long March 2C is slated to lift off from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center in southwestern China at 11:00 a.m. EST with an undisclosed payload. Then at 4:15 p.m. EST, a Long March 12 will launch from the Wenchang Space Launch Site on Hainan Island, also with an undisclosed payload.

On Friday, Nov. 6, Chinese commercial company Galactic Energy will launch a Ceres 2 rocket from Jiuquan at 6:35 p.m. EST, according to tracking from Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been disclosed. This will be the second test flight for the Ceres 2 after the rocket suffered a first-stage failure and fell short of orbit on its first flight in January.

On Tuesday, Oct. 27, SpaceX launched Starlink Group 15-16 from Vandenberg at 3:25 a.m. EDT, with the booster landing on Of Course I Still Love You.

On Friday, Oct. 30, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) launched the NVS-03 navigation satellite, also known as IRNSS-1L, aboard a GSLV Mk II rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota. The satellite joins NavIC, India’s regional satellite navigation system — the country’s homegrown counterpart to GPS.

SpaceX followed early Saturday, Oct. 31, with Starlink Group 15-18, lifting off from Vandenberg at 12:04 a.m. EDT. Its booster also touched down on Of Course I Still Love You.

No earlier than Friday, Nov. 13, United Launch Alliance (ULA) is targeting the launch of Amazon Leo (LV-01) on a Vulcan rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The flight will loft a batch of satellites for Amazon Leo, Amazon’s broadband constellation formerly known as Project Kuiper.

No earlier than Saturday, Nov. 14, Rocket Lab plans to fly The Mountain God Rises from Māhia — Electron’s 100th launch. The milestone flight goes to a familiar customer: another QPS-SAR radar satellite for iQPS, bound for a low Earth orbit.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

Satellite radar and underground electrical scans have revealed a 2,600-year-old structure at Buto, one of ancient Egypt's most sacred cities. The real surprise wasn't the walls — but what was underneath them.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Egyptian researchers have found a hidden 2,600-year-old structure the size of a football field after using satellites to peer below the ground. But what they found beneath the structure may be just as remarkable as the building itself.

The site they examined is known as Buto (modern-day Tell el-Fara'in), a sprawling mound of layered history in the northwestern Nile Delta. To the ancient Egyptians, it was the sacred home of Wadjet, the cobra goddess of Lower Egypt, and one of the most religiously important cities in the pharaonic landscape.

Archaeologists have excavated its upper layers for decades, finding remains from the rule of the Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty (305 to 30 B.C.) and Roman era (30 B.C. to A.D. 395). But the deeper, older layers at the site — including a mound called Kom C, sitting below groundwater level in waterlogged delta clay — had stayed stubbornly out of reach. Kom C itself rises above the surface as a visible mound, but earlier excavations had reached only the Ptolemaic and Roman layers before hitting the water table.

Now, researchers have turned to noninvasive tools, including satellite imagery, to delve into the mysterious subterranean layers.

First, they turned to the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellite, which can produce radar images by beaming down microwave pulses from orbit and then measuring how they reflect back; the returning signals can reveal subtle differences in surface moisture, elevation and reflectivity that can hint at buried structures beneath the ground. After looking at these radar images, the team spotted a large oval-shaped anomaly buried beneath Kom C that was 420 feet long and 203 feet wide (128 by 62 meters).

The geological profile of Tell el-Fara'in (ancient Buto) and the surrounding Nile Delta, showing the layered sequence of river sands and flood-plain clays from the last ice age and the settlement mound above.

To learn more without disturbing the site, the team ran 15 parallel lines of electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) across an area of roughly 58,100 square feet (5,400 square meters). This technique reveals the underground landscape by passing electrical currents through the earth, measuring how they travel and creating a map that archaeologists can read.

The picture that came back was layered. Between the surface and 10 feet (3 m) down, the team found scattered Ptolemaic and Roman debris, including displaced mudbricks, pottery shards and broken limestone, which point to centuries of continued occupation and rebuilding on the site. Later residents dismantled older structures for reuse and left a scatter of displaced material behind.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Using pure sand as a stabilizing cushion was a brilliant, deliberate tactic — the ancient builders profoundly understood their environment.

Deeper still, between 10 and 20 feet (3 and 6 m), the researchers found a large mudbrick structure from the 26th dynasty (688 to 525 B.C.), also known as the Saite period. They were able to date this discovery based on its layer, the unique shape of the mudbricks and other artifacts such as pottery, which the team dated by style and their archaeological layer, with carbon-14 dating applied to associated organic material. The large structure may be a tomb, a house for priests or a religious shrine, the team wrote in the study, published in March in the journal Acta Geophysica.

And below that, at 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) underground, the researchers unexpectedly found a thick, clean layer of sand.

That sand is the discovery within the discovery, the team wrote in the study.

The Nile Delta's clay is notoriously treacherous to build on. It absorbs moisture and swells, and then contracts and shifts as it dries — posing a slow-motion threat to anything heavy sitting on top of it. The Saite builders, it seems, knew this. Before laying the foundations to their structure, they packed a cushion of clean sand beneath it. This sand would have spread the building's weight, let groundwater drain through, and stopped the clay from creeping. It is the same logic behind modern load-distributing foundations — applied here more than two and a half millennia ago.

A 2D electrical resistivity scan aligned with a partially exposed mudbrick wall — the colored subsurface anomaly matches the location of the visible structure above ground.

"By combining satellite radar with deep ERT profiles, we didn't just map the walls of this massive Saite-era structure — we were also able to analyze the subsurface layers," study co-author author Abdelaziz Elfadaly, an associate research professor at Egypt's National Authority for Remote Sensing and Space Sciences, told Live Science. "The detection of a significant, clean sand foundation layer beneath the mudbrick walls explains how these heavy structures survived the high water table and shifting clayey soil of Buto."

The sand layer, in effect, acts as a barrier; it stops groundwater from wicking upward into the mudbrick, which would soften and dissolve it. The sand also lets water drain sideways instead of pooling against the foundation, according to Elfadaly.

A 3-by-3 foot (10 by 10 m) excavation trench that was around 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) deep confirmed the presence of thick mudbrick walls resting on that sand layer, and nearby, a spread of objects that hint at the site's sacred function. According to Elfadaly, these finds included ushabti and shawabti figurines — small servant statues typically placed in tombs to serve the deceased in the afterlife — and a limestone altar whose carved channels bore dried residues consistent with animal blood, pointing to offering rituals performed at the site. The study also noted a rarer find: a faience baboon figurine, the kind associated with Thoth, the god of wisdom.

Image credit: Abouarab et al.,Acta Geophysica (2026); CC BY 4.0

Layout of the ERT (electrical resistivity tomography) survey at Kom C. The blue lines mark one first set of profiles, and the red lines mark the second. Insets show the electrodes and cables deployed in the field, and a large mudbrick wall dating to the Late Roman period.

Image credit: Abouarab et al.,Acta Geophysica (2026); CC BY 4.0

A selection of artifacts recovered from the excavated square at Kom C, including small figurines and worked stone fragments from the Saite-era structure.

The Saite period was a moment of cultural revival. After generations of Assyrian and Libyan domination, Egyptian pharaohs retook the throne and poured resources into restoring Egypt's religious landscape, particularly in the Nile Delta, which had been their power base. Buto, with its deep ties to Lower Egyptian identity, was a natural focus. The Saite kings ruled from the nearby delta city of Sais, so restoring Buto reinforced their roots and their claim to the throne.

"A monumental building of this scale underscores the Saite pharaohs' intense commitment to glorifying the Delta region," Hussein Bassir, director of the Antiquities Museum at a cultural research center known as Bibliotheca Alexandrina who wasn't involved with the study, told Live Science in a WhatsApp message. "Using pure sand as a stabilizing cushion was a brilliant, deliberate tactic — the ancient builders profoundly understood their environment."

The team is planning a return visit, this time using wider-spaced electrical resistivity surveys to reach deeper layers, along with specialists who study ancient plants and also understand how geological features changed over time, which may help reconstruct what the landscape around Buto looked like when these walls were first laid.

Abouarab, M. a. R., Elfadaly, A., Elbehery, W., Wafa, O., Aboalkassim, I., Younes, A., Hiekl, A. M. A., Saada, S. A., Wilson, P., & Ibrahim, A. (2026). Multi-scale detection of buried archaeological elements across different occupation phases: an integrated approach using radar satellite imagery and electric resistivity tomography at Buto, northwestern Nile Delta of Egypt. Acta Geophysica, 74(2). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11600-026-01809-4

#6349. Can a Power Station Cut Down Your Electric Bill? Yes, Based on Your Rates and Setup.

Time-of-use mode found in some power stations utilizes an integrated battery backup to reduce the time your appliances spend on the grid when rates are highest.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Can a power station help me save money on my electric bill? I reviewed enough units to know the opportunity is there if the station has a time-of-use mode (TOU, for short). Stations with this feature utilize integrated battery backups to reduce time spent on the grid when rates are highest. That sounds pretty cool, but I’ve often wondered just how much money it can actually save.

I discovered it depends on a number of factors. For your best chance to save the most money, you need to live in an area where variable electric rates are available. You also need to primarily use portable power for a whole-home backup system or on appliances that are always running, like a refrigerator, to get the most out of TOU mode. That’s because the cost of electricity is typically lowest in a variable-rate system when demand is at its lowest, during the middle of the night, for example.

Below is everything I’ve learned about setting up TOU mode on a portable power station and how to find out how much money this feature can save you over time.

Power stations with TOU mode tend to be large or designed for home backup, such as whole-home battery-based systems or models designed to back up one or two appliances, like refrigerators. But some smaller portable power stations offer this mode. Jackery’s HomePower series, including the 1000 Plus v2, for example, offers this mode within its mobile app.

If you’re someone who primarily uses portable power for camping trips and other activities, it’s worth noting that TOU mode may not be very useful to you. To effectively switch back and forth between peak and non-peak hours, the station must be consistently connected to grid power and the devices you want to run from it. It makes more sense to plan a TOU-based setup with a more dedicated type of power station, or a portable one that you don’t plan to move around very often.

First, you need to know if variable rates are available in your region and how they operate. Electrical utilities are not regulated at the federal level in the U.S., so this varies from state to state. Utilities in states that regulate their electric utilities may offer variable rates (sometimes called time-variable pricing), while states that deregulate may have variable-rate options through the various energy providers.

For example, in my home state of Pennsylvania, the primary electric company offers only flat rates. However, Pennsylvania is a deregulated market, so if I opt for a different energy provider, I can select one that offers variable rates. Some states, like Texas, even offer times of the day when rates are free.

In most cases, variable-rate programs require you to sign up in some form or another to activate these rates, so call your local provider to get the details of what is available to you.

Once you have that worked out, setting up your station is fairly straightforward. Choose the device or devices you wish to run partially during the day from battery power and connect them to the power station. Plug the power station into an outlet in the house. From there, everything is set in your power station’s app by selecting the TOU working mode, which can usually be found in the advanced settings.

The app then prompts you to enter the high-rate (peak) hours and the low-rate hours, along with the price for each rate (dollars per kilowatt-hour). This helps the app calculate savings over time, so you don’t have to. Once that is set up, the battery automatically powers your devices during peak hours and returns to the grid during low-rate hours. It also uses the low-rate hours to recharge the battery from the grid, or you can opt to recharge it from a portable solar panel.

If only flat rates are available to you, you could still use TOU mode and choose a set of hours each day to run on battery power; there just won’t be the advantage of opting for cheaper rate times.

The potential for saving money isn’t as simple to figure out. While the apps can generally track savings over time, variable rates can fluctuate (e.g., some utilities change them every few months), so unless you are keeping up with the fluctuation and adjusting the app accordingly, those numbers can be off.

The amount of actual savings is also tricky to predict. Much of it depends on how many devices in your home you plan to run using this mode and how low the rate is during off-peak hours. The latter will have the most effect, and the savings will be harder to realize if you’re only powering one or a few things.

For example, if you’re using Bluetti’s FridgePower to power only a refrigerator in TOU mode, that appliance typically only draws 300 watts on average, so the actual savings by running it from the grid only during off-peak hours might only equate to a few dollars per month, maybe even less. Then again, if you’re powering a lot of stuff in TOU mode using a large-capacity whole-home system, the savings will likely be more significant.

Something else to keep in mind is that the most expensive devices to run in your home are usually the higher-voltage systems such as heating/ventilation/air-conditioning (HVAC) and high-voltage appliances such as ovens and electric dryers. These need to be paired with stations that can handle 220/240-volt output (only the larger ones can) and need a significant amount of battery capacity to operate over several hours. This requires a large system with at least one or two additional batteries (if not more), which can cost several thousand dollars. The cost of chasing the savings enabled by the TOU mode could likely take a few years to actually be recouped.

While the money-saving potential can be a bit hard to estimate or feel significant, especially in the short term, this feature will shave something off your monthly bill, so it’s definitely worth looking into, especially if you have a large system that powers several always-on devices.

It might not be a reason to buy a power station for home backup, but it’s certainly a good feature to have at your disposal. It may not be a huge help, but there’s no real downside either.

David is a Reviews Editor for Hearst’s Enthusiast Group, contributing to Popular Mechanics, Runner’s World, Bicycling, Best Products, and Biography. He has over 25 years of experience writing about and reviewing consumer electronics, kitchen appliances, DIY products, outdoor gear, and more. He also spent years covering the ever-changing world of online retail. To relax, he loves experimenting with new recipes, tweaking his smart home setup, and spending time outdoors on his bike or camping.

#6348. A $150 Device Can Give You an ‘Ultrasonic Brain Massage’—And Possibly Treat Alzheimer’s, Doctor Suggests

He wants to call it “The Tubulator 5000.”

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

A clinical anesthesiologist known for putting forth one of the most controversial theories of human consciousness believes that putting a $150 object the size of a hairdryer against your head for a short period each day could one day stop or reverse dementia, including Alzheimer’s disease. Stuart Hameroff, MD, says a budget brain zapper that treats the whole brain with unfocused, low-intensity ultrasound could reverse the disruption of tiny structures in the brain, called microtubules, which provide the structure for the brain’s neurons. As the system collapses, memories and cognition are lost.

There are tens of thousands of microtubules in every neuron. The most prevalent protein in them is called tau. When scientists examined the neuronal cells of people who have died from Alzheimer’s, they discovered piles of tau that appear to have fallen off the microtubules, stuck together in clumps called Neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs), or tau tangles. When tau shows up in a patient’s bloodstream or urine, you know the disease is worsening.

In Alzheimer’s disease, Hameroff says, scientists don’t know whether the microtubules disintegrate and release the tau or whether the tau falls off due to a malfunction that weakens the bond. Regardless, he says, there’s a clear correlation between this breakup and Alzheimer’s. Hameroff’s research shows that a cheap ultrasound device that targets the whole brain could encourage microtubules to hold themselves together and re-form if they’ve fallen apart.

Hameroff began wondering about the therapeutic effects of ultrasound on the brain and its microtubules while working with quantum mechanics expert Anirban Bandyopadhyay, PhD, who heads the National Institute for Materials Science in Japan. Bandyopadhyay previously discovered that numerous bands of electromagnetic and mechanical energy exist within microtubules, at multiple frequencies and time signatures.

Plus, existing studies have demonstrated that applying low-intensity transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) to the hippocampus of Alzheimer’s patients daily for three minutes increased metabolic activity in the hippocampus and improved cognition in two areas within just 26 days, all without adverse effects.

It’s important, Hameroff notes, that ultrasound therapy can either be focused or unfocused and used at three different intensity levels. For instance, we now know that at high intensities, focused ultrasound heats tissue and can destroy lesions, like tumors. At medium intensities into the brain, ultrasound opens the blood-brain barrier; at low intensities, it generally causes pleasant mood enhancement.

Hameroff’s approach, called Transcranial UltraSound (TUS) would benefit Alzheimer’s patients, he says, because memory is stored all over the brain, with emotions, skills, spatial awareness, and sensory recall located in various parts of the cortex—not just in one place, like the hippocampus. Better yet, an ultrasound machine at a hospital costs around $70,000, Hameroff says, but therapeutic TUS wouldn’t require imaging, and there are expendable, safe, and inexpensive devices available.

Sterling Cooley, an ultrasound engineering friend of Hameroff’s, had been conducting informal clinical testing with a particular device he found safe and reliable, the “USPro 2000.” (Hameroff kept his distance, given that he has a medical license to protect.) Hameroff spoke with The Institute of Noetic Sciences (IONS), an American non-profit parapsychological research institute, and they offered to use their Institutional Review Board to validate Cooley’s results. IONS instituted a pilot study in which participants “self-administer the ultrasound stimulation at home over several weeks while tracking changes in cognition, mood, and quality of life.”

The IONS Institutional Review Board insisted that if patients wanted to enroll in the study, they had to have their doctor’s permission. That slowed things down, Hameroff says. “We have to be careful what we say,” Hameroff says. “We’re not treating Alzheimer’s. We’re treating mental memory problems. And we call it brain massage, ultrasonic brain massage. Which sounds a little bit better.”

Not only could the therapy benefit Alzheimer’s patients, it could also help prove Hameroff’s theory that microtubules are where not only memories—but human consciousness itself—lives in human the brain. He is hoping for more funding to advance this treatment effort.

“My dream, I guess, is with approval and consent of course, to go to the memory care facility near my house, which has gone from one city block to five city blocks since I’ve lived there, and go room to room and give everybody, you know, five minutes of TUS.”

Then, he’d like to modify the machine to use all the microtubule resonant frequencies Bandyopadhyay has discovered. He wants to call it “The Tubulator 5000.”

Susan Lahey contributed reporting to this story.

Chemical signatures found in a Brazilian dinosaur bone may be preserved red blood cells, a new study suggests, but not all experts agree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Red blood cells found in a 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Brazil are the oldest chemical evidence of blood-related material in a dinosaur fossil, a new study claims.

However, not everyone agrees with the research team's conclusions, with some experts saying the shape doesn't match those of reptilian red blood cells.

In the new research, published Monday (Nov. 2) in the journal PNAS, the scientists said they identified microscopic structures resembling red blood cells alongside chemical signatures of heme, the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin.

The new findings come from limb bones of a roughly 10-foot-long (3 meters) dinosaur called Aratasaurus museunacionali. While previous research has detected blood in dinosaur fossils, this is the first study to use chemical processes to identify heme-based signatures in dinosaur bones.

"Traditionally, fossils give us information through bones, teeth, shells and morphology. But exceptionally preserved fossils may contain another archive of information: microscopic structures and molecular traces of the original organism," study co-author Kliti Grice, a professor in the School of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Curtin University in Australia, told Live Science via email. "That opens the possibility of asking questions about ancient biology that skeletal anatomy alone cannot answer."

The team was not originally looking for traces of dinosaur blood, Grice said. Her research was driven by a broader question: How much of an ancient organism's original biology can survive fossilization?

To investigate, Grice and her team studied the limb bones of A. museunacionali, an extinct species of small theropod that lived during the Early Cretaceous period in Brazil. Theropods were a group of mostly meat-eating dinosaurs that walked on two legs. They included famous predators such as Tyrannosaurus rex and Velociraptor.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Using microscopic and chemical analysis on the theropod's limb bones, the researchers found numerous microscopic structures within vascular canals, channels that once carried blood vessels through the bone. Their shape, size and location were consistent with red blood cells, the team said.

"We combined microscopy, mineralogical analyses and molecular geochemistry," Grice said. "Critically, we investigated the chemistry in situ [in the bone itself], so we could relate the chemical signals to the microscopic structures in their physical context within the fossil. That is much stronger than simply extracting molecules from a piece of fossil and assuming where they originated."

The team's chemical analyses detected preserved heme-related compounds associated with these structures, providing more chemical evidence to support the idea that the finding could be traces of dinosaur blood, as heme is the iron-containing, ring-shaped molecule that forms a key part of the molecule hemoglobin in red blood cells.

Grice and the team think the conditions the theropod dinosaur was buried in could have helped preserve the vascular structures and the red blood cells within them. They suggested that the animal was rapidly covered by sediment in a low-oxygen environment containing microbial mats ‪—‬ thin biofilms made of microorganisms. These conditions may have altered the normal process of decomposition, helping to preserve the microscopic structures and associated chemical signatures.

An illustration of a microbial mat covering A. museunacionali's bones after it died.

"The red-blood-cell-like structures were mineralised with hausmannite, a manganese oxide mineral (Mn₃O₄)," Grice said. "We think early mineralisation helped stabilise or replicate microscopic biological structures before they were completely destroyed, while aspects of the associated chemistry also survived in altered form."

The fossil also contained preserved amino acids associated with collagen, the structural protein found in bone.

While blood has been found in dinosaur fossils before, not everyone agrees that these latest findings are truly red blood cells.

"I very much appreciate this team bringing rigor to the study of deep time fossils," said Mary Schweitzer, a molecular paleontologist at North Carolina State University who was not involved in the study but has previously studied soft tissues from the dinosaur age. "I am in agreement that endogenous [produced within the body] molecules can persist over geological time in some form, and that there is much these can teach us. However, I am not convinced that the images they figure are remnant RBCs [red blood cells] for several reasons."

For one, the structures do not convincingly match the expected appearance of red blood cells in nonmammalian animals, Schweitzer said. Unlike mammalian red blood cells, which lose their nuclei during development, those of birds and reptiles retain their nuclei. This typically produces a characteristic nuclear bulge in the shape of the cell.

According to Schweitzer, the latest findings show the microstructures having more of a concave shape with no nuclear bulge. The structures also were smaller than most non-mammalian red blood cells, "so morphological similarity is not met," Schweitzer said.

"I appreciate these authors bringing technological innovations to the study of dinosaur fossils," she said. "I am excited to see that this team and others are moving forward with a molecular approach to ancient fossil remains."

#6346. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

#6345. Your Brain May Be Creating ‘Psychic’ Moments—Meaning Your Subconscious Tunes Into Hidden Cues, a Study Finds

A 1966 mining disaster in Wales is famous for its alleged premonitions. New research suggests what those strange “gut feelings” could mean.

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

On the morning of October 21, 1966, the Welsh mining village of Aberfan was struck by one of Britain’s most harrowing peacetime disasters. After days of heavy rain, a slag heap collapsed off a colliery (a coal mine and its connected equipment) and tore down the hillside, submerging a school beneath a torrent of black sludge; 116 children died.

Warnings had come in more than one form. For years, villagers had raised concerns about the coal waste heaps perched above their homes. But some said the signs were stranger—uncanny, even. The day before the disaster, eight-year-old Paul Davies drew a picture of men digging into a hillside, with the words “The End” scrawled above the figures. That same week, ten-year-old Eryl Mai Jones told her mother she’d dreamt that “something black” had descended over the school.

Both children died the next day in the deluge.

A study by psychologist Olafur S. Palsson, PhD, suggests that so-called anomalous experiences—events that seem to go beyond what conventional science can explain—are not rare, but in fact quite common. Additionally, people who report experiencing premonitions, déjà vu, superstitious intuition, and out-of-body sensations often share distinct psychological attributes.

These “strange-but-true” perceptions correlate strongly with a cognitive trait Palsson terms subconscious connectedness: the degree of interaction between conscious awareness and subconscious thought. The research, published in the peer-reviewed journal Psychology of Consciousness: Theory, Research, and Practice in 2025, found that individuals high in subconscious connectedness were significantly more likely to report frequent anomalous experiences, including:

“Some people have a much closer connection with the non-conscious or subconscious parts of their mind,” said Palsson, professor emeritus at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. “Their conscious and subconscious mind influence each other to an unusually high degree in everyday life.”

Using a newly developed metric called the Thought Impact Scale, Palsson surveyed more than 2,000 adults in the U.S. to assess “interactions between conscious aware thinking and nonconscious mental functions.” Respondents rated how much they agree with statements (on a Likert scale) about their various mental experiences and psychological traits, including automatic thoughts, intuitive insight, emotional resonance, spontaneous mental imagery, as well as the frequency of unusual experiences such as telepathic impressions, precognitive dreams, and uncanny coincidences. A clear pattern emerged: individuals with high subconscious connectedness reported such experiences far more often than those with low scores.

Like extroversion or neuroticism, the trait varies from person to person, but stays relatively stable over time in each person. What changes, Palsson suggests, is how the trait manifests—the ways in which people interpret intuition, memory, or coincidence. For those with stronger subconscious input, the mind may simply register more of what others discard, Palsson suggests.

“Anomalous experiences are something most people have at least occasionally,” says Palsson. “Our studies showed that 84 percent to 86 percent of adults repeatedly have at least one type of such experience. Neuroscientists suggest that the brain’s default mode network—active during daydreaming and introspection—may play a role in generating these impressions. Heightened connectivity between regions of the brain responsible for memory, emotion, and prediction could explain the intensity or vividness of so-called premonitions.”

Might psychic foresight, hunches, or “gut feelings” confer some sort of evolutionary edge? Perhaps these anomalous experiences allow humans to make better sense of subtle patterns, according to Palsson. Or, perhaps premonitions and uncanny experiences point to something more banal: they might be explained by selective recall (remembering accurate predictions while ignoring those that never came true). Consider the confirmation bias and the “availability heuristic”—our tendency to remember emotionally charged events and forget the mundane. Most of our dreams are forgotten; the one that coincides with tragedy becomes unforgettable.

Premonition might be less about glimpsing the future than about perceiving—consciously or not—subtle cues the mind is already processing. And in that sense, the inexplicable becomes part of how we navigate the world, not what’s outside it.

Adrienne Bernhard is a Los Angeles-born, New York-based freelance writer and former assistant to the deputy editor at The New Yorker. She has written for the Financial Times, The Wall Street Journal, the BBC, Smithsonian, The Atlantic, the Boston Review, and New Criterion, among others.
