#6314. Minute Review: American Airlines 737 MAX 8 First Class

American Airlines’ 737 MAX 8 First Class is not going to win awards for innovation, but on a recent flight from Dallas to Burbank, a comfortable seat and a fantastic Texas barbecue dinner made for a very pleasant journey and the subject of this week’s Minute Review.

I’m continuing my series of 60-second flight reviews, and today we’re taking a quick look at American Airlines First Class on the Boeing 737 MAX 8.

There’s nothing particularly revolutionary about the Oasis and seat and many hate it, but at least it’s a standard domestic recliner with more legroom than economy class, power, storage, and individual air vents. For a flight of a few hours, though, it gets the job done just fine. I know some of you think this should not be called “first class” or even “business class” (since it is similar to an international premium economy seat), but AA markets this flight as first class so that’s what I’m calling it.

But the real reason I booked this particular flight was dinner.

I previously wrote about American Airlines’ new Pecan Lodge barbecue platter, which I deliberately routed through Dallas to try. It included smoked beef brisket, sausage, macaroni and cheese, coleslaw, pickles, onions, peppers, and barbecue sauce.

And it was excellent…I’m still salivating over it again today.

The brisket remained tender and juicy despite being reheated onboard, the sausage was flavorful, and even the macaroni and cheese came out wonderfully. This was a genuinely delicious barbecue dinner, not just decent airlines food.

Would I deliberately connect in Dallas again just to eat it?

As always, I welcome your suggestions as to how I can make future videos better, both in terms of content and in terms of professional production.

#6313. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.

#6312. Snag These 11 Fall Travel Deals Before It's Too Late

Are you, like me, craving a Caribbean beach with a cocktail in hand? Or maybe a transatlantic cruise is calling your name? Consider these fall travel deals your excuse to start daydreaming about your next getaway. As we get closer to Thanksgiving, early Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales are starting to crop up, along with hot-off-the-press cruise offers and loads of airfare bargains worth keeping on your radar, including both international and domestic routes.

Now's a great time to start comparing prices, mapping out flexibility on travel dates, and seeing what’s on offer before the holiday shopping frenzy kicks in. As for where to go, the world is your oyster. Fall is an appealing time to book for a reason—especially for those opting for last-minute trips: Many destinations are between peak summer and winter holiday travel, while cruise lines are moving ships between regions, sometimes offering repositioning itineraries that make for memorable longer voyages. After sifting through dozens of sales, here are the very best fall travel deals to work into your next itinerary.

MSC Cruises is no stranger to luxury—nor is it a stranger to deals. Above is the MSC Poesia.

Looking for a value-forward cruise to the Caribbean, Alaska, or Europe? Top-rated cruise line Celebrity Cruises offers a weekly Exciting Deals page with discounts to all of the above, and the line-up is already pretty enticing. For one? Come late November, you can sail one of Celebrity's newest ships to the ABC Islands and take up to $700 off in instant savings, and your second guest can sail for up to 75% off. A new series of these exciting deals will launch on Monday, November 2, 2026, and continue every Monday through the end of the year.

Calling all northeast residents—your next ocean escape just got a little more tempting. Virgin Voyages is offering residents of New York, New Jersey, Massachusetts, and Connecticut up to 15% off eligible cruise fares with its limited-time Northeast Resident Rate (which can net out to over $1,000 in savings). From sailings to Canada and New England to ones in Charleston and Bermuda, the adults-only cruise line has plenty of ways to trade your usual routine for a few days at sea. I’ve sailed from NYC to Bermuda with Virgin myself and can vouch for the fun of swapping city views for ocean breezes. Even better? All-in voyage pricing includes Wi-Fi, dining at more than 20 eateries, genuinely fun entertainment, fitness classes, and nonalcoholic drinks. The resident rate can also be combined with select promotions; just use code NORTHEASTRATE when booking and don't forget to bring proof of residency when checking in.

Act quick on this one, folks: MSC Cruises' holiday sale runs through November 5 and features up to 35% off select sailings, plus children 17 and younger can sail free as third or fourth guests. With trips starting at $156 for four nights, get ready for a value-forward trip of sunbathing across the Bahamas and Ocean Cay, Puerto Rico, or the British Virgin Islands. For more deals far less timely, check out the site's deals page, where MSC constantly updates new offerings, from Voyagers Club perks to last-minute cruise deals.

Stunning views await at the Four Seasons Puerto Rico.

It's no secret that Four Seasons properties are absolute hotel havens in the world of travel. That said, a discount on these gems can never hurt. Through December 31, 2027, you can score a fourth night free when you book three consecutive nights at The Ocean Club in the Bahamas. If Puerto Rico is more your speed, take advantage of the Experience More spending credit of up to $500 when you book a stay of three nights or more at the Four Seasons Resort and Residences Puerto Rico. (I've been to this property and can't recommend it enough.) This promotion is valid for stays through January 4, 2027.

Save even more on your travel plans with Four Seasons promo codes.

The Mindful House at the JW Marriott Costa Elena Resort and Spa in Costa Rica

JW Marriott is entering the all-inclusive space for the first time this fall with the opening of JW Marriott Costa Elena Resort and Spa on Costa Rica’s Guanacaste Coast. Lucky for its first-timers, the property's Be First Experience offers up to 15% off the resort’s all-inclusive rate, plus a $150 spa credit per stay, a complimentary room upgrade, early check-in and late check-out (based on availability), and a signature JW experience for two—with a choice of a private mixology class or guided wellness journey. And it's certainly an opening to look out for: Set along a Blue Star–designated beach and surrounded by tropical dry forest, the 415-room resort will feature Costa Rica’s largest resort poolscape, JW Marriott’s largest on-property garden, 11 restaurants and bars, and a spa and wellness center. Book by the end of November for stays through December 20, and be sure to use promo code S5235.

If you’re planning to finish off 2026 in style, you may want to take advantage of Iberostar last-minute offers across the globe. Once you enter Iberostar promo code LASTMINUTE into the hotel website's discounts field—like magic—you'll save up to 60% on sun-soaked hotels this fall. In Miami, for one, you can save up to 35% on a sun-soaked stay in South Beach. Caribbean travelers can save up to 60% at Iberostar Selection Riviera Cancun, up to 50% at Iberostar Waves Costa Dorada in the Dominican Republic, and up to 45% off at the brand’s top-rated Iberostar Selection Paraíso Maya Suites. Looking for more ways to save? Check out more of Iberostar's limited time offers on its official deals page.

Save even more on your travel plans with Iberostar promo codes.

There's no shortage of things to do in the Big Apple—and a (discounted) tour is a fresh way to experience it, whether you're a tourist or local.

With Hilton’s latest perk, travelers can take 15% off experiences booked through GetYourGuide (including guided tours, excursions, and local activities, oh my!) when staying at participating new or newly renovated Hilton properties in top destinations like New York City, Las Vegas, Miami, and Oahu. Just book your hotel stay by December 31, 2026, for travel through March 31, 2027. Check the website to see if the city of your choice is considered a top destination—even if it’s not, all other participating global destinations still receive a 10% discount.

If you’ve got a sudden urge to get up and go, G Adventures has hundreds of last-minute travel deals with up to 30% off tours departing in the next 60 days. We’re talking discounts off some of their most-loved and top-rated trips, including Northern Thailand: Hilltribes and Villages and chasing Costa Rica: Coastlines and Clouds Forests. If your schedule’s flexible and your passport’s ready, this is the kind of deal you jump on before it disappears.

Nothing screams fall like a good old fashioned road trip

We're in the thick of fall travel, and Hertz is making it easy to hit the road. Book by the end of November to save up to 25% on base rates at participating locations all across Canada and the US for travel through the rest of the year. Whether you’re chasing snow-capped mountains or solitude in a charming small town, this is the perfect excuse to plan a road trip. (Though, do note that the deal is subject to availability, so double check your dates before booking a trip around it.)

Still need to book holiday flights? You're in the right place.

Expedia's November Flight Deals page is making it easy to find discounted flights. If you want a quick getaway before the winter chaos hits, Expedia's Air Hacks data argues that you don't have to book months in advance to score deals: The sweet spot for domestic airfare is actually a tight 15 to 30 days before departure, meaning last-minute planners get an automatic advantage. That said, if you're booking Thanksgiving travel, be sure to secure your seats on Expedia by November 5 to save up to $125. You can also score on international airfare when booking on Expedia, with off-season pricing on flights to destinations like Mérida or Brazil (and you'll get there before the crowds do).

Southwest Airlines has teamed up with MGM Resorts to launch Getaways by Southwest, offering travelers significant savings on flight and hotel packages. Jet-setters looking to explore major domestic destinations can save up to $250 on select five-night domestic packages, while international travelers heading to hot spots like Cancun and Punta Cana can slash up to $500 off select bookings of five nights or more. Whether you are aiming for the bright lights of Las Vegas, the beaches of Hawaii, or a tropical Mexican escape, this partnership bundles your essential travel needs into a single, budget-friendly price.

#6311. Royal Caribbean Out-Earned Hilton’s Whole 2025 In A Quarter

Royal Caribbean earned $1.7 billion in Q3 2026, or $6.45 per share, up from $5.74 a year ago. Revenue climbed 9% to $5.6 billion, and the company raised its full-year adjusted earnings guidance to between $17.85 and $17.95 per share. RCCL Management said bookings are up in the mid-teens since the last call, and 2027 sailings are up in the high teens, booked at record rates.

Net yields (revenue per passenger cruise day) rose only 0.9%, so most of the growth came from more capacity rather than higher spend per guest. That capacity is spread across three brands many travelers don’t realize share a parent. Royal Caribbean International is the big-ship family product, Celebrity Cruises is the premium line, and Silversea is the luxury line. A traveler who would never book Royal might happily book Celebrity, and plenty of Silversea guests have no idea Royal Caribbean owns it. Each serves a distinct market, and all three feed RCCL’s results.

Comparisons are fun, but until I looked at the numbers, I wasn’t aware of just how impressively cruise stacks up against even asset-light industries like modern hotel chains. The four big cruise companies with public data available earned about $8.6 billion in net income on roughly $60.8 billion in revenue. That includes Carnival at $2.8 billion, Royal Caribbean at $4.3 billion, Viking at $1.1 billion and Norwegian at $423 million (a GAAP figure; its adjusted net income was Norwegian at $423 million.05 billion). These four operate on a net margin of about 14%. MSC Cruises, the other giant, belongs to the privately held MSC Group and does not publish comparable results.

Hotels, comparatively, are less profitable for the most part. Marriott earned $2.6 billion, Hilton earned $1.5 billion, and Hyatt lost $52 million. IHG earned $759 million on $5.2 billion of revenue. The four combined for about $4.8 billion, or a little over half of what the four cruise companies made.

Car rental is worse. Avis Budget lost $995 million, including a $518 million impairment on its electric vehicle fleet, and Hertz lost about $747 million, according to the wider-than-expected losses. Together that is a $1.7 billion loss on about $20 billion of revenue. Enterprise Holdings (Enterprise, National, and Alamo) is a private company and does not report results publicly.

Airlines are the only group that earns more than cruising in nominal dollars, and only because of their sheer scale. IATA put 2025 global airline net profit at $45 billion on $1.065 trillion of revenue, a 4.2% margin, and cut its 2026 forecast to $23 billion at 2.0%. Simply, four cruise companies earned about 19% of what every airline in the world made combined, on less than 6% of the revenue.

Hotel companies like Marriott and Hilton are asset-light, so their revenue includes massive amounts of reimbursed costs and franchise fees, and most of the physical buildings are owned by other entities. A fair comparison would use margin on fees, and I would not suggest these numbers are apples-to-apples. Cruise lines own the ships, the fuel bill and the debt, with Royal Caribbean carrying about $22.4 billion of it, so their profit has to cover a much heavier balance sheet even after accelerated (and substantial) depreciation.

Passenger captivity on a ship is unrivaled throughout the travel industry. Travelers pay for the room, the meals, the drinks, the excursions and the Wi-Fi in one transaction, all on a property the cruise line controls. Royal Caribbean says close to half of this year’s guests are repeat customers and about 40% belong to its loyalty program. A hotel chain would love to know exactly how much each guest spends in its properties but they don’t; cruise lines know it down to the cent.

Royal Caribbean’s $1.7 billion, Carnival’s $1.9 billion and Norwegian’s $491 million add up to about $4.1 billion in net income in a single quarter. That roughly matches what Marriott, Hilton and Hyatt earned together in all of 2025. Hilton’s own third quarter net income was $536 million, about a third of Royal Caribbean’s. That’s absolutely incredible, especially when

Two caveats belong here. My sample includes only the hotel companies and cruise lines that publish numbers I could confirm, so MSC and plenty of private hotel owners are missing. The fiscal years also do not line up perfectly, because Carnival’s year ends in November. But it’s also worth noting that Hilton has about 18x the keys that Royal does, owns less of the product itself (and carries fewer costs), and still falls woefully behind Royal.

When I wrote about Royal Caribbean’s $3 billion Sandals deal in September, part of the claim was that Royal knows the customer base well (it does) and that it knows the market well (it does) but understanding the power of capturing the total spend for a client trip is the magic. With this much cash coming off the ships, buying 50% of Sandals, expected to close in early 2027, gives Royal Caribbean a stake in the land-based all-inclusive business. The same logic is why I argued that every big hotel brand wants your all-inclusive money. The cruise industry is not trying to beat hotels at hotels; rather it’s buying the segment of the hotel business that already works like a cruise.

My agency sells both cruises and hotel rooms, and the difference in how the two operators treat the traveler’s wallet is all the difference. Cruise companies have figured out how to capture the whole vacation budget on a floating property they control, and the earnings show it. I expect the gap with hotels to widen next year as 2027 bookings convert at record rates, and I expect more hotel companies to copy the model through all-inclusive resorts and bundled pricing. But I was still shocked that Hilton, which owns very few hotels, and is mostly a marketing arm for a far larger footprint, is dwarfed by a cruise line in a single quarter.

With many of the best credit cards on the market, earning a generous welcome bonus is a quick way to receive a lot of value. These cards from Chase are no exception.

It's important to know, however, that welcome offers often change.

Let's say you're considering adding a new Chase card to your wallet. When is the best time to apply so you can earn the best offer? We have you covered.

Read on to learn more about the welcome offer history across both Chase's cash-back cards and those earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points.

Below are some of the most popular Chase credit cards, along with their highest-ever offers and our recommendations for when to apply.

Note that these are all publicly available offers; some individual, targeted bonuses may be higher than the offers listed here. Additionally, some of these offers may no longer be available.

Also, keep in mind that Chase factors in its 5/24 rule when you apply. Other factors can dictate whether or not you're eligible for a Chase welcome bonus.

Consider your current wallet setup and cross-check with the terms of whichever card you decide to apply for.

The Chase Freedom Flex is a solid no-annual-fee, cash-back option for cardholders who want to maximize rotating quarterly bonus categories (on up to $1,500 in combined spending each quarter; activation is required each quarter).

If you have a card that earns Ultimate Rewards points, the cash back you earn on the Freedom Flex (and any Chase cash-back card, with the exception of the Ink Business Premier, which doesn't combine rewards with any other Chase card) can be turned into Ultimate Rewards points.

Here are the recent offers we have seen on the Freedom Flex.

#6309. Virgin Atlantic Ups The Ante In India, As The World Dials In

This week, Virgin Atlantic celebrates 25 years of flying to India. In Virgin fashion, it’s doing so in style, with a joint announcement among partners Delta Airlines, Air France-KLM, and a new strategic partner IndiGo.

On the sidelines of the IATA Annual General Meeting, basically the UN General Assembly of airlines, the new strategic partnership for India was announced with very interesting nods to the future.

IndiGo carries more passengers in India than anyone else and will connect US and UK/European customers flying Virgin, Delta and Air France KLM onward in India, while also helping fill seats for these European and North American partners, as their own customers head West.

That’s probably a good thing, because with recent service additions, Virgin now flies a million seats a year to India and it sounds like others are piling on more flights too. It’s now one of the largest operators to India.

I’ve been bullish on India as the next great center of the world for a while now. It’s not necessarily that I’m at all intelligent, it’s just based on the fact that India is the world’s largest population. But, when Ed Bastian, Delta’s formidable CEO says it, people tend to listen. Bastian mentioned India being the most important aviation market globally now and signaled a return of direct services for the carrier as well.

Virgin has been a small step ahead, adding service regularly on their Delhi, Mumbai and Bangalore routes. IndiGo chose this alliance over formidable competition and this will certainly be a space to watch as more global airlines and alliances focus on India.

Geo-political activity points to India becoming a new manufacturing super power, in addition to its prolific work in tech, IT and customer service, not to mention blossoming tourism. These kind of globally connected businesses are big business, huge in fact, for corporate contracts and easy onward connectivity to regional sites is essential. The partnership makes sense.

In a somewhat rare and impressive signal of unity and seriousness towards India, Virgin Atlantic made their India crews part of the core Virgin family, rather than as contractors through a third party local company, known in aviation world as a GSA. This means Virgin’s India crews are a part of the full team, with benefits too.

When asked about loyalty implications of the new alliance, Virgin Atlantic CEO, Shai Weiss, noted a mutual passion for using loyalty to enhance guest experience far beyond just the earn and burn of points and miles. For future iterations, they’ve offered the following…

The MoU (memorandum of understanding) also creates a framework for deeper collaboration between the carriers on a bilateral and multilateral basis; contemplates commercial collaboration including network, loyalty, cargo and sales, subject to regulatory approvals; explores areas of non-commercial cooperation including aircraft maintenance, sustainability, training, ground handling; and acknowledges the need to develop advanced collaboration through use of technology to efficiently service joint customers.

IndiGo will provide onward connectivity for Virgin and the other strategic partners to 32 destinations, making it easier than ever to see Udaipur, Jaipur, Mumbai, Kashmir and delights further south in Bangalore and Goa.

I just returned from the lovely Leela Palace in Delhi, as I watched the news happen live.

To me, India is a country of joy. Even people with truly nothing seem to find positivity and it’s generally a way of life here. Hospitality is as warm and steeped in tradition as it comes, too. It’s hot, it’s humid, but it’s an experience unlike any other and that’s something that’s harder to say these days than I’d like.

The food, ugh. I adore. Sure, I’ll take a dosa from the South over a heavy curry from the North most days, but I love both and if you don’t love a good black daahl there’s something wrong with you.

In short, it’s already fairly easy to get to India but it’s about to get a whole lot easier and not just to hub cities too. More seats means more chances to use points, by the way!

#6308. What Happens If Your Passport Expires While You're Abroad?

Most countries don't allow international travelers to enter their territory unless they have at least six months left before their passport expires. That might sound like an unnecessary ask for a week-long vacation, but the rule is in place for good reason.

That's because if you do find yourself in a scenario when your passport expires while you're abroad—say due to an unexpected medical issue or trip delay, for example—you could be facing a major bureaucratic headache.

However, although it might feel like a crisis, having your passport lapse while traveling is not the end of the world. There are procedures that travelers can follow to obtain a renewed document and get their trip back on track. Here’s a look at what happens if your passport expires while you’re abroad.

Many countries do not allow international tourists to visit unless they have a certain amount of validity left on their passport. A common rule of thumb that many nations observe is the six month rule: there must be at least six months before your passport expires in order to enter the country.

In some countries, including many popular destinations in the EU, your passport is required to be valid for an additional three months after your intended departure date. Before you board an international flight, airlines will verify your passport expiration and usually will not let you board the plane if your passport doesn’t meet the validity requirements. It's important to note that some airlines and cruise lines might have their own passport validity policies that differ from the country's official requirements, so be sure to check both.

Sometimes, it’s possible to enter a different country and stay past your passport’s expiration date. If that's the case, the protocol you’ll need to follow is similar to when a passport is lost or stolen abroad.

First, you’ll need to contact the nearest US embassy or consulate for assistance. If you’re not sure where the nearest embassy or consulate might be, you can use the search tool on the State Department’s website. You’ll need to then visit the embassy or consulate location in person in order to have them issue you a new passport. Keep in mind this could mean you need to travel to a different city within the country you’re visiting.

When you arrive, you’ll essentially need to apply for a new passport. That means you’ll need to bring:

“Even if you cannot present all these documents, consular staff will do their best to help you get a new passport quickly,” the State Department’s site says.

US citizens abroad who have urgent travel plans are usually issued an emergency passport, which is valid for up to one year. However, it’s also possible to get a full-validity passport that doesn’t expire for 10 years. It will depend on the specifics of your situation.

Replacement passports are usually issued by the next business day, according to the State Department.

If you’re a US citizen living overseas for an extended period of time, you might qualify for routine passport renewal by mail through the nearest US embassy or consulate. Processing times for renewal by mail are usually about four to six weeks, not including shipping time. Visit the website of the local embassy or consulate in your area and follow their instructions for passport renewal.

#6307. Can Emirates Make Denver Work Without A Smaller Jet?

At Routes World in Frankfurt, Emirates President Tim Clark named Denver International Airport, Detroit and Philadelphia as the next candidates for nonstop Dubai flights in the United States. It would be the first new US station since Miami returned in June 2021; Emirates currently serves 12 US airports. Clark would not say which aircraft would fly the route though that largely depends on the size of the market and distance. Of the three possible destinations, the distances are 7,758 miles to Denver, 7,083 to Detroit and 6,928 to Philadelphia.

Emirates Denver service has been rumored for a while. Former DEN CEO, Phil Washington, said in spring 2025 that the airport’s next new route would “likely be Dubai with Emirates,” while Emirates said it had no official plans. Emirates and United have been codeshare partners since 2023, a tie-up Live And Let’s Fly detailed when the partnership was first announced.

Emirates’ unique fleet gives it an incredible advantage in large markets, but makes smaller market expansion a challenge. According to Emirates’ own fleet figures from late 2025, 235 of its 269 aircraft, or 87%, were A380s and 777-300ERs. Those big birds carry roughly 350 to 500 seats depending on the configuration. Emirates had just 13 A350-900s at that point, and it has no 787 in service even though 35 are on order (though many have speculated they will be converted to 777-X orders assuming it eventually passes certification.)

That informs the decision on every new expansion city. Most airlines test a new market with a smaller jet, run it at three or four weekly flights and grow it if demand holds. A perfect example of that was British Airways growth at Pittsburgh. It started with subsidized service 4x weekly on a Boeing 787-8, but based on its success moved to 5x, then 6x, and now daily service and fluctuates between the 787-8 and 787-9 with some frequencies operating a 787-10 or very occasionally a 777-200. Emirates cannot do that. Its smallest widebody, the A350-900, is only now reaching the US network, entering service to Orlando on November 1 with 298 seats. A 777-300ER to Denver means filling roughly 350 or more seats, on a route 7,758 miles long, departing an airport at about 5,400 feet of elevation. High elevation (hot and high) hurts takeoff performance, and it makes a full-length route even harder especially at a frequency of more than 5x weekly.

The ideal test would be a 787-8 if it had the legs, a smaller airplane at the right size to prove the market and to link Denver to Dubai without staking a big fleet commitment on it. But Emirates has no 787s flying (it may never operate the type depending on the order book swaps I mentioned before), and the reality is that with a 20% reserve range variance, the altitude, an especially in the summer, it can’t make the trip even if they had it.

That means a Denver bet has to be a larger aircraft than ideal if it makes the cut. The other mentioned possible destinations come with their own challenges. Philadelphia has more international service but also a much larger market. It faces flights on Qatar for connecting global service along with a heavy American Airlines slate, British Airways, Lufthansa, and Aer Lingus for Europe/Middle East, and connections to Asia or Africa. Detroit has an even smaller market with more competition from Air France, Royal Jordanian, Turkish, and a heavy Delta tilt.

Denver does not have nonstops to the Middle East or Africa, and Narita is its only Asian destination, flown by United on a 787. DEN served 34 international destinations in 19 countries in 2025. The question is how many people in Denver need to get to Dubai or beyond, and cannot do it more easily another way.

Travelers who can already connect through Frankfurt or Munich on Lufthansa, through Istanbul on Turkish, or through Toronto on Air Canada, and favor Star Alliance, have little reason to switch. Many of the rest are captive to United, either because of status or because of corporate contracts, and United already flies its own long-haul routes to Europe and Tokyo. Emirates is left with a smaller pool of travelers who are not tied to a hub carrier and want to go to India, the Gulf, Africa or the Indian Ocean, along with the premium leisure market that wants Emirates’ product.

What Emirates brings from the other end is a global network. Denver would feed Dubai’s connections to South Asia and Africa, and Emirates has the reach to sell Denver as a gateway to places United cannot. But that seems like a tough challenge. I’m a fan of Denver and have visited several times personally, I grew up in nearby Omaha, my brother lived there for some time – Denver has plenty to offer to the world. But I am trying to imagine the pitch to a family in Singapore, or a upwardly mobile couple in Mumbai. Can Emirates convince locals in the UAE to choose Denver over Switzerland for those who want to hit the slopes? I’m not so sure.

My prediction is that Denver stays a candidate, but not yet a route, until Emirates has a smaller widebody aircraft in meaningful numbers. Then again, some markets where Emirates has been successful would shock readers of this site. Manchester, England had three and sometimes four daily A380s and is not a particularly premium market with even more competition. If Emirates does move forward with Denver, I expect the airline to start with a seasonal schedule, probably timed to the winter ski market, and to treat the first year as a test. Emirates built its network on massive airframes and highly premium configurations, which is great for flooding a market where you can be successful and challenging to experiment. Then again, financial performance for Emirates is less public and pressured than publicly traded companies so maybe it doesn’t matter anyway.

#6306. This Is The Summer To Tick Santorini Off The Bucket List

It’s June, and for perhaps the first time in modern history, Santorini isn’t crowded. Those earthquakes a good few months ago? Not even a flower pot was tipped over, yet incessant clickbait headlines managed to have a lasting impact.

And that’s a shame, because there’s been a lovely tourism revolution brewing there, where local hoteliers are bringing back the kind of experience and hospitality that you want to come back for over and over again.

As someone who goes at least once or twice a year, and will again very shortly, I can only advocate to tick it off the bucket list this summer, because you’ll never find prices, availability or an experience quite like it again for a while.

In the last 20 years, Santorini got totally overrun. Cruise tourism and day trip mania somewhat ruined a once idyllic, low-key fishing island and then Instagram and TikTok lit the match.

But now the TikTok crowd is in Mykonos and Santorini, as unequalled in beauty as ever, is lovely again. Hotels like The Vasilicos and Santorini Sky bring wildly different, delightfully luxurious and hospitality driven experiences to the island.

Beach clubs, yes Santorini’s beaches are underrated, have made a nice little mark on quieter coasts with great effect too. Assyrtiko, the local grape has hit the world stage as a darling of sommeliers in top restaurants and vineyards like Vassaltis offer stunning tasting experiences.

And the food? There’s no Nobu, or Scorpios here, so there are plenty of places to feel the benefit of European pricing, including a personal favorite at Kantouni.

The trouble with Santorini has historically been that many of the best hotels are small, they fill up quickly, and as they do, they charge a fortune. For the best, like the ones mentioned above, it’s still worth it. But this season, all across the board, prices are lower and even if you don’t care about price, many of the best which might typically be sold out for the season have rooms.

As an additional tailwind for travelers, flights between the US and Europe are quieter this summer, which means there’s deals to be had with both points and cash from major markets to Santorini. If you don’t see cheap flights to Santorini, try a major hub and booking an onward ticket separately.

Naturally, precaution is a good thing in life. But fear mongering for the sake of clicks is another beast and I can’t help but be fairly appalled by the many weeks and months of coverage and follow up coverage, reiterating a narrative of fear… despite no damage to anything, anywhere.

If you do bag a great deal this summer and visit one of my very favorite places, and use this great Santorini guide to make the most of your time, you can thank the media.

#6305. Copenhagen is Opening a Stunning New Bathhouse Along Its Harbor This December—And It's Shockingly Affordable

Copenhagen is a swimmer’s city. "The cure for anything is salt water: sweat, tears, or the sea," Danish author Karen Blixen, who lived up the coast from Copenhagen, famously wrote in 1934. Locals and visitors alike have taken her words to heart ever since.

In the early 2000s, floating swimming pools were introduced to the Danish capital's harbor after the city's shipbuilding industry collapsed. These pools turned an unused space into a playground for swimmers, divers, water polo enthusiasts, and boaters, especially on hot summer days. In recent years, cold plunging has also risen in popularity as a way to help with mental and physical health—nowadays, you can expect winter swimming clubs with sauna access along the harbor to have lengthy waiting lists.

The new bathing house was designed by the Japanese architectural firm Kengo Kuma Associates and has been 8 years in the making.

The next time you visit Copenhagen, there's even more reason to pack a swimsuit. The city’s historic waterfront welcomes a long-awaited new addition on Saturday, December 5: a public swimming pool set to become a new landmark along the city's harbor.

Designed by the Japanese architectural firm Kengo Kuma Associates, Kai is the new 62,500 square-foot bathing house that has been eight years in the making. It promises ten pools in total, including an open-air rooftop pool and a heated onsen overlooking Copenhagen Harbor. Delayed due to the pandemic and its knock-on effects, the pool was originally slated to open in 2021 and now joins the list of architecturally distinct buildings lining Copenhagen Harbor, including the modern Opera House and the Royal Danish Playhouse.

This designer swimming experience comes with a surprisingly affordable price tag.

Pools will be spread across the several levels of the minimalist interior, with a 82-foot pool on the ground floor. The building also offers year-round access to the harbor with designated swimming and dipping zones in and around a timber boardwalk. While the harbor itself can get pretty chilly in winter, the outdoor first-floor pools benefit from a sustainable vertical ground-source heat pump system providing year-round heating.

This designer swimming experience comes with a surprisingly affordable price tag for visitors. Tickets are expected to be in line with other local city-run swimming pools—known as "water culture houses"—where entry is typically under 100kr (about $10). Capacity overall is capped at 380 swimmers. The 989 million DKK ($150 million) project was funded by the City of Copenhagen and Nordea Fonden.

Kai will open on Paper Island on December 5, 2026.

Swimmers all over the city are delighted with the news, including Copenhagen’s Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling. “I’m really excited about the opening of the Water Culture House,” she said. “Copenhagen needs more swimming facilities, so it’s incredibly important that we are now getting new pools for adults, as well as paddling pools for children. I hope it will become the city’s new gathering point for water-loving Copenhageners and visitors alike.”

The original idea for a new pool in the heart of the city came directly from Copenhageners. Surveys had pinpointed a desire for a new, central public swimming pool and the location on Paper Island could not be better. Once the site of a beloved food market, the area had stood empty for years, before being redeveloped to play home to restaurants, cafes and hospitality businesses. Directly across the harbor from the central tourist hub of Nyhavn and accessed by pedestrian and cycle bridge, the new pool brings renewed focus to the area, that links the old town with the rapidly gentrifying former military area of Holmen and the former shipbuilding area of Refshaleøen.

Copenhagen's harbor is the heart of the city's year-round swimming culture.

If you are keen to explore Copenhagen’s swimming cultures, the harbor is the place to start—but brace yourself for chilly waters. At Sandkaj in Nordhavn in the north of the city, a demarcated swim zone invites bathers directly into the deep harbor for lane swimming. It’s a great place for a chat with a fellow winter swimmer; changing room access is members-only, but there is space to change on the quay. Warm up with a sauna at Saunanor, where you can also try the distinctive Danish saunagus tradition.

Those seeking a more spa-like experience should head up the coast to Skodsborg Spa Hotel. The former sanatorium offers a superlative spa experience with 16 different bathing experiences, including saunas, steam rooms and access to a private swimming jetty on the beach. Alternative public swimming spots include Valby’s Water Culture House, a chic grey building a world away from typical leisure centre design with a slide, lane swimming and a hot pool area.

#6304. Southwest Denies A 787 Order. Remember Its Bag Promise?

On its October 22nd, 2026 earnings call, CEO, Bob Jordan, shot down reports of a widebody order as having “no credibility.” The reports came from a Reuters exclusive two weeks earlier, citing three unnamed sources who said Southwest was looking at Boeing 787s for a long-haul push, possibly leased or second-hand, with a launch window of roughly three years. At the time, Southwest’s only comment was that it had no news forthcoming on its fleet plans. We have heard this before.

His reasoning was mostly that it would require significant changes in the business model. Operating aircraft with more than 175 seats would send the airline back to its pilots, and the pilot contract likely opens next year. Another 737 variant would be “significantly easier” than a widebody. Long-haul flying would be upside “if we decide to pursue that.” My eyerolls are likely audible at this point.

I know how this goes because I have watched the free bag story (and every other unique characteristic that Southwest would “never” change) play out. In July 2024, Jordan told investors that bags flying free was the number one reason customers choose Southwest, behind only fare and schedule. On September 17, 2024, a Southwest spokesperson told The Points Guy there was “no work currently underway” to change the policy, and Jordan, pressed on the question, would only say never say never, as CBS reported.

Six months later, on March 11, 2025, Southwest ended the policy. The airline set fees of $35 for the first checked bag and $45 for the second on flights booked on or after May 28, 2025. Jordan’s explanation was that bags flying free was not part of the airline’s DNA, and that open seating was not either. What he should have said was that it wasn’t part of Elliott Management’s DNA and they were running the show – at least while they were still heavy investors. Analysts warned at the time that dropping the policy could damage the brand and turn Southwest into just another airline. It most certainly did that, but as reported in recent weeks, it has, in fact, helped the stock price and financials significantly.

But there is no demonstrable difference between Southwest and any of the top 5 US carriers except one, no long haul international service.

The bags went first, and assigned seating arrived on January 27, 2026, with eight boarding groups, four fare tiers and extra-legroom rows on every flight. Basic fares board last. Open seating, which was the other half of the cattle-call charm, was gone. This has all been covered over the last 18 months but it’s important preamble when considering the next logical step for the airline, and the claims it is denying. What remains uniquely Southwest is one fleet type, and a partially point-to-point map and a reputation for friendliness, and the fleet may be next. Jordan said Southwest is not building toward any one thing, but the addition of 11 lounges, a premium credit card, and first class tell a different story.

It’s a sea of sameness (to steal another industry trope.) Delta and United sell the same choices at similar prices, and Southwest sells them with a smaller map and limited international reach. Every concession after the bag fee was an admission that the discount model was not enough on its own, even though I personally believe that it was.

The numbers explain why management keeps moving the goalposts. In the third quarter, revenue per available seat mile jumped a record 21.6%, but capacity fell 0.4% and unit costs excluding fuel rose 3.8%. Capacity for 2026 is up only about 1.2%. That mix tells me growth came from price and fees, not from flying more, but in order to keep up that frothy pace it will have to find new markets to enter.

Domestic markets are mature, and Southwest’s biggest rivals already own the best international partners. Southwest has partnerships with Icelandair, China Airlines, EVA Air and Turkish Airlines, and Jordan said international loyalty partnerships and partner redemption launch next spring (I can’t wait to see what the redemptions look like.) Partners only go so far, though. Will some EVA Air customers book connecting flights on Southwest for its customers, maybe, probably, but that’s not going to move the needle.

Alaska already saw this writing on the wall and made a move. The rest of the premium push doesn’t come close to working if Southwest customers still buy tickets to Rome on another carrier. Chicago Midway can technically accommodate a 787, as can Dallas Love, and at LAX and Baltimore that’s a very easy fit. But all of those markets have real competition from major carriers. Other Southwest hubs like Fort Lauderdale face serious challenges with nearby Miami, Houston Hobby against United at Intercontinental, Denver for both international carriers and United.

But Southwest wanted to assimilate the carrier to every other carrier so it has to compete with every other carrier too. And in that regard, I can’t see a lounge program as aggressive as 11 locations working without it. If the fleet was exclusively Airbus, the international case is easier with longer legs and a JetBlue-like model (though that’s not working out well for them at the moment and they already have premium cards, lounges, and international partners.)

Unless Southwest sees unprecedented growth from what it’s already doing – possible, but not probable – this is the last frontier. So why deny it? Doesn’t that indicate a lack of forward thinking?

I will take the other side of the denial. My prediction is that Southwest announces a widebody order or lease within eighteen months of the pilot contract opening, and that Jordan or his successor will explain it as a natural evolution of the brand. The pattern is set. Every sacred cow gets slain once the numbers demand it, and the statement of the day is always true until the day it is not. Travelers should treat Southwest’s promises the way they treat any airline’s, as information about the current quarter and not a commitment about the next one.

#6303. The Best Islands in the World: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

Trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in New York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best cities in the world as voted by you, our readers.

View all of the the Readers’ Choice Awards winners for 2026 here.

The six islands of the Bazaruto Archipelago—Bazaruto, Benguerra, Magaruque, Santa Carolina, Bangue, and Shell—are a protected conservation area and national park off the eastern coast of Africa. Nicknamed the Pearl of the Indian Ocean, the islands have only seen the arrival of big-name resorts within the past decade, like the impeccable andBeyond Benguerra Island in 2015.

Pro tip: This is one of the few habitats of the endangered manatee-like dugong, which sailors sometimes mistook for mermaids.

Getting there: Fly to Vilanculos on the coast of Mozambique; from there, take a seaplane to your final destination.

Instagram and Pinterest have created renewed interest in this island in the Indian Ocean, thanks to its so-called underwater waterfall—a visually stunning runoff of sand and silt best viewed from above. Roughly 550 miles east of Madagascar, Mauritius may also be home to a lost continent hiding beneath the waves.

Pro tip: Don’t trust the scales on Mauritius: The island has a stronger gravitational field, causing things (and people) to weigh more.

Getting there: The island’s Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam International Airport is your link for flights to other cities in Africa, as well as to major cities in Europe, Asia, and Australia.

With its white coral sand beaches, turquoise waters, and laid-back island vibe, few destinations offer a sense of escapism quite like Zanzibar. Add to that plenty of sunshine and consistently pleasant temperatures, and it’s easy to see its appeal. For the history buffs among us, don't skip historic trade center Stone Town, famous for its meandering lanes, minarets-crowned buildings, and the 19th-century House of Wonders where the Sultan used to live.

Pro tip: Visit the island during the dry season from June to October, when temperatures average out at 77 degrees. This time range also overlaps with the high season for safari, should a two-for-one trip be of interest.

Getting there: To get to Zanzibar, fly directly to Abeid Amani Karume International Airport (ZNZ), or arrive by ferry from Dar es Salaam in Tanzania.

Our readers aren’t the only ones who consider this African nation one of the best islands in the world: Prince William and Kate Middleton and Victoria and David Beckham spent their honeymoons on the North Island of the Seychelles. Yet some stretches of sand are so deserted that parts of the movie Castaway were filmed here. The ultimate draw, however, is the nature—the white beaches here are so beautiful that visiting them borders on a religious experience.

Pro tip: Seychelles is one of the best spots in the Indian Ocean for snorkeling. Head to the islands of La Digue and Félicité for the best variety of sealife.

Getting there: Air France, Air Seychelles, and Turkish Airlines have regular flights that connect to Seychelles International Airport (SEZ), just south of the capital of Victoria.

A chain of 26 atolls and more than 1,000 islands in the Indian Ocean, the Republic of Maldives is one of the most sought-after tropical destinations in the world. It’s dense with villas and overwater bungalows, and the diving is unreal (though, sadly, some of the coral has been threatened by bleaching). Still, there’s a dive for all skill levels at Ari Atoll, where you can swim with rays and, deeper down, reef sharks.

Pro tip: Cheval Blanc Randheli, the number one resort in the Indian Ocean (per this year’s reader survey), has 45 luxe villas—some tucked among the coconut groves, some jutting out directly over the water.

Getting there: Fly into Malé’s international airport and transfer there to the appropriate resort or atoll.

If your idea of the perfect vacation involves three-day beach parties, Koh Pha Ngan is the Thai island for you. Famous for its full-moon parties at the Haad Rin peninsula's Sunrise Beach, this island is for hardcore partygoers and the anything-goes crowd. During peak season, the island can see upwards of 20,000 visitors dancing and cavorting on the white sands under a full moon. If you can't make it at the right time of month, don't worry—there are half-moon and black-moon parties in intervening weeks, too, and there's action every night of the week at the island's beach and cocktail bars.

Pro tip: There are secluded beaches far from the crowds (like local favorite Bottle Beach, arguably one of the best beaches in Thailand), and plenty of spas where you can check yourself in for an afternoon of recovery, from the basic to the deluxe (such as the Ayurvana Spa at Santhiya Resort on Thong Nai Pan Noi Beach in the north of the island).

Getting there: From Koh Samui, take the ferry or a high-speed boat from a nearby pier like Maenam or Bangrak to Thong Sala Pier or Haad Rin Pier.

India's Andaman Islands are chock-full of beaches for thrill seekers looking to snorkel among sea life and peer through shipwrecks, as well as relaxing sandy stretches for more meditative types who prefer their quiet strolls backgrounded by sherbet-hued sunsets alike. Whether you're enjoying Havelock Island's serene Radhanagar Beach or Elephant Beach, whose shores are a veritable water sports arena, these islands provide 365 days of sun, sand, and fun.

Pro tip: Beyond the beaches, hike through the Baratang Limestone Caves' striking natural corridors through one of the most renowned natural wonders of these islands.

Getting there: Direct flights to Port Blair's Veer Savarkar airport fly from Kolkata, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Delhi, and Vizag. Alternatively, travelers may also choose to arrive at Port Blair via ferry from Kolkata or Chennai.

The Phi Phi Islands lie in the cozy cradle between Phuket and the Straits of Malacca off Krabi Province. Each of the six islands—Ko Phi Phi Don, Ko Phi Phi Le, Bamboo Island, Mosquito Island, Bida Nai, and Bida Nok—have their own charms to offer. From silky soft white sand to dramatic limestone cliffs, the beaches found on these islands are among Southeast Asia's finest.

Pro tip: For a feel of local life, stop by Ko Phi Phi Don, the largest and most populated island of the group. If flopping in solace is more your speed, pop over to Ko Phi Phi Le, which lays claim to some of the island's most stunning vistas and coastal stretches.

Getting there: As there are no airports on any of the Phi Phi Islands, visitors will have to arrive via ferry from ports such as Phuket or Krabi.

Phuket is not exactly a hidden gem, but that's because it's such a magical place to vacation, whether you want a busy immersion in city life or a quieter experience. Since it’s the biggest island in Thailand, you’re sure to find something to fit your desired itinerary. In general, though, we recommend skipping the overcrowded west coast and heading to quiet corners like Cape Panwa, where you’ll find luxury accommodations and rum distilleries that feel a bit more removed from the oft-touristed track.

Pro tip: Phuket Town receives far fewer tourists than the western beach areas. Here you can sample colorful spices at markets, visit aging Taoist temples, and snap photos of the colorful street murals.

Getting there: There are more than a dozen daily flights from Bangkok to Phuket, with most trips clocking in at an hour and 20 minutes.

Nowhere on the planet offers the same combination of surfing, spirituality, and sun-kissed pleasure as Bali. The island has sadly become synonymous with the concept of overtourism, but there are still enclaves of hidden cultural treasures and undiscovered gems—if you know where to look. For a primer on everything Insta-famous and off-the-beaten-track, check out our list of the best things to do in Bali.

Pro tip: The shoulder months of April-May and September-October are the best times to visit Bali. Not only can you enjoy lower airfares and hotel rates during the low season, but you’ll also have the rare ability to see the island without its usual crowds.

Getting there: Many airlines fly directly from the United States to Bali, including Singapore Airlines, Delta, and American.

Thailand’s second-largest island is famous for its palm-lined beaches, buzzing nightlife scene, and luxurious hotels. AVANI+ Samui Resort was voted one of the best resorts in Thailand by our readers, though the hillside villas at Four Seasons Resort Koh Samui and floor-to-ceiling bookshelves at The Library are also worth checking out. In terms of beaches, be sure to visit the five-mile Chaweng Beach, lined with coconut trees and surrounded by a natural reef. Just note that the northern end of the beach is party central.

Pro tip: If you are looking for parties, check out Green Mango, one of Koh Samui’s oldest and most famous clubs.

Getting there: You can fly directly from Bangkok to Koh Samui. A more budget-friendly option may be to fly to Surat Thani and then catch a ferry to Koh Samui—it will add a couple of hours to your travel time, but the views are pretty spectacular.

Located off the northwestern coast of Malaysia, the Langkawi archipelago has pristine beaches, coral reefs, and lush mountains—plus that famous Sky Bridge you’ve definitely seen pictures of. This collection of 99 islands is also a foodie wonderland (eating is the unofficial national sport here), with spicy peanut satay skewers and macheted coconuts sold everywhere from high-end hotels to sidewalk stands.

Pro tip: The Ritz-Carlton, Langkawi was voted the best resort in Asia by our readers this year—chalk it up to a world-class spa, multiple beachfront restaurants, and a location in a 10 million-year-old rainforest.

Getting there: Take a one-hour flight from the Malay capital of Kuala Lumpur.

#6302. Wander.com: Best Luxury Take On Airbnb (With Real Value Too?)

At first, the big hotel chains of the world laughed off Airbnb and vacation rentals. No seriously, they did. Now, they all compete in the vacation rental business and act like it was always the plan.

The problem for the traveler, is that almost all of the newer entrants just plug into a massive pipeline of already existing vacation homes and apartments and pop them on their own branded website with no added luxury, differentiation, amenity or expertise in curation.

There’s no huge unlock of new places or highly curated places that you could virtually always stamp as worth recommending to a friend, the way you’d rate an Aman, St. Regis, or Four Seasons hotel.

This is precisely where Wander.com comes in, and it’s by far my favorite luxe vacation rental platform to date. The fact that it’s boutique and limited is what makes it, at least for me. And, the $350 off Wander promo code doesn’t hurt either.

Wander is a vacation rental company which truly hand picks every property that it lists, and has the exclusive listing on. Crucially, each of the vacation properties undergoes a sort of ‘Wander’ transformation to conform with brand standards for wifi, amenity, style and vibe.

It’s above my pay-grade as a blogger on this topic, but it seems like Wander co-invests in the real estate portfolio’s, or partners with owners in a unique way that’s far more integrated than others.

Where are they? Most Wander.com properties are scattered across the US, from the shores of Malibu to the great National Parks in Wyoming and all along the Eastern seaboard too. Hawaii is also a recent addition. New destinations keep popping up!

Each of their properties feels uniquely wonderful and aspirational, and I’d say all have a very modern and contemporary slant to luxury. Grandma’s cabinets are not in any of these homes, but Tesla chargers are. One nice touch: each Wander offers a dedicated workspace with desk, chair, monitors and lightning fast wifi.

I completely respect that all tastes are individual, but the interiors and setups of these homes much more reflect my personal tastes, more minimalist chic, than many less curated vacation rental options.

Most Wander properties are around $1000 a night. Some will be half that, some will be double. On its face, that’s intimidating to many, but when you factor in the number of bedrooms and features it’s really reasonable. Families, or multi-family get togethers… amazing.

All Wander.com properties are at least two bedrooms and many are four, five or even twelve. One is an entire island with multiple residential complexes. For me, I love these sort of getaways for catching up with family or friends, and I never mind when other people are contributing too.

We’ve had some of our best ever vacations renting a house in Palm Springs for weeks or months at a time. Often, family or friends want in too, so we split the house and end up with two bedrooms each for under $500 per night.

We’ve used these bonus rooms and features to socialize or catch up with people in the serenity of the home, not annoyed by service, crowded pools or tight room setups. For a longer stay, I absolutely hate having to rely on a hotel kitchen for every meal. I love to hit a local market and grill with family or guests.

Wander is offering $350 off first bookings, which is a great way to get started. To browse the homes, you simply download the Wander app and start doom scrolling. When you find one you’re ready to book, the process is very self explanatory and easy to share with others.

I’m personally a fan of virtually California vacation and the properties offered on the platform cover everything from Palm Springs to Napa and all in between in stunning form. The $350 off is a solid discount and combined with new property discounts, which are frequent, there is a lot to love. You can browse Wander and download the app here.

If you don’t see the Wander.com discount in your account, you can add promo code AKFVDFD7 once the app is downloaded.

#6301. Lufthansa Now Requires An Account Just To Check In Online

Buying a ticket and having your booking confirmation will no longer be enough to check in online for many Lufthansa Group flights. The airline group is making a Travel ID account mandatory, adding another requirement to a process that should be simple. A major expansion takes effect today, with departures from the United States following later this month.

According to Lufthansa Group’s notice to travel partners, passengers will increasingly need a Travel ID to check in through the websites and apps of Lufthansa, SWISS, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, Air Dolomiti, Edelweiss, and Discover Airlines.

The rollout is phased by departure point:

One person can check in multiple travelers using their own Travel ID. Someone assisting another passenger may also use their own account for personal assistance.

Lufthansa presents Travel ID as a convenient way to use one login across its airlines, with stored information and fewer forms to complete. It also promotes personalized offers.

Certainly, a frequent Lufthansa Group passenger would likely find that useful. If you regularly fly Lufthansa, SWISS, and Austrian, having your information available across those airlines can save the annoying hassle of have to re-enter personal details.

A booking reference and surname have long been enough to retrieve a reservation and begin check-in. If additional identity or travel-document checks are necessary, an airline can request those during that process. I don’t understand why creating an account must now be part of obtaining a boarding pass, other than for the collection of data.

I already have more travel accounts than I care to count, but count me in here…I already have a Lufthansa Travel ID and I welcome this. But for an occasional traveler who simply wants to check in for a flight, it creates another step with another password or login process to manage.

Passengers who do not want an account can still check in at the airport. Good, but it does not make the online requirement particularly customer-friendly. Online check-in lets passengers helps passengers save time. Someone traveling with only a carry-on may have no reason to visit a check-in counter at all.

Why make that person choose between opening an account and completing check-in at the airport?

Airlines have spent years encouraging passengers to handle more tasks themselves. That works best when the digital process is easy to use. Adding an enrollment requirement seems like an odd way to improve it.

The exception for tickets issued by other airlines is also worth highlighting….an odd disincentive to book away, it seems to me.

Lufthansa Group is expanding its mandatory Travel ID requirement for online check-in throughout November, including US departures beginning November 16.

I have no objection to a shared account that makes traveling across the group easier. But passengers should be able to decide whether they want one. Buying a ticket ought to be enough to access the basic tools needed to use it like online check-in…

I wonder if this is at least in part about security. Though for now it does not seem to have made a difference to just accessing the reservation for other purposes, I have long thought that the ability to access a reservation with just the PNR and a last name was pretty insecure. It is one of the reasons I am very cautious about not throwing away used boarding passes, luggage tags (which have PNRs and names on them), and itineraries until a trip is over. I suspect it will be a bit of a headache until people figure out how this works, but having to have some additional layer of security over a reservation might be a good thing in the long run.

DING DING DING! You hit it right on the head, collect data. (that can be sold to other companies) This also makes another place for you to get hacked and have your personal information exposed. I read a story recently about a person in Oregon that requested his personal data from a major grocery chain (not Walmart) and they had 60 pages of personal info, from income to spouses and kids as well as pets. This info was sold to 30 different companies. I am not a fan of another personal info account. This data will become a profit center for airlines akin to Credit Cards.

If you ask me, this could only be about Marketing or Data Security: As long as the full booking will be shared via an unprotected email, the doors are open for fraud. Also within larger companies, you just need to check another calendar and you will see the booking code and the name. This is from my point of view not 2026 data protection. If any access to that booking would require a personal account with 2 factor authentification, this step would boost data security.
