#6299. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

Good thing you did the Edit deal as the Thompson doesn’t honor Hyatt Globalist benefits. So, no upgrade and no breakfast for Globalists.

Not true (unless something changed) stayed here in May 2023 and got Globalist benefits

Am I the only one finding Edit hotels are north of $1000 a night? Whatever the credit Chase is giving is for staying at an Edit property isn’t enough to offset the exceptionally high rate.

I’ve stayed at that Thompson many times and been upgraded to suites and the Upper Stories. The previous poster is empirically wrong.

doesn’t Edit usually require a two night minimum? How did you get the benefits for only a one night stay?

I had thought I read that the benefits are for stays of at least 2 nights. Is that incorrect?

Actually – just looked up what I read and I think it’s the $250 credit every six months that requires a 2-night stay but not the other benefits. So looks like you could have spent 12,500 points + $250 cash for a second night and gotten the $250 credited back.

#6298. Where to Stay in Big Sky, Montana, When You’re Dreaming of the Wild West

I’ve visited Big Sky, Montana, a handful of times over the past six years, and I’m still completely smitten. This corner of the Rockies, roughly 45 miles south of Bozeman, is a choose-your-own-adventure kind of city. Winter ski days beneath the hulking silhouette of Lone Peak give way to summer rafting trips and fly-fishing on the Gallatin River, while fall brings horseback rides that sprawl across open ranchlands, and spring offers hikes through wildflower-strewn meadows. The iconic Yellowstone National Park is about an hour south too, putting geysers, steaming hot springs, and roaming bison within day-tripping distance.

The city itself is a quaint yet buzzy collection of restaurants, shops, and watering holes, all adding a welcome dose of small-town charm to all that wilderness. And lately, the destination’s hospitality scene has been booming, with a new wave of stylish hotels and mountain retreats bringing some fresh takes to the city’s rugged Western roots. From luxe resorts with front-row views of the towering peaks to authentic dude ranches and design-forward Airbnbs with cozy fireplaces, there’s an accommodation for every style of Big Sky getaway on the list below. Read on for the best places to stay in Montana’s sweet mountain hub.

A peek at Big Sky's small but mighty town center, where the mountains and Main Street look great together.

Stay at Lone Mountain Ranch, just five minutes from the town center, for a dreamy dude ranch retreat.

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: Mountain access, gorgeous standalone cabins, private hot tubs, spa and wellness facilities (with indoor-outdoor lap pool, heated onsen soaking tub, cold plunge, steam room, and sauna)

Famed for its sumptuous yet tasteful resorts in far-flung destinations like Mauritius, Rwanda, and Malaysia, One&Only’s 2025 Moonlight Basin opening was the brand's American debut, as well as its first foray into the outdoor adventure space. A luxury alpine retreat like this requires a specialized type of hospitality, and the team here—a crew who can do everything from book your activities to whisk you between buildings on a side-by-side ATV—knows exactly what they’re doing. Guests get a direct line to the slopes via the One&Only gondola, as well as access to plush locker rooms, tuning equipment, and gear rentals that will impress even members of Yellowstone Club (the famously tiny private ski community next door).

Moonlight Basin is worth visiting outside of ski season too. Situated on 240 secluded acres within the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, the resort links two sections of protected wilderness in southwestern Montana’s Rocky Mountains, providing critical migration routes for species like moose and bobcats, which means you're in for some exceptional wildlife sightings. Add fly-fishing, stargazing at the on-site observatory, and unwinding at the 17,000-square-foot spa, and even the most discerning ski bums will find themselves spoiled rotten. —Hannah Towey

Neighborhood: Moonlight BasinThings to do nearby: Lone Peak, Madison River Valley, Big Sky Mountain, Madison Base Area

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: White-glove service, buzzy après bar, full spa, on-site activity center, ski-in/ski-out location

Montage Big Sky has always been more rugged than refined, but the buzz around this slopeside resort has Aspen and Jackson Hole loyalists rethinking their next ski vacation. The first five-star resort in Big Sky ushered in a whole new era of luxury for this mountain destination, with an 11,000-square-foot spa (the first true spa in the region), a buzzy bar scene, and stellar restaurants.

Most of the 139 rooms, suites, and residences have terraces and balconies with mountain views, and gas fireplaces turn on with a flip of a switch. Head to Beartooth Pub & Rec for a menu of comfort foods, like Wagyu nachos and oversized hot pretzels served alongside cold-smoked beer-cheese dip. —Jen Murphy

Neighborhood: Spanish PeaksThings to do nearby: Big Sky Resort, Ousel Falls Trail, Lone Peak, Beehive Basin Trail, Gallatin and Madison Rivers

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: True dude ranch experience, tasteful cabin design, horseback riding experiences for all levels, easy access to town

Lone Mountain Ranch, one of Montana’s longest-standing dude ranches, has plenty going for it: a wonderfully attentive staff, character-filled cabins, and a calendar of special events that draw in both longtime regulars and first-time horseback riders. The on-site wranglers are happy to work with riders of all levels one-on-one, even if that means helping you get past a few preexisting fears before climbing into the saddle. The ranch’s roots reach back to the early days of Yellowstone, with its owners involved in conversations around Big Sky’s formation and the region’s ranching, logging, and wilderness preservation. Yet unlike many of Montana’s more remote ranches, it’s conveniently less than a 10-minute drive from town.

You may still find little reason to leave: Set among towering aspens, the 150-acre guest ranch has 25 restored historic cabins, each with its own Wild West–inspired name and one to six bedrooms. And then there are the signature experiences, including Cowgirl Up, a weeklong retreat that brings women from around the world together to experience ranch life and release their inner cowgirl.

Neighborhood: Lone MountainThings to do nearby: Big Sky Town Center, Ousel Falls Trail, Moonlight Basin, Gallatin River, Big Sky Resort

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski-out access, hot tub, gas fireplace, mountain views, outdoor seating on the patio

There’s something pretty splendid about staying at 8,300 feet, especially when the mountains are quite literally at your doorstep. This standalone cabin in Big Sky’s (iconically named) Cowboy Heaven neighborhood is a haven for folks who wish to spend their days outside, whether that means skiing straight from the deck in the winter or taking advantage of the area’s hiking and wildlife spotting in the warmer months. It’s especially ideal for couples, small families, or friend groups, with one caveat for your crew: The second bedroom has a queen-over-twin bunk, so five adults looking for equal amounts of space may want to look elsewhere. A big plus? The town center is less than a 10-minute drive away.

Neighborhood: Cowboy HeavenThings to do nearby: Big Sky Resort, Lone Mountain, Moonlight Lodge, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Private hot tub, in-unit washer and dryer, indoor wood-burning fireplace, fully equipped kitchen, patio with outdoor furniture, longer stays allowed

With three floors and two separate living areas, this Big Sky rental gives small groups room to spread out between outings. And there’s plenty to get out for: Big Sky Resort is about 1.2 miles away, Beehive Basin Trailhead is roughly 2.6 miles, and Ousel Falls Park is another nearby option for low-key but scenic walks.

Inside the light-filled abode, fun Western touches are everywhere. In true Big Sky fashion, you’ll find everything from hanging longhorns and antlers to framed photographs of bison and horses. Through a wall of windows, you can look past the cozy fireplace into the hilly woods—the towering trees are gorgeous year-round. Do note this base might be best for four, rather than six, despite what the listing says. There are two generously sized bedrooms, but two sofa beds in the living room.

Neighborhood: Moonlight BasinThings to do nearby: Big Sky Resort, Beehive Basin Trailhead, Gallatin River, Lone Mountain, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, firepit, spacious design, game room, fully equipped kitchen, patio space with seating and grill, proximity to Yellowstone National Park

For a fun departure from the usual cabin-in-the-woods vibe, this modern mountain retreat sleeps up to eight and puts you in a handy spot for mountain treks, foodie-forward itineraries, and all the trips in between. It’s incredibly spacious, with a large patio for grilling local ingredients, warming up around the fire, and stargazing. In winter, take advantage of the trails practically right next to the property for snowmobiling; you're also in a prime position for skiing at Moonlight Basin, Big Ski Resort, or Bridger Bowl ski area (a bit further north). According to the listing, a sauna is set to open on the property—check in with the hosts to see if it will be set up by the time you visit.

It’s worth noting that this is the closest Airbnb to Yellowstone on this list. You can drive to the West Yellowstone entrance in around 45 minutes.

Neighborhood: Gallatin ValleyThings to do nearby: Gallatin River, West Yellowstone, Lone Indian Peak, Buck Ridge Trailhead, Crown Butte, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: Private hot tub, shared firepits and sauna, board games and books, kid-friendly amenities

This gem of a rental is high on my Big Sky bucket list for more reasons than one. To start, the tastefully designed home is all about panoramic views of misty, moody Ramshorn Ridge. With heaps of walking paths and a mountain-facing hot tub under string lights, guests will be almost poetically connected to Montana’s wide-open landscape. But you won’t be too far from the mountain town’s buzz: This home is part of Aspects, a 10-home village set in a ryegrass field in the Gallatin Valley, meaning you’ll have access to the community’s saunas and two firepits, which you can share with like-minded travelers.

Downtown Big Sky is just a five-minute drive away, while hiking trails branching from Yellowstone are within 15 minutes of the home. Along with its great location, I’m personally captivated by this home’s aesthetic design touches—from the light wood walls that warmly envelop the dining space to the vibrant art that brings fun, unexpected pops of color throughout the home.

Neighborhood: Gallatin ValleyThings to do nearby: The Riverhouse BBQ, West Yellowstone, Downtown Big Sky, Cinnamon Mountain, Gallatin River

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Unique design, minutes from Big Sky Resort, sauna, private walking/biking trail from the property

A little off-grid, a bit otherworldly, and just a couple of miles from Big Sky Resort, this Earthship Airbnb is a unique kind of Montana hideaway. Set on 20 private acres in Michener Meadows, the solar-powered house is designed to bring the outdoors in, with its own potable spring water and a private walking and biking trail winding around the property.

Neighborhood: Michener MeadowsThings to do nearby: Ousel Falls Park, Dudley Creek Trailhead, Table Mountain, Horn and Cantle, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Walkable to Big Sky Town Center; patio with grill; indoor fireplace; fully equipped kitchen; shared access to indoor pool, hot tub, and sauna

For those in search of an easy, breezy Big Sky stay, this convenient condo is a boon. Tucked just outside of the city’s small but mighty town center, you’ll be within walking distance of cozy cafés, outdoor gear and gift shops, and hyper-local pubs and restaurants. Back at “home,” your launchpad is as design-friendly as it is inviting. There’s a snug living room with an electric fireplace, a raised patio with a barbecue, string lights, and a table for enjoying meals made in your fully equipped kitchenette. It’s pretty spacious for a condo—each of the bedrooms boasts a king bed, and there’s a bathroom for each duo.

You’ll also be a short drive to the ski resort and practically right next to Big Sky Golf Course, where you can enjoy an award-winning 18-hole expanse and Nordic skiing, depending on the season. A plus for those chasing the snow? There’s an in-unit washer and dryer for all your ski gear, so it’ll be clean and dry for more mountain fun the next day.

Neighborhood: Meadow VillageThings to do nearby: Big Sky Golf Course, Big Sky Resort, Big Sky Town Center, Lone Mountain Trail, Blue Moon Bakery, Historic Crail Ranch, The Reflector Trail Loop

#6297. American Airlines Pilots Told Not To Eat The Tiramisu, Now Union Says Never Mind

UPDATE: The Allied Pilots Association has withdrawn its warning about tiramisu served in American Airlines crew meals in Phoenix. Following an investigation involving American’s safety team, Phoenix inflight staff, and the caterer, the union now says it was a false alarm.

Yesterday, APA ​Aeromedical was advised by the ​PHX ​Flight ​Office that ​a dessert ​included ​with ​some crew meals may ​have contained ​alcohol.

Out of ​an abundance of ​caution, APA issued an immediate ​advisory recommending that crewmembers ​not ​consume the dessert, ​specifically ​the ​tiramisu, ​until ​additional information ​could be obtained. ​Following coordination ​with ​AA ​Corporate ​Safety, PHX Inflight, ​the catering ​provider, and ​other ​involved ​parties, APA has confirmed ​that ​the desserts ​in question ​are safe ​to ​consume ​and ​do not pose a ​risk to ​aviation safety.

We appreciate the ​PHX ​Flight ​Office ​for promptly ​raising the concern and ​working with ​both American Airlines ​and APA to investigate the potential ​issue. The ​initial ​advisory ​was ​issued ​based on the information available ​at ​the ​time ​and ​with crew ​and ​flight ​safety ​as ​the priority. ​We appreciate your patience ​while additional fact finding ​was ​conducted.

For those pilots ​involved ​in a HIMS ​program ​we ​would like to ​use ​this ​as an opportunity to ​remind you that ​consuming ​certain ​food additives ​and extracts in large quantities may pose a ​risk to ​abstinence ​monitoring. Please consult ​the APA ​HIMS Subcommittee ​for additional ​information.

As ​always, ​please reach out to APA ​Aeromedical ​with any ​questions or ​concerns.

APA explained that its initial warning was precautionary, based on information available at the time…though I’m wondering what information

American Airlines pilots have been warned to skip the tiramisu in some crew meals out of Phoenix because it contains alcohol. That is an awkward ingredient to find in a meal provided to people who are supposed to be flying airplanes…

JonNYC shared a warning attributed to the Allied Pilots Association’s Aeromedical–HIMS Committee concerning meals supplied by American’s contracted caterer in Phoenix:

“The contracted catering provider has included tiramisu containing alcohol on some crew meal trays. Because the dessert is not cooked after the alcohol is added, alcohol may remain in the finished product.

“We recommend that no crew member consume this dessert.

“APA cannot determine the amount of alcohol contained in an individual serving or what effect consumption could have if a crewmember were subsequently required to undergo DOT alcohol testing.”

"PHX Crew Meal Alert – Tiramisu Containing Alcohol

The APA Aeromedical–HIMS Committee has been made aware of an issue affecting crews based in or transiting PHX.

The contracted catering provider has included tiramisu containing alcohol on some crew meal trays.…

The notice says the committee is coordinating with the Phoenix Flight Office to have the dessert removed and replaced. In the meantime, crews are advised to accept an incomplete meal rather than eat it.

Pilots who have already consumed the tiramisu and have concerns about their fitness to fly are instructed to contact their union domicile representatives immediately. The warning expressly tells them not to let schedule pressure influence that decision.

The notice does not establish that a serving would cause impairment or a failed alcohol test. The committee says it does not know the alcohol content or the potential testing consequences. But crews should not have to evaluate that uncertainty while eating an airline-provided meal!

The FAA explains that a confirmed alcohol concentration of 0.02 to 0.039 requires temporary removal from safety-sensitive duties, even though that result is not itself a federal testing violation. A confirmed result of 0.04 or greater carries more serious consequences.

American’s Phoenix caterer apparently supplied an alcohol-containing dessert in crew meals, prompting a union warning to leave it untouched while a replacement is arranged. I like tiramisu, but this is one setting where the alcohol-free version is the obvious choice. Pilots have enough to think about without wondering whether their crew meal could complicate an alcohol test…

#6296. Planning Your First Trip to New Zealand? Here's Where to Go

Living in Sydney, I’m guilty of thinking of New Zealand as somewhere I can always go next month. It’s close enough for a skiing trip, which is usually my first excuse to book. I love Queenstown for that, but what I’ve particularly enjoyed discovering on my travels is how naturally New Zealand brings together its spectacular outdoors and a tradition of luxury hospitality, in every season.

Aotearoa is easy to admire from a car window, but I’ve found that the places I remember most are those where I’ve stopped and spent a little more time. Wellington is overdue for another visit, and Fiordland is somewhere I'd like to explore properly. Then there are the lodges, each with its own character and reasons to return: Huka Lodge for its history, Cabot Lodgefor its working-farm roots, and many others worth discovering.

Below are the five places I’d build a trip around, leaving enough room in the itinerary to linger a little longer wherever I find myself wanting to stay.

I’d start with Queenstown if you’re coming for the mountains, with time allotted for Arrowtown and a few days in Fiordland National Park. For the North Island, Auckland is a useful starting point before heading towards Rotorua for its geothermal landscapes and Māori culture, then Lake Taupō. If food is your priority, I’d make Wellington part of the trip. My main advice is to choose a few places you’re interested in and give each at least a few days.

It can be, although a luxury lodge and a helicopter aren’t compulsory parts of an itinerary. I’d spend on a stay I really wanted, then balance it with somewhere simpler, ideally with a kitchen so you can cook some of your own meals. Skiing and guided activities can take a sizable bite out of the budget, so decide which matter most before booking everything else. If you’re considering a camper van, compare the total hire cost, including fuel and campsite fees, with a car and accommodation. I’d also leave room on the budget for eating out and wine tasting.

Seven days is sufficient for a trip, but I wouldn’t try to cover both islands in that time. On the South Island, you could spend the week around Queenstown and Arrowtown, adding Te Anau if Milford Sound is a priority. Or drive from Christchurch to Lake Tekapo and spend time in the Mackenzie region. On the North Island, Rotorua and Taupō work well together.

I always prefer to spend an extra night somewhere than keep repacking. Leave some flexibility, too: if you’ve come for stargazing and the sky clouds over, you’ll appreciate having another evening available.

Arrowtown, 20 minutes from Queenstown, is an idyllic place to visit.

Queenstown is great for the skiing, but I’d make time for nearby Arrowtown even if it meant losing a day on the slopes. I love the old cottages and shopfronts, and how much of its gold-mining history is still visible. The partially restored Chinese miners’ settlement beside Bush Creek is worth walking through before lunch.

Food is another reason to stay. At Aosta, northern Italian cooking makes good use of Central Otago produce. Nearby Ayrburn occupies a former 150-acre farm, with restaurants spread across its restored buildings. Billy’s, in the original homestead, serves modern Chinese food. I’ve visited both Arrowtown and Ayrburn, and would happily organize another Queenstown trip around eating here, with some skiing fitted in.

Where to stay: Arrowtown House is a small boutique hotel in town, making walking to dinner easy. Millbrook Resort, nearby, has more of a resort feel, with apartments as well as rooms and a spa for sore ski legs.

I still think about the water outside Huka Lodge. The Waikato River is this extraordinary emerald color, and I could have spent much of my stay watching it. Huka also got me interested in New Zealand’s lodge history: it began as a fishermen’s camp in 1924. There’s something appealing about discovering that a place has been welcoming people for the same reason for more than a century.

You don’t have to stay there to spend time beside the river. Follow the riverside walks towards Huka Falls, where the water forces its way through a narrow rock channel. I’d also get out on Lake Taupō, with a boat or kayak trip to the Ngātoroirangi Mine Bay Māori rock carvings. Created by Matahi Whakataka-Brightwell and his team, they’re a striking example of contemporary Māori art.

Where to stay: Huka Lodge has a certain stateliness, with its manicured grounds beside the Waikato River and a history of royal guests. I have dreams of running away to Poronui Safari Camp, in the wider Taupō region. Its two canvas tents sit beside the Mohaka River, with hot showers and food supplied by the kitchen. It’s booked exclusively for up to four people.

The Cairns Alpine Resort’s Alpine Lodges on crystalline Lake Tekapo

I visited Dark Sky Project while reporting on quiet destinations for Traveler and loved having someone explain what I was looking at. The indoor experience brings Māori astronomy and science together, and houses an enormous restored 19th-century telescope. It gives you a way into the subject even if your astronomical knowledge is limited. For nighttime stargazing, book the Summit Experience at Mount John Observatory, within the Aoraki Mackenzie International Dark Sky Reserve. I’d arrange it early in the stay, leaving another night available if the weather doesn’t cooperate.

There’s plenty to look at during the day, too. Lake Tekapo gets its milky turquoise color from fine glacial rock flour floating in the water. It’s a good place to spend a few days on a South Island drive from Christchurch, with time for the Southern Alps and a separate excursion into Aoraki/Mount Cook National Park.

Where to stay: The Cairns Alpine Resort’s Alpine Lodges take their inspiration from musterers’ huts. Inside, there are two bedrooms and a kitchen, with timber-lined rooms and a wood-burning fireplace. After a late night stargazing on Mount John, you can have a lie-in and cook breakfast whenever you’re ready.

The city of Wellington, a great place to visit for good eating and galleries.

New Zealand received its first Michelin restaurant selection in 2026, although you hardly need the guide to eat well here. For me, Wellington would be a few days of galleries and restaurant bookings, with enough time between them to walk around and see what’s changed since my last visit some years ago City Gallery’s reopening has moved it up my list and is the sort of thing I’d build a weekend around. I’d leave plenty of time for eating, though.

Puffin is on my list for a glass of natural wine. I’m also keeping an eye on Rita, a small restaurant in an Aro Valley cottage known for its changing set dinners. The team is also opening a daytime deli called Super Rita, expected to open in early next year.

Where to stay: The Intrepid Hotel is the one I’d book: 18 rooms in Te Aro, near Cuba Street, with Puffin downstairs. I like the idea of a nightcap in a locals-filled wine bar and a short walk upstairs to bed.

The Cabot Lodge, a working farm, is an intriguing stay in Fiordland

Milford Sound and Doubtful Sound are still on my list, and I’d like to give Fiordland a trip of its own. I’d stay around Te Anau rather than make the long journey out and back from Queenstown. There are glowworm caves across Lake Te Anau, while nearby Manapouri is the starting point for the most direct land-and-water route to Doubtful Sound: a boat across Lake Manapouri, followed by a coach over Wilmot Pass to the fjord.

I also have a shopping recommendation for the journey. At The Key, on the approach to Te Anau, Davaar sells knitwear (that has a cult following) made from wool grown on the family’s working sheep station, Davaar Station. Founder Kate Macdonald is the fifth generation, and her sister Anna runs the food caravan next door. I bought a jumper a few years ago when she had a pop-up in Arrowtown that I still love. It’s exactly the sort of place I want to find when traveling: a homegrown product with a family story; make the best souvenirs.

Where to stay: Cabot Lodge interests me because it’s on a working farm overlooking Lake Manapouri, and near Doubtful Sound departures. For a night at Milford itself, Milford Sound Lodge has chalets overlooking the river and rainforest. I’d decide which sound I wanted to spend more time exploring before choosing where to stay.

#6295. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6294. Introducing “Delta Disruptive” Class For Flights Within Florida (Hilarious SNL Skit)

Forget Delta One. Saturday Night Live has imagined another cabin for Delta Air Lines it calls “Delta Disruptive Class,” and this one addresses a problem even a lie-flat seat cannot solve: the passenger who makes everyone else’s flight miserable.

In a spoof commercial from its October 31 episode, Saturday Night Live introduces “Delta Disruptive,” a separate section for passengers whose behavior makes them particularly unwelcome elsewhere on the aircraft.

The premise is simple: instead of letting these travelers ruin the flight for everyone, put them together behind a thick plexiglass partition.

— Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl), November 1, 2026

The fictional cabin accommodates everything from obnoxious personal habits to full-blown onboard meltdowns. There are passengers clipping toenails, fighting over seats, and shouting conspiracy theories. One customer offers a testimonial while duct-taped to her seat. A Tiffany Gomas character also makes an appearance..

Naturally, the airline presents all of this with the polished enthusiasm of a commercial announcing an exciting improvement to your travel experience.

“All Delta Disruptive flight attendants are the toughest, gayest, ex-Spirit Airlines employees who have seen much worse.”

I love how Kenan Thompson, who plays flight attendant “Kevin,” grabs an emotional support iguana and throws it off the plane. He also has a ring on every finger, lol.

The new cabin class is rolling out soon…on flights within Florida. Book now…

“Delta Disruptive” is a joke, but the desire to enjoy a flight without becoming an unwilling participant in someone else’s viral video is quite real. Part of me wishes that we could throw unruly passengers into padded part of the plane instead of diverting and costing everyone time and money.

As usual with SNL skits, the joke captures a frustrating truth about flying: as carefully as you may choose your airline seat, you cannot choose the person sitting nearby. One passenger can make an otherwise pleasant flight unbearable.

#6293. A New York City Weekend Guide for Design Lovers

The thing that makes visiting (or living in) New York worth every penny is that you don’t have to go out of your way looking for inspiration. You might be struck by a vintage sign advertising color TVs in the East Village; a grandpa on the Upper East Side pairing bright red socks with his loafers; or that never-gets-old view of the Brooklyn Bridge from an elevated subway track. Design is, indeed, everywhere in NYC, but sometimes you need a bit of a roadmap to plot your next moment of awe.

Like many New Yorkers, I derive a lot of joy from looking at pretty things and existing in cool spaces. When I feel like I’m staring at a blank page—or I just want to spend a weekend more intentionally—the places below are the ones I turn to for a creative spark. These spots span boroughs and cover art, architecture, and fashion—from former artist residences and Japanese-inspired stationery stores to restaurants and spas with covetable interiors.

For the aesthetes who have already seen the latest exhibition at MoMA, this weekend guide for design lovers is intended to point you in a few other directions (and no, this does not include that viral room full of dirt in SoHo).

The Cooper Hewitt is the only museum in the United States devoted exclusively to both historical and contemporary design.

For many New Yorkers, to go uptown is to go to the museum. And while the Metropolitan Museum of Art holds down the fort, there are a few other players along Museum Mile that always seem to take me by surprise whenever I visit. The Cooper Hewitt, for instance, showcases “design objects” in the broadest sense that span across centuries—you might find an Egyptian ceramic from 1100 BCE in one room, and a Swedish midcentury-modern lamp in another. It’s also a lovely hangout spot; earlier this year, the museum hosted a Hi-Fi listening room, and when the weather’s nice, visitors can take advantage of the garden (tickets are not required and Wi-Fi is free), admiring the gorgeous architecture of Andrew Carnegie’s former mansion.

The “Einspänner” at Sabarsky—double espresso with whipped cream.

A short walk away, the Neue Galerie, which specializes in early 20th-century German and Austrian art, is where I go to gush over furniture designed by the likes of Josef Hoffmann and Adolf Loos. The museum is set to reopen on November 12 for its 20th anniversary, but in the meantime, you can visit the stunning Café Sabarsky—the Viennese restaurant located within the museum—and pretend you’re at the helm of the next great intellectual movement with your friends over fancy whipped-cream-topped coffees.

Further downtown, in Midtown East, the Paul Rudolph Institute is a must for anyone who enjoyed The Brutalist. Join the monthly open house at the Rudolph-designed duplex within the iconic Modulightor building, once the headquarters of the lighting company the architect co-founded with his life partner, Ernst Wagner. Docents are on-site to answer any questions as you wind your way through the all-white apartment, with its disjointed staircases and built-in shelving units, though private tours are also available.

When it comes to shopping, I believe one can gain a lot from staring into the windows along Madison Avenue, or even heading inside to get a feel for the luxe fabrics, sans purchase. But for second-hand designer clothing, Upper East Vintage (by appointment only) and Designer Revival (Gentleman’s Resale is also right next door), both on the Upper East Side, are your best bet. I’m also always delighted by what I find at Spellman Gallery, a small showroom owned by an art appraiser with fantastic taste—you can discover all kinds of treasures, from a rare vinyl record to a painting worth a few thousand.

Browsing beautiful items will inevitably stir up an appetite, and for a restaurant that has tables equipped with landlines during live art auction sales, check out Marcel 945 Madison, housed inside the historic Breuer Building that is now the global headquarters of Sotheby’s. While the restaurant serves (very expensive) French bistro fare, it’s all about the rotating art on the walls—including works by Roy Lichtenstein and Willem de Kooning, to name a few past residents—which are also available for purchase.

With its glass blocks, chrome light fixtures, and black leather booths, Bridges in Chinatown is a design-lover's dream.

If you prefer to walk amongst grittier cast-iron buildings or people-watch from plastic stools, then it’s best you head downtown. Start with a trip to the Judd Foundation, where you can book a slot to explore 37 of minimalist Donald Judd’s artworks, each permanently installed in the late artist’s former residence and studio on Spring Street, and get a glimpse of how an artist lived and breathed in SoHo before the luxury flagships arrived. Over in Greenwich Village, the Renee and Chaim Gross Foundation boasts over 12,000 of American artist Chaim Gross’s sculptures, drawings, and prints, as well as his personal collection of global art. The late artist’s personal home, which he shared with his wife Renee, is light-filled and lived-in—an intimate experience that cannot be replicated at a traditional museum.

The Lower East Side, specifically Orchard Street, is where to go to shop independent designers. Browse Colbo—more of a multidisciplinary space than a retail store—for unisex neutrals as you sip an espresso. Adjacent to the shop, Colbo Next Door is a great spot to grab a glass of wine and listen to vinyl. Further along Orchard Street, you’ll find Lara Koleji for vintage Miu Miu, as well as Tumbao, a curation of the very best in Latin American fashion design. On East Broadway, also in the LES, Aeon Bookstore is one of my favorite bookstores in New York, a basement-level shop with a small-but-mighty selection of used titles, whether you’re looking for a coffee table book on the Bauhaus or a beautiful edition of Lolita.

Gem Home on Mott Street saves the day whenever I’m in need of a unique, last-minute gift—say, a stainless steel ice cream bowl or spiral toothbrush holder—and the shop, which is also a café, has recently started hosting dinners in collaboration with French pop-up Mon Petit Canard. Continuing on with the theme of downtown cool, Bridges is a swoon-worthy restaurant space that’s bound to get your interior design wheels turning, and there’s a famous Comté cheese tart that’s a work of art in and of itself.

If you've ever wondered what the subway looked like decades ago, the New York Transit Museum has your answer.

If you’re spending a day in Brooklyn, make sure to pop over to the New York Transit Museum in Downtown Brooklyn—talk about a celebration of design. In addition to touring over 20 different vintage train cars, you’ll view an otherwise quotidian part of New York City life in a new light. Graphic design nerds in particular will geek out over the exhibits dedicated to Massimo Vignelli, who designed the 1972 subway map we love and use today. For a different kind of museum experience, Pioneer Works in Red Hook was born out of a former 1866 red-brick warehouse, and today it’s dedicated to all kinds of arts and science programming. On view right now, for instance, is a multimedia exhibition by Helsinki-based artist Tuomas A. Laitinen, drawing on more than a decade of research on octopus intelligence, sleep, and consciousness.

There’s only one place I trust for buying jeans, and it’s Front General Store's Outpost, which boasts an entire wall of vintage Levi’s and then some—think worn-in Burberry trench coats, military deadstock, and new shoes from Japanese or British brands you might not have heard of. The vintage shopping in Brooklyn, of course, doesn’t stop there: 10 ft Single by Stella Dallas in Williamsburg is a reliable favorite for threadbare T-shirts and Ralph Lauren sweaters, and if you’re on the hunt for a conversation starter of a chair, Dream Fishing Tackle in Greenpoint is part fishing supply center, part midcentury-modern furniture store. If it wasn’t already clear, NYC loves a retail space that’s also something else: Chyelle in Bushwick and Apartment Ra’el in Bed-Stuy both serve up coffee and beautiful homeware. For those obsessed with paper and pens (guilty), Yoseka Stationery in Greenpoint stocks the very best in Japanese stationery design—from Hobonichi journals to Kaweco fountain pens.

In a sea of white-marbled wellness spaces, Spencer’s Spa in Williamsburg proves good design is integral to relaxation. I’ve had excellent facials at both the Brooklyn and SoHo locations, lingering for as long as possible afterwards in the lounge areas, which seem to take inspiration from traditional Japanese, Art Deco, and Scandinavian design (I like to take pictures of all the unique lamps and objects so I can reverse image search them for my apartment later on). But if you’d rather find your zen within New York City’s nightlife scene, James Murphy–owned club Nightmoves in Williamsburg, music venue Public Records in Gowanus, and listening bar Eavesdrop in Greenpoint all boast incredibly impressive custom sound design.

The Noguchi Museum is one of the most peaceful pockets of the city.

Akari Light Sculptures abound at the Noguchi Museum, and you can even bring one home.

A trip to Queens would not be complete without a visit to the Noguchi Museum in Astoria, where you can feel a sense of serenity walking around Isamu Noguchi’s biomorphic sculptures, then buy one of his Akari light sculptures in what is perhaps the best museum gift shop in New York City. While the museum is home to its own sculpture garden, there’s also one practically across the street—make sure you allot some time to strolling Socrates Sculpture Park, where you’ll encounter a whole host of experimental installations (they’re always rotating), with the Manhattan skyline as the backdrop.

In Long Island City, the industrial hub-turned-creative enclave in western Queens, MoMA PS1 is at once nostalgic and of-the-moment, showcasing contemporary art within former elementary school halls—it’s especially fun in the summer when it's running its Warm Up series, when everyone gathers outside for DJ sets and music performances. Also in the neighborhood, Somerset House is a staging and interior design gallery that sells collectible furniture and art—think Pierre Jeanneret armchairs and Poul Henningsen lamps—by appointment only. For something a bit more accessible, Lichen in Ridgewood sells a similar catalog of vintage furniture, plus its own in-house designs ranging from glass coffee tables to futuristic sconces.

This bank-turned-hotel features original vaulted ceilings that rival those of Grand Central Station. Sip a martini at the Swan Room, the property's see-and-be-seen lobby bar.

Situated in NoMad, The Fifth Avenue Hotel gives you access to both Museum Mile and downtown shopping. The 19th-century, Renaissance-style mansion is dressed in maximalism.

Once a barrel factory in the early 1900s, this hip Williamsburg hotel is your gateway to industrial-chic rooms, a cinema with red velvet seats, and the acclaimed Le Crocodile restaurant.

The Mercer is SoHo in a nutshell, with loft-like suites, a neutral color palette, and a buzzy restaurant. Minimalists, this one’s for you.

#6292. The 10 best places to visit in November 2026

November is peak shoulder season: The weather can be unpredictable (but you can get really lucky), crowds are small nearly everywhere and prices are often the lowest they'll be all year for many destinations. It is an ideal time to travel in many ways, if you're willing to risk less-than-ideal weather in some places.

Thanksgiving also takes place in the U.S., and if you are not obligated to visit family, you can enjoy a wonderful four-day vacation without missing any school or work. And for those who love Christmas markets and lights, several spots start their displays at the end of the month.

Here are 10 great destinations to consider for your November getaway.

This stunning desert and mountain region enjoys cooler weather in November that's ideal for hiking in the Atlas Mountains. Meanwhile, the nearby city of Marrakech is as vibrant as ever, with more people coming out in the less-than-scorching temps that linger all summer. Wander the souk, stroll the gorgeous gardens, and visit architectural highlights without breaking a sweat.

Nov. 18 is Morocco's Independence Day, and this year's Marrakech Coffee & Tea Festival will run Nov. 5-7, with more than 400 exhibitors and various workshops and classes. This year's Marrakech International Film Festival runs from Nov. 20–28.

Use points to stay at the Park Hyatt Marrakech, which opened in 2025 (rates from $594 or 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night), or check out the new Riad Beij, in the heart of the Medina (rates from $168 per night). To stay in the Atlas Mountains, you can use Virgin Red points at the luxe Virgin Limited Edition Kasbah Tamadot (rates from $577 or 140,000 Virgin Red points per night).

TPG tip: Marrakech has increased seasonal direct flight access, including a direct flight from Newark on United Airlines, which launched in 2024, and from Atlanta on Delta Air Lines, which debuted at the end of 2025.

Oaxaca's celebration of Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, is legendary, especially in Oaxaca City, where festivities and commemorations take place every year from Oct. 31 to Nov. 2. Expect elaborate costumes, parades, street festivals, cemetery and altar visits, and plenty of music, food and drinks.

After the city festivities, plan to stay at one of the region's design-forward hotels. Boutique hotel 7 Casa Laurel opened in April this year, and Casa Yati opened in Ventanilla on the beach last summer. La Valise Mazunte is a member of Small Luxury Hotels of the World with just six suites and a villa (rates from $400 or 130,000 Hilton Honors points per night).

TPG tip: You can fly directly to Puerto Escondido on United Airlines' Houston-to-Puerto Escondido route, which debuted in 2025. American Airlines launched its direct flights to Puerto Escondido from Dallas-Fort Worth in December 2025.

November is the very beginning of the dry season in Thailand, so it's a good time to beat the winter crowds and score good airfare and hotel pricing. Nov. 24 is Loy Krathong, the beautiful floating lantern festival that lights up the Bangkok waterways on the night of the full moon in the 12th month of the Thai lunar calendar. Various events happen along the Chao Phraya River, in public parks and at cultural landmarks.

The city, which has several new hotels this year, with something for almost every loyalist. Voco Bangkok Surawong opened in January 2026 (rates from 19,000 IHG One Rewards and $137 per night). Canopy by Hilton Bangkok Sukhumvit opened in August 2026 (rates from 45,000 Hilton Honors points and $170 per night). The long-delayed Fairmont Bangkok Sukhumvit finally opened, also in August, with LEED Gold certification, a jasmine-inspired spa, seven food and beverage outlets and 474 rooms (rates from 12,345 ALL Accor points and $278 per night).

TPG tip: Last year, United Airlines launched a new daily flight to Bangkok via Hong Kong from Los Angeles and San Francisco, making it the only domestic airline to offer a daily one-stop flight to Bangkok from the U.S.

Looking for an adventure? November is the last month of the dry season to visit the Amazon, so there's still time to squeeze in an adventure before the end of the year. If colorful birds, jaguars, river dolphins and caiman sightings aren't enough for you, the first-ever Global Citizen music festival in the Amazon, in Belem, is Nov. 1. Global Citizen Festival Amazonia brings Brazilian music stars Anitta, Seu Jorge and Gaby Amarantos and Coldplay's Chris Martin together with Indigenous leaders to amplify climate action campaigns.

TPG tip: Avianca flies to Belem via Bogota, Colombia, from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), and LATAM flies there through Sao Paulo/Guarulhos International Airport (GRU). Book a room at Ibis Styles Belem Batista Campos ($67 per night) or Grand Mercure Belem do Para ($474 per night). Both are members of Accor Live Limitless.

If you've dreamed of a vacation in St. Barts but thought you couldn't afford it, November may be the best time to visit the gorgeous Caribbean island. You'll enjoy warm weather, beat the winter crowds and enjoy better prices on hotels and flights. And while the French island is known for always having excellent food, November brings even more culinary star power to the isle.

The Saint-Barth Gourmet Festival is Nov. 9-15 and features five chefs from Michelin-starred restaurants, including chef Amaury Bouhours of Restaurant Le Meurice Alain Ducasse and Thibault Sombardier of Les Parisiens.

TPG tip: Getting to St. Barts can be a bit of a journey if you don't have a private jet (ahem), but Cape Air flies twice daily from well-connected St. Thomas.

Looking to the other hemisphere is always a good idea, and in Australia, they're experiencing the other shoulder season: spring. In Western Australia, this means gorgeous wildflowers and some excellent festivals worth traveling for.

Foodies should plan to attend the world-renowned Pair'd Margaret River Region food and wine festival (Nov. 19-22), which brings world-class wine, food and music to the Margaret River region. This year's lineup includes chefs Rodney Scott, Matt Abe, and Mindy Woods, as well as wine writer Erin Larkin.

TPG tip: Hyde Perth opened in March of this year (rates from $239 per night) as the first Hyde hotel in Australia, a brand from Ennismore (also behind the Hoxton, Mama Shelter, Delano, and 25Hours brands) that also has locations in London, Ibiza, Dubai, and Miami.

Some November trips require compromising on the weather, but not in the desert. Palm Springs in November is ideal: With a daytime high of 79 degrees Fahrenheit and a low of 52 degrees Fahrenheit at night, you'll still avoid its peak tourist months, which begin in January. It's also ideal weather to hike in nearby Joshua Tree National Park.

Though most Pride events occur in June, the Palm Springs Pride Festival is a fall event. This year, it runs from Nov. 6–8, with the big parade on the final day. Expect live music, comedy, local vendors and artists, and plenty of food and drink stands in several areas across the downtown area. The Sunset Music and Comedy Festival runs concurrently each night at the Agua Caliente Casino.

There are several new and improved attractions in the desert: The Palm Springs Air Museum recently completed a $2.5 million renovation, and reopened in September, featuring a turbine-inspired façade, new exhibits, and the Ronald M. Auen Learning Center, and DSRT Surf, a manmade surf lagoon that creates the perfect wave, every time, opened this summer in Palm Desert.

TPG tip: The iconic La Quinta Resort & Club celebrates its centennial in 2026, with special events and guest experiences all year long. It's now a part of Hilton's Curio Collection, so you can use and earn rewards points there (rates from 85,000 Hilton Honors points and $329 per night)

Florence in summer can be a hot, crowded mess, but come November, there are fewer crowds and mild weather (although rain is likely). It's also truffle-hunting season in Tuscany.

Film lovers should mark Oct. 31-Nov. 8 for the Festival dei Popoli, Europe's oldest international documentary film festival. And Nov. 29 brings runners from around the world to the Estra Firenze Marathon. Finally, most Christmas markets open around the city in the last week of November.

TPG tip: The city recently welcomed Borgo Pignano Florence, set on a 5-acre estate with 11 historic buildings and 32 rooms and is part of Relais & Chateaux. La Resérve Firenze opened Oct. 15 inside a restored 15th-century palazzo. If you want to use points, W Florence (rates from $507 or 70,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night) opened last year.

Rev your engines for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, when Formula 1 racing comes to Sin City from Nov. 19-21.

Outside the hugely popular event, you can find some hotel and flight deals this November. And there's still plenty to do in November beyond F1. At the Sphere, you can catch the 4D version of "The Wizard of Oz" daily throughout the month, or see Metallica Nov. 4-7, the Eagles Nov. 13-14 and 27-28.

Christmas also starts early in Vegas on Nov. 5, when the 3-acre Cactus Garden at Ethel M Chocolate Factory opens its annual lights show, and Nov. 14 at the Bellagio Conservatory, where they pull out all the stops to create a lit-up floral winter wonderland.

Foodies should also be excited: Taylor Swift favorite and NYC hotspot The Corner Store is opening its second location at the Cosmopolitan of Las Vegas on November 9.

TPG tip: United restored its nonstop service between Cleveland and Las Vegas in September, with five flights a week and budget airline Breeze Airways added a daily route between Las Vegas and John Wayne Airport in Orange County.

November is the tail end of hurricane season so the possibilities of one hitting are slim—and there are great deals to be had, and usually, excellent weather. Miches — located on the northeast coast of the Dominican Republic — has been increasing its number of high-end all-inclusive resorts, and it's typically much less crowded than Punta Cana, which is near the airport.

Hilton loyalists can turn Hilton Honors points into an all-inclusive stay at Zemi Miches Punta Cana All-Inclusive Resort, Hilton's first Curio Collection all-inclusive resort in the country. Hyatt has also planted its all-inclusive flag in Miches with two openings: Dreams Playa Esmeralda Resort & Spa and Secrets Playa Esmeralda Resort & Spa. At Dreams, families and kids are welcome to enjoy the beautiful beaches, pools, and many restaurants and bars, while Secrets is adults-only.

TPG tip: No matter where you stay, let the hotel arrange your transportation from Punta Cana International Airport for ease and affordability. The transportation area at this airport can be overwhelming, and after a long flight, who doesn't want everything made easy?

#6291. United Airlines Adds Five Routes From San Francisco, Including Four Surprising Transcons

United Airlines is adding five routes from San Francisco next spring, including four transcontinental flights to smaller East Coast markets. The latest additions, Richmond and Norfolk, are particularly interesting because both will operate just twice weekly. United is also taking on Breeze Airways directly in Richmond.

Across two rounds of announcements in late October, United unveiled new or returning service from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) to Charleston, Hartford, Oklahoma City, Richmond, and Norfolk.

I had not yet covered the earlier additions, so let’s look at all five together:

The new routes were flagged by Ishrion Aviation.

The first round of additions, from SFO to CHS, BDL, and OKC were loaded on October 22–23.

Charleston International Airport announced its seasonal San Francisco route on October 22, listing Boeing 737-800/MAX 8 aircraft. The airport emphasized both travel to the Bay Area and connections beyond United’s West Coast hub.

Bradley International Airport followed with its announcement of daily, year-round Hartford service. Unlike Charleston’s limited weekly schedule, this represents a daily commitment to the Connecticut market.

A Boeing 737 MAX 9 will be used for Hartford and a SkyWest-operated Embraer E175 for Oklahoma City. The OKC flight will operate daily.

The newer announcements extend that expansion into Virginia. Interestingly, none of these five new routes were formally announced by United.

Richmond International Airport announced its twice-weekly service on October 30. Meanwhile, Norfolk International Airport confirms its new San Francisco flights begin March 31.

The twist on the RIC and ORF flights are the frequencies. Twice-weekly service is familiar territory for leisure-focused airlines but rather atypical of the daily-or-better schedule many passengers associate with a United hub route or that of another network carrier. That certainly suggests United is approaching these markets differently from Hartford. A Richmond traveler can choose a Thursday departure and Sunday return for a long weekend. Someone needing to travel on other days will still need a connection or another option.

The Richmond addition also creates a direct competitive overlap with Breeze Airways, which already offers nonstop service between Richmond and San Francisco.

Breeze is an annoyance to United at SFO and while Breeze is smart enough not to full Independence Air (ramping up at a major United hub too much, too fast, then going bust), I would be incredulous if Breeze did not influence United’s decision to launch this route, particularly given the twice-weekly schedule.

The bigger question is whether both airlines can make the route work over time. More competition is useful when it lasts.

Both Hartford and Charleston’s airport announcements explicitly promote those onward connections…that’s true for all five routes. Ultimately, this is just United trying to grow its network and dominance at its primary West Coast hub.

United Airlines will add or restore five San Francisco routes in March 2027, with daily service to Hartford and Oklahoma City, four weekly flights to Charleston, and twice-weekly flights to Richmond and Norfolk. Richmond brings direct competition with Breeze, while the broader expansion strengthens United’s reach into smaller domestic markets. These are less glamorous additions than another international route announcement, but quite useful as United also continues to rebuild its domestic network.

#6290. United Airlines Launches New 6-Hour Boeing 737 MAX Nonstop Routes: See Map Now

United Airlines has added two new transcontinental routes from San Francisco International Airport (SFO). It'll operate from its Pacific hub to both Norfolk and Richmond, both of which are in Virginia.

Last month, the carrier disclosed two transcon routes from SFO to Charleston, South Carolina, and Hartford, Connecticut. While Charleston, Norfolk, and Richmond have not previously had United flights from SFO, Hartford has, most recently in 2018.

While United will serve both long domestic routes next year, only two weekly flights will exist on both of them, all on the 166-seat Boeing 737 MAX 8. This configuration has 16 domestic first seats, along with 54 seats in economy plus and 96 seats in main cabin. The schedule, more or less the same for both routes, will allow connectivity to/from various Asia-Pacific destinations. Manila, Seoul, and Tokyo will be especially important.

UA2364: 8:15 AM-4:41 PM (5 hours and 26 minutes)

UA1297: 5:45 PM-8:57 PM (6 hours and 12 minutes)

UA1853: 8:15 AM-4:50 PM (5 hours and 35 minutes)

UA1807: 5:45 PM-9:08 PM (6 hours and 23 minutes)

The Star Alliance member will be the sole operator between SFO and ORF. Cirium Diio shows that it is a brand-new market, with no nonstop services with any airline in the past. It is, therefore, historical in nature. With 43,400 round-trip local passengers, ORF was SFO's tenth-largest unserved domestic market.

SFO to RIC is very different. United will coexist with Breeze Airways, which commenced the long route in May 2022. Running twice-weekly on the Airbus A220-200, it will be the first time the airport pair has had two carriers operating nonstop. Fortunately, both airlines will operate on different days of the week. While United will focus on the local market and some connectivity via SFO, virtually all of Breeze's traffic is point-to-point. With 70,000 local passengers, it was SFO's fifth-largest domestic market that did not have United flights.

While the list of upcoming routes in 2027 will almost certainly increase, the latest information, as of November 2, shows that the following routes will launch. They'll all take off at the end of March, as northern carriers, including United, will switch to summer schedules based on IATA slot seasons on Sunday, March 28, 2027.

The additions join four markets that materialized in 2026 or will do so in the remainder of the year. The first to launch was SFO to Carlsbad, California, on March 29, with two daily services on SkyWest E175s. Flights to Portland International Jetport Airport (PWM), Maine, followed on June 27, with a weekly 737 MAX 8 operation. Both airport pairs are brand-new, which is always great to see. PWM is the longest nonstop domestic service from SFO.

On November 17, United will lift off from SFO to West Palm Beach, with up to a daily MAX 8 service. Then there's SFO to Sapporo, Japan, with three weekly flights on the 787-9. Neither destination has previously been served from SFO. In fact, it'll be the first time that Sapporo has had nonstop flights from the Lower 48. Meanwhile, SFO is West Palm Beach's new longest domestic route.

#6289. Sleep Under the Stars at These Incredible Igloo-Like Airbnbs Around the World

Few travel experiences are as otherworldly as watching the night sky from the cozy cocoon of a glass-topped igloo. In the far north, that might mean watching the aurora borealis shimmer overhead, surrounded by pine forests and frozen lakes. But you don't have to travel to the Arctic Circle to experience an igloo-like stay. From snow-covered mountain landscapes in Germany to peaceful corners of Spain, these unusual stays can be found in some unexpected places across Europe and beyond.

The impressive northern lights in Finnish Lapland

Many interiors lean into a Nordic theme—think Scandi-style decor, underfloor heating, faux-fur throws, and panoramic windows designed to maximise stargazing. In Nordic destinations, many of these igloos give you the chance to enjoy classic experiences nearby, such as husky and reindeer sledding, cold-water swimming, or a spell in a geothermal spa. Elsewhere, the appeal might be waking up to mountain views, exploring the surrounding countryside, or simply enjoying the novelty of sleeping inside a transparent dome.

Wrap up, pour a hot chocolate, and settle in—here are the best igloos to bed down in for a memorable night under the stars.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Pet-friendly, private deck, hot tub

Set within 45 acres of secluded private woodland, this spacious dome is a cozy base for exploring the surrounding walking trails by day and stargazing after dark, thanks to the area's limited light pollution. Inside, there's a king-size bed, two fold-out single beds, armchairs, and a dining area, as well as a private bathroom with a hot shower and a small kitchenette equipped with a microwave, kettle, toaster, and fridge. Outside, the deck has plenty of seating and a barbecue, while a covered Scandinavian wood-fired hot tub overlooking the surrounding countryside can be used for an extra charge. Dogs are welcome too, making this a good option if you don't want to leave four-legged family members behind.

Location: Shropshire, United KingdomThings to do nearby: Ludlow Castle, Tenbury Museum, Mortimer Forest

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Lake views, fireplace, air-conditioning, hot tub

Perched on a hillside above Lake Superior, this geodesic dome combines the feel of camping with all the comforts of home. Designed to be enjoyed year-round, it has a gas fireplace and heating for chilly Minnesota winters, as well as air-conditioning for warmer summer days. There's room for up to four guests, with a queen bed and a second lofted bed, plus a fully equipped kitchen and bathroom with a walk-in shower. The highlight, though, is the large private deck, where a hot tub overlooks the lake and can be used throughout the year. The town of Two Harbors is also just a short drive away, with cafés, restaurants, shops and a local brewery.

Location: Two Harbors, MinnesotaThings to do nearby: Two Harbors town, Pierre the Voyager, Two Harbors Pierhead Light, Rock Beach

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: Studio, shared bathWhy we love it: Fjord views, secluded location, terrace

Perched on rocky terrain above Trondheim Fjord, Dome Smiberget makes the most of its spectacular waterfront setting. The geodesic dome feels wonderfully secluded, surrounded by trees with little between you and the water below. Inside, a wall of honeycomb-shaped windows wraps around the bed and seating area, framing sweeping views across the fjord and letting you watch the sky change without stepping outside. Come evening, you can stargaze from bed, while a small private terrace overlooking the water makes an idyllic spot to sit out when the weather plays along.

Location: Indre Fosen, NorwayThings to do nearby: Ulvestøtta monument, Sukkertoppen mountain hikes

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Outdoor grill, swimming pond, boules court

Drive through the scenic Dresden Elbe meadows to reach this rüdehof, which serves as both the headquarters of a family distillery and a tranquil countryside retreat—best enjoyed under a layer of icing-sugar snow in winter. The igloo is more like a hobbit house, with all you need to shelter from the cold, including a double bed, compact kitchen, shower room, and a dining area with panoramic, bucolic views. You're secluded as can be, around 90 minutes from Hamburg within a two-hectare wild and rugged estate, now yours to explore at your leisure. Stoke the fire and grill outdoors at suppertime, then settle in for some stargazing. If you're feeling brave, there's a swimming pond; then warm up in the hot tub afterwards. A boules court is available for a few leisurely games before supper.

Location: Amt Neuhaus, Niedersachsen, GermanyThings to do nearby: Stixer Wanderdüne hiking paths, Alte Eiche Forsthaus grüner Jäger momumental oak tree, Hamburg

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Fireplace, sledding, northern lights viewing

This is glamping, but not as most know it. On the cusp of Rovaniemi's thick pine forests, this igloo is furnished in true Nordic style with thick down blankets, plenty of wool rugs, cozy bedding, and a crackling log fireplace to huddle around in the evenings. Wrap up and head into the garden for wintry fun, including sledding—or simply huddle under the duvet to watch as frost forms and snow falls gently behind the windows.

Location: Rovaniemi, FinlandThings to do nearby: Ounasvaara Ski Oy ski resort, Ounasvaara Winter Trail, Forestry Museum of Lapland

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: Studio, 1 bathWhy we love it: Panoramic views, breakfast included, kitchenette station

Spain isn't the first place you'd think of for igloo adventures, but this Airbnb might just change your mind. Deep in Spain's Selva de Irati forest, this immersive retreat pairs stylish design with wild beauty, perched on a hilltop overlooking the lush Aezkoa Valley. Interiors are simple and sparse, leaving space to focus on the comfortable silence and the nature that surrounds—there are dreamy panoramic views over the mountains from every angle. Previous guests have loved this experience, saying the sunsets from here are especially lovely. For something a little different, it's hard to beat.

Location: Orbaizeta, SpainThings to do nearby: Mirador de Zamariain viewpoint, Museo de Roncesvalles, Irati Forest

#6288. United went big on credit cards in 2026. More changes are coming, MileagePlus boss says

Before he ran United Airlines' MileagePlus program, Jarad Fisher was the type of traveler who went "all-in" for elite status.

He read TPG, collected miles and occasionally went on ambitious end-of-year "status runs."

"My wife thought I was nuts," he joked, recalling an epic out-and-back trip to Hawaii 12 years ago — where he never even left the airport — in order to qualify.

Now, Fisher is in charge of United's loyalty program as it undergoes one of its biggest transformations in recent memory.

Ironically, one of his first orders of business was eliminating flight segments as a status metric.

Starting in 2027, "Premier Qualifying Flights" are out. That means United loyalists will no longer be "graded" on how many actual flights they rack up.

Instead, the carrier will rely exclusively on PQPs, which are based on a combination of members' spending, both on flights and on their United credit cards.

United has framed the change as a way to make qualifying for status simpler — though it could make it more challenging for some United flyers.

It will also end the need for eleventh-hour "segment runs" that once had frequent flyers (like Fisher) crisscrossing the country in December to rack up enough elite-qualifying flights.

"That was an old relic," he said, speaking about United's recent changes in an exclusive interview with TPG.

"You're taking seats away from people who actually want to get to a certain destination. It's not great for the environment. It's not a great use of time," he explained. "We thought it made more sense for them to have one, consistent metric."

That's not the only change United has made to MileagePlus in 2026.

Earlier this year, the carrier upended several of its loyalty policies, heavily tilting its program toward members who carry one of its credit cards.

Together, these moves were among the most aggressive any U.S. airline has made to nudge flyers toward its cobranded credit cards.

It's part of a larger strategy Fisher often sums up with this mantra:

"It's good to fly United, it's great to be a MileagePlus member," he said. "But the best way to engage with us is to be a MileagePlus member and actually have one of our cards."

Speaking publicly this year, United's chief commercial officer, Andrew Nocella, has hinted that United's loyalty shakeup isn't done.

It appears some changes may have to wait until the airline can re-negotiate its credit card deal with banking partner Chase.

"While we continue to work under a long-term cobrand contract," Nocella said on an earnings call in April, "We're making changes to what we can control today."

United's current Chase deal is set to run through 2029, according to past TPG reporting.

For now, the carrier has significantly upped the incentives for customers to carry one of its cards in the first place: Over the past year, United's cobranded credit card holders have clearly gained the upper hand in its program.

Fisher said the airline plans to continue adapting the program in ways "that will be more consistent" with that ethos in the coming years.

"And so I think as a function of that, we're looking at not only the core loyalty program, we're looking at our partnerships," he said. "And we're trying to make it so that we will continue to be — not just the best airline loyalty program — but we're really aspiring to be the best loyalty program in the world."

What future changes could MileagePlus members ultimately see when they go to redeem miles, earn on their Lyft rides or enter a United Club?

And Fisher will play a big part in those decisions, after taking the helm of MileagePlus this year with an intriguing pedigree.

Seven years ago, he was heavily involved in the launch of Apple Card.

Before that, he spent time at top rival Delta Air Lines, helping turbocharge its partnership with American Express — which today is the industry's most lucrative tie-up, set to bring Delta $9 billion this year.

That resume has Fisher thinking beyond earn rates and status benchmarks as he looks to build on changes that gave United flyers plenty to digest in 2026.

"We're really trying to think about what will truly help us break away from the pack," he said of the carrier's future plans.

Of course, that's easier said than done in the airline world.

Flight delays are inevitable. Loyal flyers can grow frustrated when they go to book a redemption and are shocked by how many miles they'll need.

Not to mention, complimentary status upgrades don't clear as often as they used to, as first-class seats are increasingly filled by customers who actually paid for their tickets. By the way, balancing paid first-class seats with those long upgrade queues is a dilemma Fisher said the airline is "consistently looking at."

"More folks are paying for [premium seats], which of course is putting pressure on the system," he acknowledged.

But for an airline that has made plenty of waves in recent years — from its on-board internet to its international routes — it's safe to say United won't shy away from trying new things on the loyalty front, either.

And it's a likely bet that customers who carry its credit cards will benefit most.

"If you think about the amount of time people spend with us, and on board our aircraft, we want them to feel known. We want them to feel recognized," he said. "You will continue to see us become even more focused and deliberate about that approach."
