#6287. Review: Emirates 777-300ER “Game Changer” First Class Dubai To Brussels

Seven years after my first flight in Emirates’ fully enclosed Boeing 777 first class suite, I returned to the same route and same flight, EK183, from Dubai to Brussels. The “Game Changer” suite remains extraordinary, but this flight demonstrated that even a superb seat cannot compensate for disappointing service, though perhaps my exceptions were too high? My latest review follows, with the original 2019 review preserved below for comparison.

I first reviewed this product in 2019 and came away impressed. Returning in 2026, I was curious whether it would feel quite as special after experiencing more of the world’s leading first class products. The suite certainly did. The experience around it was less consistent, especially compared with my excellent Emirates A380 flight from Mumbai to Dubai.

As I explained in the introduction to this trip report, I booked Mumbai–Dubai–Brussels for 102,000 Emirates Skywards miles and approximately $700 in taxes and fees. That included my A380 flight the day before and this flight to Brussels on a Boeing 777-300ER featuring Emirates’ “Game Changer” first class suites.

I took an Uber from my hotel to DXB. Emirates has a dedicated terminal for business and first class check-in and within area, there’s a posh first class check-in lobby.

However, with so many first class passengers, there is not the sort of personalized ground service you might experience with Air France or Lufthansa. After checking in, I was on my own to get through security, passport control, and to the lounge.

I visited both the Concourse A and Concourse B Emirates First Class lounges before my flight.

I reached the gate (further than I thought) about 30 minutes prior to scheduled departure and the flight had fully boarded, with a “final call” announcement from the gate agent and on the monitors.

I settled in onboard, noticing the cabin was booked full. What war?

The first class cabin has six suites in a 1-1-1 configuration with the middle suites having virtual windows (with a live feed of the world outside).

My suite, 1K, included a large table, screen, closet, cabinet for hand luggage, and an oversized, plush “dentist” chair. Sounds simple enough, but the accents were tremendous and I loved that Emirates’ first class cabin has ditched most (but not all) of the gold bling for a more refined look…it’s just so odd that after all these years Emirates has only retrofitted nine jets with this product.

There’s also a flip-up cabinet with a mirror that houses the amenity kit skin products and a cool souvenir notebook and pen.

The suite has universal A/C, USB-A, and USB-C power (plus HDMI for those still living in 2012).

There are also plenty of lighting options.

Within the suite, you can customize your experience not only via adjusting the seat from upright to reclined to fully-flat, but you can adjust the temperature and lighting (even the color of the lighting).

I didn’t need to sleep on this daytime flight to Brussels, but I ended up taking a 4-hour nap: the bedding is superb and the 79-inch bed very comfortable in 180º lie-flat mode.

In terms of the hard product alone, this seats beats out the JAL A350-1000 suite. But of course a flight is about more than the seat, especially in first class….

Emirates’ “ICE” entertainment system includes hundreds of movies, TV shows, live TV, music, and games…more than enough for a journey around the sun, let alone a quick trip to Europe.

Noise cancelling headphones are from Bowers & Wilkins.

While this flight did not have Starlink Wi-Fi, the OnAir internet was complimentary and worked reasonably well, even if it felt more like dial-up than high speed.

It was also a lovely day just to look out the window, especially as we neared Brussels.

Upon boarding, I was offered a refreshing glass of Champagne and chose Dom Rosé 2010.

Menus were distributed prior to pushback, with a la carte breakfast and lunch choices available throughout the flight. along with an exceptional collection of wine and spirits plus a “movie snack bar” menu.

I thought the breakfast choices were limited. My omelet was fine, but I’ve had much better omelets on other carriers and even had a better one out of Mumbai on Emirates the day before.

Service began with fresh fruit, a cappuccino, orange juice (with ice cubes?), rhubarb yogurt, and delicious bakery items like a cinnamon bun and almond croissant.

The omelet had beans, potatoes, and cooked spinach with it…utterly forgettable.

After waking up from extended nap, it was time for the main feast. While my meal was being prepared, I was offered mix nuts and hydrated with some sparkling water.

The caviar course was excellent and I had more Dom Pérignon Rosé with it.

Next came fabulous Arabic mezze with humus, grape leaves, tabbouleh, falafel, kibbeh, and fattoush salad..everything was great.

With time running out, I skipped the soup and went right for my main course: pan-fried lamb loin and cutlet, served with olive caramel sauce, tomato fondue, beetroot jus, potato pavé with pistachio dukkah-crusted kale, and blanched sugar snap peas.

Sadly, it was so overdone that I did not finish it. However, I did enjoy some excellent garlic bread and red wine (a Bibi Graetz Colore 2015 from Tuscany) with it.

Lunch ended with a cheese course and chocolate truffle cake (with roasted hazelnuts and pistachios). The cheese included:

The “new” 777 has two lavatories in the front of the cabin, shared by crew. They are spacious, though not like upstairs on the A380:

I was never proactively offered an amenity kit. When we landed, I asked about it and was told, “They are on request only.” So be aware of that…

Slippers and pajamas (what Emirates class loungewear) was proactively offered. I took size medium, which fit me (I’m 6’1″) and was very comfortable.

As I mentioned above, skin products from Byredo were present in the suite.

I’ll repeat what I wrote in my first impressions of this flight.

After breakfast, my dishes sat for over 20 minute untouched. Not the service I was expecting.

I woke up a couple hours before landing for the meal and was totally ignored for almost 30 minutes (and my suite door was open). I realize that I could have just pressed the call button (and eventually did), but I don’t think that should be necessary in first class…I think that the FAs should have been far more proactive in monitoring the cabins.

When I did call the FAs to begin meal service, there was 90 minutes left in the flight, which in theory should have been time for everything. I provided the full order and the caviar came quick, but once again the crew was not attentive. I finished the caviar and waited. Finally, the mezze came and I finished it…and waited. I waited and waited for the main course and it came (having been left in the oven far too long).

I waited again. The captain announced our descent into Brussels. My glass was empty, my plate was pushed way, but no one was coming.

Do I really have to push the call button after I finish each course? That’s not the kind of first class service I like.

With 40 minutes left in the flight, I finally flagged a FA down and asked her to bring the cheese and dessert at once. She seemed very agitated, not in the hostile sense, but because she was so stressed…because it wasn’t only me trying to finish my lunch, but the other four in the cabin (it was booked 5/6).

She brought over the cheese and dessert and I ate it…it was fine…but I felt too guilty ordering coffee with so little time left…again, not a feeling I should have in first class. Drink refills were not offered.

The pre-arrival service could have been so much better executed. The service flow was so perfect on my A380 flight because the flight attendants took charge and proactively executed service. Not so on this flight and it wasn’t because the FAs were too busy: they were chatting in the galley.

So was it was the best flight ever? Nope. The A380 flight the day before was perfect…this one was not.

I think it’s always appropriate to mention here that I am incredibly grateful to fly first class on Emirates and this sort of “first world problem” is not meant to condemn Emirates or gripe so much as it is to offer an honest comparison between this and other premium cabin products. Comparatively speaking, Emirates fell short here.

Despite the questionable service, what a pleasure it was to fly on this product and enjoy the beautiful suite and multi-course meals. I look forward to doing this again. Next time, though, I think I’ll skip breakfast and just have one meal in the middle of the flight.

The review below was originally published on June 7, 2019, and covers my earlier flight from Dubai to Brussels.

I booked my ticket from Dubai to Brussels a couple night before the trip using Emirates Skywards. The points transfer on a 1:1 basis from American Express Membership Rewards and the trip cost 85,000 miles and about $420 in taxes/fees. The same trip would have been 75,000 miles with Qantas, which has now been added as an American Express transfer partner.

I began the day with a 4:00 A.M. cab ride to Dubai International Airport from the Park Hyatt. Although I tired to sleep, I was too excited for the upcoming journey. Pulling up to the Emirates premium class check-in area Dubai, a line of uniformed staff were waiting to assist with luggage, but today I was traveling only with hand baggage.

Inside, I  found myself the only passenger in a huge terminal…it felt a bit surreal. After checking in, I proceeded down a long hallway toward the security checkpoint and passport control.

After a couple hours in the first class lounge, I headed to the gate for boarding, which began ahead of schedule about an hour prior to takeoff.

B1 is used for aircraft departing from remote stands and passengers were being funneled down a single escalator and onto a waiting bus. I tried to board but was told to wait and that first class boarding would begin “soon”. So I waited. And waited. And waited. 25 minutes passed. I was getting antsy. So were the three other first class passengers. We were the only ones left in the gate area.

Finally, we were invited to head downstairs where our “first class” bus was awaiting. I don’t know if “first class” was the right word, but the bus was very comfortable. We soon began what turned out to be a 15-minute bus ride to the aircraft…which seemed to be parked in Abu Dhabi (I jest…). Upon reaching the aircraft, we were invited to carry our own bags up the fairly steep air stairs onto the 777-300ER that would shortly be departing for Brussels.

Onboard, three FAs were waiting at the door. After a warm welcome, one escorted me to my suite.

I was grinning ear-to-ear as I stepped into the beautiful six-seat cabin. Wow, this was spacious! The cabin is arranged in a 1-1-1 configuration with four window/aisle suites and two suites in the middle, one with an entrance on aisle one and the other with an entrance on aisle two.

My suite, 2K, included a large table, screen, closet, cabinet for hand luggage, and an oversized, plush chair. Sounds simple enough, but the accents were tremendous and I loved that Emirates’ latest first class cabin has ditched most (but not all) of the gold bling for a more refined look.

What I appreciated most about this new cabin was the attention to detail Emirates placed in making it practical. For example, my rollerboard carry-on fit perfectly in the cabinet, which was so much more convenient and aesthetically pleasing than having to leave it under the ottoman (like in Singapore or Etihad First Class) or store it in a closet (Lufthansa First Class) or overhead bin (Air France First Class).

There was also a closet that easily accommodated my garment bag and clothes on a hangar and smaller storage cabinets along the window.

A power port and USB charger was conveniently located within arm’s reach, as was a USB-C charger (which my laptop has…).

Adjacent to my seat was a touch panel that allowed for control of the lighting (including customizable mood lighting) and the temperature of the suite. The armrest also had a four-button seat control.

In addition the drink cabinet, there was a basket with snacks sitting on the table along with beautiful orchids:

But the attention to detail went even further. The careful stitching on the seat and embroidered Ghaf (prosopis cineraria) tree above the window further showed how much thought Emirates put into this cabin. And the overhead lights were shaped like diamonds.

Each suite had binoculars to look out. These were not souvenirs; FAs collected them as we approached Brussels.

The suite across the aisle from me stayed vacant, so I had a chance to check out the “fake” windows”. Kudos to Emirates for trying, but I was not impressed.

I structured the flight around a nap…not because I wanted to sleep through a pricey flight, but because I slept poorly the previous two nights and wanted to try out the bed and bedding.

Thus, shortly after my post-takeoff breakfast flight attendants prepared the bed for me while I changed into my pajamas. The bedding is simply tremendous, with a satin-like finish that was soft and so comfortable.

Window shades lower by button (sheer blinds and blackout) but Emirates also added real curtains. While I figured these were purely for aesthetic reasons, light seeped through one of my three windows so it turns out the curtains were quite practical.

The only annoying thing was that I could not figure out how to shut off the small band of blue light overhead:

I slept for about 3.5 hours, asking the FAs to shake me awake with about two hours to go until landing.

Prior to pushback, I was offered a drink of choice and chose orange juice, which was freshly-squeezed. Later on in the boarding process, I was also offered Arabic coffee and a choice of dates.

After takeoff, I examined the menu for today’s flight:

Having had steak for “breakfast” I was actually in the mood for some eggs, but only a light continental breakfast was offered. No problem…I wasn’t all that hungry. The purser, Ashwin, came by to introduce himself and took my breakfast order. I just wanted some fruit and yogurt along with a cappuccino. Almost immediately, my table was prepared by Tetiana and I was offered more orange juice along with a basket of warmed breakfast breads.

The table folds out from the console in front:

Mixed nuts were also offered and I enjoyed a glass of Dom Pérignon 2008 Champagne.

I do try to stay away from these fatty carbs, but the croissants smelled so good I ended up eating two of them…and some danish. So much for my light breakfast…

The fruit, yogurt, and cappuccino (notice the chocolate powder stencil art is the Emirates logo?) were all tasty and the whole breakfast service took only about 20 minutes. I still had plenty of time for sleep and a big feast prior to landing.

I was presented with a hot towel after my breakfast dishes were cleared.

After my nap, Tetiana again set up my tray table for lunch.

Hot bread from the oven and my favorite Isigny Sainte-Mère butter from France were offered.

I started the meal off with some more Dom, though this time some Dom Pérignon Rose 2006. It was served at the perfect temperature and was a spectacular accompaniment to the meal which would follow.

I began with caviar, admittedly more so for the trip report than because I felt like it. Still, I ate it and enjoyed it. I appreciated that Emirates warmed the blinis.

While I was eating my soup, Maria brought over my next course, a green salad with French dressing.

For my main course, I ordered a beef filet with asparagus and boiled potatoes. The dish was beautifully presented and the asparagus with truffle hollandaise sauce was spectacular…even better than Lufthansa First Class.

But the beef filet? Not so much…it was served beyond well-done and I ended up only nibbling at it. Such a shame that it was served overcooked. Tetiana was concerned that I did not eat and offered to bring me something else, but by this point I was already full and there were still two courses left.

As you can read in the menu above, the cheese course was quite extensive. I had a sample of each piece, but could not finish it.

Finally, I completed my meal with warm chocolate cake with raspberry sauce and another cappuccino.

Kudos to Emirates for an excellent dining experience in first class.

Emirates does not offer amenity kits on daytime flights. That said, there were several toiletries available in the lavatory and a box at each seat contained Byredo (Swedish) amenities like eye cream and skin toner. The amenities were “hidden” away in a cabinet along the table that folded up to reveal a mirror with lights. A leather-bound notebook and writing pen were also present.

Pajamas were available by request. Emirates uses “breathing” pajamas that are supposed to help the body stay ventilated. While that may just be a gimmick , I loved the soft pajamas and they have become my new favorite airline pajamas…my old favorites were also from Emirates.

Finally, the slippers were also quite comfortable and also large enough for my feet.

Ok, this is what surprised me the most. I knew the flight would have wireless internet, but like all (and I do mean ALL) my previous Emirates flights, I just assumed it would not work. Boy was I wrong. Not only was the internet functional and free (as a Skywards member), it was FAST!

Make sure your Skywards number is associated with your reservation in order to take advantage of the complimentary wi-fi.

On the other hand, the IFE was no surprise. I knew Emirates would offer a comprehensive library of movies, TV shows, live TV, games, and music and of course it did. There were even two cameras to allow for live views from outside.

What did impress me, however, was the wireless remote in the suite and the detachable tablet that served as a secondary IFE device, especially suited for games and music. When detached, it was totally wireless and also controlled the seat, could summon FAs via video conference for service, and easily controlled my customized soundtracks.

Newspapers were offered prior to takeoff.

Lastly, the Bowers & Wilkins noise-cancelling headphones were comfortable and worked very well.

Two first class lavatories were compact, but kept very clean and offered towels, Buglari toiletries, and other amenities like toothbrushes and combs. There were even little bars of soap like airlines used to offer decades ago.

Tetiana, Maria, and Ashwin provided excellent service from start to finish. Tetiana and Maria primarily took care of me and were not only lovely and charming, but highly polished. I appreciated how precisely the table was set, drinks were poured, and food served. I never had to wait long between courses and plates and utensils were always promptly cleared. Throughout the flight, I was addressed by last name.

Upon landing in Brussels I requested a picture of the flight crew and they happily obliged:

The only problem with this flight was that it ended so quickly. 6.5 hours was not enough time to fully enjoy the wonderful hard and soft product onboard. I was simply ecstatic throughout the flight…Emirates takes first class to a whole new level.

Was this my best first class flight ever? I don’t know if I’d go that far, but it was absolutely the best first class hard product (suite) I have ever experienced. While the old Emirates suite is still very nice, the new suite is even more spacious, even more comfortable, and even more cutting-edge.

Emirates has room for improvement with its first class ground product, but its in-air product is top-notch.

#6286. United card bonuses: Best-ever offers on 2 of the personal cards

If you're planning a dream getaway soon, now is a great time to determine your earning strategy and rack up those points and miles. One of the easiest ways to amass a large chunk of rewards is through credit card welcome bonuses, and several United cards are currently offering elevated, limited-time offers.

All six United credit cards currently have elevated welcome offers that meet our threshold for when to apply. Two of those offers — on the entry-level and mid-tier personal cards — are at the highest we've seen, making now the perfect time to apply.

Chase issues United's cobranded cards, so make sure to keep its application rules in mind.

Let's look at each card's current welcome offer.

Here's a comparison of the current United credit card offers:

*Welcome offer value is determined using TPG's November 2026 valuations and is not provided by nor reviewed by the issuer.

The information for the United Club Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The United Club Card is the top-tier United card. It's aimed at loyal United flyers who want an elevated experience.

Welcome bonus: Earn up to 100,000 bonus miles: Earn 90,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn an additional 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,200 (including miles from adding an authorized user).

While not the highest offer in the card's history, it meets our recommendation for applying (when at least 90,000 miles are offered). If United status is on the table for you, it may make sense to wait for an offer that includes bonus Premier qualifying points.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Club Card.

The United Business Card is the more affordable of the two United business cards. It's a good choice if you're a small-business owner watching your budget but wanting to earn United miles and enjoy some perks when flying.

Welcome bonus: Earn up to 100,000 bonus miles and 2,000 PQPs: Earn 90,000 bonus miles and 2,000 PQPs after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,200 (including miles from adding an authorized user; excluding the value of the PQPs).

While not the highest bonus we've seen on this card, it meets our threshold for when to apply and is especially valuable if you want to qualify or requalify for status.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Business Card.

The United Club Business Card is the higher-tier option of the two United business cards. It's suited to high-spending small-business owners who want premium perks with United.

Welcome bonus: Earn up to 100,000 bonus miles and 2,000 PQPs: Earn 90,000 bonus miles and 2,000 PQPs after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,200 (including miles from adding an authorized user; excluding the value of the PQPs).

We've seen higher offers on this card, but the current bonus is still valuable, especially if you are chasing status.

Learn more: United Club Business Card review

The United Quest Card is the airline's upper-mid-tier card for frequent flyers. It's best for frequent United flyers who want travel perks without paying a steep annual fee.

Welcome bonus: Earn up to 90,000 bonus miles and 500 PQPs: Earn 500 PQPs after your first purchase and 80,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $1,080 (including miles from adding an authorized user; excluding the value of the PQPs).

Although not the highest offer we've seen, it meets our threshold for when to apply.

The 500 PQPs included in the bonus can also help you move closer to earning United Premier elite status. TPG credit cards writer Stephanie Stevens earned United Premier Silver status thanks to the PQP jump-start she earned through her Quest Card.

For United flyers who check bags regularly and fly multiple times per year, the additional perks may justify the higher annual fee compared to lower-tier United cards.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Quest Card.

The United Explorer Card is a great option for those who want to enjoy United benefits at a reasonable cost.

Welcome bonus: Earn up to 80,000 bonus miles: Earn 70,000 bonus miles after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $960 (including miles from adding an authorized user).

This matches the highest bonus we've seen on this card. Just note that this time you need to add an authorized user to reach the full 80,000-mile bonus.

Annual fee: $0 introductory annual fee for the first year, then $150

To learn more, read our full review of the United Explorer Card.

The entry-level United Gateway Card has no annual fee. It's a good option for those who fly occasionally with the airline and want to earn United miles.

Welcome bonus: Earn up to 50,000 bonus miles: Earn 40,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $600 (including the miles from adding an authorized user).

This is the best-ever bonus we've seen on this card, making now the best time to apply.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Gateway Card.

While United's dynamic award pricing can make it difficult to score high-value redemptions, the airline does offer some solid benefits for loyal flyers. Its award sales provide excellent redemption options, sometimes starting at just a few thousand miles per ticket.

The airline also doesn't impose fuel surcharges on award tickets (which can easily save you hundreds of dollars).

It's also a Chase transfer partner, which can help you earn United miles across multiple credit cards. The airline's Star Alliance membership means you can redeem miles with the other roughly 25 member airlines, including Air New Zealand, Lufthansa and Turkish Airlines.

By taking advantage of low-cost domestic award tickets (such as flying from Houston to Orlando for as little as 3,500 miles), you can stretch the miles you earn with your credit cards to help you plan your upcoming trips.

Or, go big and start saving miles toward a fancy United Polaris business-class flight.

Related: How to get maximum value from the United MileagePlus program

Taking advantage of a United welcome bonus can get you closer to your next trip. Plus, if you're interested in the elevated bonuses available, now is a great time to apply.

Before you put in your application, ensure you're aware of Chase's 5/24 rule: If you have opened five or more accounts in the past 24 months, you may have difficulty getting approved for these cards.

If you're successful in applying, you'll be well on your way to a more elevated flying experience with United and its partner airlines.

#6285. The 15 Most Haunted Places in the World and How to Visit Them

The most haunted places in the world may seem like something out of a fable that defies all logic. They're places where UFOs hover over Transylvanian forests, headless queens roam through castle corridors, and ghosts take shape of bears, children, and any other creature imaginable. No matter where you’re traveling, you’re sure to find some sort of haunted landmark, hotel, even landmark-turned-hotel—and usually a ghost tour to go along with it.

You might be guided more by scholarly than ghastly pursuits, though these locations are still worth your time. Spectral hauntings often come with spectacular history, architecture, and artwork, not to mention proximity to incredible cities and natural beauty. Whether you’re scheming up a Halloween trip or simply want to entertain the chills with a dash of the macabre, explore 15 of the most haunted places in the world below, if you dare.

Over the span of nearly one millennium, the Tower of London has served as an armory, prison, menagerie, and palace. Though best known today for its housing of the Crown Jewels, the UNESCO World Heritage Site also falls among the most haunted places in the United Kingdom. It's not uncommon to hear strange noises echo through the White Tower, while over a dozen ghosts—with backstories that range from ridiculous to outright tragic—are said to lurk in its limestone hallways.

The most infamous apparition is that of Anne Boleyn, Henry VIII's second wife, who was executed in the tower in 1536 for being found guilty for treason and adultery. Today, some visitors may encounter her headless body roaming about, head in hand. Other specters include two young princes who were mysteriously murdered in the 1400s and even multiple accounts of a phantom bear, who made multiple appearances in the 1800s and was said to leave any witness dead.

There are two long-running explanations for the curses that plague this 16th-century fort in Rajasthan. The first is that a religious ascetic had destroyed the fort and nearby towns after its height surpassed that of his own home, casting Bhangarh in perpetual shadow. The second, equally melodramatic, is that a black magic priest fell in love with a princess and was crushed to death by a boulder after she rejected him; right before he passed, however, he condemned the premises to a fate of destruction.

Today, the scene at the fort is quite serene, and visitors can wander throughout royal palace ruins, Hindu temples such as Gopinath and Hanuman, as well as old marketplaces and townhouses like Nartakiyon Ki Haveli. The fort is open each day from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m., as no visitors—those living, at least—can legally stay after sunset.

Built by lumber magnate Carl Beck for his family in the late 1800s, this house in Penetanguishene is one of Ontario's most troublesome. Legend goes that after Beck's wife passed away, his eldest daughter Mary was put in charge of raising her younger siblings. Years later, when Carl died, he inexplicably left Mary $1 in his will. Today, an angry female ghost—presumably Mary—is said to appear in the upstairs windows (you’d probably haunt the house too if your dad gave you a $1 inheritance). For any travelers curious about Victorian architecture with a side of paranormality, consider renting the Carl Beck House on Airbnb.

What's far scarier than a haunted graveyard? A haunted graveyard 50 feet underwater. Micronesia’s Chuuk Lagoon (formerly Truk Lagoon) served as a fortified base for the Japanese Navy during World War II and was attacked by American forces during a three-day air strike in 1944. Dozens of warships, planes, tanks, and railroad cars sank to the bottom of the lagoon, where they still remain in what is known as the “Ghost Fleet of Truk Lagoon.”

The ship graveyard is immensely popular amongst scuba divers, with PADI dubbing it “one of the best wreck diving destinations on the planet.” Underwater explorers can swim up close to the wartime vessels, which are littered with weapons, gas masks, and, according to some superstitious divers, a few waterlogged ghosts.

This Victorian-era prison in Belfast is often referred to as Europe’s Alcatraz and for good reason. During its 150 years of operation, the jail contained some 25,000 inmates (men, women, and children), publicly hung many prisoners, and buried their bodies within the prison walls. The institution officially shut its doors in 1996, but the ghosts of deceased inmates are said to still roam the iron walkways today.

If this sounds like the sort of place you want to spend time in, you’re in luck—Crumlin Road Gaol offers daily tours, live concerts, and reasonably priced meals at its in-house (in-prison?) restaurant. It even serves as a venue for conferences and, believe it or not, weddings.

Though travelers have been coming to Estes Park since 1909 to enjoy The Stanley Hotel’s stately Georgian architecture and world-renowned whiskey bar, its reputation took a dark turn on October 30, 1974, when Stephen King and his wife, Tabitha, checked in. The hotel was about to close for the season, and the couple were the only guests there. King was particularly struck by the endless empty corridors that he walked through after dinner, and the property as a whole ended up serving as inspiration for The Shining’s Overlook Hotel.

Of the eerie stay, King said, “[The hotel] seemed the perfect—maybe the archetypical—setting for a ghost story. That night I dreamed of my three-year-old son running through the corridors, looking back over his shoulder, eyes wide, screaming. He was being chased by a fire-hose. I woke up with a tremendous jerk, sweating all over, within an inch of falling out of bed.” In the years since, the hotel has leaned into the reputation King bestowed upon it with ghost tours and a resident psychic.

Named after a shepherd who, along with his flock of 200 sheep, vanished without a trace in the forest, Hoia-Baciu hit it big in 1968 when a military technician photographed a supposed UFO hovering over the trees. Some believe it to be a portal capable of transporting visitors to places unknown. Those who pass through (and live to tell the tale) have reported rashes, nausea, and anxiety. The curved, spindly trees that make up the forest are particularly conducive to a twisted feeling, as is the location in Transylvania—a real nexus point of abnormal activity.

The St. Augustine Lighthouse is visited by over 200,000 people annually, though it's just as well-known for its otherworldly guests. Several tragic events that occurred at the now-historic site have contributed to the alleged paranormal activity. The ghost of a lighthouse keeper who fell to his death while painting the tower has been spotted watching over the grounds. Ever since the horrific death of three young girls, who drowned when the cart they were playing in broke and fell into the ocean, visitors have claimed to hear the sounds of children playing in and around the lighthouse.

Less than half a mile from the canals of Venice, Poveglia Island has served as a quarantine zone for bubonic plague victims, storage space for Napoleon’s weapons, and the site of an early 20th-century psychiatric hospital. The latter played host to horrific medical experiments and finally closed for good in 1968 after a doctor threw himself off the institution’s bell tower. Locals still claim to hear echoing chimes from the island—even though the bell was removed decades ago. Though it's illegal to visit Poveglia, you can see the island and decaying hospital at a safe distance from the beaches of nearby Lido or by hiring your own boat charter to pass a little closer (do not disembark onto the island).

Himeji Castle dates to 1333 and is regarded as one of the greatest remaining examples of Japanese castle architecture. It also has some rather eerie folklore associated with it—most notably the story of Okiku, a palace servant who was falsely accused of losing valuable dishes and thrown to her death in the castle’s well as punishment. Her ghost now sulks in the castle at night, counting dishes in a mournful tone; she reaches nine before shrieking and returning to the well’s depths. A visit to Himeji Castle is best done as a day trip from Osaka, about two hours away by train.

On the northern edge of Ireland's Wicklow Mountains, at the summit of Montpelier Hill, the ruins of a lone building remain. As many tales begin, the hill was originally site to an ancient grave, which wealthy Irishman William Conolly disregarded (even taking stones from) while building a hunting lodge in the 1720s. It's no surprise that terror ensued, and after Conolly's death, private club Hell Fire Club occupied the space, where they were said to engage in black masses, ritual murder, and other occultish happenings. At one such meeting, an unfamiliar guest with horse hooves as feet disappeared as mysteriously as they arrived. A curious farmer who had witnessed another night unfold was apparently left so terrified he no longer remembered his own name. Today, an enormous black cat with striking eyes is said to haunt Montpelier, which, beyond its murky past, offers forest trails and guided paths that make for an otherwise pleasant walk (before dusk).

Hidden among the canals of Xochimilco, Isla de las Muñecas (“Island of the Dolls”) is something of an internet legend and dark tourism mecca. The backstory centers on a man named Julian Santa Barrera, who reportedly encountered the body of a girl floating in the channels. Shortly thereafter, he found a discarded doll in the same canals, and he hung it from a tree on an artificial island in her honor—and to ward off evil spirits. So he continued, adding more and more dolls to appease the ghost of the young girl.

After Barrera passed away in 2001, his family opened the island to the public, and travelers have been seeking it out ever since. As if the mere idea of the island isn’t unnerving enough, there have also been reports of the dolls whispering to each other and moving their eyes.

Often considered the “king of Czech castles,” this early Gothic fortress in South Bohemia has undergone sieges and assaults from the 1400s onward, though, today, the source of its terrors is an impish creature called Rarášek, who is said to trip and poke at any unassuming visitor. A ghastly woman, known only as “the White Lady,” also resides here, while hellhounds allegedly guard a secret passage to the castle tombs.

Beyond the paranormal, visitors can enjoy self-guided tours through Zvíkov's cellars, courtyards, and rooms—be sure to stop and take a look at St. Wenceslas Chapel's frescoes.

The entire city of Savannah is essentially one giant ghost story, due in large part to the mysterious tunnels that run below the town’s streets. The underground structures play a major role in many of Savannah's most haunted locations, including Forsyth Park, the fountained green space you probably recognize from a postcard or two.

According to Savannah Magazine, doctors at the adjacent Candler Hospital (now the Savannah Law School) performed autopsies in the tunnels below. Maria Pinheiro, a historian and spokesperson with Ghost City Tours, says these below-the-surface rumblings make Forsyth Park particularly ripe for sightings of shadowy shapes that, even if unclear, it's certain they are not of this world.

This article has been updated since its original publish date.

We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

A few years ago, on a damp evening in late March in London, I learned the hard way that countries don’t all change their clocks for daylight saving time simultaneously. After ordering a glass of white wine at a cozy bar in Bermondsey, I mindlessly scrolled on my phone while the bartenders chatted about the clocks jumping forward that coming Sunday. I nearly spit out my Chablis.

Back home in New York City, I had already skipped ahead one hour on the second Sunday in March. As I frantically Googled, I learned that in the United Kingdom, the clocks go forward one hour on the last Sunday in March (and back one hour on the last Sunday in October).

Don’t be like me and lose two hours of sleep in one month. When you travel, remember the following to avoid daylight saving time-related snafus and other time zone mistakes — and if you're in the U.S., most states fell back one hour on Sunday, Nov. 1.

The U.K. isn’t the only country that changes its clocks on a different weekend than we do in the U.S. For example, most European countries follow the same calendar as the U.K., moving clocks forward one hour on the last Sunday in March and back one hour on the last Sunday in October.

Generally, when traveling in the spring and fall, it’s always best to check when the country you’re going to falls forward or backward — and also whether that country observes daylight saving time at all. In fact, according to the Pew Research Center, about 66% of the world doesn’t.

Though daylight saving time is commonly observed in North America and Europe, many non-European Union countries in Europe — including Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Iceland, Russia and Turkey — stay on standard time year-round.

In 2023, Egypt became the only country in Africa to change its clocks when it reintroduced daylight saving time for the first time in seven years. Now, each year, its clocks move forward one hour on the last Friday in April and backward one hour on the last Thursday in October.

It’s also worth double-checking these things even if you're traveling within the U.S. In 48 states, daylight saving time runs from the second Sunday in March to the first Sunday in November. Arizona and Hawaii are the outliers that stay on standard time year-round. While it’s less of an issue on an island like Hawaii, Arizona shares enough borders with other states that do observe daylight saving time that it can be problematic.

“Always double-check timing when flying in/out and on road trips through the state,” Becky Blaine, TPG’s newsletter managing editor and former Arizona resident, said. Otherwise, you can risk missing a flight or a reservation.

To keep it simple, remember that Arizona is in the Pacific Daylight Time zone from mid-March to early November, and the rest of the year it’s in the same time zone as other states in Mountain Standard Time.

It’s a similar situation in Canada. Generally, Canada follows the same daylight saving schedule as the U.S., but most of Saskatchewan, the Yukon and some parts of Quebec and British Columbia stay on standard time year-round.

In Australia, daylight saving time starts the first Sunday in October and ends the first Sunday in April in the Australian Capital Territory, New South Wales, South Australia, Tasmania and Victoria; meanwhile, the Northern Territory, Queensland and Western Australia don’t observe it.

Outside of daylight saving time changes, there are some general time zone issues to be aware of while traveling.

In countries as large as the U.S., Canada and Australia, it’s easy to see why there are so many time zones. But Eric Rosen, TPG’s director of travel content, also pointed out that the airport in the Maldives is in a different time zone than some resorts in the tiny island nation.

Technically, the Maldives has only one official time zone: Maldives Time, which is five hours ahead of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). However, some of the archipelago's private island resorts add an hour to Maldives Time to maximize their guests' evening light.

For example, The St. Regis Maldives Vommuli Resort sets its clock one hour ahead of the official clock to what it calls "Island Time," but also provides guests with butlers who coordinate transfers to and from the airport so nobody accidentally misses a flight.

Before you go to the Maldives, be sure to check if your resort also does this.

Due to its geographic location, the Canadian island of Newfoundland is 90 minutes ahead of Eastern Time instead of just 60 minutes ahead, as in the rest of Atlantic Canada. On a July trip, Nick Ewen, TPG’s editor-in-chief, found this challenging for calendar purposes.

While traveling in Newfoundland, he received an Outlook invitation to a 7:30 p.m. dinner meeting the following week and accepted it without much thought. However, the actual dinner back home in the U.S. started at 6 p.m. — a detail he completely missed until the reminder popped up 15 minutes before. At that point, he realized he would be late.

Other places offset from UTC by 30 minutes include India, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, Iran and some states in Australia. Want to be confused even more? Nepal's time zone is offset by 45 minutes due to its geography.

Even when not dealing with half-hour time zones, it can be easy to make similar mistakes when adding events back home to your digital calendar while traveling in a different time zone.

"Last year, I brought my middle son to a birthday party. We were running a few minutes late, but when we arrived, it seemed like the party was almost over," Tarah Chieffi, a senior writer at TPG, said. "While the kids were eating cake, I double-checked my calendar to make sure we had gotten the time right, and it seemed like we had. But then I went to check the invitation, and we had, in fact, arrived one hour late."

Her mistake? When she entered the party into her calendar while traveling, her calendar app defaulted to the time zone she was in and showed her the incorrect time back home.

"Now, I always toggle the time zone to my home time zone if I enter appointments into my calendar while I'm traveling," she said.

"Outlook lets you have up to three time zones showing on the calendar," Madison Blancaflor, a managing editor at TPG, said.

Go to "Settings," then "Calendar," then "Time zones." Then, check the box for "Show second time zone in Day and Week view" underneath your default time zone. If you need a third one, you can also check that box.

It's also important to remember that it's possible to quickly encounter multiple time zones on cruises — especially on transoceanic cruises, where you'll change time zones daily or almost daily. And if you're on a cruise traversing the Pacific Ocean, you could lose an entire day if you cross the international date line, like Clint Henderson, TPG's principal spokesperson, did when he sailed from Seward, Alaska, to Tokyo last year.

Related: I made a rookie travel mistake that nearly cost me $4,000 — here's how I fixed it

Even on shorter cruises, check if you'll have to change time zones. When I was on a five-day Alaska cruise earlier this summer, I changed time zones twice as we moved in and out of Alaska Daylight Time on a round-trip sailing from Vancouver (which was one hour ahead, on Pacific Daylight Time).

Cabin stewards usually leave notes on your bed at turndown to remind you of upcoming time changes. Clint said he had to set his clocks back between one and two hours each night on his cruise. But you can't always rely on your cellphone to display the correct time when it’s in airplane mode and using satellite-based internet. Bring an analog watch or an alarm clock to ground you if you're unsure whether your device will update properly.

However, some cruise ships may ignore time changes at select ports. "I've had that happen on Royal Caribbean ships in the Caribbean, for example, to avoid the ship time changing three days in a row," said Christine Gallipeau, a senior editor on TPG's points and loyalty team. "So if you're doing shore excursions, make sure you know what time the ship is following, as it may not necessarily match the local time."

Related: Can a cruise help with jet lag? The answer might surprise you

When traveling, don’t assume every country or state follows the same daylight-saving-time rules and schedules as where you live, and be mindful of time zone anomalies. Losing or gaining an unexpected hour can lead to lost sleep, arriving late to an event and, worst of all, missed flights.

#6283. How Travel Can Be an Antidote to Optimization Culture

I’m seconds away from jumping into the Adriatic Sea from the platform of a 55-foot catamaran aptly named Slice of Heaven when one of my friends says she misses her routine Pilates classes. I try to bite my tongue—I don’t want to be rude!—but I can’t help myself. “Look around,” I say, exasperated. “This is your workout.”

I fling my hand toward the pebbly shore where our captain, Tony, has just dropped anchor in an idyllic bay somewhere between Stari Grad and Vis, along Croatia’s Dalmatian Coast. A forested hillside rises above the beach, and there’s not a single other boat in sight. Tony is busy launching the paddle board into the water, while our hostess, Matea, cooks up a surprise Croatian lunch. The cerulean water is so clear I can see all the way to the seafloor, where colorful fish glimmer in the light.

The author sailed from Split to Dubrovnik on a chartered catamaran dubbed Slice of Heaven.

By any measure, this is paradise, which is exactly why I’m baffled. Who could think about Pilates classes when this is right in front of you?

I love traveling with my friends, many of whom live all over the world—in Latin America, Europe, Africa, the US, and beyond—and this is one of the only ways we get to see each other. The Pilates comment doesn’t come out of nowhere, as we’re a group that keeps things balanced: Each trip usually contains equal parts revelry and cultural activities, loads of wine followed by electrolytes for recovery, and enough belly laughs and deep conversations to sustain us until we book the next getaway.

But recently, I’ve noticed a shift: our trips are becoming less of a break from normal life and moreso an extension of it. We spend more time stressing over holding onto the very routines we seek to escape than we do living in the moment. I understand the pressure to not only be healthy, but to look healthy, because it affects me, too. And now, with wearables like Whoop bands and Oura rings telling us how we feel, rather than the old-fashioned way—listening to our bodies to intuitively know how we feel—we can track our wellness progress. Or lack of it.

Sail Croatia operates the 55-foot catamaran Slice of Heaven for private charters of up to eight guests.

According to the Global Wellness Institute, the wellness economy reached $6.8 trillion in 2024 and is predicted to soar to $9.8 trillion by 2029, while wellness tourism alone reached $894 billion in 2024 and is on track to surpass $1.4 trillion by 2029. McKinsey’s Future of Wellness research even found that 84% of US consumers consider wellness a top priority in their everyday lives. It’s clear most people want to be well, and now more than ever, they’re refusing to leave their routines at home when they travel.

We’d been talking about this trip for months: an eight-day private catamaran tour with Sail Croatia that I intend to enjoy every minute of. I’m not immune to the pressure to be well and look well—especially when I’ll be in a swimsuit for eight days—so I’ve made the ocean my gym for the week, stand-up paddle boarding and swimming in the Adriatic. I know I’ll eat and drink more and sleep less over the next several days, but I also know I’ll swim and walk more and have memories that will last forever.

I take a deep breath and stretch before diving into the sea. When I surface, Tony throws me the paddle, and one of my friends joins me in my “workout.” We wobble around on the board until we successfully balance our weight, which proves even more interesting when Matea hands us two Aperol Spritzes.

I work up a sweat as I paddle us to the cliff walls, where we down our drinks before taking to the shore, acting like children as we take turns cannonballing into the water and climbing the rocks, looking for shells.

Perhaps I’m doing the same thing as my friend, but I’m more secretive about it—turning moments of this trip into an opportunity to stay fit—but for me, getting outside and into the landscape is what I call balance.

Mljet National Park's saltwater lakes are open to the public for swimming.

Over the next few days, we sail from Vis to Hvar, then on to Korčula and Mljet. Croatia exceeds all of my expectations. All I can think about is how blissful it feels to split a lavender cheesecake at San Marco restaurant above Hvar’s St. Stephen’s Square, the biggest in Dalmatia; how dizzying it is to climb the wooden ladder to Massimo in Korčula, a 15th-century tower that’s now a bar, where our cocktails arrive by pulley; and how freeing it feels to cycle the wide lanes beneath Mljet’s forested canopy, where the island’s saltwater lakes offer some of the most serene swimming of the trip.

But as we sail on, I start to notice just how intensely our routines follow us. In the galley next to the coffee maker, our collagen powders are in a neat row. We add some to our coffee every morning. All of us brought our favorite brand of electrolytes, the individual packs so many that they have their own shelf. My contribution is a basket holding as many NAD+ liposomal packs and sheet masks as my carry-on suitcase could fit. As I look at it all lined up, I start wondering where my limit is and whether bringing every protocol with me defeats the point of leaving home in the first place.

As soon as I notice it, I can’t unnotice it. Comments that would have usually blown over my head—or that I would have made myself—start stacking up like our supplements in the galley. Over lunch on the bow, someone mentions she’d kill for her protein smoothie instead of the fresh seafood pasta that Matea just made us. While strolling the limestone streets of Korčula, someone announces she’s in desperate need of a collagen sheet mask. On Mljet, while walking back from the lakes with our wet hair dripping down our backs, someone asks whether anyone has a hair mask, because the sea salt is wrecking hers and ruining her extensions.

Tracking technology isn’t inherently bad. In many cases, it’s helpful—but counting every minute of exercise or every calorie does give me pause. My friends are some of the sharpest, smartest, and most intuitive women I know, and we are all being sold the same promise—the same lie—that I am: That we no longer can gauge if we are well on our own, and that with the right protocol we can somehow outsmart aging, exhaustion, and the general chaos of being human. This is a seductive proposition, even for me.

I’m healthy; I’ve built an entire career writing about wellness and hospitality in all its forms. I die for a week at a medical spa in the mountains. I have an Oura ring I check religiously. I try to hit 10,000 steps a day. I have an unlimited membership to a Pilates studio. I take peptides, creatine, magnesium—the works; I do all of this because I want to feel my best. But when a trip full of paddle boarding, cycling, and hiking somehow isn’t enough—when the sea itself gets reframed as an interruption to a protocol—even I have to call it.

Dubrovnik's Old Town is a complex maze of staircases and alleyways.

This is where I realize I need to draw the line. For me, setting out on a trip has always been about discovery and connection. It’s a given that I’ll have unexpected moments of chaos while navigating an unfamiliar place, often in a language I don’t know, which makes it exhilarating. I find it kind of hilarious to sit down at a restaurant and order a meal and have it arrive nothing like I expected, and the most tremendous of honors to be invited into a home and eat a meal with strangers who quickly become friends. It’s this sense of spontaneity, of surrender, that makes travel worth it for me. Not whether or not these meals hit my macros.

That’s why, when we stop in Ston, known for its oysters and the Great Wall of Europe, and one of my friends comments that she’s finally getting her steps in as we climb the stone stairs and rattles off her Oura ring stats, I pretend not to hear. I’ve already made up my mind; I’ll no longer make my trip about this.

Instead, I choose to marvel at the ancient salt pans glittering below us and the farms scattered across Mali Ston Bay. I take even more joy in savoring freshly shucked oysters at the bayside Bota Šare restaurant.

Ston's Great Wall of Europe is a five-kilometer medieval stone wall with three forts.

On our last day of the trip, we arrive in Dubrovnik just before sunset. We go to one of the best restaurants in town, Gradska Kavana Arsenal, overlooking the Old Port, and for one night, it’s like all of our guards fall. We laugh uncontrollably as we enjoy rounds of champagne, two types of tartare, and a thick piece of chocolate cake. Back on the boat, we do what happens at the end of every trip. We stay up for hours in an attempt to squeeze out the last of our time together, all while lamenting that none of us want the trip to end. It’s been one of the most refreshing trips of my life, and I finally know why.

Aside from Croatia being downright gorgeous, the private catamaran experience felt freeing for a particular reason: It was the opposite of what so many hotels are becoming. It was inherently wellness-oriented without anyone handing us a biohacking menu; healthy meals were prepared for us daily without a detox protocol attached; and without a single workout class included. It was all salt water and sunshine, no supplement or gym equipment required.

Slide of Heaven's salon area hosts meals overlooking the Adriatic Sea

When I finally tuck myself into bed, I do the exact thing most wellness protocols would tell me not to do: I look at my phone. Immediately, I’m served a video from an influencer who has just completed our same itinerary through Croatia, sailing from Split to Dubrovnik.

What catches my attention isn’t her videos of the Dalmatian Coast, but her morning routine. It’s a montage of her waking up at 6 a.m., peeling off her mouth tape and collagen sheet mask, removing a weighted décolletage wrinkle pad, then launching into what seems like a 100-step beauty routine full of serums and LED masks. I don’t judge her for this. If anything, it makes me question if I’m doing enough.

I look through my own photos. Mine tell a different story: an impromptu dance party in Vis with a group of younger French men, grinning from ear to ear at a seaside tavern in Mljet, squid-ink risotto staining my entire smile. A selfie of the girls taken in Korčula during the hour I’d usually meditate but have one of the deepest conversations of our trip instead.

For some travelers, the influencer’s version of the trip isn’t so much a dream as it is a necessity to keep up with ever-evolving beauty standards. Even if I’m leaving the catamaran a little under-rested, sunburned, and salt-crusted—I’d choose our version of the trip every single time.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6282. How Many Flights In One Day? We Tracked A Wideroe Dash 8 For 24 Hours

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

On Wednesday, October 21, a Widerøe Bombardier Dash 8-100 registered LN-WIE flew 17 sectors between eight airports in Arctic Norway. It left Tromsø (TOS) at 04:12 UTC and finished at Lakselv (LKL) at 21:28, spending 8 hours and 34 minutes airborne across an elapsed day of 17 hours and 16 minutes. The shortest flight, Båtsfjord (BJF) to Vadsø (VDS), lasted seven minutes. Five sectors ran under 20 minutes. The aircraft returned to Hammerfest (HFT) five separate times.

None of it exists on commercial merit. These are public service obligation routes, tendered by the Norwegian government and operated under subsidy because no airline would fly them otherwise. Widerøe won all 13 PSO routes in the 2017 tender round, and the Dash 8-100 is the aircraft that makes the arrangement work at 39 seats on short Finnmark runways. Keeping those airframes flying has required De Havilland Canada to certify the type to 160,000 flight cycles, double its original design life and the highest of any commercial aircraft.

On Wednesday, October 21, a Widerøe Dash 8-100 registered LN-WIE operated 17 flights across eight airports in Arctic Norway. The aircraft departed Tromsø Airport (TOS) at 04:12 UTC and arrived at Lakselv Airport (LKL) at 21:28, a span of 17 hours and 16 minutes. We followed the rotation on Simple Flying's Live Flight Tracker, the same approach we took when tracking a Ryanair Boeing 737 through a full day of European short-haul flying.

The two days look nothing alike. LN-WIE spent 8 hours and 34 minutes airborne across its 17 flights, averaging just over 30 minutes per sector. The longest was Tromsø to Kirkenes (KKN) at 1 hour 7 minutes, the only flight of the day to exceed an hour. The shortest was Båtsfjord (BJF) to Vadsø (VDS) at seven minutes. Eleven of the 17 flights lasted 35 minutes or less, and the aircraft completed its first four sectors before 07:30 UTC.

The route pattern is equally unusual. The aircraft arrived at Hammerfest (HFT) five separate times and at Tromsø four, working between those two points and a cluster of smaller airports across Finnmark, Norway's northernmost county. It also reached Alta (ALF), Vardø (VAW), Vadsø, Båtsfjord, Kirkenes and finally Lakselv, where it finished the day rather than returning to where it started. Four of the eight airports were visited more than once. This is not point-to-point flying in any conventional sense. It is one aircraft circling back repeatedly through the same handful of fields, which is a pattern dictated by something other than commercial route planning.

The third sector of the day was Båtsfjord to Vadsø. The aircraft departed at 06:09 UTC and arrived at 06:17. Seven minutes airborne, which is shorter than the taxi time at most major airports. It is the kind of sector that exists nowhere in a conventional airline network, and on this day it was not even unusual.

Four other flights ran under 20 minutes. Vadsø to Båtsfjord in the opposite direction took 10 minutes that evening. Vardø to Vadsø took 11. Kirkenes to Vardø took 15. Hammerfest to Alta took 16. Five of the 17 sectors, nearly a third of the day's flying, lasted under 20 minutes, and together they accounted for 59 minutes of airborne time out of 514. Several were shorter than the turnaround that preceded them, inverting the usual relationship between time airborne and time on the ground.

These sectors are the reason the network exists in this form. The Bombardier Dash 8-100 is the backbone of Widerøe's public service obligation operation in Norway, particularly in the north. The routes connecting Vardø, Vadsø, Båtsfjord and the other Finnmark fields are subsidized by the Norwegian Ministry of Transport and Communications precisely because the distances involved and the populations served do not support commercial air service. The evening sequence makes the logic plain: Kirkenes to Vardø to Vadsø to Båtsfjord, three consecutive sectors totaling 36 minutes airborne, strung together to connect four communities in a single rotation. A seven-minute flight is not an inefficiency in the schedule. It is what the government contracted for.

Air Transat launches Montreal–Istanbul flights, strengthens its Turkish Airlines partnership, and announces five new European routes for 2027.

Across the full rotation, LN-WIE accumulated 8 hours and 34 minutes airborne against an elapsed day of 17 hours and 16 minutes. That leaves 8 hours and 42 minutes between sectors, marginally more time on the ground than in the air. For an aircraft operating 17 flights in a day, the arithmetic is counterintuitive until sector length is taken into account. When half the flights last under 35 minutes, turnaround time becomes the dominant constraint on how many sectors fit into a day.

The turnarounds were quick. The shortest was 18 minutes at Hammerfest, between arriving from Vadsø at 07:26 and departing for Tromsø at 07:44. Several others ran close: 20 minutes at Hammerfest later that morning, 20 minutes at Båtsfjord in the evening, and 22 minutes at Hammerfest, Alta and Vardø. Across the 16 turnarounds, nine were 30 minutes or less, and the median sat at roughly 23 minutes.

The two long stops were both at Tromsø. The aircraft sat for 78 minutes between arriving from Alta at 11:19 and departing for Hammerfest at 12:37, then 62 minutes in the early afternoon before operating to Kirkenes. Those two pauses account for more than two and a half hours of the day's ground time on their own, meaning the remaining 14 turnarounds averaged under half an hour between them. Everywhere else, the pattern held: land, turn, depart. Hammerfest saw the aircraft five times and Tromsø four, with the rotation repeatedly returning to both rather than progressing along a line. The final turnaround of the day, 34 minutes at Tromsø, preceded the 40-minute positioning sector to Lakselv.

None of these flights exist on commercial merit. They operate under public service obligation contracts, under which the Norwegian Ministry of Transport and Communications subsidizes air service on routes that would not otherwise be flown. Widerøe has held those contracts across the regional network, winning all 13 PSO routes in the 2017 tender round after the government determined it wanted a single operator across all subsidized regional routes in the country.

The Dash 8-100 is the aircraft that makes the arrangement work. Dom Sipinski described the type as the backbone of Widerøe's public service obligation operation, noting that Widerøe is not only the largest operator of the Dash 8-100 but the only one running the aircraft to the end of its service life. At 39 seats, the type matches what these communities generate in demand. Widerøe itself is the largest regional airline in Scandinavia, carrying approximately 2.8 million passengers annually across more than 40 domestic and international destinations, operating from a base at Bodø and now part of Norwegian Group.

Widerøe's fleet structure shows how central the smallest type remains. AvioRadar lists 26 Dash 8-100 and -200 aircraft at 39 seats, three Dash 8-300s at 50 seats, 16 Dash 8-400s at 78 seats, and three Embraer E190-E2s at 110 seats. ch-aviation counts 19 Dash 8-100s specifically within a total fleet of 51. Either way, the smallest aircraft in the fleet carries the network that justifies the subsidy. AvioRadar noted that extending the structural life of the Dash 8-100 allows the airline to preserve a network tailored to Norway's geography without prematurely moving to larger aircraft that would undermine the economics of lower-demand routes. Oslo has since opened a new tender covering southern Norway's PSO routes.

Seasonal and year round frequencies are trimmed, forcing travelers to reroute through neighboring airports for connections.

A flight cycle is one takeoff and one landing. On a day like the one LN-WIE flew, the aircraft accumulated 17 of them before midnight, which is where the Dash 8-100's structural problem begins. De Havilland Canada designed the type for 80,000 cycles. Several of Widerøe's aircraft are already well past that figure, because no other operator in the world works the type this hard. The Extended Service Program raised the certified limit to 120,000 cycles. Widerøe went past that too.

In 2022, the airline became the launch customer for Extended Service Program PLUS, which lifts the limit to 160,000 flight cycles. De Havilland Canada states that this gives the Dash 8-100 the highest certified flight-cycle life of any commercial aircraft. Widerøe initially enrolled ten aircraft with options for ten more, and expanded the agreement in 2026 by adding four, bringing the total under ESP+ to 14 with options for six further airframes. It remains the only customer. Dom Sipinski observed that the gap to the second-most-intensive operator of the type is large enough that Widerøe will quite likely remain the only one. The airline also participates in De Havilland Component Solutions, the manufacturer's component support programme, and extended the intervals between A and C checks across its Dash 8-100, -200 and -300 fleets in 2021.

Werner Skaue, Widerøe's Director of Aircraft Trading, framed the decision in operational terms: "The Dash 8-100 remains an important part of our regional network, and ESP+ provides us with a practical and cost-effective way to extend the life of these aircraft while maintaining the safety, reliability and performance on which our operations depend." The alternative is not a newer small turboprop, because none is in production at this size. Extending the airframes Widerøe already owns is the only route to keeping Finnmark's airports connected.
