#6281. The Best New Restaurants in NYC Come in All Cuisines and Sizes

New York City has a new restaurant flinging its doors open seemingly every hour—and that's on top of the time-worn institutions, from old-school steakhouses and delis to bagel shops run by the same family for decades.

When it comes to the new, we're spoiled for choice: One week, it's a fabulous Korean small-plates bar with a commendable natural wine list downtown; the next it's an imported taverna from Argentina in the Village where the steaks are juicy as hell and, well, there's even more great wine to work your way through. To help you parse through all the opening news and find the buzzy spots worth fighting for a reservation at, our editors are eating out night after night, trying new Mexican mariscos joints and modern Indian fine-dining spots, to report back on the ones that stand out.

This is our Fall 2026 status report on the best of the new—the places to try your luck walking into, or commit to a Friday night dinner at, whether you're a NYC local or a visitor in town for just the weekend. These are the best new restaurants in New York right now.

The best new restaurants in New York City stretch across Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island. Every business on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has personally tried the restaurant in question. When choosing new restaurants, our editors consider both high-end and affordable eateries that offer an authentic and insider experience of the city. We’re always looking for standout dishes, a great location, and warm service—as well as serious sustainability credentials. In terms of how we define ‘new,’ we've chosen to focus on restaurants that have opened within a year of the publish date. When you work your way through the list, check back in: We'll update this guide regularly as new restaurants open in New York City.

Read our complete New York City travel guide here, which includes:

This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

Neighborhood: Williamsburg, BrooklynGo for: Martini hour and Shrimp Voodoo

After around seven years of living in Williamsburg, I’ve finally found the moody, cozy refuge this pocket of the neighborhood was missing. Booth’s Extra Fine, which just opened on October 9, feels like a sexy little secret. Hidden behind discreet oxblood curtains, the space simulates a vintage 20th-century supper club with dark walnut, rich leather booths, and deep, amber, brain-massage-like lighting. The heart of the restaurant stems from chef Nick Pfannerstill’s grandfather, Booth—an effortlessly stylish Milwaukee car salesman whose 1920s-50s photos line the walls.

Lean into the nostalgia and splurge on the porterhouse steak for two (or three—it's massive), but don't skip the Caviar Royale or the chef’s-kiss Shrimp Voodoo appetizer, cooked and swimming in Creole garlic butter. Personally? I can't wait to return and try the dry-aged Extra Fine Burger and a nice martini. Speaking of martinis, look out for Booth's "martini hour" launching soon, putting $12 cocktails—gin or vodka—at your disposal. —Jessica Chapel, commerce writer

Neighborhood: Hudson Yards, ManhattanGo for: A standout egg curry

Indienne, a tasting-menu-driven Indian restaurant, comes from chef Sujan Sarkar, who has worked in kitchens across Mumbai, New York, and San Francisco and runs a Michelin-starred restaurant of the same name in Chicago. Sarkar’s shtick? In his words: he reimagines Indian cuisine by “blending classical Indian flavors with refined European technique.” Think: deconstructed and then reconstructed. It takes a couple of courses to get a feel for what Sarkar is doing. The dhokla, for instance, isn’t spongy; it’s cubed, dehydrated, crackly, and tinged with white chocolate. The zingy passionfruit pani puri arrives in the shape of an oyster shell over reindeer moss. But once you get past the initial surprises, things really pick up. The “egg curry”—a whole steamed egg sitting on top of curry foam encrusted with potato sev and topped with caviar, served with buttery babka pao and house-churned butter—is an absolute standout. Things get a little more traditional with the chicken makhani that my husband got: chicken, three ways (chicken breast topped with spiced chicken mince wrapped over malai mousseline), served with buttery dal and even butterier naan. I didn’t miss the meat for a second, being on the vegetarian tasting menu myself, because my celeriac kebab was smoky and melt-in-your-mouth. And then came another surprise: the ghewar, a traditional Indian sweet that arrived like a mini layer cake with edible gold leaf (there’s a lot of this) and a bouncy coconut foam. A Penicillin-adjacent drink made with apricot whisky, mead, and ginger kept me company along the way. As we left, we were shown Sarkar’s other venture in the same premises, the British-Indian chophouse Elder, that was busy on a Tuesday night. —Arati Menon, global digital director

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: ribeye among many other things

From the man (Pablo Rivero) behind one of Buenos Aires's most iconic steakhouses (Don Julio) comes Graciela—an Argentine tavern on a cozy corner in the West Village, where the wine list is long and commendable, the food is fire-cooked, and the room is star-studded in that quiet, in-the-know way. All the hype made me suspicious, but if you're expecting a Corner Store or Carbone experience, this is not that. It's just fantastic cooking that is elevated and pristinely executed enough to be covetable, with an experience that stays focused on the food. And the space, with dried herbs hanging from the ceiling and heavy wooden furniture and warm, low light, feels both moody and inviting; cool yet welcoming.

It's easy to rack up a major bill here, because every corner of the menu is worth exploring—from a red pepper dip with wood-fired oven-made bread, to the sliced bondiola coppa with lemon zest and olive oil (a very true must), to, of course, the salty, sizzling steaks. (The iconic whole tomato starter has been lost to the turning of the seasons, but I am certain something autumnal will replace it.) Some flavors are more complex, but much of what you'll find are crowd-pleasers, like the milanesa neapolitana which our serve aptly described as being "like a pizza milanesa" which is impossible to complain about. —Megan Spurrell, senior features editor

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: Roti, actually, to accompany the beef cheek panang curry

The preponderance of new restaurants in the West Village specifically should be studied—sometimes it feels like we could dedicate a whole list to that neighborhood alone. The best of them, like Hommali, take the cuisine of choice and present it in an eminently stylish, upscale dining room. Every time I asked general manager Kritayanee “Air” Promsarin where something—the stemware, any number of the vividly colorful paintings on the walls—had come from, the answer was JJ Market, or Chatuchak Weekend Market, in Bangkok. It just looks good in there, I can't stress it enough. And then there's the matter of the food, which is buoyant, delightful, and oftentimes a wonderful introduction to Thai flavors for many Americans. I'm talking about a cold tom yum seafood cocktail, a heavily-spiced beef tartare on tripe cracker, and tao jiew lon, a fermented soybean-coconut dip scooped up with fried veggies. The mains are enormous and well-priced, and the best bite of the evening was not the beef cheek panang curry (although that was great on its own), but rather the piece of delicate roti used to scrape up the last remnants of sauce. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: SoHo, ManhattanGo for: sashimi and sake pairing

For this toro-obsessed tuna lover, Noury’s torotaku tartare topped with uni was love at first bite. As I greedily piled the pale-pink tuna belly, pillowing orange uni, and pickled yellow daikon radish with a dash of sushi rice onto a sheet of toasted nori to make a DIY handroll, I knew at once that I had reached appetizer ambrosia. And the saké pairing? Divine nectar.

I had high expectations for chef-and-sommelier duo Alex Chang and Lina Goujjane, who opened Kiko together in 2024, which I believe remains one of the city’s most underrated restaurants simply because of its isolated locale in so-called Hudson Square. Now, with Noury the pair finally has an address to match their ambitions in prime Soho, on Sullivan Street between West Houston and Prince.

While Kiko is cozy and chic, Noury is stylish and sexy. The restaurant is modeled after a Japanese “izakaya,” relaxed dining establishments that serve shareable plates and drinkable tipples. As such, small bites, raw seafood, and saké are the star, but the vibe isn’t so puritan as an omakase counter. In addition to the daily changing sashimi and futomaki, there are also non-fish entrees like the steak haché (not my favorite bite, but a popular crowd pleaser) and pork and cheese mille feuille katsu; plus a surprisingly addictive chrysanthemum salad. To pull it all together, Chef Alex tapped Joji Miwa as Noury’s chef de cuisine, whose career spans award winning restaurants like Sushi Sanshin in Osaka and Sushi Noz in New York. That’s where he first met Lina, the mastermind behind the beverage program, which includes both extremely rare and accessible sakes and a selection of shochu cocktails and refined spirit-free options. Like at Kiko, the service at Noury is knowledgeable and their hospitality kind. Come. Eat. Drink. Be merry. —Hannah Towey, news editor

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: ox tongue

Somssi, like Arthur, is new but doesn't feel it. It's a West Village restaurant with no flash or bombast, just a short and clever menu that jumps off from operator Ahris Kim's Korean origins and a casual, dimly-lit couple of dining rooms with lace accoutrements and eclectic hanging art giving the most comfortable feeling that you're at a friend's supper club rather than a sterling food and beverage operation. There's the semi-viral "Potato, Potato, Potato and Caviar" croquette, which is what it sounds like and will appeal to all, but more fun is to be had with things like the Grilled Ox Tongue, which comes undisguised as such on the plate with its uneven triangular shape atop romesco. I only gagged once while eating it, when my teeth came too close to my own tongue and I thought too hard about what I was eating, but then quickly continued my feast for love of the novel and tender dish. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Nolita, ManhattanGo for: crudo spotted with stracciatella and a late night

It was fitting that I ended up at Tashca just a few days after returning from Portugal, because I could fully appreciate how plucked-from-Lisbon this special spot in the LES is. Open only on Thursdays (the space is available for private events on other nights), this breezy little restaurant feels like being at a friend’s slightly chaotic but very endearing dinner party. Your table may or may not be ready when it’s supposed to be (we were given sparkling wine when ours took 30 minutes longer than planned, which is a trade I would have willingly made), and on that note, all reservations are made by Instagram DM (and you will need one; I saw several walk-in hopefuls turned away). But when you do flit through the open doors into the dining room, you won’t want to leave. Candles burn low throughout the night, and flowers hang from light fixtures—and the food, most importantly, sings, toeing the line between beauty and comfort, with distinctly Portuguese dishes that feature great seafood, bright produce, and a long list of tasty wines to pair. On the night I visited, there was a $95 prix-fixe made in partnership with visiting chef Joao Magalhaes Correia (who is usually in the kitchen at his Lisbon spots like Bar Alimentar). It featured a couscous bathed in squid ink and topped with a perfectly charred skewer of grilled octopus; melon draped in presunto ham; and a crudo topped with globs of stracciatella that I never could have imagined would work as well as it did. Come early, and plan to stay late. —Megan Spurrell, senior features editor

Neighborhood: NoMad, ManhattanGo for: fried chicken, actually!

When the Jungsik team closed sleek offshoot Sea in NoMad in May, it wasn't to abandon ship. They worked with commendable quickness to open a new concept, Mūje, by July. Like Jungsik proper, Mūje serves a tasting menu. Unlike Jungsik proper, Mūje is casual and focused on Asian food more generally rather than Korean exclusively. It's also more affordable at $150 for eight courses (Jungsik will cost you $335 for 10). There's a lot of fun to be had here with such a premise, like the tender short rib that comes with four different wraps nodding to Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese approaches, respectively. The best bite by a mile is the chicken wing, which is insane. It comes deboned and stuffed with pork, a Chinese technique, but is fried with the Korean Prinkle seasoning (a combination of cheese and onion and other good stuff) to create something really special. You only get one, so savor it. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Greenpoint, BrooklynGo for: an immaculate and affordable champagne list, plus the half chicken of the moment

I loved being at Arthur. With its lively and long dining room, buoyant soundtrack of soul music, and warm service, it's a place that feels like it's been around for a long time despite having opened in April. Food and drink are reasons to visit, in equal measure. Charlotte Mirzoeff's wine list is extensive and counts the French along with the Corsican and Portuguese, with a Champagne list 30-plus bottles deep (Mirzoeff is obsessed with the stuff, wants us all to be drinking more of it, and has two options for less than $100 to help make that happen.) Kevin Finch's food is rustic and comforting, the type you want to eat on the regular, but never boring—escargot comes grilled on a skewer beneath a bed of chives so ample it looks like a wig, for example. Two favorites: the kohlrabi with anchovy, herbs aplenty, and hazelnut (sop up the sauce with the pillows of housemade brioche) and the sasso chicken, with its crispy skin served atop crispier rice. Burgerheads take note: they've got an excellent one, with dijon, blue cheese, caramelized shallots, and a thick brisket patty between a sesame seed bun, but it's only available on Wednesdays. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Dumbo, BrooklynGo for: oysters broiled with bone marrow butter

Mexican food is back in the former Gran Electrica space on Front Street, a stretch of Dumbo real estate bustling with tourists moving to and from the Brooklyn Bridge vantage point. This time, the operation is run by Alan Delgado, the chef behind Fort Greene burrito spot Los Burritos Juarez, with drinks from bartender Ivy Mix. The great backyard garden patio remains, although I enjoyed my meal in the front dining room, which manages a moody mise en scène with its terracotta walls and glowing light despite lovely, huge windows overlooking the street and its passersby. Mix's beverages are stellar and inventive, in particular the rotating micheladas and frozen beverages that are tart and perfect. On the food front, the must-order comes first in the oysters, which are broiled a delicious brown color in bone marrow, and arrive bubbling. It's the perfectly decadent start. People talk about the fish tacos in particular, but I preferred the suadero, a confit brisket with guac on a corn tortillas rather than the flour Delgado is known for (and which can be purchased plain on the side, something I recommend.) There are flashier entrees, but the Chile Colorado—a braised pork shoulder with pinto beans and pickled onions that takes on a stew-like consistency, is subtly smoky, extremely filling, and something I'll be returning for. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Williamsburg, BrooklynGo for: potato bread, celery salad, and a breezy dining room

In the location of the former Llama Inn, a beloved modern Peruvian eatery in Williamsburg, the new Cafe Bar J.F. has arrived. Despite a name that feels designed to be confused and/or forgotten (both of which I keep experiencing), the space inside—and the food they serve—is an honorable replacement for Llama Inn. The concept, which comes from the Llama Inn team and is spearheaded by chef Francisco Castillo, is a “South American Tavern”. To me? It feels like eating at one of the many breezy, design-eyed restaurants I love to splurge at in Lima or Buenos Aires, with dishes that build on beloved foundations like ceviche and asado. Madrid-based Plantea Estudio has elevated the room from the plant-filled corner it once was to a more demure combo of dark-wood and metal furniture (and while the rooftop remains open, the interior is so lovely I chose to stay indoors). The prices will get ya if you don’t pay attention, but certain items—the potato bread and the celery salad, two surprising ones—really lingered. Go for a date night, or a celebratory dinner with a friend, and take the excuse to work through the satisfying cocktail menu. —Megan Spurrell, senior features editor

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: Guinness, oysters, and whatever seafood special is on the chalkboard

My friend Sarah put it best. There we were—me leaning back in a booth, she perched on a stool—at Dean's, the lively new pub from King team leaders Jess Shadbolt and Annie Shi, the windows flung open in celebration of one of spring's first sunny days, and she says, “This feels like what the Hamptons is supposed to be like.” The parts that make it so: a location in the Village and the according clientele, nautical stylings (lots of dark wood and blues of the navy variety), abundant seafood done the British way. All to say that, somehow, we felt as though we'd stumbled into something of a seafood shack. The halcyon weather won't be a constant, of course, but the place will do just as well comforting the cold in winter with its pies and beers—the stargazy pie, a hopefully perennial special, is strikingly fish-forward when it appears on your plate, head and tail of a milky-eyed mackerel protruding. Whether or not you eat its eyeballs, the rest of the dish beneath the buttery crust is basically chowder, not at all intimidating but very much delicious. It's also rather heavy, so if you want to try as many dishes as possible while also downing excellent Guinness pour after excellent Guinness pour, perhaps stick to such happy hits as the oysters, fish and chips, and scallops in malt vinegar. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

#6280. United CEO Hints at Potential Destinations

United is exploring potential new markets in a part of the world not served by any of its U.S. competitors.

CEO Scott Kirby told the hosts of the Cheeky Pint podcast that global network planning chief Patrick Quayle and his team were recently in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan.

“We can’t fly there today because we can’t fly over Russia,” he said. “But he’s there. This could work down the road.”

Kirby did not elaborate on plans for the region but cited United’s seasonal service to Nuuk, Greenland, as evidence that unconventional destinations can work.

No U.S. airlines currently fly to Central Asia. Russia’s ban on Western airlines – enacted in the early days of the Russia-Ukraine war – would make the trip uneconomically long.

Historically, there was little demand among American travelers for connections to Central Asia, but that is changing. American arrivals in Uzbekistan, for instance, increased from around 17,000 in 2019 to more than 26,000 in the first seven months of 2026 alone. The newfound interest has been attributed to visa liberalization measures in Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan, the relative affordability of the region, and trips by travel influencers.

In Kazakhstan, international airlines mainly serve Almaty, the country’s most populous city. In Uzbekistan, the main international gateway is Tashkent.

The only Central Asian carrier with flights to the U.S. is Uzbekistan Airways. The airline serves New York-JFK from Tashkent.

#6279. 11 Gorgeous Mountain Cities in the US, Plus Where to Stay

Whether you're seeking snow that's smooth as butter or high altitudes that keep summer comfortably cool, there's nothing quite like America's mountain cities to scratch an itch for the outdoors. With over 100 distinct mountain ranges across the US, there are endless peaks to summit and après-ski offerings to enjoy. The possibilities range from astoundingly good omakase in Salt Lake City to heliskiing in Colorado's San Juan mountains.

Whatever your vibe is, there's something for you—it's not all log cabins and snow shoes in the country's best mountain cities. These are year-round destinations that offer world-class art, adrenaline-pumping slopes, and family-friendly activities. From Appalachia to the Rockies, these are the mountain cities to call home for your next adventure, plus our favorite, editor-approved places to stay.

Nestled in the foothills of the Rocky Mountains’ Ten Mile Range, Breckenridge is one of the country's most treasured ski towns, home to five peaks peppered with skiers of all abilities come winter. The once crown jewel of Summit County's mining towns, its lined streets are hugged by weathered saloons and colorful homes harking back to its boomtown days. Breck's—as regulars call it—real claim to fame though, is its nearly 3,000 acres of lift-served terrain. After you hit the slopes, there's plenty to love beyond the skiing, whether you're looking crawling through its craft beer and distillery scene or appraising the thriving arts district.

Stay here: A new kind of boutique hotel tailored to outdoor enthusiasts, the dog-friendly Gravity Haus Breckenridge draws out-of-towners with a wide variety of guest rooms (from bunk rooms to two-bedroom suites), a Japanese-inspired onsen, private ski lockers, and an in-house team to help you explore outside.

As Crested Butte lies just 24 miles from Aspen, the two are practically next-door neighbors, but you'd be remiss to skip this hidden gem because of that fact. There's something that feels more intimate about Crested Butte’s historic downtown, which looks like it was stolen out of a snow globe or used as the set of a holiday Hallmark movie, but it can keep up with the best of them. There's the world-class skiing and mountain biking with some memorable restaurants and watering holes to boot. In other words: all the beauty and nightlife, none of the pretense.

Stay here: If you want to stay an arm's length away from it all, check into Old Town Inn, which sits three miles away from Lake Grant and two miles away from Peanut Lake. The property also offers free shuttle service to Mount Crested Butte.

Mountain cities nearby a national park are automatic winners, but Whitefish somehow goes a step above the rest. Being steps away from Glacier National Park certainly helps as travelers gain access to some incredibly beautiful lakes and glaciers, but there's also the namesake ski resort in town that plus tons of summertime activities like hiking and zip-lining; and its mountain-backed, saloon-lined downtown has more than enough Old Western vibes to fill an entire vacation.

Stay here: Larch House is a new 39-key hotel is the first design-forward boutique hotel of its kind in Whitefish. It’s in the heart of downtown’s historic Railway District, a short walk away from all the town’s shops, restaurants, and bars.

Aspen, Colorado’s reputation precedes itself; it’s the quintessential mountain city that's been winning praise since 1879 (when it was originally founded as Ute City). Why? Its surroundings are simply awe-inspiring—snow-capped peaks in winter that turn into perfect hiking weather in summer—and its comfortably small footprint makes your whole itinerary easy to reach, from the famed slopes to downtown's designer boutiques and top-notch restaurants. Aspen has long been a hotspot for skiers searching for fresh powder and a lively après scene, but the town has been on a roll more recently with all types because of its worldly mix of cultures on display at institutions like the Aspen Art Museum. In addition to those seeking snow, Colorado's premier mountain city welcomes families, food lovers, and design seekers alike.

Stay here: There’s an inimitable charm to Aspen’s Hotel Jerome. From rustic to high fashion, the 135-year-old historical landmark sits in a perfect location for both rest and play. Offering both complementary hotel-to-hill transit and walkable proximity to designer shops, a stay at the Jerome is as convenient as it is decadent.

Two years after Hurricane Helene descended on Asheville, the creative spirit of the artsy Appalachian city is back and better than ever. With hundreds of artists bringing life to repurposed spaces, whether it's a glass studio, ceramics workshop, or open gallery, Asheville is abuzz again.it seems Asheville's pure energies are vibrating at a higher frequency than ever, even as it continues to rebuild. As Jeffrey Burroughs, a local jewelry designer shared with Condé Nast Traveler, “What music is to New Orleans art is to Asheville,” and visitors come here for much more than the bucolic scenery.

Stay here: Enfolded within the grounds of the opulent Biltmore Estate, the Inn uniquely summons what it was like to be a guest at the Vanderbilt family’s magnificent 19th-century mansion, but with 21st-century luxury and comfort.

Ouray calls itself the Outdoor Recreation Capital of Colorado, and it's an epithet well-earned. See why on the Perimeter Trail, a 6.5-mile loop that hugs the rugged mountain city. Set aside (at least) four hours for the full hike; shortly after your ascent, you'll be taken aback by views of the entire box canyon—a sight that continues along much of the journey. Among the trail’s highlights are the towering Cascade Falls, its Baby Bathtubs (smooth, carved rocks kids can play on), and the Box Canyon Falls high bridge. Because the Perimeter Trail is never more than a half mile from town, there are several points where hikers can cut the walk short and head back into Ouray.

Stay here: The adults-only Beaumont Hotel and Spa is made for those looking to rejuvenate their bodies after long days spent romping around Ouray's thrill-seeking offerings. Plan to spend a day soaking in the property's hot springs, which has been soothing visitors since 1886.

Salt Lake City is becoming something of a cultural haven in the Mountain West. Foodies flock to the city for its inventive dining—from speakeasy cocktails to picture-perfect omakase—while the mountains are never far for skiing or hiking—don’t miss out on the quirky annual events like Winter Roundup skijoring (skiers and snowboarders get towed by horses through the snowy streets) and the ultra-hip, indie-forward Kilby Block Party Music Festival. Boutique shopping and independent galleries are emerging alongside long-standing museums, lending downtown an even more vibrant, walkable energy. Between all the buzz, postcard mountain views, swanky bars, and hotels that balance history, style, and service, Salt Lake City has genuinely become a place you’ll want to return to—not just pass through.

Stay here: Downtown Hyatt Regency SLC is the city’s workhorse: spacious, modern rooms, consistent service, and direct access to the convention center and buzzy streets. It’s perfect for business travelers or anyone valuing convenience and reliable amenities.

The powder here is perfect, and so is the quirky, small-town vibe. But it’s when the mercury starts to rise that this historic mining community in the San Juan Mountains really shows off its shine: Warmer temperatures bring vibrant wildflower blooms, its famed film festival, and beloved bluegrass performances to Telluride. Come for the robust art scene where you’ll find a mix of creatives, outdoorspeople, blissful retirees, and the odd celebrity or two (Oprah Winfrey is among those who reportedly own a home here). Even with all the new hype, Telluride has gracefully managed to hang onto its authentic character and remains a favorite, down-to-Earth Colorado destination.

Stay here: The Madeline Hotel & Residences, Auberge Resorts Collection, located at the base of Telluride Ski Resort, is an ideal basecamp for your trip. This updated 83-room alpine retreat, which also features 71 residences, is surrounded on three sides by the San Juan Mountains and offers stunning views from its 4,000-square-foot outdoor terrace, complete with a heated pool, massive hot tubs, fire pits, and an al fresco lounge.

Jackson Hole is the epitome of why they call this region of the country big sky country. There are endless open spaces to admire the handsome soaring mountains, and it's no secret what makes so many first-time visitors never want to leave. The resort skiers and adventurous outdoorsy types have been coming for decades, and in recent years, the dining scene has only been getting better. All of which gives it an outsized place in the mind of travelers. Jackson Hole brings in a whopping 2.6 million visitors every year; the entire state of Wyoming has a population under 600,000. It’s a gateway to the National Parks, a winter wonderland, and an idyllic paradise year-round.

Stay here: Four Seasons Resort Jackson Hole, nestled at the base of Jackson Hole Mountain Resort in Teton Village, is the only ski-in/ski-out hotel in the village, and comes with unobstructed views of the Tetons, full-service alpine spa, an outdoor pool and jacuzzi (open year-round), ski concierge, and all the pampering you’d expect.

If the air feels lighter in Silverton, maybe because the landmarked former mining town rests at a cool 9,300 feet above sea level. The scene here feels closer to the industrial history than many of Colorado's other rehabbed mining outposts, with a good number of its colorfully painted storefronts catering to passengers from the out-and-back, steam-powered train from Durango. It's the perfect home base to spend a couple of days hiking and fishing in nearby San Juan National Forest. In the winter, this is one-horse town completely transforms into a mecca for serious backcountry skiers.

Stay here: For a real step back in time, step through the threshold of The Bent Elbow Hotel, whose façade nods to the Victorian architectural style that was rampant in Silverton's hey-day. Paired with the mountain-view balconies, you might just wonder which century you're in. But worry not about the loss of modern amenities, the rooms come equipped with special comforts from complimentary streaming services to white noise machines to complete your wind-down ritual.

Townsend is called the “peaceful side of the Smokies” for a reason. Instead of neon lights and chain brands, you'll find a small downtown area alongside the Little River with easy access to the national park. The eastern part of town is closest to the park’s most incredible waterfalls: Meigs Falls and Spruce Flats Falls. The Smokies lay claim to more than 700 fishable rivers, including the Little River, that can be visited with Townsend-based Little River Outfitters. In Townsend, Dancing Bear Appalachian Bistro is a local favorite, with seasonal Appalachian-inspired dishes like striped bass and sorghum glazed chicken on offer.

Stay here: Head to nearby Walland for Blackberry Farm, a Relais & Châteaux resort spread over 4,000 acres—and hands down the most notable stay in these parts. It has James Beard award-winning restaurants including The Barn (which accepts reservations from non-guests), known for its dishes crafted from seasonal and local ingredients.

#6278. Where to Eat, Stay, and Play on Easter Island, the Wild, Remote Island in the Pacific

At 1,292 miles from its closest inhabited neighbor, Pitcairn Island, and 2,200 miles from continental Chile, Rapa Nui (Easter Island) takes isolation to the extreme. Here, at the lonely eastern edge of Polynesia, the empty horizon seems to curve with the Earth itself. It’s an extraordinary setting for one of archaeology’s enduring mysteries: Why did a group of Polynesians carve nearly 1,000 monolithic human figures (known as moai), haul them across the island to distant ceremonial platforms over the course of centuries, and then topple them all to the ground? There are plenty of theories, and fewer answers. It adds an element of mystery to an already dramatic landscape, and one that has proven to be timelessly alluring.

Today, this Chilean territory is essentially an open-air archaeological museum, with many of its enigmatic moai (representations of Polynesian ancestors) returned to their upright positions following seven decades of restoration. Of course to see Rapa Nui only through its superhuman past is to miss much of the story: The island’s distinct Polynesian culture remains a vital presence, particularly in its sole town, Hanga Roa, where nights come alive with cheerful ukulele music and hip-swirling dances. There’s also a vast, vibrant sea, windswept volcanic plains, and a food culture that draws on the island’s rich heritage and maritime setting.

As a repeat visitor to the island, this is my guide to Rapa Nui.

There are thousands of stone moai—representations of Polynesian ancestors—on Rapa Nui.

Unless you sail over on one of the dozen or so annual cruise ships that dock here, including National Geographic Resolution and Silversea’s Silver Cloud, you’ll likely arrive via air at the world’s most remote commercial airport, Mataveri International. LATAM is the only carrier serving Rapa Nui with at least one daily flight from Santiago, 5.5 hours (and two time zones) away. Once on island, visitors typically sleep in the town of Hanga Roa and organize day trips to the archeological sites, which are never more than a half-hour drive from each other.

The Chilean Government officially transferred administration of Rapa Nui National Park in 2017 to the Ma'u Henua Indigenous Community, an organization run by elected members of the Rapa Nui community. Recently, they’ve increased entrance fees (currently CH$95,000, or about $100 USD) to stave off overtourism, while establishing initiatives encouraging longer stays, deeper cultural connections, and stronger protections for the fragile moai. Chief among the changes is a requirement to visit all archeological sites beyond Hanga Roa with a certified guide. Consequently, it’s become less common these days for visitors to rent a car (or bike) and explore on their own.

Head to La Kaleta for lunch along the rugged coastline.

La Kaleta's ceviche is served within view of working fisherfolk.

Seafood is a highlight of the Rapa Nui dining scene where the tuna is so fresh, you’ll invariably want to eat it raw in a ceviche, carpaccio, or tiradito (thinly sliced in a spicy citrus sauce). Te Moai Sunset makes a particularly painterly version of the latter. Paired with a pisco sour and views over the modern Moai de la Paz (“Peace Moai”), it’s the most idyllic place to wind down during—you guessed it—sunset. Similarly, the mahi-mahi is sublime over roasted Rapa Nui sweet potatoes at the tiki-style Te Moana, while the dockside ceviche lunches at La Kaleta let you watch the fisherfolk in action.

Kotaro has long been Hanga Roa’s hidden treasure: a small, quirky Japanese restaurant with an impeccable tasting menu and strict dining rules outlined on the website (no kids or chitchatting with the chef, for example). Neptuno Sunset is another off-piste favorite thanks to its seafront location near the end of the airstrip, slightly removed from the action. Bountiful seafood pastas are the specialty, but do save some space here or elsewhere for a dessert of po’e, a sweet, dense sponge cake made from mashed ripe bananas.

The wide open spaces are less jungly than most expect from Polynesia, but gorgeous nonetheless.

Many assume that Rapa Nui will have the jungle-clad hills of other Polynesian destinations like Hawaii or Tahiti. Instead, it’s covered mostly in grassy plains and looks more like Ireland. While there are two fine beaches on the northern coast at Ovahe and Anakena (which is apt for swimming), this is not your standard resort island, and sunbathing is secondary to the mystique of the moai.

Rapa Nui National Park has two chief archeological sites from the moai-building era: Rano Raraku and Ahu Tongariki. The latter is the island’s largest ahu (moai platform) with 15 statues often viewed in silhouette at sunrise. The former is a volcanic crater and quarry site where the ancient Rapa Nui designed some 95% of the island’s sculptures; about 400 remain in situ in various states of construction. There are dozens more ahu sites (many with restored maoi) spread throughout the island. The other major historical attraction is Orongo, a stone village perched on the rim of the Rano Kau volcano, which served as the ceremonial center for religious festivals dedicated to the creator god Makemake.

Just offshore from Orongo are Los Motu, small islets that were central to the annual Tangata Manu “Birdman” competition from the 17th to 19th centuries, which involved a death-defying race down Rano Kau, into the Pacific, and up sea cliffs to secure the unbroken egg of a sooty tern. Today, Los Motu is a popular snorkeling site where you can ply the gin-clear waters in search of vibrant corals and 142 marine species found nowhere else on earth, including the rare Easter Island butterflyfish. Mike Rapu Diving Center is one of Rapa Nui’s longest-running and most respected operators for snorkeling and scuba diving. Back on land, there are excellent hikes to be had up Terevaka, the highest point on the island at 1,675 feet, or around the barren Poike Peninsula, which holds several little-explored archeological sites, including petroglyphs and an enormous rock carved in the shape of a human face.

Modern Polynesian culture is alive and well on this island of 7,750 people. Though there are many souvenir shops with kitschy moai and colorful shell necklaces, for top local craftsmanship, seek out the paintings, woodcarvings, and jewelry at Mana Gallery, on the north end of Hanga Roa. The music school Toki Rapa Nui, co-founded by classical pianist Mahani Teave, offers occasional concerts and guided visits of its sustainable Earthship building, which is shaped like an eight-petal flower. More popular are the evening Polynesian dance shows from groups like Kari Kari and Te Ra’ai, the latter of which comes with a traditional (if highly theatrical) umu feast cooked in an underground earth oven with hot stones. For something less overtly touristy, check out the contemporary Polynesian music at Iti Lafken.

Explora Rapa Nui offers all-inclusive stays with daily adventures led by local guides.

For an all-inclusive stay with daily adventures led by local guides, book at Explora Rapa Nui, an architecturally striking hotel about 15 minutes outside Hanga Roa. Of all the Explora properties, this one has the finest food and shrewdest guides. Right on the edge of town, the Leading Hotels of the World property Nayara Hangaroa gives you a bit more flexibility to book things à la carte. It boasts an oceanfront pool, three unique dining concepts, and oval-shaped rooms styled after homes in the nearby Orongo ceremonial village.

More affordable options include the centrally-located (and playfully designed) Hare Nua Hotel Boutique, or the lush garden rooms of Pikera Uri Eco Lodge, from which you can explore the island on horseback. In general, prices are significantly higher here than in mainland Chile due to the remote location and lack of local resources.

Earn 2 Delta Comfort Flight Certificates + 50K Miles

The Business Platinum Card® from American Express

As High As 300,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

Is airline elite status worth it anymore? It’s an age-old question that’s back on plenty of travelers’ minds — especially after two of the four largest U.S. carriers overhauled their loyalty programs this month.

And one theme is becoming clear: To get the best rewards, members are going to have to spend ... a lot.

Starting in 2027, taking the most United Airlines flights won’t necessarily translate to the highest United MileagePlus status.

Instead, the airline's top elite members will be the customers who spend the most money — either on flights or the airline’s cobranded credit cards.

Top-tier 1K status will also be harder to earn.

Meanwhile, Southwest Airlines took its biggest step yet toward nudging flyers toward its lineup of credit cards.

Beginning next year, every dollar its members charge to their Southwest Rapid Rewards cards will count toward status.

Southwest also closed a key shortcut to its most alluring perk: the Companion Pass. Going forward, members hoping to score the "buy-one, get-one" flight pass will have to spend their way to the airline’s top status tier (or take 100 flights in a year).

These changes weren’t entirely surprising.

Over the past decade, airline status has become less about the time you spend in the sky and more about the cash you’re willing to spend.

For years, American Airlines and Delta Air Lines have awarded status based purely on the money their frequent flyers spend.

And across the industry, carriers have become more agnostic about whether those dollars come in the form of a flight booking or card swipe at the grocery store.

On some airlines, you can now technically swipe your way to status without ever setting foot on a plane.

Here’s how much you’d need to pay for top-tier airline status in 2027 — if you went exclusively by credit card spending.

*Note: American has not announced what its status thresholds will be in 2027.

Note: United requires a minimum of four United-operated flights for members to be Premier-eligible.

Note: Cardholders earn a one-time 10,000 TQP boost upon hitting 130,000 TQPs in 2027.

Note: Elite credit earned by flying or other eligible spending reduces the card spending needed to qualify for elite status. Southwest still also offers elite qualification via flight segments.

It’s not just the eye-popping dollar amounts travelers must now spend to reach status.

Airlines have also made carrying a credit card a more important part of the overall loyalty experience.

United and Delta cardholders now get access to better mileage redemptions than members who don’t carry a card.

JetBlue will soon offer exclusive elite perks to JetBlue TrueBlue loyalty members who carry its top-tier card.

And even more airlines offer cardholders shortcuts to elite status.

Delta this month said it’s on track to pull in a record $9 billion through its banking partnership with American Express.

American expects to make $8 billion this year through its tie-up with Citibank.

Those are eye-popping numbers, of course.

Beyond the raw cash flow, though, airlines also see turning flyers into cardholders as one of the best ways to become part of customers’ day-to-day lives, even when they’re not on a trip.

“It really is about making sure that we are top of mind for our members every single day, whether or not they’re able to be on board our aircraft," Jarad Fisher, United’s president of MileagePlus, said in a recent interview.

On one hand, airline status still offers a host of ways to save money, get better seats and travel with more flexible policies.

And, in some ways, qualify has become more realistic for travelers who aren’t true “road warriors," since everyday spending counts toward status.

At the same time, free first-class upgrades have gotten harder to score and status benchmarks keep getting pricier to earn.

It's created a real dilemma for travelers who fly a lot — but only have so much money they're willing to put toward earning status: Is it worth dumping tens (or hundreds) of thousands of dollars onto your favorite airline’s credit card to reach your status goal?

Think about what you’re getting out of status, and whether it’s worth the investment.

If not, you could be a candidate to hop off the status "hamster wheel" and be an airline "free agent."

But if you've crunched the numbers and decided status is still worth it, you may need to double down on your favorite airline.

And that might mean prioritizing credit card spending on that carrier's card. Because in 2026, that is almost as important as flying when it comes to unlocking the best perks.

Here’s how much you’d need to pay for entry-tier airline status in 2027 if you went exclusively by credit card spending.

*Note: American has not announced what its status thresholds will be in 2027.

$25,000 with the Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® (see rates and fees)

Assumes 12 flight segments on American to fully unlock the card’s “Flight Streak” benefit.

$25,000 with the Delta SkyMiles® Reserve American Express Card

Note: United requires a minimum of four United-operated flights for members to be Premier-eligible.

$35,000 with any cobranded credit card, including the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card

Of course, the most efficient way to earn status is by combining your card spending with flying.

Spending on flights does typically earn you more elite credit (and points) than you'd get with typical credit card spending.

While airline credit cards can offer strong value with that carrier, other cards may offer a stronger return for your spending.

For instance, there's basically no airline card that truly competes with the American Express® Gold Card on rewards for dining worldwide and grocery purchases.

And some Capital One credit cards offer 2 miles per dollar spent on every purchase.

Most of us only have so many dollars to dole out, and sometimes the best rewards to earn are the flexible points you can transfer to a wide range of partners.

Plus, as a frequent traveler, I also carry hotel cards that are key to unlocking perks once I arrive at my destination.

If you're rethinking your loyalty with a particular airline, there are status matches you can take advantage of to effectively “change airlines.”

Just remember: Most U.S. carriers are now playing the “spending to status” game in some form. So, you may encounter similar sticker shock with your new carrier of choice.

Plus, even after matching, you’ll likely have to hit an ambitious challenge goal to keep your status for the entire year.

While United and Southwest announced major overhauls to their loyalty and status programs, Delta opted to stay the course for next year.

Its Medallion qualification requirements will not change in 2027.

Delta’s last major shake-up to its Delta SkyMiles program came in 2023, which led to significant backlash among its SkyMiles members.

American likely won’t update its AAdvantage members for a few months since its loyalty year technically doesn’t begin until March 1.

So, it remains to be seen whether the status game will continue getting harder for more flyers in the new year.

#6276. Southwest Premier Card Review: Is The $149 Mid-Range Card Worth It?

Chase and Southwest have a great portfolio of personal credit cards at three different price points. This is my in-depth review of the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card, the Southwest personal card with a $149 annual fee (which is neither the highest nor lowest annual fee product).

Now is an especially good time to consider this card, both because it’s offering an elevated welcome bonus, and because it’s your last chance to use credit card welcome bonuses to qualify for Southwest’s Companion Pass benefit under the old system.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card

Before I get into my Southwest Premier Card review, here’s a broad look at the card and its key features:

In my opinion, here are the pros and cons of the Southwest Airlines Premier Card:

When applying for credit, cards, the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and fees, are obviously major factors that potential cardmembers consider. So let’s cover those details for the Southwest Premier Card, as the card has a great bonus, nuanced eligibility requirements, and a relatively manageable annual fee.

The Southwest Premier Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus where you can earn 85,000 bonus points after you spend $2,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. This is a limited time, elevated offer, as the most recent base offer was for 55,000 points.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So to me, the points from this welcome bonus are worth $1,020, making this a solid welcome offer.

When it comes to Southwest credit card eligibility rules, the Southwest Premier Card isn’t available to anyone who currently has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest Rapid Rewards business credit card.

Beyond the restrictions related to which Southwest cards you have, there are general application rules for Chase cards, including the Chase 5/24 rule, whereby you usually won’t get approved for a Chase credit card if you’ve opened five or more credit card accounts in the past 24 months.

The Southwest Premier Card has a $149 annual fee, and you can add authorized users to the card at no extra cost. Southwest’s personal credit cards have annual fees of $99, $149, and $229, so this is the “middle child” of the Southwest and Chase personal card portfolio.

The Southwest Premier Card has no foreign transaction fees, so you can use it abroad without worrying about extra charges.

In addition to the benefits, one of the main reasons you’ll want to consider picking up a card is because of its return on spending, so you’re sure it aligns with what you’re looking for. In the case of the Southwest Premier Card, it has a limited number of bonus categories, and spending can also help you toward earning elite status with Rapid Rewards. So let’s cover those details.

As far as the Southwest Premier Card’s rewards structure goes, the card offers the following:

It’s good that the card has some bonus categories, though there are ultimately more rewarding cards out there for everyday spending. Based on my valuation of 1.2 cents per point, that’s like a 3.6% return on Southwest purchases, a 2.4% return on grocery stores and restaurants (up to the cap), and a 1.2% return on everything else.

The Southwest Premier Card also lets you earn unlimited Tier Qualifying Points (TQPs) toward Southwest status. Through the end of 2026, you can earn 1,500 TQPs toward A-List status for every $5,000 spent on the card. Starting January 1, 2027, every Southwest credit card will earn 1 TQP per dollar spent, so $35,000 in spending on any of them would get you to Silver status.

A-List is Southwest Airlines’ version of elite status, and offers perks like priority boarding, a 25% points bonus, same-day standby, priority check-in and security lane access, and a dedicated phone number. A-List status ordinarily requires earning 35,000 TQPs in a calendar year, so spending on a Southwest Premier Card could help you earn that. Whether or not that’s worth it depends on how much you’d otherwise fly with Southwest.

Currently, Southwest Rapid Rewards elite status has two levels: A-List and A-List Preferred. Beginning January 1, 2027, though, the program will grow to three tiers, with new names: Silver, Gold, and Platinum. Qualifying for Silver status will require the same 35,000 TQPs needed for A-List, while Gold and Platinum will require 65,000 TQPs and 140,000 TQPs, respectively. I covered these Southwest Rapid Rewards program changes in detail here.

This brings me to another big upcoming change to the Southwest program and how cards like the Southwest Premier Card fit into your strategy — and this is a pretty unwelcome one.

One of the best values in travel is the Southwest Airlines Companion Pass. With a Companion Pass, you can have someone travel with you for the entire year (whether on a cash ticket or award ticket) and just pay taxes and fees for them. This is such an incredible deal and basically doubles the value you can get from flying Southwest.

For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting January 1, 2027, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

This eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only change: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending, won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

This change isn’t specific to the Southwest Premier Card, as it applies to welcome bonuses across all Southwest credit cards. But the good news is that welcome bonuses earned before the end of 2026 do count toward Companion Pass qualification, so now is your last chance to take advantage before this opportunity ends.

I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but I’ll briefly cover how redemptions work.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, which means that the value you’ll get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. That said, there are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares.

Basic award fares tend to offer the highest redemption value, and in my experience the best-value Southwest point redemptions are usually for international routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. For instance, I’ve seen Basic awards from Tampa (TPA) to Liberia, Costa Rica (LIR) for 12,000 points and $24.21. The same fare cost $200 in cash, giving you a very strong value of 1.46 cents per point.

One great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

The Southwest Airlines Premier Card offers some benefits that could make the card worth keeping long term. How do the perks compare to Southwest’s lower and higher annual fee cards?

The Southwest Premier Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person. With even a couple of roundtrip flights per year, this benefit can offset the annual fee.

The Southwest Airlines Premier Card lets you pick a Preferred seat on Southwest, if any are available, starting 48 hours before departure. The cost for a Preferred seat can vary from $28 to nearly $50 depending on the flight, so this perk is another potential money-saver.

Another Southwest Premier Card benefit is early boarding. You’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group. Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last.

On your cardmember anniversary every year, you’ll receive 6,000 bonus Rapid Rewards points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you can generally expect that you’ll need around 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book.

In other words, 6,000 bonus points get you around $72 in Southwest airfare annually. That covers nearly half of the annual fee right there.

Each year on your Southwest Premier Card cardmember anniversary, you’ll get a 15% promo code that applies to Southwest flights. Just note that this excludes Basic fares.

The Southwest Premier Card offers 25% savings on inflight purchases of Wi-Fi and drinks. Simply pay with your card, and you’ll automatically receive a statement credit for that amount.

The Southwest Premier Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:

You’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

The Southwest Airlines Premier Card is Southwest’s mid-range card, and the $149 annual fee is in line with many other co-branded airline credit cards. The card is offering a fantastic bonus, which is one good reason to consider this product.

On an ongoing basis, the 6,000-point anniversary bonus can get you around $72 worth of airfare. Whether the Southwest Premier Card is worth it in the long run depends on how much you value the other perks like a free checked bag, and whether you plan to use spending on the credit card to qualify for Southwest elite status.

As I mentioned above, the Southwest Premier Card is the mid-range option in Chase’s lineup of Southwest cards. Here’s a look at how it compares to the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (learn more), which is the entry-level option:

If you don’t care about working toward Southwest status through credit card spending and you want to keep your annual fee to a minimum, the Southwest Plus Card is likely a better option for you.

On the other end of the spectrum, there’s the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card, which is the most expensive of the three personal Southwest credit cards. Here’s how it differs from the Southwest Premier Card:

If you fly Southwest all the time and want as many benefits with the airline as possible, the Southwest Priority Card could be the right choice. It’s also the best pick if you want to spend your way toward status before the end of 2026, since it earns TQPs at the fastest rate of the three cards.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. This means that you could earn points at a faster rate through Ultimate Rewards than through Rapid Rewards, and your points will be more flexible (since you can also transfer them to other airlines and hotel programs).

So, should you earn Rapid Rewards points directly with a Southwest Airlines credit card, or with a Chase Ultimate Rewards credit card?

For context, some of the best cards for earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points include the following:

On top of that, the following four no annual fee cards earn points that can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points at a 1:1 ratio in conjunction with one of the above cards:

The Southwest Premier Card is a solid mid-range airline credit card. It has a nice welcome bonus, plus ongoing perks that justify the annual fee. However, if you’re not particularly interested in extra perks when you fly Southwest, you’re much better off earning points with Chase Ultimate Rewards and then transferring them to Southwest Rapid Rewards, given that it gives you higher points earning rates and more flexibility.

#6275. 3 New Routes, 1 New Destination: JetBlue Expands Its Network Today

JetBlue is launching three new nonstop routes today, expanding its network with two services from Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL) and another connecting Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI) with San Juan. The new additions bring Columbus back into its network and introduce Indianapolis as an entirely new destination for the airline. All three routes will operate daily using Airbus A320 aircraft.

The launches come amid a significant transformation of JetBlue's network, with Fort Lauderdale recently overtaking New York JFK as its busiest airport. The airline is capitalizing on the demise of Spirit Airlines to expand its South Florida presence, while preparing to introduce additional premium transcontinental services later this month.

JetBlue's latest expansion introduces daily nonstop flights from Fort Lauderdale to Indianapolis International Airport (IND) and John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH). The two new services are part of a broader expansion announced earlier this year, when the airline outlined plans to add 11 destinations from the South Florida airport.

Indianapolis represents the biggest milestone, becoming a new city in JetBlue's network. Columbus, meanwhile, welcomes the carrier back after an absence, giving travelers another option for reaching South Florida. The additions strengthen JetBlue's domestic connectivity from Fort Lauderdale, where the airline has been expanding aggressively throughout 2026. JetBlue CEO, Joanna Geraghty, had the following to say:

"We're building on our already strong foundation by adding more destinations, creating more connections and giving customers even more reasons to choose JetBlue. As Fort Lauderdale's leading airline, we see an opportunity to continue growing together with this community."

The new route from Baltimore to San Juan's Luis Munoz Marin International Airport (SJU) builds on JetBlue's return to Baltimore back in July, when it introduced three daily flights to Fort Lauderdale. The new Puerto Rico service expands its reach from Maryland while reinforcing San Juan's importance within the airline's Caribbean network. Baltimore airport officials welcomed JetBlue's arrival, emphasizing the benefits of additional competition and connectivity.

The Fort Lauderdale expansion has led to it becoming JetBlue's busiest airport by scheduled departures, overtaking its longtime New York JFK Airport (JFK) stronghold. The change illustrates how dramatically the airline's network has shifted toward South Florida. Based on the winter schedule figures highlighted in a recent Simple Flying analysis of JetBlue's network changes, Fort Lauderdale now leads JFK by approximately six daily departures.

The expansion has been accelerated by Spirit Airlines' collapse and JetBlue's changing route network. JetBlue has introduced 15 destinations from Fort Lauderdale while increasing frequencies on existing routes. Its share of scheduled seats at the airport is expected to reach approximately 37% in the fourth quarter, an increase of 14 percentage points year-over-year. Peak daily departures will also exceed 150 this winter.

Crucially, the expansion is also delivering encouraging financial results. During the third quarter, Fort Lauderdale revenue per available seat mile (RASM) increased nearly 15% despite capacity growing by more than 65%. The expansion is also driving increased ancillary revenue, with co-branded credit card acquisitions in the region up 55%. The airline expects the maturing Fort Lauderdale operation to generate further unit revenue improvements as capacity growth moderates.

JetBlue will launch new routes and add more Mint flights from Fort Lauderdale.

JetBlue's next significant Fort Lauderdale launch is scheduled for later this month on November 19, when daily nonstop flights to San Diego International Airport (SAN) begin. The route will feature the airline's premium JetBlue Mint business class, including fully lie-flat seating. This will give the airline a distinct advantage over Southwest Airlines and Alaska Airlines, which also operate the route, by making it the only airline with a lie-flat offering between the two airports.

The San Diego launch is part of a much wider transcontinental push. JetBlue is also adding Mint-equipped flights to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and San Francisco International Airport (SFO) this winter, creating its largest-ever Mint schedule from Fort Lauderdale. The airline ultimately plans to offer up to eight daily flights to Los Angeles and three to San Francisco, although these totals include services without Mint.

The premium expansion signals JetBlue's ambition to transform Fort Lauderdale into more than a gateway for leisure travelers heading to Florida and the Caribbean. By adding lie-flat business class capacity on key West Coast routes, the airline hopes to capture higher-yield passengers while differentiating itself from competitors. Combined with today's new domestic and Caribbean routes, the Mint expansion demonstrates how central Fort Lauderdale has become to JetBlue's future growth strategy.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Maybe a flight that left in the afternoon from FLL, stopped in IND and/or CMH; then continued to JFK. Have the opposite happen from JFK to IND/CMN, then continues to FLL. This way, you provide service to two focus cities, not just one.
