#6232. Singapore Airlines’ New First & Business Class Cabins Will Be Unveiled This Week

In November 2024, Singapore Airlines announced a huge investment into its premium passenger experience, which will see the introduction of all-new cabin products, plus the expansion of first class. These cabins will be retrofitted on dozens of Airbus A350s, and will also be available on newly delivered Boeing 777-9s in the future.

The product was initially supposed to roll out as of the spring of 2026, though as is all too common nowadays, the project was delayed due to supply chain constraints, etc. The good news is that the wait is almost over — the new product will be unveiled on Friday, November 6, 2026, with an entry into service planned for the first quarter of 2027. Let’s recap all the details we know as of now.

Singapore Airlines will be investing 1.1 billion SGD (~835 million USD) to update the interiors of its entire long haul Airbus A350-900 fleet. This consists of a total of 41 jets, and includes the carrier’s seven A350-900ULRs, with the “ULR” standing for “ultra long range,” as these planes operate the world’s longest flights.

The only A350-900s that won’t be reconfigured are the ones that are specifically designed for regional flights, featuring the same cabin products you’ll find onboard Boeing 787-10s.

With this project, we can expect changes across cabins. We’ll see first class added to the carrier’s ultra long range A350s, an all-new business class product, refreshes to premium economy and economy, plus an updated inflight entertainment system and the installation of Starlink Wi-Fi.

How will the layouts of these jets change, once reconfigured? Singapore Airlines’ standard long haul A350-900s:

Singapore Airlines’ ultra long range A350-900s:

Singapore Airlines will be introducing new first and business class products. This isn’t just some new interim product, but rather this is intended to be the carrier’s new premium product in the long run. The same seats that are being installed on the Airbus A350-900s will also be installed on the carrier’s Boeing 777-9s, so these are very much “flagship” cabins.

Singapore Airlines initially intended to debut new premium cabins on its 777-9s, which were first supposed to be delivered in 2020. However, those have now been pushed back to late 2027 at the earliest. So clearly Singapore Airlines decided that it’s finally time to introduce new cabins, even if the 777-9 keeps getting delayed.

Singapore Airlines will introduce a new first class product on its subfleet of A350-900ULRs, which operate the world’s longest flights. This same product will be available on 777-9s in the future, but won’t be available on standard A350-900s. Furthermore, there are no plans to retrofit existing 777s with this product. A350s will have four of these seats, while 777s will have six of these seats.

Below is the first teaser picture of Singapore Airlines’ new first class.

Currently Singapore Airlines only has first class on its A380s and 777-300ERs, so it’s cool to see this product expand.

Official details about the new first class are limited, other than that it’s “designed with increasingly discerning travellers in mind,” and that the first class seats “promise to deliver an unparalleled in-flight experience.”

We have reason to believe that the new cabin will be in a 1-2-1 layout. Why? Well, Singapore Airlines filed a patent some time back, clearly for the carrier’s new first class product. The patent is for the 777-9, where the airline will have a first class cabin with six seats.

The plan seems to be to have individual suites along the windows, plus a double suite in the center. However, the center suite can be used by either one or two people, so if people are traveling separately, there’s a partition that can go up.

As you can see, there’s a bit of staggering with the cabin, to maximize the width of the suite, as the aisle curves a bit.

This looks like a very nice product, though to be perfectly honest, it doesn’t look like anything revolutionary. Nowadays some of the top first class products are in a 1-1-1 configuration, like what you’ll find on Japan Airlines and Emirates. Admittedly the flexibility of the double suite in the middle is great for those traveling with someone, since that’s not something that was really considered with the new Japan Airlines and Emirates products.

For that matter, we have reason to believe that Cathay Pacific may offer the world’s best first class on its 777-9s, as it could very well be in a 1-1 configuration.

This is super exciting. Singapore Airlines is one of the best airlines in the world, with incredible service, food, drinks, and more. However, at this point the carrier’s business class hard product isn’t really cutting edge anymore.

With details being so limited, all we can do is speculate as of now. So I have a few thoughts:

In late 2024, when this project was first announced, Singapore Airlines shared the following timeline for debuting the new first and business class seats:

Unfortunately that timeline didn’t stick. Several months ago we learned how the first retrofitted aircraft wouldn’t enter service until the first quarter of 2027, best case scenario, with the expectation being that some long range A350s would be reconfigured before the first ultra long range A350 gets a makeover.

The revised timeline reflects industry-wide supply chain constraints, as well as delays in the certification of one of the new seats (a common industry problem). The aircraft will be retrofitted by SIA Engineering Company in Singapore.

So, is that still the timeline we’re looking at? It would appear so. Singapore Airlines has confirmed on social media that it will unveiling its all new products on Friday, November 6, 2026.

From the first sketch to the final detail, discover how the new Singapore Airlines travel experience comes together across every cabin class and every part of the journey.Unveiling on 6 November 2026. pic.twitter.com/dTML7QmOXe

This announcement is actually being marketed as being about more than just seats, as it’s described as “the new Singapore Airlines travel experience,” and we’ll learn how it “comes together across every class and every part of the journey.” We’ve already seen the airline tease details of a new dining concept as well as new amenities across cabins, so presumably this will all come together to form the new experience.

Which routes are likely to get the new cabins first? While we’ll see how this plays out, based on historical precedent, it’s likely that Sydney (SYD) and London (LHR) will be the first two destinations, since those are the first destinations where the airline has sent all of its new long haul products.

Singapore Airlines plans to introduce all-new cabins on its Airbus A350-900s, which will also eventually be installed on Boeing 777-9s. Most exciting is an improved new business class product, which is long overdue. Singapore Airlines will also be adding first class to its subfleet of A350-900ULRs, with a boutique cabin having just four seats.

While this product was supposed to enter service as of the second quarter of 2026, the timeline has been pushed back to the first quarter of 2027, due to supply chain constraints and certification issues… a familiar story! The expectation is that the new cabins will be unveiled this week, on November 6, 2026. I’m mighty curious to learn the details, so I’m happy that the wait is finally (almost) over.

What do you make of Singapore Airlines’ plans to introduce new long haul cabins?

#6231. Buy Finnair Plus Avios For 50% Off (1.06 Cents Each): Best-Ever Price Worth It?

The Finnair Plus program has just launched its newest promotion on purchased Avios, offering up to a 50% discount, which is an opportunity to acquire Avios for as little as 1.06 cents each. This is the best offer from the program of the year, and you can use this to acquire any “flavor” of Avios at an advantageous rate.

Strategically buying points for premium travel can be a great value, especially with a specific use in mind, so this is an offer I’d seriously consider.

Between 12:01AM EET on November 2 and 11:59PM EET on November 16, 2026, Finnair Plus is offering a limited time promotion on purchased Avios. If you purchase Finnair Plus Avios, you can receive the following deal:

Beyond the discount, you can also receive tier points toward status equivalent to 10% of the Avios purchased. This is of course useful if you’re going for elite status with Finnair, but otherwise, is of limited value.

Now, here’s where it gets interesting — Finnair lets you select the currency in which you want to buy Avios (you can find the option to switch currencies at the top of the screen), and the price differs:

So based on current exchange rates, you’re best off paying in JPY, followed by USD, followed by EUR. If you maxed out the promotion with a 50% bonus and paid in JPY, the best deal you could get would be to pay $2,110 for 200,000 Avios, which comes out to 1.06 cents per Avios (in USD), inclusive of all taxes and fees.

Note that this offer is only available to Finnair Plus members who joined the program before October 30, 2026, and have a minimum balance of 50 Avios in their account (though those Avios can be transferred from another “flavor” of the currency).

When Finnair Plus offers a promotion on purchased Avios, it’s common to see either a 50% bonus or a 40-50% discount. The 50% discount gives you the absolute best price, so this is definitely the time to buy Avios, if interested.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from the program, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Finnair Plus Avios purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

Since the purchase of Finnair Avios can potentially be billed in a foreign currency, there is one other great option. The Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card (learn more) offers 3x points on foreign purchases, so that’s a fantastic card for this kind of purchase.

What should you expect from Finnair Plus award pricing, and the best ways to redeem to Finnair Plus Avios?

Below you can find the one-way Finnair Plus award redemptions rates for travel on Finnair.

Awards also have surcharges, though they’re at least mild. If you have a connecting itinerary, you’ll only be charged the surcharge correlated to the most expensive segment flown.

When your award booking includes a connecting flight, Avios are charged separately for each flight, except for flights within Finland and Northern Europe. For example, a Frankfurt to Helsinki to New York business class award would cost you 82,500 Avios (20,000 Avios plus 62,500 Avios). One awesome thing is that Finnair Plus has an award seat guarantee, meaning there’s pretty consistently award availability when booking far in advance.

Finnair Plus also allows redemptions on partner airlines, though the pricing isn’t particularly attractive, for the most part. The more important thing to keep in mind is that it’s possible to transfer Avios between the various “flavors” of the currency.

Therefore this promotion is also an opportunity to earn Avios that you can transfer 1:1 to programs like Aer Lingus AerClub, British Airways Club, Iberia Club, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, etc. That opens up more redemption opportunities.

Finnair Plus has launched a promotion on purchased Avios. With this, you can receive up to a 50% discount when purchasing Avios, which is an opportunity to buy them for 1.06 cents each (in USD, when paying in JPY). This is the best price of the year from Finnair Plus on purchasing Avios (and the best price for purchasing any current of Avios this year, for that matter).

There’s absolutely value to be had here, especially since this is an opportunity to earn any “flavor” of Avios, thanks to the 1:1 transfer options.

#6230. United’s CEO Loves New American Airlines Boarding Gates—Here’s Why They Make Flying Worse

He saw it as something worth copying. When American announced the equipment, I thought it would make flying worse.

Kirby says he’s flown American, Delta and Southwest at least three times each over the past year, looking for things they do better than United. He lives in Dallas, and is regularly spotted on American but Southwest is based at Dallas Love Field as well.

American supplied this rendering when it announced the gates in April:

The glass barriers open after the system validates a boarding pass. American says the equipment can control the pace at which passengers enter the jet bridge, reduce manual work (cost savings on gate agents), and let employees spend more time helping customers (or just pocket the labor savings). The airline has since opened its new DFW Terminal C pier with the technology at all nine gates.

Airports are increasingly moving to e-gates, where facial recognition is used to confirm identity. So far this has mostly been used for international departures. The government wants more than a person looking at you and confirming it against the photo in your passport.

At many international departure gates, a camera is mounted at the gate or held by a government customs officer or airline staff member, to take a live photo of each passenger during boarding.

That image is sent to the Customs and Border Protection cloud-based Traveler Verification Service, which compares each person’s mugshot to a gallery built from your passport or visa photo and compares it to the flight manifest. The government has already checked the flight manifest and decided who can travel and who can’t. Now they want to match people against the manifest. If there’s a match, you’re allowed to depart the country. If there’s no match, you get a manual document check.

The biggest boarding bottlenecks aren’t actually the act of scanning a barcode. In fact, without human assistance each passenger may take longer to scan and wait for the gate to open.

Too many carry-ons, limited overhead bin space, gate-checking bags, families bunching up during preboarding and standby processing at the gate seem to be bigger issues. These gates do not solve any of that – just queue management and access control. The worst part of the experience is actually what Kirby says is his standard for judging this:

“I think of air travel for customers through the lens of traveling with small children,” Kirby said. “I have seven kids. I know what it’s like. I’ve tried to make it easy for people to travel with young children because if we do that, it’s going to be great for everybody.”

#6229. Save On Air France-KLM Flights With Amex Offers (Targeted)

The Amex Offers program has just rolled out a great new targeted offer for the purchase of Air France-KLM flights, which could be worth considering for anyone planning travel. We’ve seen this offer in the past, and I’m happy to see it return, as I always get significant value from it. However, this offer isn’t quite as lucrative as past ones.

With a new targeted Amex Offers deal, you can earn a $250 statement credit when you spend $2,500 or more with Air France-KLM by December 15, 2026. (Enrollment required)

It’s possible that there’s also a version of the offer for 25,000 bonus points rather than a $250 statement credit, and if so, I’d consider that to be more valuable. That’s because based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, so I’d value the 25,000 points at $425.

For what it’s worth, in the past when I’ve purchased sustainable aviation fuel with Air France in order to earn XP (the metric by which you qualify for status), that triggered an Amex Offers deal. So at least anecdotally, that seems to work. Furthermore, taxes and carrier imposed surcharges on award tickets also seem to qualify.

I’m always happy to see this offer available, though let me note that this isn’t as lucrative as in the past. In past situations we’ve seen a $200 statement credit or 20,000 bonus points after spending $1,000+, so as a percentage return, this definitely isn’t as good.

This Amex Offers deal is targeted, though it’s possible you’ll see it on multiple of your cards. If so, I’d highly recommend registering your American Express Platinum Card® for this offer. That’s because the Amex Platinum offers 5x points on airfare purchased directly with airlines on up to $500,000 per calendar year and then 1x.

Based on my valuation of 1.7 cents per Membership Rewards point, the 5x points offers an incremental 8.5% return on spending. On top of that, the Amex Platinum offers valuable travel protection, should you experience irregular operations.

In other words, if you took advantage of this offer with the Amex Platinum for a $2,500 ticket, you’d receive a $250 statement credit plus 12,500 points. By my valuation, that’s a return of $462.50 on $2,500 of spending, which comes out to an 18.5% return.

There’s a new targeted Amex Offers deal for a $250 statement credit when you spend $2,500+ on an Air France-KLM ticket. If you’re planning travel on Air France or KLM, this has the potential to be a solid deal. Ideally you’ll see this offer on the Amex Platinum, so that you can really maximize your points.

Were you targeted for this Amex Offers deal, and if so, do you plan on taking advantage of it?

#6228. Adani Expects ‘One or Two’ Foreign Airlines to Pause Mumbai Flights Rather Than Move Airports

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: The check-in counters at Navi Mumbai Airport. NMIA

Adani says a few airline exits would barely dent passenger numbers, but that’s not the only measure of a new airport’s success. If well-known long-haul carriers refuse to fly to Mumbai, Navi Mumbai’s international network will be mostly Indian airlines, which limits its appeal to global travelers.

Some international airlines may temporarily suspend their Mumbai services rather than shift operations to Navi Mumbai International Airport, said Arun Bansal, CEO of Adani Airport Holdings.

“There might be one or two airlines that decide not to operate from Mumbai for a couple of years, but that will have almost no impact on the overall passenger count,” Bansal said during Adani Enterprises’ second-quarter earnings call last week.

He added that the airport is close to wrapping up discussions with most international airlines, with only a few dialogues still to be resolved.

The proposed shift is part of a larger operational change at Mumbai’s Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport (CSMIA), which Adani also operates.

Adani Airport Holdings expects a handful of international airlines to pause Mumbai service rather than relocate to Navi Mumbai International Airport, and CEO Arun Bansal said the loss would barely register in overall passenger numbers. The shift is driven by the April 2027 redevelopment of Terminal 1 at Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport, which will push domestic flights into Terminal 2 and squeeze out some international carriers that Adani wants to move 45 kilometers away to Navi Mumbai. Foreign carriers have asked for more time, and Air France-KLM said in September that splitting its Mumbai operations "is not an option." Indian carriers are moving first: Akasa Air shifts its Mumbai–Jeddah flights in December, IndiGo plans to build to 12 international destinations between February and July 2027, and Air India Group has announced seven international routes. IndiGo CEO Willie Walsh said Navi Mumbai matters to the airline's long-haul ambitions and that it will operate at both airports, but that its timing will follow its own network plans rather than the operator's requirements. Adani is targeting full use of Navi Mumbai's 20 million passenger initial capacity by the end of the next financial year, with Terminal 2 construction due to start this month.

#6227. Save On Etihad Flights With Amex Offers (Targeted)

The Amex Offers program has just rolled out a great new targeted offer for the purchase of Etihad Airways flights, which could be worth considering for anyone planning travel (that’s not to say you should or shouldn’t plan travel on Etihad, for a variety of reasons — I’m just sharing a deal!).

To my knowledge, this is the first time that we’ve seen an Amex Offers deal for Etihad purchases, so it’s nice to see another airline join the Amex Offers “circuit.”

With a new targeted Amex Offers deal, you can earn a $200 statement credit when you spend $1,000+ or more with Etihad Airways by December 31, 2026. (Enrollment required)

It’s possible that there’s also a version of the offer for 20,000 bonus points rather than a $200 statement credit, and if so, I’d consider that to be more valuable. That’s because based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex points are worth 1.7 cents each, so I’d value the 20,000 points at $340.

Let me emphasize that while the terms suggest that you need to book an Etihad flight through the US website that originates in the US, I’ve had similar Amex Offers triggered in the past for flights that didn’t originate in the US, so it’s anyone’s guess how that’s actually enforced here.

This Amex Offers deal is targeted, though it’s possible you’ll see it on multiple of your cards. If so, I’d highly recommend registering your American Express Platinum Card® for this offer. That’s because the Amex Platinum offers 5x points on airfare purchased directly with airlines.

Based on my valuation of 1.7 cents per Membership Rewards point, the 5x points offers an incremental 8.5% return on spending. On top of that, the Amex Platinum offers valuable travel protection, should you experience irregular operations.

In other words, if you took advantage of this offer with the Amex Platinum for a $1,000 ticket, you’d receive a $200 statement credit plus 5,000 points. By my valuation, that’s a return of $285 on $1,000 of spending, which comes out to a 28.5% return.

There’s a new targeted Amex Offers deal for a $200 statement credit when you spend $1,000+ on an Etihad ticket. If you’re planning travel on Etihad, this has the potential to be a solid deal. Ideally you’ll see this offer on the Amex Platinum, so that you can really maximize your points.

Were you targeted for this Amex Offers deal, and if so, do you plan on taking advantage of it?

#6226. "Short-Sighted": Delta CEO Vows To Fight Heathrow’s Move To Split It From Virgin Atlantic

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian has publicly criticized Heathrow Airport's decision to move the airline to Terminal 4 in 2028, calling the decision "short-sighted" and "bad for airline consumers." The criticism comes after a once-in-a-decade review at Europe's busiest international airport resulted in five airlines being ordered to move terminals in 2028, including Delta.

This change has been met with upset after both Delta and Virgin Atlantic, in which the American carrier holds a 49% share, argued that it will move the US carrier away from its UK partner and put the airline at a disadvantage to its competitors. Bastian has vowed to "pursue all available remedies" to reverse the decision.

As part of Heathrow Airport Limited's review, Delta will be required to relocate to the airport's Terminal 4. This comes after more than a decade in which Delta and Virgin have cohabitated in Terminal 3. This one-terminal approach for the two airlines has enabled convenient connections, premium shared amenities, and a collaboration to provide travelers access to the airlines' two extensive long-haul networks.

Having the two airlines co-located in Terminal 3 has provided a valuable competitive alternative to other legacy carriers operating transatlantic flights. When separated, this will undermine the years of investment that the two airlines have spent in the last decade, and it is suggested that the decision has disregarded the customer benefits that are offered by the co-location. In a lengthy statement released on Monday, Bastian said:

"Heathrow Airport Limited’s decision to relocate Delta’s operation to Terminal 4, away from our partner Virgin Atlantic, is short-sighted, deeply disappointing and bad for airline consumers . . . Separating our operation undermines years of investment and disregards the tightly integrated customer benefits that we offer in our co-located terminal."

As detailed in Bastian's statement, both Delta and Virgin are planning to fight this decision, and Delta is urging Heathrow Airport Limited to reconsider the decision. Virgin is considering its legal options, and SkyTeam, of which both airlines are partners, has argued that the move would put its members at a disadvantage to other airlines sharing terminals.

For Delta, the move matters as they are arguing that the relocation to Terminal 4 would split the airline from its joint venture partner after more than a decade. This would result in connecting passengers between the two airlines being forced to connect across the airfield by bus transport.

Heathrow Airport Limited has said that the once-a-decade review would free up available capacity at the airport, while easing congestion at one of the most slot-controlled airports in the world.

Heathrow's decision to separate Delta and Virgin Atlantic sparks competition concerns and potential legal challenges.

For US carriers, Delta is tied second with United Airlines by total destinations served at Heathrow, with both airlines serving seven year-round US gateways. They trail behind American Airlines, who operate year-round to nine US airports, and add a sole seasonal service.

Virgin Atlantic operates year-round to ten destinations in the US, with a seasonal service added during the Northern Hemisphere summer season to Seattle. The full Heathrow network for both airlines is below:

Atlanta (ATL), Boston (BOS), Detroit (DTW), Minneapolis/Saint Paul (MSP), New York-JFK (JFK), Salt Lake City (SLC), Seattle/Tacoma (SEA)

Atlanta (ATL), Boston (BOS), Las Vegas (LAS), Los Angeles (LAX), Miami (MIA), New York-JFK (JFK), Orlando (MCO), San Francisco (SFO), Tampa (TPA), Washington-Dulles (IAD), Seattle/Tacoma (SEA) – seasonal

Antigua (ANU), Barbados (BGI), Bengaluru (BLR), Cancún (CUN), Cape Town (CPT) – seasonal, Delhi (DEL), Dubai (DXB), Grenada (GND), Johannesburg (JNB), Lagos (LOS), Malé (MLE) – seasonal, Montego Bay (MBJ), Mumbai (BOM), Seoul (ICN), St. Vincent (SVD), Toronto (YYZ), Phuket (HKT) – seasonal

In Heathrow Terminal 3 currently, Delta and Virgin share a number of facilities and infrastructure, including the Virgin Atlantic Clubhouse, providing an iconic lounge for eligible business class passengers and top-tier frequent flyers. Travelers also have access to the Virgin Revivals Lounge, which provides lounge facilities for arriving passengers.

Shared ground labor, check-in, and transfer coordination also see the two airlines working collaboratively for the benefit of passengers and airline operations.

#6225. American Airlines Spent Years Making Its Cabins Worse—Now It’s Racing To Win Passengers Back From United And Delta

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby says one of his biggest competitive advantages won’t last. Other airlines will catch up with Starlink internet. He says he’s investing anyway, because two or three years is enough time to get passengers to try United, discover other things they like, and move their loyalty and credit card spending. That answers the argument Doug Parker made at American Airlines in 2017 for not investing in product: better products just get copied so can’t offer an enduring advantage. Delta spent nearly two decades showing how investment in the operation, product and employees could work together. United has improved more than any other U.S. airline over the past decade. American has made an impressive amount of progress since its premium pivot roughly 21 months ago. But it’s trying to win back customers while losing money, carrying heavy debt, and with fuel costs up. They’re in a race against time to show results before Wall Street gets impatient. I attended American’s September 2017 media and investor day. The airline’s theory was that competitors would match a better product, leaving corporate culture and employees to differentiate the airline. Take care of employees, who would take care of customers, who would take care of shareholders. (Of course American alienated all three groups.) They didn’t explain how that was going to happen. There were nicer employee facilities coming, help using their health and wellness benefits, and they spent a disproportionate amount of time on company-sponsored weight loss programs. I left without understanding the mission employees were supposed to rally around, or how American would install its workforce with a desire and knowledge to deliver exceptional service. Meanwhile, American was preparing to fly its new domestic interior with less legroom, less padded seats and no seatback screens. At that same media day, they didn’t even think they needed native booking in their mobile app. Sending customers to a mobile website was good enough. A year later, Parker told employees: we work really hard to match our service to our competitors, and they do the same to us. He described watching what competitors put onboard, including meals, to ensure American was comparable. He was surprised by the idea that customers might choose United or Delta because of a different inflight product. In contrast, Richard Anderson became Delta CEO in 2007. Along with Glen Hauenstein and Gil West, he built an airline around keeping its promises to passengers and driving hard bargains with its counterparties. Anderson later explained how much of the advantage came from line maintenance. An older airplane could be reliable if mechanics could work on it where it spent the night, fix recurring problems and have it ready in the morning. Delta also worked toward eliminating involuntary denied boarding. A customer who bought a ticket, arrived on time and followed every instruction shouldn’t be told they weren’t going to travel because the airline had sold too many seats. Finding enough volunteers protected the relationship with that customer. They leaned into seatback screens. Their non-union crews were somewhat friendlier than at competitors. Then Delta made itself relevant in the markets where customers had the most money to spend. The 2011 LaGuardia slot swap with US Airways was one of the great airline asset trades. Parker’s airline gave Delta 132 daily LaGuardia slot pairs in exchange for 42 pairs at Washington National and $66.5 million. Required divestitures reduced Delta’s net gain (they eventually got the slots back that were transferred to WestJet) but it gave them the platform to build the New York business. Delta fleeced Parker. US Airways strengthened Washington, but when it merged with American it had to give up slots there anyway. The combined airline couldn’t keep all of both carriers’ holdings. American – once headquartered in New York – would never be able to position itself in New York the way that Delta had. Delta invested in facilities at LaGuardia, JFK and Los Angeles. That all positioned Delta to overtake American in cobrand credit card spend. I’ve been critical of how much Delta has coasted on that reputation. Its operational advantage isn’t what it was (they’re still a bit more reliable than peers but when things go south they struggle to recover, and no longer go months without a mainline cancel). Their 767s out of New York are arguably the actual worst product across the Atlantic and among those who compete for premium transcon business. And Delta’s success despite weak mileage value shouldn’t have taught competitors to devalue their own programs. Delta offered a better experience – that’s eroding – and had strong positioning in some of the best spend markets, and lack of competition in their other key markets (Atlanta, Upper Midwest, Salt Lake). Kirby took a long time to arrive at his current view. He was president of American when it cut meal service in 2014. Planning for the domestic interior without screens began while he was still there, even though the first aircraft with that interior entered service after he left. He initially carried the same approach to United. They cut full domestic first class meals on flights under four hours outside the dinner window, before customer complaints forced a reversal. They eliminated Polaris wine flights and cocktail carts, then reduced business class staffing by one flight attendant and moved to pre-plated entrees. Some of United’s early product investment was probably overboard – greenlighting most everything when Oscar Munoz came back from medical leave. The later United NEXT commitment to screens, bigger bins and a better domestic cabin, combined with sustained investment in its mobile app, represented a different approach under later Kirby. Most passengers sit in coach. Improving their experience gets them to pay more and builds a reputation that qualifies the airline for their future purchases in business. Even business class passengers internationally are often coach passengers domestically, and bad experiences in domestic form the bulk of a passenger’s opinion when it coms time to buy long haul business. The app is part of the coach product just as well as the premium cabin one. Passengers can manage changes, get help improving their seat assignment and receive clearer explanations when something goes wrong. It gives them more control over their trip. They use it repeatedly, and it’s reason they may hesitate to move their flying elsewhere even after another airline matches the cabin. By 2025, Kirby was explaining a different test for food spending. He told Brian Sumers: Every year we’re going to consciously spend more for customers in a bet that we’ll just win more brand-loyal customers. He couldn’t prove exactly how much additional ticket revenue better food would generate. He was willing to make the investment anyway. The old approach could identify the savings from moving a meal window by 15 minutes, while the revenue lost through a series of small disappointments was much harder to see. United’s network rebuilding started earlier. Kirby restored domestic connectivity that had been cut back under Jeff Smisek, and explicitly explained in October 2017 that better connections would help sell credit cards. If United’s schedule didn’t work for someone, that person wasn’t going to take the card. American went the other way in New York, Chicago and Los Angeles. Retreating made the airline less useful in the country’s most valuable spending markets. Offering a less desirable product alienated customers from spending on the American card. And an airline’s route accounting can miss this. A Chicago customer’s work trips may be what persuade them to get an airline’s card, even if they eventually redeem the miles for Hawaii. Credit the Hawaii flight with all the benefit, cut Chicago because it looks weak, and you lose the spending that generated the miles in the first place. In contrast, aviation watchdog JonNYC shares excerpts attributed to Chief Commercial Officer Andrew Nocella laying out where the airline sees itself: United reached 50% of revenue from Chicago-based passengers in the second quarter of 2026, according to Nocella, and gained share in its other hub cities as well. It expects to largely complete United NEXT’s connectivity goals at its midcontinent hubs by summer 2027. More attention then shifts to coastal gateways and international expansion, including a planned return to New York JFK next year. Premium capacity will grow faster than main cabin capacity as United adds Airbus A321neo and A321XLR aircraft at scale. Comments by Andrew Nocella, shared by JonNYC United’s hubs in some of the best cities for card spend and long haul pre-existed Kirby (and those cities are more contested than other airlines face in their most important hubs). Kirby’s Starlink explanation in his Cheeky Pint interview describes how he plans to accelerate United’s gains. John Collison characterized the opportunity as a two-to-three-year window to win customers, and Kirby agreed. Other airlines will eventually have comparable low Earth orbit connectivity. American, Southwest, Alaska and even Frontier are all adding Starlink (and Southwest expects to complete its install around the time United does). they’re going to try us for Starlink, and they’re going to stay because all the other technology, and everything else is better. A temporary advantage can generate a customer relationship that outlasts it. And the biggest gap will be with Delta, which has committed to Amazon Leo that will maybe start becoming available in 2028, and where they’ve committed only to eventually outfit 500 aircraft. Delta’s current wifi is generally poor now that demands on the system by giving it away free have overwhelmed available bandwidth. Parker was right that competitors could copy a feature. Copying the feature doesn’t on its own win back the customer. American is finally reversing course. I first reported its explicit premium pivot in January 2025. In roughly 21 months they’ve changed an extraordinary amount, from better coffee and wine to improved lounges, new business class suites and more attention to the coach experience. They’ve committed to bringing back domestic seatback screens and adding more first class and extra legroom seats. They’ve announced Starlink installations beginning early next year. They’ve even instructed employees to stop involuntarily bumping passengers, giving airport leadership more authority to secure volunteers. American is changing what it asks employees to prioritize, and giving them tools to do it. And Flagship Dining at Los Angeles is finally reopening after more than six years, with access expanded to qualifying business class passengers. It’s a defensive move because Delta’s business class lounge is so much better, and United’s even had been better than American Flagship. I want this to work. I’ve spent years criticizing American because it had so much potential to be better. They’re making real changes and some customers will come back simply because the airline stops giving them reasons to avoid it. But matching what they already get elsewhere likely isn’t enough – American needs a value proposition for what they deliver to customers that no one else will. That’s Delta’s reliability argument (paired with service and screens that for years others eschewed). That’s United’s Starlink argument (paired with a stronger global network). American entered the pandemic with heavy debt after spending more than $12 billion on share buybacks under Parker. Borrowing while returning that much cash to shareholders left it weaker than competitors. It has too much debt service, less room to borrow, and less well-positioned to do acquisitions. The risk is that investors demand results before enough customers have experienced the improvements, or demand cuts to the spending that could produce real results. American’s domestic seatback screens won’t begin arriving on new aircraft until 2028, and the broader fleet project extends into the next decade. It needs the improvements it can deliver sooner to get customers back onboard and spending more before then. The interest and fuel bills are arriving now. A temporary advantage can generate a customer relationship that outlasts it. And the biggest gap will be with Delta, which has committed to Amazon Leo that will maybe start becoming available in 2028, and where they’ve committed only to eventually outfit 500 aircraft. Delta’s current wifi is generally poor now that demands on the system by giving it away free have overwhelmed available bandwidth. Parker was right that competitors could copy a feature. Copying the feature doesn’t on its own win back the customer.

American is finally reversing course. I first reported its explicit premium pivot in January 2025. In roughly 21 months they’ve changed an extraordinary amount, from better coffee and wine to improved lounges, new business class suites and more attention to the coach experience.

They’ve committed to bringing back domestic seatback screens and adding more first class and extra legroom seats. They’ve announced Starlink installations beginning early next year.

They’ve even instructed employees to stop involuntarily bumping passengers, giving airport leadership more authority to secure volunteers. American is changing what it asks employees to prioritize, and giving them tools to do it.

And Flagship Dining at Los Angeles is finally reopening after more than six years, with access expanded to qualifying business class passengers. It’s a defensive move because Delta’s business class lounge is so much better, and United’s even had been better than American Flagship.

I want this to work. I’ve spent years criticizing American because it had so much potential to be better. They’re making real changes and some customers will come back simply because the airline stops giving them reasons to avoid it. But matching what they already get elsewhere likely isn’t enough – American needs a value proposition for what they deliver to customers that no one else will. That’s Delta’s reliability argument (paired with service and screens that for years others eschewed). That’s United’s Starlink argument (paired with a stronger global network).

American entered the pandemic with heavy debt after spending more than $12 billion on share buybacks under Parker. Borrowing while returning that much cash to shareholders left it weaker than competitors. It has too much debt service, less room to borrow, and less well-positioned to do acquisitions.

The risk is that investors demand results before enough customers have experienced the improvements, or demand cuts to the spending that could produce real results. American’s domestic seatback screens won’t begin arriving on new aircraft until 2028, and the broader fleet project extends into the next decade. It needs the improvements it can deliver sooner to get customers back onboard and spending more before then. The interest and fuel bills are arriving now.

Not until Robert Isom is gone and AA has true leadership will this airline ever recover. Morale is miserable in ALL work groups. Airlines are all alike and it simply comes down to the people that take care of the customers. Whenever I have to fly AA I brace myself for the absolute worst experience. After being scolded asking for a third glass of water during a dinner service in business class I simply have had enough. Like TWA, Braniff, Eastern and Pan Am before them there’s plenty of room in the desert to park planes when it’s all said and done.

I bet NO. We don’t forget the barking dog tapes. They treat passengers like dogs

American’s on time performance and overall reliability remains at the bottom end of the industry peers, slightly above JetBlue. That’s not good.

The fleet is enormous, and a lot of it still flies around in the Parker-era bare bones aesthetic, which is not aging well.

American’s finances are challenged by the buy-backs, yes, and the massive 2011 re-fleet which was needed, but very costly.

American has to work harder in NYC, Chicago, and LA to win back premium customers and position itself not as one that has matched DL and UA but does something a bit better. The wealth on credit card spend in America does not sit in Charlotte or the Sun Belt. It resides in the big blue cities that MAGA hates. Just look at United’s route map and rising premium revenue, and you can see why. It’s hubs are in the right markets.

Delta’s performance in NYC is slipping. Too much flying to Europe is performed on 767-300ERs and 767-400ERs, and A330CEOs that have old, dated cabins. Ground staff at JFK are often rude but Delta still has the ability to find a revenue yield premium like the rest cannot.

Alaska is the winner in the service wars. They have the best employees and give them the authority to do their jobs. That’s not to say that AS hasn’t backslid the last two years but their recent announcement indicated they still get what’s important.

Is that enough to grow to the size of the big three? No not so long as airport slots are constrained. But where they fly Alaska asks for and appears to get a premium which indicates that passengers are willing to pay more to fly with them.

Bigger picture whatever happens the customer is going to see substantial benefits from AA’s change in direction not only when they fly AA but other carriers as well because premium flyers obviously don’t take well to being abused and with loyalty no longer very valuable are much more likely to go with the airline with whom they have had good experiences.

That marginal revenue the airlines have been able to extract by upselling has come at a cost. No longer beholden the carriers have to perform in order to get a passenger’s repeat business.

Ironic but a good outcome for those of us who fly frequently and want more than just a cheap seat.

To respond to another commentator… you’re wrong about Alaska. They absolutely suck. Their Firsr Class food is a joke. And Alaska is already dumbing down Hawaiin Airlines, a once great airline. American will catch up over time. Delta is sliding. Their seats on the a321 Neo in First Class are absolute garbage… there is a metal box for electronics that sits right between the 2 “First Class” seats, severely impeding your legroom. The seats are cheap and you feel like you’re sitting on concrete after a couple of hours. And Delta’s WiFi is pure garbage too.

The US Airways/Doug Parker take over was an unmitigated disaster. The US Air planes right after the merger were horrendous. Charlotte, Phil, PHX are not DFW, MIA, ORD for corporate travel. I get AA was bankrupt and Arpey and Carty before him were not Crandall and Parker had the upper hand of a profitable airline, at that time. Going forward the legacy US AIR team needs to be moved out and bring in fresh blood that can make American Airlines great again.

I haven’t had the same reaction to their food in F. In your opinion how would you say it compares to UA, AA and DL?

It’s not all about ‘systems’. The people at Delta are so friendly and helpful – that can’t be replicated. The 757-400s are being replaced by new planes. That is coming.

The unions simply didn’t like the way Horton ran AA which is a shame as he’s one of the only people I’ve ever heard who not only was able to get bondholders their 100 cents to the dollar, but didn’t have shareholders wiped out during BK.

As the saying goes, “you reap what you sow”.

As an American Airlines retiree I agree with Texas Fly Girl. When someone asks I tell them I worked for airline and hope they don’t ask which one. It is embarrassing the downfall since the arrival of Parker and the USAIR guys.

I think it’s great to see AA finally realize its mistakes and move towards improvements. Hopefully they figure out ways to actually leapfrog the competition. They need to figure out a way to somehow buy or lease the JetBlue slots and gates at JFK, BOS and LAX. Would be next to impossible given the JetBlue+United partnership, but they need to explore options. Having United with its huge EWR fortress AND with a huge number of JFK slots would put WAY too much power in the hands of one airline.

#6224. War Insurance Dries Up for Gulf Events as U.S.-Iran Conflict Continues

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: The Riyadh Skyline Wikimedia Commons / B.alotaby

Gulf events can still insure against cancellation but not against war. That is pushing organizers to postpone events or to take on the risk themselves. It’s a growing issue, and Saudi Arabia’s calendar has been paying the price.

Event organizers in the Gulf can still insure against cancellation for many reasons, such as bad weather, a declared period of national mourning, or an IT failure. What they increasingly can’t buy is protection if an event is canceled because of war or political violence, industry executives told Skift.

Standard event-cancellation policies exclude war and political violence, so organizers routinely have to buy that coverage as a separate layer. Since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, it is something that has become very hard to find for Gulf events.

Only one insurer, possibly two on very limited terms, is currently willing to consider war exposure for events in the region, according to Panteha Peters, head of sports, entertainment, media and special risks at insurance broker Marsh Middle East and Africa. It does so case by case, and generally no earlier than about one week before the event.

War and political violence cover for events in the Gulf has largely disappeared, and organizers are absorbing the risk themselves, industry executives told Skift. Standard event-cancellation policies exclude war, so that protection is normally bought as a separate layer — and since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, only one insurer, possibly two on limited terms, will consider war exposure for Gulf events, according to Marsh Middle East and Africa's Panteha Peters, typically case by case and no earlier than about a week before the event. Marsh said in May that political violence premiums in the Gulf have risen at least 20-fold since the war began, while capacity to write that cover shrank from about $1 billion to roughly $200 million. Saudi Arabia is the sharpest pressure point: Morningstar DBRS's Marcos Alvarez said the Houthi missile and drone campaign on Riyadh, Abha, and Dammam in October turned war from a theoretical exclusion into a live, priced peril, and a long list of events has slipped, including the Future Investment Initiative conference, the EU-Gulf summit, Intersec Saudi Arabia 2026, the Saudi Retail Forum, the 2027 Dakar Rally, the Saudi International golf tournament, the Red Sea Film Festival, and Riyadh Fashion Week. Pricing for standard cancellation cover has generally held stable this year, Gallagher's Yasmin Dacuycuy said, so the squeeze is concentrated in the war layer. Events that proceed are doing so with lower limits, more exclusions, and in some cases no cancellation insurance at all.

Delta Air Lines is adding another route from its fastest-growing “focus city.”

Over the weekend, the Atlanta-based carrier filed plans to launch nonstop service from Austin Bergstrom International Airport (AUS) to Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA) outside Bentonville.

Flights will begin in March 2027, with Delta offering service on board a Delta Connection regional jet.

The service will give the Texas capital a nonstop link to northwest Arkansas — not to mention parts of Oklahoma, Missouri and Kansas, which are all a relatively short drive from XNA.

SkyMiles news: Delta announces Medallion qualification requirements for 2027

The airport is also the closest option for travelers heading to the University of Arkansas.

For Delta, it’s the latest in a series of expansions in Austin.

The carrier has grown its flight offerings at AUS at a fast pace over the last couple of years, targeting the airport as one of its top non-hub “focus cities.”

That growth included the airline’s first nonstop service from Austin to Europe, which Delta revealed in August. Those flights to Paris will begin in April.

That’s on top of new routes to major tech hubs like San Jose in California's Silicon Valley and popular leisure destinations like Bozeman, Montana, and Cancun in Mexico.

All told, the airline plans to operate up to 70 daily departures by March, Delta chief commercial officer Joe Esposito told me this summer.

In 2019, it had 28 peak daily departures from AUS.

“The boom is incredible,” Esposito told me in August, noting that a growing number of Delta flyers will also start seeing itineraries with connections in the Lone Star State. That said, Delta has stopped short of saying it will ever make Austin a hub.

“We want to be the business carrier of Austin — we’re quickly moving in on the leading corporate carrier for Austin,” he said. “Then you wind up connecting people.”

It's likely no coincidence, then, that Delta would be interested in service to Bentonville: the region is home to Walmart's corporate headquarters.

As for this latest route, Delta’s service from AUS to Northwest Arkansas will launch on March 7.

It’ll be a late-night departure, with flights taking off just before 9 p.m. The return flight from XNA to AUS will launch the next morning, on March 8.

The service will be on board an Embraer 175 regional jet operated by regional partner SkyWest.

“This new direct route is another example of Delta’s continued investment in Austin and our commitment to making it easier for Austinites to get where they want to go as we continue growing alongside this important community,” Luis Guitart, Delta’s Austin-based regional sales manager, said in a statement to TPG Monday.

While Delta has grown its flight offerings in Austin rapidly over the past couple of years, Southwest Airlines remains the market leader at the airport.

Southwest, like Delta, plans to offer its biggest schedule ever from AUS in 2027.

The airport will also be home to one of its inaugural airport lounges.

Delta, for its part, is planning a second — larger — Sky Club at AUS for the coming years.

By the way, Delta's new route to Northwest Arkansas will add to a strong run of air service growth for that region, too.

This year, the airport will see 28% more total flights than it did just two years ago, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium.

Beyond its future route to Austin, Delta serves Bentonville from five other airports — all hubs: Atlanta, Detroit, Minneapolis, Salt Lake City and New York's LaGuardia Airport (LGA).

#6222. Ouch: Flying Blue Makes Earning XPs Through SAF 50% More Expensive

The Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has just rolled out a quiet devaluation, and it’s one that many savvy Flying Blue members won’t be happy about. The airline group has increased the cost to contribute toward sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), and in turn, has reduced the ability to earn elite status through this method. And we’re not talking about a minor price increase either…

Personally I consider Air France-KLM Flying Blue elite status to be valuable, not just for the SkyTeam Elite Plus perks, but also for the more Air France- KLM specific benefits, like access to more award availability.

Earning Flying Blue elite status is based on the concept of XPs (“experience points”), and how many of those you rack up. One really innovative thing that Flying Blue has done is that it has been possible to earn XPs through environmental contributions:

As I see it, this is a win-win — this program can genuinely help you earn status, while doing something that’s good for the environment, and also contributing to Air France-KLM’s long term environmental goals.

Well, seemingly overnight, Flying Blue has increased the cost to purchase SAF, and in turn, earn XPs. With these changes, you earn one XP for every €15 contributed toward SAF, compared to the previous amount of €10.

A 50% overnight increase is rough. It gets even worse than that, though. There’s no longer any “rounding” with this, so for short haul economy flights you might find that you’re not offered any XPs if the contribution amount is €14, and you’re offered one XP if the amount is €28.

The past year or so has definitely been rough for the overall value of the Flying Blue program, including for elite members:

This is of course all frustrating, though I guess the other side of the equation is that Flying Blue Platinum status has become more valuable over time, but primarily through punitive measures:

How do we make sense of increasing the cost to contribute to SAF, and in turn, earn XPs? I wonder if Flying Blue management thinks that people will still buy SAF at the same rate as before? I know I certainly won’t, though maybe I’m in the minority (I’ll instead increasingly earn XPs through Flying Blue’s co-branded credit card in the US, since that opportunity was recently improved).

For that matter, I’m curious to what extent the number of people buying SAF matters to Air France-KLM? Does this materially contribute to any environmental initiatives, or is it not a priority?

I still get value from my Flying Blue Platinum status, and don’t have plans to change my strategy. Honestly, that partly comes down to how hard it has become to find award availability in business class on long haul flights through other programs.

But I’m definitely slowly becoming less enthused by the program. Then again, I guess that sums up the reality of miles & points more broadly — this isn’t what it once was, and it’s getting harder and harder to make the case for being loyal. It’s no different than World of Hyatt, where they’re clearly trying to cash in. I guess that is the goal of any for-profit business, eh?

Flying Blue has just devalued the rate at which you earn XPs for SAF contributions. You used to earn one XP for every €10 contributed, while you now earn one XP for every €15 contributed. A 50% increase in cost overnight is huge.

I always thought this was a unique aspect of the Flying Blue program, since it’s a win-win for consumers, the airline group, and the environment. Obviously they’ve decided on a different equation now, and for us members, this isn’t good news.

What do you make of this change to Flying Blue when it comes to earning XPs for SAF?

These offsets are just virtue signaling. Let them all go away!

Another European here. Thank God for this. We are so tired of all those credit card milers taking up award space and ruining lounges for us over here. Unlike US programmes, FB is clearly reserving benefits for those who actually fly AFKL. I think it's great, lure in Americans who never fly AFKL with a half-baked Visa Signature, then slowly take away all benefits.

As someone who had qualified for Elite Plus for 15+ years, I'm really pleased with my decision to relegate FB to a backup programme shortly before the shocking devaluation that moved intercontinental awards from 50k to 85k. I now do virtually all of my revenue flying on *A and have been able to get cheap status matches for 4+ years (AZ, KQ, SK) so that I can still enjoy the perks on the odd cheap short-haul flight and when redeeming (non-FB) miles in premium economy etc.

This has become an all too familiar script. Devalue a program, wait a few months, find another way to devalue it, and repeat. Flying Blue is hardly alone. Numerous frequent flyer programs have followed the same playbook. I'm sure these programs analyze member behavior after each devaluation and, seeing little meaningful impact, feel emboldened to do it again. But loyalty erodes gradually. At some point, members will stop chasing status, accumulating miles, or going out of their way to remain loyal. The real danger isn't that members will get angry and leave. It's that they'll simply stop caring. And indifference is far more damaging to a loyalty program than outrage.

#6221. Hotel Guests Report Mold And Mice—It Still Passed Inspection The Next Day

A mother says mice crawled across her sleeping three-year-old at a Wyndham hotel near the Albany, New York airport. Other residents reported mold, cockroaches and soaked carpets. The hotel passed a county health inspection the next day even though the inspector recorded six violations. The rooms with violations weren’t occupied on the day the inspector arrived and were supposed to be repaired before being rented. We trust hotels to do some very basic things: Change the sheets Clean the bathroom Make sure the door locks And the brand on the hotel is supposed to give you confidence! Baymont by Wyndham Latham Albany Airport markets rooms to travelers. It also houses people placed by county social services. That’s often a good indication… One woman, staying with her nine month old daughter, described cockroaches, mice, mold and bedbugs in some rooms. Other residents described wet carpets and a strong smell. A guest said she’d filmed mice crawling over her sleeping child and had stopped letting the girl sleep in her own bed. There were complaints about mouse droppings and dead flies on a bed, and mold and dead flies in a refrigerator. The County moved some social service clients. Another county with one room there relocated their client as a precaution and suspended use of the hotel. What The Inspection Found Albany County inspected the hotel October 13, finding no public health hazards, but six violations: A removed smoke detector. Three exterior doors that didn’t self-latch. A stained bathroom ceiling tile. Evidence of pests in a room. The plan to fix the rooms before renting them helps explain how the hotel could continue operating, though a missing smoke detector matters even in an empty room. And it seems to me that pests in one room can easily spread. There were earlier maintenance concerns, too. A March 13, 2025 entry in New York’s inspection database notes water stains and possible active leaks at this property. You’re Supposed To Be Able To Rely On A Brand A big part of what a hotel brand sells is confidence that somebody has vetted the property. You know what you’re getting. The hotel may be franchised but it’s supposed to deliver to brand standards. Years ago I covered an Inside Edition investigation that found three of nine hotels tested hadn’t provided completely fresh sheets between guests. The beds were re-made with the previous guest’s used sheets. Then came pandemic promises of enhanced cleaning. Inside Edition went back in 2020, using washable marks visible under ultraviolet light. It reported unchanged bedding at a Hyatt Place and a Hampton Inn in Times Square. At Trump International, the sheets had been changed, but the report said a pillowcase hadn’t. More recently, I covered a Hyatt Place guest who went through three rooms and still wound up with filthy bedding. Hyatt refunded the stay and provided 15,000 points. You’re not supposed to have to even check recent reviews and traveler photos, and pull back the bedding immediately on arrival. I Wouldn’t Let An Airline Choose Where I Sleep, Either I’ve made the same argument about hotels airlines provide during overnight delays. I’ve reported on roaches, floors was so dirty they turned guests’ feet black, and worse. Airlines offering lowest-cost rooms aren’t necessarily delvering places you’d ever want to stay. More recently, I covered a Hyatt Place guest who went through three rooms and still wound up with filthy bedding. Hyatt refunded the stay and provided 15,000 points. You’re not supposed to have to even check recent reviews and traveler photos, and pull back the bedding immediately on arrival. I Wouldn’t Let An Airline Choose Where I Sleep, Either I’ve made the same argument about hotels airlines provide during overnight delays. I’ve reported on roaches, floors was so dirty they turned guests’ feet black, and worse. Airlines offering lowest-cost rooms aren’t necessarily delvering places you’d ever want to stay. And the brand on the hotel is supposed to give you confidence! Baymont by Wyndham Latham Albany Airport markets rooms to travelers. It also houses people placed by county social services. That’s often a good indication…

One woman, staying with her nine month old daughter, described cockroaches, mice, mold and bedbugs in some rooms. Other residents described wet carpets and a strong smell. A guest said she’d filmed mice crawling over her sleeping child and had stopped letting the girl sleep in her own bed.

There were complaints about mouse droppings and dead flies on a bed, and mold and dead flies in a refrigerator. The County moved some social service clients. Another county with one room there relocated their client as a precaution and suspended use of the hotel.

Albany County inspected the hotel October 13, finding no public health hazards, but six violations: A removed smoke detector. Three exterior doors that didn’t self-latch. A stained bathroom ceiling tile. Evidence of pests in a room. The plan to fix the rooms before renting them helps explain how the hotel could continue operating, though a missing smoke detector matters even in an empty room. And it seems to me that pests in one room can easily spread. There were earlier maintenance concerns, too. A March 13, 2025 entry in New York’s inspection database notes water stains and possible active leaks at this property. #6220. Belavia Can Once Again Do Business With Boeing, As US Lifts Sanctions On Belarus

Belarusian national carrier Belavia has faced sanctions from the United States and European Union for quite some time, due to a combination of the “hijacking” of a Ryanair flight, along with the country’s support for Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Well, if Belarusian media is to be believed, these sanctions are now being lifted, so the country’s airline can once again buy planes from Boeing…

Belarusian state owned national news agency BelTA is reporting that the United States Department of Commerce has granted Boeing a license to resume full cooperation with Belavia. This was announced by Valentin Rybakov, the Belarusian representative to the United Nations. If true, this means that Belavia can once again purchase planes and parts directly from Boeing.

This all seems to be related to a visit to Belarus by an American delegation in September, where the country’s president, Alexander Lukashenko, met with US Special Envoy John Cole. This meeting included a larger lifting of sanctions. It also comes at a time when we’re seeing the Trump administration increasingly lifting sanctions on Russia in relation to the invasion of Ukraine.

In 2021, the United States imposed sanctions on Belarus, after the country engaged in what was referred to as a state sponsored hijacking. A Ryanair Boeing 737 was flying between Greece and Lithuania, and as the plane approached Belarusian airspace, an air traffic controller claimed there was a bomb onboard, and that the plane needed to divert to Belarus.

As it turned out, an opponent of the Belarusian government was onboard, so the real motive with this was to have him arrested. Obviously this violates all sorts of international laws and aviation treaties, which is why action was taken against the country. Then in 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, additional sanctions were imposed against Belarus, given its support for Russia.

Obviously having sanctions imposed on you by both the United States and European Union makes it challenging to buy new aircraft, given the aircraft manufacturing duopoly we have (unless you consider the aircraft manufacturers in China and Russia to be competitors).

So most of Belavia’s aircraft acquisitions in recent times have been smuggled into the country using shady middlemen. For example, in 2025, Belavia acquired Airbus A330s through an imaginary Gambian airline, as one does.

Belavia can reportedly once again buy aircraft and parts from Boeing, after the United States lifted sanctions that were imposed around five years ago, when the country hijacked a Ryanair plane. This easing of sanctions comes as part of a larger reversal by the Trump administration, as it takes less of a stance against Russia and Belarus.

It’ll be interesting to see what comes of this, and if Belarus places some big Boeing aircraft order in the near future…

What do you make of the US lifting sanctions on Belarus on the airline front?

#6219. Inside the Unraveling of the Tollman Family Travel Dynasty

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

The company was doing fine. The family wasn’t.

For 104 years, The Travel Corporation was owned by a single family, and that ownership was a key selling point of the company.

The Tollmans built TTC into one of the world's largest guided-tour companies and kept full control. It presented itself to travel agents and customers as a family business with no outside investors to answer to.

Then, in July 2024, Brett Tollman, TTC’s chairman, announced a sale to Apollo. He gave only one reason: there was no next generation to lead the business. While that was true, it wasn’t the whole story.

Credit rating reports, UK filings and interviews with more than half a dozen former executives and advisers point to a profitable tour business that was underfunded, while the family’s luxury hotel chain, Red Carnation, lost money and relied on financial support from TTC on cheap terms. Ultimately, the family sold the tour business and kept the hotels.

Skift's review of credit rating reports, UK filings, and interviews with more than half a dozen former executives and advisers fills in what sat behind The Travel Corporation's 2024 sale to Apollo. Brett Tollman publicly cited the absence of a next generation to lead the business. The documents show a profitable but underfunded tour group — roughly $190 million in EBITDA on an implied $1.3 billion in revenue — sold for about $1.1 billion, less than six times earnings, despite Uniworld's roughly 45% share of luxury river cruise and Trafalgar's 15% of guided tours. S&P and Fitch both described reduced marketing spend and agent commissions, weak direct sales, and outdated systems, with an EBITDA margin of 14% against more than 20% at competitors. Apollo set aside $50 million to upgrade operations. The family kept Red Carnation Hotels, which UK filings show had been funded by a loan of more than £50 million from Travcorp Financial Services at the Bank of England base rate — terms the hotel group's own audited accounts call below market. The London hotel group's losses widened from £1.6 million in 2023 to £7.2 million in 2025, while capital spending rose from £2 million to £7.6 million over the same period.

#6218. Passenger Says Delta Flight Attendant Photographed Her Sleeping—‘You Might See It On Facebook’

Tasia Jewel had just arrived in Mexico City and checked into her hotel when she shared the story. She’d been at the Formula One race in Austin, stayed in Texas rather than going home, and was exhausted. She slept for about an hour and a half or so on the roughly three-hour flight.

Then she got to the aircraft door. She says three or four male flight attendants were standing there saying goodbye to passengers. One told her:

Hey, yo friend, I took a picture of you while you were sleeping.

She says the other crewmembers laughed with one adding, “Yeah, she was knocked out.” And the first flight attendant repeated, “You might see it on Facebook.”

Here’s her account, flagged by Paddle Your Own Kanoo:

The woman acknowledges he could have been joking. She also says she hadn’t spoken to him at all on the flight.

My first reaction was that, while Delta has built up its Austin flying, they don’t actually operated Austin – Mexico City. But in a follow-up video she says she flew from Dallas to Atlanta to Mexico City with the flight in question being Delta 602. She says she chose Delta’s Boeing 757 because she didn’t want the Aeromexico Boeing 737 MAX.

And she reports that Delta responded well to her complaint. Her original video caption said she’d filed a complaint. In later replies, she reports a phone call, an apology and an investigation. I guess what matters here was whether there was a fundamental breach or a bad joke. Either way, she says she felt unsafe.

I’ve written about a sleeping passenger who said a man photographed her, where the crew intervened and police met the flight. Here, the person allegedly taking the photos was an employee she was supposed to go to for help.

And last year I covered a flight attendant who caught a passenger secretly filming her and sending her image to someone else. It’s easy to understand why that bothered her. But a passenger can have the same objection when the roles are reversed.

I don’t want a ban on taking pictures inside an aircraft. Passengers need to be able to document how they’re treated. Delta’s customer photography guidance recognizes that people take photos and videos, while asking them to avoid interfering with safety and to be “respectful in your intent” when including employees. Employees ought to show customers that same consideration.
